metal pipe grid transforms personal rituals of control into participatory playground
what does it take to feel secure? south korean sculptor won ji lim transforms personal rituals of counting, checking, and seeking balance into participatory sculptural environment.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Interactive playground by WON JI LIM EXPLORES rituals of control
Created by Chicago-based South Korean artist Won Ji Lim, Shifting Center (2026–ongoing) is a participatory sculptural installation that translates personal rituals of control, such as counting, checking, and aligning objects, into a physical, interactive environment. Measuring approximately 9 × 9 × 6 feet, the modular structure is constructed from metal pipes and connectors, forming a framework reminiscent of a playground jungle gym. The installation integrates suspended objects, woven membranes, transparent pockets, balancing mechanisms, and a series of rule-based activities that visitors can physically enter and navigate.
The artwork is a self-contained system, open to physical additions
The project by artist Won Ji Lim pairs structural framework with unstable or organic materials. Hog casing is tightly woven across sections of the metal frame, undergoing physical shifts as it stretches and dries over time to demonstrate the limits of fixed structural order. A suspended plumb bob set within a hand-woven square visualizes the process of seeking physical balance, while transparent pockets hold archived written thoughts that are photographed and re-integrated into the system to document the installation’s ongoing assembly. Additional interactive components include a converted baseball rebounder with a target graphic, numbered tags, and colored beads. Designed to be reconfigured over time, the modular installation functions as an evolving system where visitor movements continuously alter the spatial dynamics.

Five-hour search

Omar recalled waking up at about 6am to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
Omar came with her family to the US at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a US citizen five years later, in 2000.

Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:47:39 UTC
10:47:39 KST

Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?
Rights groups are worried that the agency at the heart of Trump’s immigration crackdown could sway the vote on election day.
Since returning to office for a second term, United States President Donald Trump has embarked on a campaign to root out and deport the country’s undocumented immigrants.
Spearheading that campaign is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal agency housed in the Department of Homeland Security.
Under Trump, the agency has grown substantially, boasting 22,000 officers and agents as of January, a staffing increase of 120 percent.
Thanks to recent spending packages, ICE is also considered the best-funded federal law enforcement agency in the US.
But the agency, founded in 2003, has come under increased scrutiny for its aggressive tactics and expedited hiring techniques.
Immigration agents, under the authority of ICE and other agencies, have been responsible for at least 25 shootings since the start of Trump’s second term, six of which have been fatal. At least 60 people have also died in ICE custody since January 2025.
That track record has made democracy advocates and human rights groups worried about ICE’s activities in the lead-up to the November 3 midterm elections.
Organisations like Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have voiced concern that the Trump administration could use ICE to intimidate voters.
The threat of encountering ICE agents could also keep some voters away from the ballot box, the groups say. One national poll, conducted in September by the University of California, San Diego, found that 40 percent of respondents expected ICE agents to be present near polling stations on election day.
Can ICE agents legally operate at or near polling stations?
Federal law prohibits the use of armed federal agents at polling stations. Some states have similar provisions.
The federal prohibition dates back to 1865. The law reads that it is illegal for anyone “engaged in the civil, military or naval service of the United States” to order or bring “any troops or armed men” to election sites.
There is, however, a loophole if such force is needed “to keep peace at the polls” or “to repel armed enemies of the United States”.
Another federal law prohibits members of the military from interfering with elections, and several other laws prohibit efforts to “intimidate” voters.
Those measures have been tested this year. During the primary elections for the midterms, there were at least two incidents – one in San Antonio, Texas, and another in Ventura County, California – where ICE agents reportedly conducted routine operations near polling stations.
In both cases, the ICE agents left after being asked to do so by local police.
How has the Trump administration used ICE agents before the election?
Though there are prohibitions against law enforcement near polling stations, advocacy groups say the Trump administration has nevertheless used ICE agents for election-related matters.
ICE has different offices under its control, one of which is Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
In the months leading up to this year’s midterm elections, HSI has reportedly been ordered to prioritise its investigations of non-citizen voting, an illegal act. Only US citizens are allowed to vote in federal elections.
Starting in August, the Department of Homeland Security deployed HSI agents for “field investigations” in at least nine states to probe questions of voter eligibility.
Some have reportedly gone door to door, asking residents if they are citizens and if they plan to vote.
This week, a federal judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to pause those investigations, citing the risk that a US citizen could be “wrongly swept up” and “subjected to intimidation”.
The judge also noted a “high likelihood of error” in how the federal agents were identifying alleged non-citizens.
Trump has pointed to non-citizen voting as support for his false claims of pervasive voter fraud.
Experts, though, say such fears are unfounded, with tiny numbers of non-citizens actually taking part in elections, despite Trump’s depictions of the issue as a widespread problem.
What has the Trump administration said about deploying ICE during the midterms?
Trump officials have refused to rule out using ICE agents to stop illegal voting, an effort that could extend to election day itself.
In May, Trump was asked by reporters: “For the midterm elections, would you send the National Guard or ICE to voting locations in November?”
Trump declined to answer directly. “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections,” he replied.
Other leaders in his administration have issued similar statements. In September, for instance, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin affirmed that ICE would not “patrol” polling stations, but he suggested its agents could be there for other reasons.
“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said.
Another member of Trump’s cabinet, Attorney General Todd Blanche, has questioned the uproar over the issue, framing it as misguided.
“Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations?” he asked in March at a conservative conference. “Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.”
What has been the response from advocacy groups?
The Trump administration’s rhetoric has raised alarm with a number of rights groups, who fear an ICE presence on election day could dampen voter turnout.
On Tuesday, Human Rights Watch called on the Trump administration to order ICE agents not to deploy near polling stations or other midterm election sites.
“ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, the executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.”
On October 16, the rights group Amnesty International issued a similar appeal.
“Eligible voters must have the meaningful opportunity to participate in elections without discriminatory and arbitrary barriers, intimidation by armed forces, or fear of harm when seeking to exercise their rights,” the group said.

“I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report.
On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling.
Though the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty.
Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and the Trump administration officials trading blame.
Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said in a social media post on October 14, using the acronym for “president of the United States”.

Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly calling him “difficult” in comparison to his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.

While Europe has backed Ukraine’s defence against the invasion, Trump has suggested Ukraine itself could be to blame for the conflict.
In 2025, for instance, Trump blamed Ukraine’s ambitions of joining NATO. “ I actually think that that was the thing that caused the start of the war,” he said at the time.

As the war continues, Trump has been criticised by Democrats and some members of his own Republican Party for easing US pressure on Russia.
Recently, his administration issued a series of announcements to buy Russian diesel and ease restrictions on Russia’s energy sector.
Those decisions come as Trump is struggling with the political fallout of high fuel prices caused by his decision to join Israel in launching a war on Iran.
He has also suggested he would be open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which would be a first for the three leaders.

ABC staff targeted in sophisticated cyber attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:41:30 UTC
10:41:30 KST

ABC wipes staff devices exposed to new, sophisticated cyber attack
In short:
The ABC is wiping a small number of staff devices as a precaution but says it has found "no signs of compromise" from ads linked to a spyware campaign from an Israeli company.
Researchers uncovered an operation using online ads to infect devices, targeting Australian high-profile and sensitive organisations.
What's next?
More than two dozen other Australian organisations are part of a "significant cluster" of targets, but they have not yet been identified.
The ABC has wiped staff devices that were exposed to a new, sophisticated cyber attack carried out as part of a broader campaign to track and even hack into networks of some of Australia's most high-profile and sensitive organisations.
It can be revealed the ABC is among more than two dozen Australian government, critical infrastructure, universities and media organisations that researchers claim were targeted by an Israel-based company abusing the online advertising system.
The public broadcaster confirmed a "small number" of devices had been exposed but said so far it had not identified any impact from the attack discovered by researchers at The Citizen Lab.
"The ABC is aware of the Citizen Lab report that describes exposure to advertising that may contain spyware. There is no evidence of a resulting compromise," a spokesperson said.
'No evidence' ABC impacted by cyber attack
The ABC attack was part of a bigger campaign, dubbed "Adfection", revealed by Citizen researchers last week.
The Canadian-based group found evidence that company Discover-Tech exploited digital advertising technology from major platforms like those run by Google to deliver spyware that could infect devices merely by viewing an online advertisement and without clicking.
Researchers were able to confirm Discover-Tech's technique was used to infect devices at international news network Al Jazeera with spyware from another Israeli company, Candiru.
A spokesperson for the ABC confirmed that this had included the public broadcaster but had found no evidence so far of any adverse impact.
"Our review found that ads from this network were shown on a small number of ABC devices. We have found no evidence that any staff member has been identified or tracked," they said.
"For the small number of ABC devices identified, we have found no signs of compromise, and are wiping any still in service as a precaution. We take the privacy of staff and the protection of journalists' sources seriously."
New method of cyber attack exploits known risks of online advertising
Even if this infection is unsuccessful, researchers said, the same method also allowed the attackers to profile tens of millions of devices that were shown these malicious advertisements — measured by "impressions" — potentially giving information about their identities and online habits.
University of Queensland Professor Nicholas Carah, whose research focuses on digital advertising, said the attack was proof of the well-known risks about online advertising technology.
"On one level, it's horrifically surprisingly, but on another level it's like, well, yeah of course, online advertising is really useful infrastructure for doing something like this," he said.
Professor Carah said the report showed how bad actors could exploit existing characteristics of online advertising technology to thwart protections that were supposed to stop tracking for nefarious purposes.
"You can get an [internet protocol] address, or a mobile, then, hey, presto, you're able to identify those individuals," he said.
Greens leader and digital rights spokesperson David Shoebridge said the report's contents were alarming.
"When foreign zero-click adtech is aimed at our public broadcaster, and other sensitive government agencies, that of course raises serious questions about foreign interference," he said, adding that this shows the need for privacy reform and to include advertising in the government's proposed digital duty of care.
Australian government, critical infrastructure and media organisations targeted
While there were devices targeted across the world using Discover-Tech's techniques, Citizen Lab researchers noted a "substantial cluster of impressions in Australia, including on government and private-sector networks associated with critical infrastructure".
The researchers did not know who Discover-Lab or Candiru were carrying out the attacks on behalf of, if anyone.
The report singled out Australia's nuclear science agency, ANSTO, as being a hot spot in their data for the number of malicious ads shown. It did not specify the other organisations.
An ANSTO spokesperson told the ABC earlier this week it had not identified any impacts.
Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, declined to comment.
Researchers also claimed three Australian media organisations had seemingly been targets.
Media organisations and journalists are common targets for commercial spyware operations, alongside politicians, dissidents and human rights groups.
"The use of spyware against journalists is on the rise," international group Reporters Without Borders wrote late last year.
"Digital attacks often go unnoticed, so it is vital that journalists regularly check if their devices are compromised."

How Hong Kong can go from passive trade hub to regional control tower
Hong Kong’s challenge is to reposition itself as a regional supply-chain management hub linking diverse Asian production networks with Western markets
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ningrong Liu is deputy vice‑president (international strategy) and professor of globalisation and business at City University of Hong Kong. 
This year has opened a rare window of relative calm in global commerce. On October 8, the World Trade Organization doubled its forecast for global goods trade growth, from 1.9 to 3.9 per cent. The easing of US-China and Europe-China tensions has given open economies some breathing space.
Hong Kong has seized the moment. Its exports rose 42.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, with figures from August alone up 53 per cent, driven largely by AI-related equipment and high-value electronic components.
A deeper transformation lurks beneath the headline numbers. Hong Kong is no longer merely a passive trade hub. For decades, its role in global commerce was defined by its position as a buffer in geopolitical cross-currents. The traditional model of “Made in China, shipped via Hong Kong, consumed in the West” made the city a passage point rather than a decision point.
The question now is whether Hong Kong can reposition itself as a regional supply-chain management hub linking diverse Asian production networks with Western markets. Three structural shifts are creating this opportunity.

Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:21:47 UTC
10:21:47 KST

Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chunhui Yao, Jie Ma, Ningning Wang, Peng Bao, Wei Zhuo, Tao Zhang, Wanlu Zhang, Kangning Xu, Ting Yan, Liang Ming, Yuxiao Ye, Tawfique Hasan, Ian White, Richard Penty, Qixiang Cheng. Optical convolutional spectrometer. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (6): 664 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01891-6

Recent attempts to restrict Ukraine's access to satellite systems have triggered a blame game among officials in US President Donald Trump's administration and their allies, who have offered conflicting explanations for the sudden restrictions on Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attacks.
Source: Associated Press, citing sources
Details: Restrictions imposed on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service and a key part of Ukraine's drone operations and communications, alarmed Ukrainian military and government officials last week. Commanders reported lost drones and interrupted missions. After several days of uncertainty, Trump said on Thursday 22 October that the service was operating again at full speed.
However, AP quoted a senior European official familiar with the situation on the ground in Ukraine as saying that nothing had changed in Starshield's operation and that the speed limit remained at around 160 km/h.
Ukraine has received no clear official explanation of who ordered the restrictions or why, according to the official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The incident and the subsequent lack of accountability have sparked outrage among Ukraine's allies and supporters of a tougher policy towards Russia on Capitol Hill. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal announced a new investigation into how the speed of Ukraine's defence systems had been restricted.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the disruption of the satellite internet network created by Elon Musk, which Ukraine has relied on for years to counter attacks by Moscow.
As recently as Thursday, Trump insisted that he had not issued such an order. Vice-President JD Vance hinted at coordination between the White House and Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied any involvement by the administration.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump said that the White House had nothing to do with the restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starlink.
- According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink and Starshield operations in Ukraine.
- On 17 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a test conducted by Ukraine in EU countries had confirmed that the restrictions on its use of Starlink were imposed as part of a planned operation.
- Rubio said Trump's administration "had nothing to do with" the restriction of Starlink's operation in Ukraine.
- On 18 October, Zelenskyy told NBC that the signal to restrict Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine had come from the US government.
- Hegseth said the US was not involved in restricting Starshield's operation in Ukraine and had issued no such orders.

Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose ‘sequentially’ like a doctor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:15:00 UTC
10:15:00 KST

Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose ‘sequentially’ like a doctor
- Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses step by step was more than twice as accurate as general physicians in complex cases, according to a study in Science on 22 October.
- The system uses an “orchestrator” and a simulated panel of clinical experts to ask questions, order tests, and update its diagnosis like a doctor.
- It also cost less than human doctors in work-ups, and the team will next test it for emergency department triage with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
AI generated
Washington – Microsoft researchers say an artificial intelligence tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published in the journal Science on Oct 22.
The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam.
Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview.
Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems with human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dominic King, the corporate vice-president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms. REUTERS

Apple launches into foldable market as iPhone Duo sales begin
- Apple has entered the foldable phone market with the iPhone Duo, which went on sale on Oct 23 and drew strong demand, with delivery dates slipping to late January.
- Early reviews praise the Duo’s design and hinge, but note camera limits and app changes. Some reviewers say it feels like a polished prototype, not a finished product.
- Apple faces tight supply in many countries, but IDC says its entry could widen foldable adoption. IDC expects Apple to lead the market by 2027 in both value and units.
AI generated
SYDNEY – Sales of Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Oct 23, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market just like the iPhone did for smartphones.
The Duo’s reception could prove an early test for new chief executive John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.
It could also have large implications for a niche category in which rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years.
Within minutes of pre-orders opening on Oct 16, Apple’s estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply.
The US company called the response from customers “nothing short of extraordinary”.
In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones on Oct 23, a queue of customers formed outside before opening at 8am local time.
Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 (S$3,500) for a Duo with 512GB memory.
“This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it’s so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life’s too short,” he said.
Mixed reviews
Early reviews have praised the Duo’s design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.
But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for many Apple customers.
“It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype – not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry,” long-time Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball, wrote in a review.
Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD, said in a YouTube review that “if you’re just a regular person who doesn’t do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the US$2,000 doesn’t mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone.”
Tough to find
The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo.
Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe.
In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online.
In the China-governed territory of Macau, where the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers only, fans lined up hours in advance of the store opening, social media posts and media reports showed.
“Foldables have been an established category for years, but adoption has remained relatively limited compared with conventional smartphones. Apple’s entry could bring the format to a much broader audience,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president at market researcher IDC.
IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable value in 2026 on 31% of foldable units. By 2027, it will become the market leader in the category both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.
“Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor,” Jeronimo said after spending a week with the passport-shaped Duo.
“Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market,” Jeronimo said. REUTERS

Chinese astronomers find real 3-body system. It is not what Liu Cixin thinks
In a case of life imitating art, Chinese researchers have discovered an ‘extremely rare’ three-star system that is not science fiction
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ling Xinin Ohio
In author and computer engineer Liu Cixin’s science fiction hit The Three-Body Problem, three suns throw a doomed world into chaos. Chinese astronomers say they have found a real three-star system that is far better behaved.
Using FAST, the world’s biggest single-dish radio telescope in southwestern China, the researchers found two dead stars and a “living” one locked in a steady cosmic dance about 7,000 light years from Earth.
One of the dead stars is a pulsar that spins more than 300 times a second, about as fast as the blades of a kitchen blender. It whirls around its partner, a white dwarf – the dim, burnt-out core of a smaller star – every eight days.

Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:54:51 UTC
09:54:51 KST

Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.
Thousands of people have protested in more than 20 towns and cities across Poland, calling for access to free and legal abortion services.
Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.
Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress.
The demonstrations come days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the mostly Catholic country, but are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative President Karol Nawrocki.
Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.
She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki’s veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women’s support to win elections next year.
In the capital, Warsaw, about 1,000 protesters demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain.
“Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36-year-old Emilia Niemiec, who manages the AboTak abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out a pharmacological abortion.
Abortion laws tightened
Restrictive abortion laws have been in place in Poland since 1993, with Polish women leading calls for the legalisation of abortion ever since. In 2016, nationwide demonstrations took place, with women donning black as a sign of protest.
But rather than being relaxed, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of foetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, with the overwhelming majority carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared with 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.
Campaigners organising Thursday’s protests are claiming the Tusk government has betrayed Polish women – and that Tusk’s claims that women’s access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.
“The government’s promises act as a type of disinformation,” Marcinek said. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is OK, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it’s very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”

Venezuelans call for elections in first national protest in nearly two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:52:28 UTC
09:52:28 KST

Thousands of Venezuelans took to the streets on Thursday in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years, demanding free elections and other political changes, with security forces present in notably small numbers.
The United States has been working closely with the interim government led by acting President Delcy Rodriguez since US forces captured President Nicolas Maduro in January. Both US President Donald Trump and Rodriguez, Maduro's former deputy, have said elections will be held, but have not set a date for either a legislative vote or a national presidential contest.
Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027.
Her Vente Venezuela movement organized the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas and other cities, including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo.
“Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible," said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. "I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader, president, Maria Corina."
Venezuela's socialist movement has been in power since 1999
"I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added as music boomed around protesters waving Venezuelan flags.
Venezuela's socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters decrying political repression, dizzying inflation, poor public services and other problems in the economically battered country, including after the 2024 presidential election.
Security forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Thursday, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark.
The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas' Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location.
Negotiations continue
US-backed talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government, aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council with an eye toward ensuring fairness at eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time. The negotiations do not include Machado's political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress.
Machado's proxy roundly won the 2024 election according to vote tallies released by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country's legal and electoral institutions.
"We want presidential elections now. We want an electoral timetable to be announced now. We are not going to wait until 2028," said Maria Debora Marin, 57, who runs a clothing store in central Valencia, referring to rumors elections may only take place the year after next. "What we want is to move forward and finally get out of this nightmare."
Amid the arrests of some of her closest collaborators, Machado went into hiding. Her last public appearance in Venezuela was at protests to mark Maduro's third inauguration in January 2025, where she was briefly detained.
Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro, through links to drug gangs, represented a direct threat to US national security. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.
But Trump has repeatedly praised Rodriguez's management and her willingness to welcome US investors, saying last month it is too soon to consider elections.
Machado's desire to return home, especially after devastating twin earthquakes in June, has caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters has reported.
"We're in limbo," said recent graduate Rayeska Puesme, 18, as she attended the protest in Caracas, adding she had considered leaving because of a lack of opportunities. "The United States removed one big problem, which was Maduro, but the rest are still there."
"I feel in my heart that things are going to change, but I don't see when."
Demonstrators were also calling for the release of prisoners they say are held for political reasons.
Legal rights group Foro Penal, which represents opposition figures and others who have been detained, often on charges like treason, says there are still more than 320 political prisoners in Venezuela, despite releases that took place under an amnesty law backed by the legislature earlier this year. The government has repeatedly denied holding political prisoners and says the amnesty is generous.
US welcomes progress in Venezuela political reconciliation talks
The US State Department said on Thursday it welcomed the conclusion of a third round of political reconciliation talks between Venezuela's 2015 National Assembly and its interim government.
The State Department said the process "continues to strengthen democratic institutions" and "lay the groundwork for free, fair and credible elections" in the South American country.
The US continues to urge the immediate release of all political prisoners in Venezuela, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

Former hostage Elkana Bohbot recalls how faith, family helped him survive Hamas captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:52:24 UTC
09:52:24 KST

Former Hamas hostage Elkana Bohbot described how his determination to reunite with his wife and son, along with his religious faith, helped him survive captivity in Gaza, in an IDF podcast featuring Lt.-Col. (res.) Tamar Aviv, the officer who supported his family throughout his captivity.
"First of all, what kept me going there, more than anything, was the belief that I would see my son Re'em again, my wife and my family," he said.
Bohbot explained that he was determined not to give Hamas the satisfaction of seeing him give up.
"I would do everything I can to come back and show them what resilience and renewal really mean. To show them that we're here and we're going to stay here. There's nothing you can do about it.”
Bohbot also said he continued observing religious practices during captivity, starting each morning with prayers of gratitude for surviving another day and saying Kiddush on Friday night and Saturday.
"Even when the terrorist was right next to me, literally right next to me, I would quietly recite my Kiddush and preserve my identity. Absolutely," he said.
Elkana Bohbot recalls his first meeting with Tamar Aviv after his release
Describing the moments following his return from captivity, Bohbot recalled being surrounded by IDF soldiers and struggling to recognize the people around him, including Aviv.
"Only later, when she got into the helicopter with me, did I understand who Tamar was," Bohbot said. "My mother told me, 'Meet Tamar. She's been accompanying us for two years,' and it immediately clicked."
Aviv, who had spent more than two years supporting Bohbot's family, said the meeting marked the culmination of a deeply personal mission.
She explained that she initially knew Bohbot only through a photograph but gradually came to know him through conversations with his relatives and friends.
"It is no longer just a mission. It becomes something emotional. I don't actually know him. We've never met, but I have tremendous love for him, concern and anxiety," she said.
Aviv described the prayers and anticipation that accompanied the long period of uncertainty, saying her own religious faith had strengthened during that time.
"But the moment we received the report at Re'im that they had reached him and that he was, so to speak, with us, that was the moment I truly felt an enormous release of tension and overwhelming excitement," she said about the day he was released by Hamas.
The emotional toll of accompanying a hostage's family
Aviv said she had been responsible for supporting Bohbot's entire extended family throughout his captivity, including his parents, wife, son Re'em, siblings, and sisters-in-law.
Her role involved maintaining constant contact with relatives, arranging meetings with military and government officials, providing intelligence updates, and helping families manage everyday needs.
"Things happen along the way that we don't want the family to wake up in the morning and discover on the news," she said, explaining that she was responsible for updating relatives, even in the middle of the night.
Aviv described the emotional difficulty of becoming so familiar with someone she had never met, without knowing whether he would return.
"You're learning about someone who isn't here, and you don't even know whether he's ever coming back."
One of the greatest challenges, she said, was supporting Bohbot's young son, Re'em, who was growing up without his father.
She recalled a video Bohbot's wife, Rivka, sent her showing three-year-old Re'em sitting on his bed, looking at a picture of his father and pleading for him to return.
Aviv said she struggled to answer Re'em's questions about his father's absence while shielding him from the full reality of captivity.
"You sort of bend the truth," she said.

SpaceX said on Thursday that its stake in Elon Musk's The Boring Co. netted the company an investment gain of $561 million during the third quarter.
The gain accounted for more than half of SpaceX's "other income" in the period and boosted its net income, which landed at just over $4 billion, the company said in its quarterly financial filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later, Boring Co. says its mission is to "revolutionize transportation" by creating underground tunnels with stations where passengers can board and exit. Last month, Boring Co. raised $3 billion at a $23 billion valuation, with backing from the United Arab Emirates and a roster of other longtime Musk supporters.
Boring Co. has announced about a dozen city projects, but its only tunnels currently open for public use are in Las Vegas, where passengers can travel in Tesla vehicles between the downtown convention center and various casino resorts using its Las Vegas Convention Center Loop.
In July of last year, Boring Co. struck a deal to build about 20 miles of tunnels in Nashville, Tennessee. The Music City Loop, as it's known, is being designed to carry paying passengers between downtown and the airport in Tesla vehicles. The fast-tracked project sparked a partisan feud when it was greenlit and has drawn new safety concerns over sinkhole risks this week.

Earlier, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in parliament that he favored Armenia’s expulsion from the CSTO and would be pleased if that happened. The country does not intend to step up its participation in the CSTO over the next five years, he said, adding that Armenia’s interest in the CSTO had run its course. The Kenya Red Cross said late Thursday that it was scaling up emergency assistance for families fleeing deadly clashes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states, with an initial humanitarian response targeting 1,000 households in northern Kenya.
"Our priority is to make sure every family arriving in Moyale is safe, sheltered and treated with dignity. Our volunteers and staff are on the ground and will continue to respond as needs evolve," Kenya Red Cross Secretary General Dr. Ahmed Idris said in a statement.
Marsabit County Commissioner Stanley Kamande confirmed that displaced Ethiopians had entered Kenya, with many seeking shelter among relatives and residents on the Kenyan side of the border.  
Hundreds of Ethiopians crossed into Kenya following violence in Moyale, a town divided by the international border, where gunfire erupted amid tensions between Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regions as the cause of the clashes remained unclear.
The Red Cross said many displaced families had arrived in Kenya's Marsabit County with few belongings and urgently needed shelter, food, clean water and medical assistance.
Working with county and national authorities, the humanitarian organization said it had begun establishing temporary shelters and distributing tents, blankets, sleeping mats, water containers and kitchen supplies.
It is also providing fortified porridge flour for young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers alongside first aid and assistance to reunite families separated during the displacement.
The organization warned of urgent shortages of food, safe drinking water, sanitation facilities and health services, particularly affecting women, children, older people and people with disabilities.
The violence erupted in Moyale on the Ethiopian side of the border following tensions over the display of the Somali Regional State flag at a local administrative office in an area administered by Ethiopia's Oromia Regional State.
Oromia and the Somali Regional State are two of Ethiopia's federal regions, home predominantly to Oromo and ethnic Somali communities respectively. Both communities have longstanding ties to the border area.

Homes and trading centers were burned, disrupting commercial activities and forcing residents to abandon their properties.
The exact number of people killed or injured remained unclear, with no independently verified casualty figures available.
Moyale, approximately 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and about 770 kilometers (478 miles) south of Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, by road, is a major commercial crossing between the two countries.
The border town serves communities in both countries, with close family and trading connections making it an important route for people fleeing insecurity.
The Kenya Red Cross said it was conducting a rapid assessment to determine the most urgent humanitarian needs and would continue coordinating with government authorities and other partners.
The organization also said it was restoring family communication links to help displaced people reconnect with relatives.
Although the initial relief operation is expected to assist 1,000 households, the total number of people displaced within Ethiopia or crossing into Kenya has not yet been established.
The violence comes amid renewed conflict in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, adding to concerns over civilian safety and humanitarian needs in the Horn of Africa.

Netanyahu helped Kushner hide $1 billion in UAE funds at Israel's central bank, book claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:37:19 UTC
09:37:19 KST

A secret network of bank accounts allegedly connected Jared Kushner, senior adviser to President Donald Trump, with powerful Gulf rulers and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during Trump's first term, according to allegations detailed in a forthcoming book by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, excerpts of which were published by Vanity Fair. 
The book claims that at least $2 billion was made available through financial arrangements spanning the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Israel, including an alleged $1 billion transfer to an account at Israel's central bank. Kushner's lawyer categorically denied the alleged arrangements.
The claims appear in Cole's book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East. According to Cole's account, Emirati leader Mohamed bin Zayed and Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman initially discussed establishing a fund exceeding $10 billion to advance political objectives important to the incoming Trump administration. The plan reportedly narrowed into several accounts allegedly giving Kushner access to foreign funds outside conventional U.S. government oversight.
One of the most significant allegations concerns approximately $1 billion that bin Zayed allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan in 2018. Citing a person briefed on the arrangement, Cole writes that Netanyahu encouraged Kushner to place the money in an account at the Bank of Israel, where it would appear to be associated with government funds rather than with Kushner personally. The source claimed the money was intended for Kushner's personal benefit, although the book excerpt does not establish how the funds were ultimately used.
The Bank of Israel does not operate personal accounts, and government accounts require authorization from two individuals to conduct transactions. According to Cole, Netanyahu wanted Kushner to inform him before any transfers, with messages allegedly conveyed through David Friedman, then the U.S. ambassador to Israel. One source claimed that significant sums were subsequently transferred through Cyprus. Friedman emphatically denied any knowledge of the alleged arrangement or involvement in transmitting messages, while Kushner's lawyer insisted that "there are no accounts and never were."
How Dutch intelligence allegedly uncovered the financial trail
Cole traces the alleged financial network to an extraordinary intelligence operation that began in late 2017, when the Netherlands' military intelligence service reportedly discovered that a hacker working for Russia's GRU military intelligence agency was preparing to travel to Britain. With British cooperation, Dutch intelligence officers allegedly persuaded the operative to provide access to a Russian intelligence server rather than face arrest. Investigators reviewing material on that server reportedly discovered screenshots from Kushner's iPhone, prompting an effort to determine how Russian hackers had compromised the device.
By early 2018, Dutch cyber specialists had allegedly found a vulnerability that allowed them to monitor images appearing on Kushner's screen as he used his phone. According to the book, the surveillance revealed that Kushner was accessing a UAE bank account that had received hundreds of millions of dollars through an Azerbaijani bank. The account, identified by Cole as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank and had allegedly received approximately $750 million beginning in 2017, with funding attributed to Saudi and Emirati sources.
The use of Azerbaijan was particularly significant, Cole argues, because certain banks there allegedly facilitate large foreign-currency transfers that obscure the original source of the funds. Rather than transferring Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams directly to their destination, clients could reportedly use intermediary transactions that delivered equivalent amounts in U.S. dollars. For investigators examining the final transfer, the money could appear to originate from an Azerbaijani institution, concealing the financial arrangements behind it.
The Alpha account was allegedly held by the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, an Emirati government-funded charity, rather than by Kushner personally. Cole alleges that Kushner was made an authorized signatory, giving him potential access to the funds without formal ownership. The foundation, headed at the time by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, allegedly served another purpose: facilitating covert Emirati arms purchases and foreign operations. A confidential source cited by Cole described the charity as a vehicle that could reduce scrutiny of sensitive transactions. Kushner's lawyer denied that his client knew Al Falasi, had any connection to the foundation or possessed access to a UAE bank account.
According to Cole, the alleged financial arrangements developed alongside ambitious diplomatic plans involving Washington, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Jerusalem. Mohammed bin Salman was seeking to consolidate his position as Saudi crown prince, while bin Zayed wanted the Trump administration to abandon Barack Obama's nuclear agreement with Iran. Kushner, meanwhile, was pursuing an Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative and closer relations between Israel and Gulf states. The book alleges that access to the funds was connected to those overlapping political objectives, although the precise terms of any arrangement remain disputed.
Israeli security arrangements and questions of oversight
Cole's book also describes a third, separate account allegedly established during secret contacts between Israel and the UAE before the countries formally normalized diplomatic relations in 2020. Kushner reportedly helped negotiate an understanding under which Israel would assist the Emirates in defending against a major Iranian military attack. According to Cole, Abu Dhabi deposited additional money into an Israeli central bank account to finance such emergency assistance. The excerpt does not specify the amount involved or establish whether the funds were ever used.
Cole argues that the three alleged accounts effectively created an unofficial financial framework through which Kushner could pursue Middle East diplomacy with senior regional leaders. The arrangements, if substantiated, would raise questions about transparency and government oversight. Kushner was an unpaid senior White House adviser but remained a federal employee subject to financial disclosure requirements, including obligations associated with access to classified information. Cole says four former senior Trump administration officials, including national security advisers and a former CIA director, were unaware of presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government account.
The book excerpt also examines potential legal implications. A former prosecutor who worked on Robert Mueller's investigation told Cole that any agreement to provide official influence in exchange for money could potentially violate federal bribery laws or foreign-agent registration requirements. Such an assessment depends on whether the alleged arrangements existed and what, if anything, was promised in return. The allegations presented in the book do not amount to a judicial finding that Kushner committed a crime, and his attorney denied any legal violations or undisclosed financial arrangements.
Kushner's counsel maintained that his dealings with foreign officials were conducted with Trump's approval and in the interests of the United States. Friedman separately rejected the allegations involving him as entirely false. The competing accounts leave major questions unresolved, including whether the reported bank accounts existed as described, who controlled the funds and whether any money was used for personal purposes. Cole's account, published in excerpt form by Vanity Fair, nevertheless places the alleged financial relationships at the center of the diplomatic efforts that preceded the Abraham Accords, raising questions about whether an undisclosed system of financial arrangements operated alongside official U.S. Middle East policy.

Macron bans protests
French President Emmanuel Macron has announced a crackdown on public demonstrations, ordering authorities to ban protests and restrict even officially organized marches as nationwide unrest over soaring living costs and deteriorating public services continues.
The restrictions, announced Thursday following an emergency meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, come ahead of another wave of demonstrations planned for Saturday, after some of France’s worst street violence in years.
Macron said local authorities would prohibit deemed “illegitimate” gatherings organized by individuals or groups deemed to lack authority, while demonstrations arranged by recognized organizations, such as trade unions, would be considered for approval but could be required to use alternative routes.
“The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days,” Macron declared, insisting the measures were necessary to restore calm and protect businesses and public buildings.
“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” he claimed, accusing organized radicals of orchestrating violence and looting.
The announcement significantly tightens restrictions on mass gatherings in a country where the right to protest is constitutionally protected. Under French law, authorities can prohibit demonstrations if they are believed to pose a threat to public order, although such decisions must be proportionate and can be challenged in court.
A Paris administrative court overturned a police ban on a student demonstration on Thursday, allowing thousands of protesters to gather despite official objections. The rally proceeded peacefully under heavy police presence, according to AP.
However, authorities have already prohibited Saturday’s demonstrations in central Lyon, where hundreds of businesses were ransacked last weekend. Similar restrictions have been imposed in Marseille, Nice and Toulon. In Paris, one authorized march has been diverted away from the city center, while another involving students and members of the Yellow Vest movement has been banned.
France has been gripped by escalating unrest since protests over teacher shortages and deteriorating school conditions spread into a broader movement against rising prices, inequality and cuts to public services.
Around 550,000 people joined demonstrations last Saturday, which descended into clashes with police, arson and widespread looting. Nearly 2,500 people have since been arrested, while approximately 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, according to figures reported by French media.
Opposition leaders have blamed Macron’s policies and failure to maintain order for the crisis. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen described him as a president “without credibility or authority” who has “lost all touch with reality,” while left-wing leader Jean-Luc Melenchon accused his government of undermining public services over the past decade.
Even police unions have turned against the administration. Alliance Police Nationale has announced plans to sue the state, accusing officials of abandoning officers during the riots and failing to provide adequate equipment and clear instructions.
Macron has also clashed with US President Donald Trump, who blamed France’s turmoil on uncontrolled immigration and radical groups. The French leader dismissed comments by foreign politicians about the unrest as “stupid” and “unacceptable.”
The president is expected to chair another emergency defense council meeting on Friday to decide whether further restrictions are needed ahead of Saturday’s protests.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, while the statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia," President Vladimir Putin told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin.
In its contacts with Washington, Moscow reached an agreement to be ready to resume Russia-US-Ukraine talks that will focus on ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved.
Moreover, Putin spoke about the situation in the Ukrainian army: the number of deserters there is half a million, if not more. The motivation of Ukrainian citizens is declining.
TASS has gathered the main statements by the Russian leader.
"Political schizophrenia" in Europe
Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, the president said.
"If we look at the political processes underway in Europe, we will see that the peoples of Europe don’t want to fight with Russia. I would like us to be heard: we don’t want [to fight with Europe] either," he said.
EU statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia": "This [Donbass and Novorossiya’s decision to reunify with Russia], as is well known, became the reason or the pretext for some of our ill-wishers abroad - primarily, as we see today, in European countries - to launch an anti-Russian campaign in all directions. Now they are also constantly talking about a threat from Russia and the start of preparations for the war with Russia, which, in my view, is a kind of political schizophrenia," Putin said.
"This too shall pass," he added.
Ukrainian conflict and trilateral talks
Russia called for a peaceful solution to the Ukraine conflict from the very beginning, "from the very first days, in 2014," offering its help to facilitate a negotiated solution, but Kiev resorted to force instead.
The Russian leader also mentioned the Minsk agreements. "We have always sought to ensure that they could reach an agreement with the part of Ukraine that does not accept coup d'etat. However, they refused to do so," he said.
For its part, Russia does not want war, it’s Kiev that wants to go to war with Moscow, "let it have it," Putin stressed.
That said, the war against Russia in order to weaken it cannot be Ukraine’s national idea. "Certain countries of Europe, for example, or from other global regions want to wage war against Russia in order to weaken it. But is this really a national idea for Ukraine itself?" the president asked rhetorically.
Defeating Russia on the battlefield is impossible, and inflicting a strategic defeat on it is improbable, Putin emphasized, adding that it is "better to live in friendship" with Russia: "I think people who have sought to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia - and, unfortunately, such people still exist today - will come to terms with reality and understand that it is better to live in friendship with Russia. This is in the interests of their nations."
Regarding trilateral talks on Ukraine, Russia has reached an agreement with the US to be ready to resume them. They will focus on ensuring security of both Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved, Putin stated.
According to the president, US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff said at the October 21 meeting that, when discussing issues related to ensuring "the future security of both Ukraine and Russia, it will be surely necessary to address the European security architecture as well." "Basically, I agree with that," Putin added.
Prior to the start of the Russia-US-Ukraine talks scheduled for November, Moscow will be monitoring the situation "in the coming days."
Russia remains ready to make agreements and seek solutions to the situation surrounding Ukraine, Putin said, adding that Russia has always called for settling the conflict peacefully. However, if Kiev wants a different solution to the conflict, that is its will. Moscow will continue the special military operation and achieve all its goals through it, the president noted.
Loss of motivation among Ukrainians and 500,000 deserters in Ukrainian army
Ukrainian citizens are being picked up off the streets like stray dogs and forcibly conscripted, which results in lower motivation among Ukrainians. "This is leading to severe consequences as troops' motivation declines. Yes, there are still formations made up of motivated nationalists. There are some. But it’s not always them fighting on the frontline. Those who have been forcibly rounded up are being thrown onto the frontline," Putin said.
The president pointed to the fact that the Kiev regime and its Western sponsors are treating Ukrainian citizens as expendable. "They [in the West] have always said they are ready to fight until the last Ukrainian is standing. And what about the Ukrainian authorities and their attitude to their own people? Do they share the approach of those abroad who want to fight with us and treat Ukrainians as expendable? They are their fellow citizens, after all," Putin noted.
Meanwhile about 500,000 servicemen have already deserted from the Ukrainian armed forces, but the real figure may be even higher, the Russian leader added. "Well, the figures are almost official: [there are] half a million deserters. Officially, over 300,000 criminal cases have been initiated, but in reality - and they are already talking about this almost publicly as well - it is 500,000, half a million," he said.
On territories lost by Ukraine
The lands lost by Kiev are not Ukrainian territory, those are historically Russian lands. Putin believes it is inappropriate for Kiev to speak of any territorial losses after Donbass and Novorossiya residents voted to reunite with Russia.
"The people who live there voted for, first, state independence, and, second - I would like to point out - for reunification with Russia," the Russian leader stated. "This is why I think it’s inappropriate to speak of any territorial losses. Still, it’s a debatable issue, and debates can go on indefinitely," he added.
Russians and Ukrainians genetically one people
Russians and Ukrainians are not merely close, they are genetically one people, Putin stressed. That said, the head of state expressed respect for the fact that a political division of the broader Russian nation occurred historically.
"Someone has a different opinion, fine," he admitted. "Alright, we agree, this is how the history of Russia shaped out, and such are the realities of today. But everything is negotiable."
