Critically endangered Bangka slow loris documented after decades without scientific records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:14:26 UTC
08:14:26 KST

Critically endangered Bangka slow loris documented after decades without scientific records
The Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate classified as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) on the the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, has been documented across Indonesia’s Bangka Island, according to a new study published in the scientific journal Spixiana, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The findings are based on records of more than 90 slow lorises rescued by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center between 2015 and 2025. Although the species had not been documented in scientific literature since the 1930s, local residents continued to find the animals in gardens, along roadsides and on power lines.
The study was co-authored by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center, Timon Glaw of the Haus des Meeres Aqua Terra Zoo in Vienna and the Taman Safari Prigen Conservation Breeding Ark. Of the more than 90 animals rescued, 86 recovered and were released at seven sites on the island.
“We are glad to contribute to the scientific record to show that the Bangka slow loris is not lost, but the species is still very close to extinction,” said Langka Sani, director of the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center.
Sani said the species’ natural habitat had shrunk significantly because of illegal tin mining and extensive land clearing for oil palm plantations.
According to the study, human settlements, roads and power lines also threaten the species, while slow lorises are targeted by the pet trade across their range in Asia.
“Bringing the Bangka slow loris back onto the scientific radar is only the first step,” said Glaw, one of the study’s co-authors. He called for population surveys, genetic studies and protection of the species’ remaining habitat.
The researchers recommend a conservation program to protect suitable forests and continue monitored releases. They also propose a conservation breeding program to learn more about the species’ biology and behavior.
Benji Barca, exploration program manager at Re:wild, said the rescue center’s records had helped bring the primate back into scientific view.
“A species can disappear from the scientific record without disappearing from the lives of the people who share its home,” Barca said.
The Bangka slow loris was first scientifically described in 1906 and recognized as a distinct species in 2013. Slow lorises are the only primates known to be venomous. They mix secretions from a gland on the inside of their upper arm with saliva, producing a bite that can cause pain and swelling.
Qazinform previously reported that a rare Central Asian river otter, listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book of endangered species, had been captured on camera at Charyn National Park. The footage highlighted the role of wildlife monitoring in studying rare species and supporting conservation efforts.

Breaking: Commonwealth makes offer to send Australian of the Year to space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:01:32 UTC
08:01:32 KST

Federal government makes offer to send Australian of the Year to space
In short
The federal government has submitted a counteroffer to a European Space Agency proposal to send Katherine Bennell-Pegg to space.
Ms Bennell-Pegg has already completed her basic astronaut training with the agency in 2024.
What's next?
If accepted, Ms Bennell-Pegg would become the first person to fly to space as a formal representative of Australia.
The federal government has submitted a final bid to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send Australian of the Year Katherine Bennell-Pegg to the International Space Station.
If ESA agrees to Australia's offer, Ms Bennell-Pegg will be required to attend training at the European Space Agency’s astronaut training centre in Cologne, Germany and NASA facilities in the United States.
"We have submitted a final bid to our friends in the European Space Agency," Science Minister Tim Ayres said on Friday morning.
"We are grateful for the opportunity to apply for this important project. It is an important opportunity. It does require careful fiscal management and making sure that we are balancing the fiscal pressures appropriately."
If ESA accepts Australia's bid, Ms Bennell-Pegg will become the first person to formally represent Australia in a space agency mission.
Previous Australians have either flown to space with private companies, or taken US citizenship to fly with NASA.
A spokesperson for the minister said "the government has long held ambition to see an Australian astronaut go to space wearing an Australian flag on their space suit".
"The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight — which is a significant cost," the spokesperson said.
"We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6 million in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments."
It is understood these contributions are encapsulated in the industry-led "flyKatherine" campaign, which this week had reached a reported $25 million.
South Australia is the only state or territory to have publicly confirmed it would provide financial support to the endeavour.
On Friday, SA Health Minister Blair Boyer said the decision showed ambition from Australia.
"I think there is something big around the inspiration of sending anyone into space but, again, a South Australian, and a South Australian woman to do that," Mr Boyer said.
"It’s welcome news and it’s good of us to have some ambition about this kind of stuff as well. I would hate to think we’ve lost that kind of ambition around doing these things."
ESA originally offered Australia a mission seat for Ms Bennell-Pegg at the beginning of this year, for a reported cost of $100 million.
The federal government did not give details on how much money it had committed in its final bid.
A government spokesperson told the ABC a response to its bid was expected by the end of the year.

Sudan: El Fasher civilians suffer unlawful killings, detention and torture one year after city’s capture by the RSF – new testimony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:01:00 UTC
08:01:00 KST

- Surveillance and detentions rife in city
- With limited humanitarian aid, risks of child malnutrition remain high
- “A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today” – Agnès Callamard
Civilians in El Fasher in North Darfur, Sudan, are still suffering detention, torture and limited access to humanitarian aid one year after the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured the city and committed brutalities against civilians, Amnesty International said today.
In new testimony, residents who recently escaped the city told Amnesty International how schools had been turned into detention centres, how their movement was strictly controlled, and that unlawful killings were rife.
According to figures gathered by humanitarian organizations working in the city, fewer than 70,000 people are present in El Fasher, compared to its pre-war population of more than one million. Humanitarian access remains limited, and humanitarian workers and other civilians in the city are constantly surveilled or monitored. Arbitrary detention risks, for both civilians and humanitarian workers, remain extremely high.
A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“The RSF’s claims that El Fasher is safe for civilians to return to after the horrific massacres that took place one year ago could not be further from the truth,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today. Men and women live under constant RSF surveillance, and with the ongoing threat of detention, torture and killing.
“One year since El Fasher fell to the RSF, the international community has failed to take the necessary actions to address the desperate plight civilians face as the conflict rages. There has been little accountability for abuses in North Darfur. The moves towards a ceasefire have been half-hearted, and Amnesty International is not aware of any diplomatic attempts to establish an international force that would meaningfully protect civilians.
“Crucially, the United Arab Emirates has continued to support the RSF, while governments with the required influence have largely failed to name and denounce their role or hold them to account.
“Without a ceasefire, accountability, and a protection force, civilians will continue to suffer in El Fasher and across Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces have consistently opposed the extension of an arms embargo and a ceasefire, continuing to believe that a military ‘solution’ to the conflict remains possible, thereby also setting aside the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
In August and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 25 civilians, including 19 residents and six humanitarian workers, regarding the situation in El Fasher. Of the residents, 15 left El Fasher between July and August 2026 and one was still in the city; the other three had fled earlier.
On 9 October, Amnesty International wrote to the RSF regarding the findings. At the time of publication, no response had been received.
In July 2026, Amnesty International released a major report that documented how the RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing during its campaign to seize El Fasher, with certain ethnic groups, including the Zaghawa, singled out for abuse. Amnesty International continues to document flagrant abuses committed by both parties to the conflict in Sudan, including in El Obeid, North Kordofan, as well as in South Kordofan and Blue Nile States.
Detention, torture, and unlawful killings in prisons
Of the 19 residents interviewed, 17 were detained by the RSF. Most were arbitrarily detained during the RSF capture of the city, while several were detained when they returned to retrieve belongings from their homes or to search for missing family members. They were all held in captivity for months. Several noted that people of particular ethnic groups, notably Zaghawa and Masalit people, were more likely to be detained and abused.
Most men were held in detention centres or prisons, where they witnessed unlawful killings, suffered torture and other ill-treatment, and were given minimal food or water. All were released only after family members paid ransom, or by escaping.
If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, who was detained in Shala prison
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained in Shala prison. He was regularly beaten and witnessed unlawful killings. He told Amnesty International: “Torture is something which is permanent in any [RSF] detention. They executed people who tried to look at them… If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you. They ask, ‘You want to take a rest? We will give you permanent rest’.” In July 2026, Modathir escaped, fleeing from house to house in order to reach safety.
Mamoun*, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man, was also held in Shala prison until July 2026. He said he witnessed the RSF shooting prisoners, and the death of a man with untreated diabetes who the RSF refused to help. Mamoun was regularly beaten, and said: “They take people out [of the cell] randomly, they accuse you of being with the Joint Forces or the military… And they beat you until you faint… Sometimes I was beaten four times a day… It just depends on their mood.” Mamoun was eventually released after his family paid a ransom.
Paying ransom was not always a guarantee of freedom. Musa*, a 23-year-old Zaghawa man, said that he and his father were detained at El Fasher Children’s Hospital in October 2025. They were released more than a month later after they paid a ransom. However, instead of being allowed to leave the city, Musa said the RSF took them to an RSF-guarded house and held there until around May 2026 when they were able to escape.
Musa and his father were forced to work for the RSF including collecting corpses, and were sometimes forced to speak on camera to say that the city was inhabitable, encouraging people to return. He said: “They paraded us inside the city and told us to talk [about how] El Fasher is good and safe.”
Detention in schools
Women, children, and some older or injured men were held in schools that were de facto detention centres. They described high rates of malnutrition, including among their own children.
Amnesty International interviewed nine people who were detained by the RSF in schools. They had extremely limited access to food and medical treatment; some women said that their children became malnourished during their detention there. All of these individuals were released or managed to escape by July or August 2026.
Haram*, a 45-year-old Zaghawa woman, and her young children were detained at a school in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood. She told Amnesty International: “[The RSF] were verbally abusing people… Zaghawa people were beaten, [the RSF] would just select and randomly beat [people]. They called us falangayaat women [a slur that indicates slavery or servitude].”
Hadia*, a 30-year-old Gimir woman whose husband was shot by the RSF during their capture of El Fasher, was detained in a school with her children, along with hundreds of other women and children. The RSF provided them very limited food and water.
Hadia was too malnourished to provide her youngest child, aged 18 months, with sufficient breast milk. When she finally escaped and reached Tawila in August 2026, all three of her children were diagnosed with malnutrition; one was hospitalized. Hadia told Amnesty International: “My children were very skinny and weak.”
Aloya*, a 54-year-old Zaghawa woman, spent several months detained in a school. She was afraid that her Zaghawa identity would be discovered and so never spoke the language while there. She said: “Daily there were four to five people dying… mostly from lack of food.”
Hatim*, a 38-year-old Berti man with a serious shrapnel injury in his jaw, was detained by the RSF when he returned to El Fasher to retrieve personal belongings from his house in spring 2026. He was taken to a school where he was kept for about four months with an estimated 300 people, mostly women. He told Amnesty International: “You could not move freely, you had to stay there… [The RSF] beat me up two times I tried fleeing… including on my wounds.” On his third attempt, Hatim was able to escape.
Amnesty International analysed satellite imagery of school detention sites between October 2025 and September 2026. While several sites indicated signs of human activity in previous months, by September 2026 there was little daily activity, suggesting that these detention sites may have been closed. Shala prison and Mina al-Bari detention centre, another facility where residents were held, still showed significant signs of human activity.
‘Everybody is terrorized’: RSF surveillance and limited humanitarian access
El Fasher residents told Amnesty International that while a small number of humanitarian organizations were operating in the city again as of September 2026, the RSF closely monitored their movements and prevented residents from speaking freely to them.
One resident who had returned to El Fasher in June 2026 told Amnesty International: “The El Fasher I knew is gone, it is a completely destroyed city. The public infrastructure, the schools, government institutions, hospitals, all are destroyed… It seemed like everybody is watched very closely, they don’t give humanitarian workers any private space to talk… Everybody is terrorized.”
Another resident said: “There is no complete blockage of [humanitarian] access, but… when organizations are implementing activities [the RSF] will monitor implementation… There are no pictures, no interviews, no interactions of any kind.”
Humanitarian workers expressed concerns about malnutrition, particularly amid a poor harvest season. According to official assessments, IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, is highly likely in North Darfur, including in El Fasher, in the months ahead.
Forced labour
Both men and women were subjected to forced labour, such as collecting dead bodies and rubble from El Fasher’s streets, or cooking and cleaning for the RSF without pay.
Misbah*, a 32-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained by the RSF in October 2025. He was brought to a house in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood, where he was forced to cook and clean for RSF officers. He was tied up and given very little to eat. He said he was beaten every day, and said: “I never thought I would survive.”
The RSF should immediately release all those who have been arbitrary detained, and end torture and unlawful killings in detention and elsewhere. The use of forced labour, which is prohibited by international law, must also end.
Amnesty International is again calling for an immediate ceasefire and for the urgent deployment of an international force to protect civilians. All countries must also immediately stop providing arms and ammunition to all parties to the conflict in Sudan. In particular, all countries must cease arms transfers to the United Arab Emirates until it stops supplying weapons to RSF in violation of the UN embargo on Darfur. The UN Security Council must also expand the existing arms embargo on Darfur to the rest of the country.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (or AIPAC), a major pro-Israel lobbying group in the United States, has changed tactics ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, announcing that it will cease direct endorsements and donations to candidates.
AIPAC’s decision comes following a decline in public support for Israel in the US over its genocide of besieged Palestinians in Gaza.
A letter sent by AIPAC to its members on Wednesday, and first published by Jewish Insider, demonstrated the erosion of the Israeli lobby's influence on public opinion in the United States.
In its letter, AIPAC stated that the committee would end its "direct endorsements of candidates" and "donations up to certain amounts" beginning with the US midterm congressional elections on November 3.
Accordingly, AIPAC will no longer directly endorse any candidate as a committee and will end its direct donations to candidates under the political action committee (PAC) umbrella, which were limited to $5,000 per election or a total of $10,000 for primaries and general elections.
However, this decision will not affect the multi-million dollar donations that the pro-Israel group receives under the umbrella of its "super PAC."
According to Federal Election Commission (FEC) data, AIPAC was the largest PAC donor in the country in 2025, with $26.8 million donated to candidates and other political committees.
It has already poured tens of millions of dollars into races nationwide through its main election-spending vehicle, the United Democracy Project (UDP).
Discontent among Democrats
The decision, seen as a reflection of growing discontent among Democrats regarding Israeli policies following Israel's genocide in Gaza, resonated in the US media.
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) and CNBC, reported that AIPAC was forced to "change tactics" after some prominent Democratic candidates announced they were rejecting AIPAC's support.
The reported that AIPAC's shift in election tactics regarding US politics was influenced by the growing resentment towards Israel among Democratic voters, particularly due to the Gaza genocide.
The news reports highlighted that prominent Democrats such as Senators Cory Booker and Ruben Gallego, and California Governor Gavin Newsom, as well as many "progressive" figures, had pledged not to accept AIPAC donations due to pressure from their constituents.
Tensions between Democrats and the Israel lobby escalated in July when 103 Democratic members of the House of Representatives supported a resolution to cut aid to Israel.
The motion was rejected, but AIPAC later removed the names of the Democratic members of Congress who voted for it from its website.
Support for Israel declining
A recent poll conducted by the Pew Research Center indicated that 80 percent of Democrats and independent Democrats hold negative views towards Israel.
The survey indicated that this rate, which was 53 percent in 2022, has increased significantly, particularly due to the humanitarian crisis caused by Israel in Gaza.
The shift extends beyond Democratic voters. The poll noted that negative views towards Israel, particularly among Republicans aged 18–49, have risen from 50 percent to 57 percent in the last year.
Conversely, the poll highlighted that the percentage of those with positive views towards Israel dropped from 55 percent in 2022 to 37 percent in 2026.
Israel has been carrying out genocide in Gaza since October 2023. Palestinians have recorded killings of more than 74,000 people — equivalent to about 3.4 percent of Gaza’s estimated prewar population of 2.2 million — most of them women and children, in the Israeli annihilation campaign.
Thousand of Palestinians are feared buried under rubble of bombed homes.
Experts contend that the actual death toll significantly exceeds what the Gaza authorities have reported, estimating it could be around 200,000.
The latest UN Trade and Development report has put recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.5 billion, warning that the estimate could rise as further damage is recorded.

Use MFA, patch, beware of scammers: 5 ways to keep safe online in the wake of AI-supercharged hacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Use MFA, patch, beware of scammers: 5 ways to keep safe online in the wake of AI-supercharged hacking
Much of the world woke on Oct 22 to news that PHP, a coding language most people have never heard of but that underlies roughly 70% of all websites, had a hackable vulnerability, sending businesses and governments scrambling to fix it.
While the PHP glitches sit in the underlying code itself, the NSA warned that attackers could use them to take control of web servers to steal data, disrupt services or move through networks on services the average person relies on every day.
Experts say responsibility mostly lies with software providers and organisations that serve customers. But there are basic steps everyone should take to protect themselves.
Use multi-factor authentication
MFA, or multi-factor authentication, requires two forms of verification to access a protected site, such as a password plus a text-based code or security key. Emily Austin, principal security researcher at cybersecurity firm Censys, recommended unique passwords for individual websites, and for people to monitor any transactions.
“But realistically, for situations like the PHP vulnerabilities, there really isn’t much an end user can do beyond hope the services they rely on either don’t use PHP or have people actively working on patching,” Austin said.
The PHP flaws are the latest in a series of severe software bugs made worse by increasingly capable and accessible large language models. Long-hidden flaws in widely used software, once too obscure or complex for humans to exploit, are now much easier to surface and weaponize.
Make hardware updates automatic
Dan Guido, CEO and co-founder of cybersecurity firm Trail of Bits, recommended people “turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, and home router.” Companies typically issue security updates when patches are available for known vulnerabilities, so installing them promptly limits the window for bad actors.
Even so, consumers remain at the mercy of the services they rely on, Guido said.
“Someone visiting a website can do everything right, like use two-factor authentication, and still have their information exposed,” Guido said. “You can’t patch your hospital’s website.”
Most of the work falls on companies running services, Guido said. “They need to deploy fixes faster and limit the damage that compromised systems can cause.”
Runa Sandvik, the founder of Granitt and a digital security expert, said people need to update apps and services on their devices whenever they’re available, and to not forget about internet-connected devices around the house.
“I can see a scenario in which some people have some sort of IoT device at home that maybe doesn’t get frequent updates, maybe doesn’t get any updates at all,” Sandvik said. “It’s worth double checking with the vendor to see if there is anything available.”
Patch, patch, patch
Dr Daniel Gardham, a lecturer at the Surrey Centre for Cyber Security and the University of Surrey, said organizations must know what software they run, patch promptly and check whether they’ve already been compromised. In the AI age, attackers have the advantage, Gardham added.
“Finding vulnerabilities is becoming faster and easier, but fixing them across the range of systems that rely on this software is much harder,” Gardham said. “How well organizations manage that gap will determine whether AI makes the internet safer or more vulnerable.”
Beware of scammers
Any time a major cybersecurity threat makes the news, scammers and cybercriminals will try to take advantage, said Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, a cyberkinetics company.
Be wary of unsolicited links. “When these headlines hit, check the affected company’s instructions by opening its app or typing its website address yourself,” Adams said. “An urgent message telling you to ‘secure your account’ deserves extra scrutiny.”
Your money is safe
Banks have been preparing for this moment since frontier models came out, and have “worked extremely hard to ensure there is no more low-hanging fruit for the bad guys to go after,” said Paul Benda, executive vice president of risk, fraud and cybersecurity at the American Bankers Association.
However, Benda added, “we are in a new normal” in terms of cyber threats, and consumers need to be aware, especially in the wake of the PHP vulnerabilities, when shopping with random retailers or websites “where their security is not going to be as good as your bank.”
Benda said consumers should not reuse passwords across shopping sites, and should consider using passkeys where possible, which are digital keys specific to certain websites, that avoid the need to enter a password into a website and a phishing resistant. REUTERS

Putin reaffirms Russia’s readiness to resume trilateral peace talks on Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:56:45 UTC
07:56:45 KST

Burç Eruygur
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed Moscow’s readiness to resume trilateral peace talks on the war in Ukraine, saying the negotiations would focus on ways to ensure postwar security for both sides.
In an interview Thursday with Vesti news outlet, Putin discussed Russia’s negotiations with representatives of US President Donald Trump’s administration, recalling an agreement to resume trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
“The objective of these talks will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements – specifically definitive, long-term agreements rather than merely a temporary cessation of hostilities,” he added.
Putin said they are ready to resume contacts to achieve this goal, noting that during their meeting in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stressed they must address the broader architecture of European security if they are to discuss future security arrangements for both Russia and Ukraine.
“I agree with that too. Well, let’s see how the situation develops over the coming days,” he added.
His remarks came a day after he hosted the US envoy at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, after which Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that Putin conveyed Moscow’s readiness "in principle" to resume trilateral peace negotiations on Ukraine in November.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations around the 10th of November,” Ushakov said following the talks, adding that Moscow’s readiness for trilateral negotiations particularly concerned the issue of building a post-war “security system” for Russia and Ukraine.
Separately, Witkoff announced on US social media platform X that he and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner held “constructive” discussions in St. Petersburg and the Norwegian capital Oslo, the latter of which took place Tuesday, and that these discussions will continue with trilateral talks “at the technical level.”
Russia and Ukraine last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks on Jan. 23-24, Feb. 4-5, and Feb. 17-18. The first two were held in Abu Dhabi, while the third took place in Geneva.
Commenting on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's remarks on Wednesday to Fox News on being open to freezing the front line in Ukraine in an effort to end the war, Putin argued that it seemed "inappropriate" to describe the issue as amounting to “any territorial losses.”
"To begin with, my view on this matter is that this is not their territory. It is the territory of historical Russia," Putin said, further arguing that the residents of these territories "chose" to be part of Russia through referendums in September 2022.
The referendums were widely condemned as illegal by the international community.

Hundreds of Ethiopians cross into Kenya to flee regional fighting
Hundreds of Ethiopians have crossed into Kenya, fleeing fighting in the border town of Moyale, which was reportedly prompted by loyalists publicly raising the flag of a neighbouring majority-Somali state.
Kenyan police said on Thursday that hundreds of Ethiopians, mostly women and children, crossed into Kenya through several entry points in Moyale, including the Sessi, Kore, Biashara, Foundation and Miti areas.

UK museum removes Egyptian mummies over lack of ‘consent’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:41:34 UTC
07:41:34 KST

UK museum removes Egyptian mummies over lack of ‘consent’
A British museum has removed ancient Egyptian mummies from public display, citing a lack of “consent” from the deceased and drawing accusations of excessive political correctness.
The Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in Glasgow, Scotland, is one of the country’s most popular cultural attractions, drawing more than 1.3 million visitors annually. Its collections include Egyptian antiquities and mummified remains that have been exhibited for years.
Among the items taken off display were a painted coffin containing the remains of an Egyptian priest named Nekht, a mummified male head, a right foot, and a right hand recovered from the Valley of the Kings in Luxor, Egypt, the Glasgow Times reported on Thursday.
My daughter has a book on the ancient Egyptians and has been quite animated by it so we took her to Kelvingrove Museum to see their mummy. Except, it’s no longer there. All ‘human remains’ gone with the following sign up in place of exhibits that have been there for years. https://t.co/DKGOx4VjpR
— Jonny McFarlane (@jonnyrmcfarlane) October 17, 2026
The changes came to public attention after a visitor said he had taken his daughter to see an Egyptian mummy, only to discover that it was no longer there. He shared a photograph on X of a museum notice stating that the remains had been removed “as a mark of respect.”
Mummies have been removed from display at the Kelvingrove Museum in Glasgow because of a 'lack of consent from the deceased individual'. A Glasgow Life spokesman said: ‘The removal of human remains from display at Glasgow Life museums reflects contemporary museum practice. ‘The International Council of Museums’ revised Code of Ethics, published in June 2026, states that museums “should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance”. ‘The All-Party Parliamentary Group on Afrikan Reparations 2025 report, “Laying Ancestors to Rest”, also raises ethical concerns about the display of ancient Egyptian human remains due to the consistent disregard of the potential wishes of the ancestors and the intention of the communities that originally laid them to rest.
— UNN (@UnityNewsNet) October 22, 2026
Glasgow Life, which operates the museum, said the move reflected contemporary museum practices, citing revised ethical guidelines published by the International Council of Museums in June. The guidelines call for human remains to be treated with dignity and respect.
The organization’s draft policy proposes that such exhibits should be displayed only with documented, informed consent from the deceased or, where appropriate, their descendants.
“In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals,” a Glasgow Life spokesperson said.
The decision drew criticism from Scottish Conservative politician Murdo Fraser, who described it as “woke madness.”
“Even Egyptian mummies are now being cancelled by a society so obsessed with modern sensibilities that it has lost all sense of perspective,” said Fraser.
Chris McGovern, chairman of the Campaign for Real Education and a former adviser to the British prime minister’s policy unit, also condemned the move as “virtue-signaling, woke nonsense.”
“It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago,” he said, adding that museums in Egypt continue to exhibit mummified remains.
Egypt itself has defended the display of its antiquities in foreign museums. Mohamed Ismail Khaled, head of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, said last year that thousands of artifacts legally exported to Britain serve as the “best ambassadors of Egypt,” attracting international visitors to the country. Cairo has nevertheless continued to demand the return of looted treasures, including the Rosetta Stone held by the British Museum and the bust of Nefertiti in Berlin.
Glasgow Life said it is also working to remove further archaeological human remains from Kelvingrove and plans to remove a coffin and mummified remains from the nearby St Mungo Museum afterward.
The controversy follows a similar decision by Manchester Museum, which removed the 2,700-year-old mummified remains of an Egyptian woman named Asru in September after more than two centuries on public display.

What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:26:57 UTC
07:26:57 KST

France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this pathogen, there is no risk to the general public. It emphasized, however, that health authorities are continuing to investigate.
The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon. The patient, who died earlier this month, suffered from severe immunosuppression, making this likely an exceptional case. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus,” the official statement notes.
According to preliminary evidence, the patient contracted Shamonda virus from an insect bite. A tiny gnat known as the biting midge is known to be the primary route of transfer between animals. Since the virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, sporadic infections have been reported in livestock across Africa as well as in Japan. Cattle are considered the primary host because they develop visible symptoms. (Although sheep and goats can become infected, no obvious clinical signs have been documented in these animals.)
After animal is bitten by a midge carrying Shamonda virus, the infection has an incubation period of two to three days. Symptoms observed in animals include fever, diarrhea, and a decrease in milk production. When pregnant cows have become infected, the virus can cause miscarriages or severe deformations in the calf.
To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents. That doesn’t mean you should panic. Public health authorities are considering the case to be “exceptional,” because the deceased patient was severely immunocompromised.
Still, several European countries are on alert, because until a few months ago, this region was considered free of the virus. However, this summer, a new variant known as Shamonda-Europe was detected in livestock in Switzerland. Other cases were subsequently identified in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy, and Spain.
Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states that two genetically distinct forms of the virus, known as Shamonda Type 1 and Shamonda Type 2, have been identified circulating in Europe. It adds that, in early September, infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 provinces across France.
The case documented in France constitutes the first known infection in a person.
X content
“This is an important scientific finding. However, it is important to put this into perspective. The patient had a serious underlying illness that left them particularly vulnerable to infections, and we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death,” Ben Brennan, professor of virology at the University of Glasgow, said in a statement.
It’s premature to draw conclusions about the virus and it’s potential to infect humans, agreed David Roiz, a scientist Institute for Game and Wildlife Research in Spain. Many viruses “circulate naturally amongst mammals in tropical regions and cause sporadic cases in humans,” he said. “In a globalized world, where animals and goods are on the move and the climate is changing, it is not unusual for cases of human transmission to occur, and we should not be concerned; we simply need to monitor the situation, remain vigilant, and be proactive in addressing potential health risks.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula about even ahead of Brazil runoff, Datafolha poll shows

Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula about even ahead of Brazil runoff, Datafolha poll shows

Archimedes screw-inspired molecular machine boosts electrical conductivity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:26:16 CST
07:26:16 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- An international team of researchers has developed a molecular machine inspired by the ancient Archimedes screw, revealing a new way to connect mechanical movement and electrical conduction at the molecular scale, Israel's Weizmann Institute of Science said on Thursday.
The Archimedes screw is a simple machine that moves water uphill by rotating a screw-like blade (helical surface) inside a hollow pipe.
Inspired by the ancient invention, the molecular structure features a helical molecule produced by stretching it between two gold tips. The researchers can stretch or compress the molecular screw by adjusting the distance between the gold electrodes.
According to the findings published in the latest issue of Nature, the molecule rotates when a voltage is applied, and the rotating molecule conducts electricity significantly better than a stationary one. Above a certain voltage level, the electrical current is increased by up to 100 times.
The researchers' calculations showed that the positions the molecule avoids when at rest conduct electricity best, and rotation makes these positions accessible.
Based on the calculations, researchers developed a simplified model that reproduced the experimentally observed rotation and current increase.
The researchers highlighted the close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries. The study drew together scientists from research institutes in Israel, Germany, Denmark and China.
Molecular machines are inspired by biological motors that convert energy into movement. The field gained international recognition with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded for the design and synthesis of molecular machines.
The new findings could inform future research into molecular electronics, spintronics and microfluidic systems, holding potential to provide a way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. ■

Gaza faces starvation as Israel blocks commercial trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:52:03 UTC
16:52:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza faces spectre of starvation as Israel continues to block commercial trucks
The war-torn coastal enclave may go hungry again as Israeli restrictions on the entry of commercial goods deepen shortages, drive up food prices and threaten to shut down remaining operational bakeries.
Abdel Nasser al-Ajrami, head of the Bakery Owners Association in Gaza, warned on Thursday that the seven remaining operational bakeries could close within 48 hours as flour stocks run low.
Speaking to The New Arab, he said several other bakeries that had operated in partnership with the World Food Programme (WFP) and received fuel support had already closed in Gaza City, central Gaza and the south.
Although the Kerem Shalom crossing reopened after several days of closure, no flour shipments had entered Gaza by Thursday, al-Ajrami said. Efforts to secure essential supplies had also yielded no response by late Wednesday.
Commercial shipments have been blocked since mid-October amid disruptions linked to an Israeli festival. Trucks expected to enter Gaza on Thursday were reportedly prevented from doing so by Israeli settlers, further worsening shortages in local markets.
In a press statement, Gaza's Ministry of Social Development warned that the closure of bakeries and restrictions on flour and other essential food supplies could have catastrophic humanitarian consequences.
The ministry said the shortages threatened to worsen malnutrition, particularly among children, sick people and older residents.
It called on the international community to pressure Israel to open the crossings and allow humanitarian aid and commercial goods to enter.
Soaring prices
The disruption to commercial supplies has already driven up prices and made basic goods increasingly difficult for residents to afford.
Radi Kamal, a resident of al-Zawaida refugee camp in central Gaza, told TNA that a 250-gram packet of coffee now costs $10, up from $6. A kilogram of tomatoes costs around $6, potatoes $4 and frozen red meat about US$20. Eggs and fruit have also become scarce.
"Almost everything has become more expensive, and we can no longer buy as much as we used to," Kamal said. "Even when goods are available in the market, many families cannot afford them. We have to choose what we need most and go without other things because we do not have enough money."
He said families feared the situation would deteriorate further if commercial trucks continued to be blocked.
"If supplies do not arrive, prices could rise further, and some goods may disappear from the markets," he said. "Families are already struggling to buy food. If bread also becomes unavailable, feeding our children will become even harder."
Um Mohammed, a 42-year-old mother of five from Gaza City, told TNA that rising prices had forced her to cut back on household purchases to ensure her children had enough to eat. "When I go to the market, I buy only what we need most, but even these things have become expensive," she said. "I put my children's needs first and give up other things so I can provide food for them."
In Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, Abu Ahmed, 51, who supports a family of six, said many households could no longer afford the goods available in local markets.
"We have to buy less and put other needs aside because prices keep rising," he told TNA. "If the bakeries close, things will become much worse because bread is a basic food that we depend on every day."
While Israeli restrictions on the entry of goods remain a major obstacle to supplies reaching Gaza, a apparent dispute over commercial imports and alleged financial demands on merchants has added another layer to the crisis.
Before Israel's genocidal war, around 1,500 merchants and importers operated in Gaza. Commercial-sector sources say Israel has since restricted the coordination of commercial shipments to just eight merchants, leaving supplies vulnerable to disruptions when disagreements arise.
Merchants have accused Hamas of imposing fees of up to 10,000 shekels (around US$3,300) per truck. Disagreements have also emerged over the proportion of sales that merchants must collect in cash rather than through bank transfers.
Hamas and Gaza's Government Media Office have denied imposing mandatory fees on goods. The Ministry of Economy has said the proposed contribution is voluntary and intended to support a national fund providing social assistance, including help for orphans, widows and displaced families.
Riyad al-Sawafiri, head of the Economic Committee at the Gaza Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told TNA that the chamber opposed imposing additional fees or taxes on merchants.
Some traders said they were required to pay 30 per cent of their sales in cash, while Nahed Shuhiber, head of the Private Transport Association in Gaza, put the figure at 25 per cent.
Shuhiber told TNA that the dispute was linked to measures taken against one of the eight merchants authorised to coordinate commercial shipments into Gaza following disagreements over sales procedures.
The situation is further complicated by a cash shortage. Merchants struggle to obtain money for transactions, while residents face difficulties withdrawing their savings.
Despite these internal disputes, the entry of commercial trucks remains subject to Israeli approval and border procedures, leaving the flow of essential goods vulnerable to restrictions and interruptions.
Food insecurity
Political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that the suspension of commercial shipments could not be understood solely as a dispute over import procedures or financial contributions.
"Restrictions on the entry of goods have direct and severe consequences for the lives of Gaza's population," he said. "Disruptions to supplies worsen the food crisis, drive up prices and make it harder for people to secure their basic needs."
He added that low-income families and displaced people were bearing the heaviest burden, particularly as bakeries warned of closure and flour stocks dwindled.
"Even if disagreements exist between merchants and local authorities, resolving them should not come at the expense of the population or leave people without access to food," Ibrahim said.
He also questioned the gap between images of trucks at the crossings and the shortages in Gaza's markets, arguing that the presence of vehicles at the border did not guarantee that goods would reach consumers.
With commercial supplies blocked by Israel, food prices soaring and bakeries warning they may soon run out of flour, Gaza's residents face mounting difficulties in securing basic necessities.

ANKARA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) will focus on the concrete implementation of climate policies, said Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Berris Ekinci on Thursday.
Speaking at an event commemorating the upcoming United Nations Day, Ekinci said the conference would be designed as an "implementation COP," reflecting growing expectations that the second decade of the Paris Agreement should focus on delivering climate commitments rather than primarily negotiating new decisions.
She highlighted the importance of linking national climate priorities with financing through the Climate Implementation Bridge, an initiative developed with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to help turn climate ambitions into bankable projects.
According to the Turkish minister, the summit will also combine formal negotiations with a climate action agenda that involves cities, businesses, investors, researchers, civil society, and young people. Ekinci said the agenda includes six global targets for 2035.
Babatunde Ahonsi, the UN Resident Coordinator in Türkiye, said that addressing climate change requires broad participation across society, including businesses, local authorities, women and young people, as well as governments.
Describing the approach as "inclusive multilateralism," Ahonsi said preparations for COP31 had involved dialogues with businesses, municipalities, youth groups and women's organizations.
Also on Thursday, Murat Kurum, minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, said Türkiye expects 85 world leaders to attend COP31 in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya next month, while 26,000 security personnel will be deployed to ensure the event proceeds smoothly.
Kurum made the remarks during an inspection of the summit venue. According to the minister, nearly 300 ministers are expected to visit Türkiye, and applications for 159 pavilions and 90 delegation offices have been approved, a record number for the UN conference.
More than 1 million visitors are expected during the event, which will feature dedicated meeting halls, exhibition areas and a media center designed to accommodate 4,000 journalists, he said.
Meanwhile, Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said 26,000 personnel from the police, gendarmerie and coast guard would be assigned to security duties, with measures covering land, air and maritime operations.
COP31 is scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. ■

High fuel costs squeeze major U.S. airlines' profits despite strong revenues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

An American Airlines aircraft takes off from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York City, the United States, Oct. 22, 2026. As major U.S. airlines reported their third-quarter (Q3) operating results, rising fuel costs put pressure on their profit margins despite strong travel demand. (Photo by Ziyu Julian Zhu/Xinhua)
NEW YORK, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- As major U.S. airlines reported their third-quarter (Q3) operating results, rising fuel costs put pressure on their profit margins despite strong travel demand.
Despite record-breaking revenues and strong travel demand, higher operating costs continue to eat up profit and weaken earnings expectations heading into the final quarter of 2026.
American Airlines reported a net loss of 269 million U.S. dollars in Q3, despite generating record revenues of 16.3 billion dollars.
Its fuel expense increased by 1.9 billion dollars, or 67.5 percent, with an average fuel cost of 3.85 dollars per gallon.
The carrier expects to pay 4.7 dollars per gallon in the fourth quarter, nearly double the price paid in the fourth quarter of 2025, with quarterly fuel expenses projected to increase by approximately 2.8 billion dollars year over year.
American Airlines also lowered its full-year outlook, forecasting an adjusted loss of 1 to 1.6 dollars per share, compared with its previous projection of a loss of 65 cents to a profit of 65 cents per share.
Southwest Airlines, on the other hand, reported a similar challenge on Wednesday, even as its Q3 earnings exceeded Wall Street expectations.
The Dallas-based carrier generated a net income of 270 million dollars with operating revenues rising 21.2 percent to 8.4 billion dollars, a third-quarter company record, according to a press release from Southwest Airlines.
However, the fuel expenses of Southwest Airlines increased by 821 million dollars compared with the same period last year, and its Q3 fuel cost was 3.92 dollars per gallon, which is above the prior assumptions of 3.7-3.75 dollars per gallon.
"Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," said Southwest Airlines CEO Bob Jordan in the company's Q3 revenue press release. "We remain confident in our ability to further strengthen earnings, improve returns, and expand margins over time."
Southwest Airlines assumed a fourth-quarter 2026 fuel cost of approximately 4.55 dollars per gallon based on the forward curve as of Oct. 15, 2026.
United Airlines on Tuesday reported its Q3 revenue of 17.9 billion dollars, up 17.4 percent year on year, with net income reaching 1 billion dollars. However, its fuel expenses increased by 1.8 billion dollars, or 62 percent, compared with the same period last year, according to the company's third-quarter earnings release.
United Airlines expects to pay approximately 4.8 dollars per gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, compared with 3.9 dollars in Q3. The carrier forecasts adjusted earnings of 50 cents to 1.5 dollars per share for the fourth quarter, which is below Wall Street expectations. ■

Backgrounder: 5 things to know about Israel's upcoming parliamentary election
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:26:04 CST
07:26:04 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Israelis will vote on Oct. 27 to elect the 26th Knesset, the country's parliament, with about 7.3 million eligible voters.
It will be Israel's first election since the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and triggered a devastating Israeli offensive in Gaza, followed by a wider regional escalation involving Lebanon and Iran.
HOW DO ISRAEL'S ELECTIONS WORK?
In Israel, winning the most seats does not necessarily mean winning the premiership. The next prime minister will be the lawmaker who can assemble a governing coalition with the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
Israel's system of nationwide proportional representation means voters choose party lists rather than individual candidates. Seats are allocated according to each party's share of the vote, provided it crosses the electoral threshold of 3.25 percent.
No single party has ever won an outright majority in the Knesset, making coalition-building essential.
WHICH PARTIES ARE CONTESTING THE ELECTION?
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party has dominated Israeli politics for much of the past two decades and draws support largely from conservative and nationalist voters.
Likud heads a bloc of far-right and religious parties, including Otzma Yehudit (Hebrew for "Jewish Power"), led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir; Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, and the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.
The main opposition parties include Yashar (Hebrew for "straight" or "honest"), headed by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and Together, an alliance of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that brings together right-wing and centrist voters opposed to Netanyahu.
The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, advocates civil liberties and a two-state solution, while Avigdor Lieberman's right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Hebrew for "Israel Our Home") party traditionally draws support from Russian-speaking Israelis, who account for approximately 15 percent of Israel's population.
Two predominantly Arab lists are also running: the Joint List, comprising Hadash, Ta'al and Balad, which advocates Palestinian citizens' rights and an end to Israel's occupation; and Ra'am, an Arab-majority party that focuses on improving conditions in Arab communities and has previously joined a governing coalition.
Smaller parties near the electoral threshold could also prove decisive, as votes for lists that fail to cross it are excluded from seat allocation.
WHAT DO OPINION POLLS SHOW?
In most recent polls, Netanyahu's Likud party has trailed Eisenkot's Yashar party.
An early October survey by Israel's Channel 12 News projected Netanyahu's bloc to win 49 seats, compared with 54 for the main non-Arab opposition bloc, leaving Arab parties and smaller lists holding the balance of power.
A poll published by Israeli public broadcaster Kan earlier this week projected 51 seats for Netanyahu's bloc and 52 for the main non-Arab opposition bloc.
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the main opposition bloc appears poised to secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, according to the polls.
WHO IS NETANYAHU'S MAIN CHALLENGER?
Eisenkot, 66, has emerged as Netanyahu's leading rival, with Yashar ranking the largest party in most polls.
A former minister in Netanyahu's wartime government, Eisenkot has campaigned on restoring public trust and investigating the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attack.
On Wednesday, he ruled out serving in a government led by Netanyahu, even in a power-sharing agreement involving a rotation of the premiership.
Despite their rivalry, both politicians take a hard line on national security and oppose the establishment of an independent Palestinian state. They differ on some other issues, including settlement policy.
WHAT ARE THE MAIN ISSUES?
National security and accountability for the Oct. 7 attack are central campaign issues, alongside Israel's military operations in Gaza and Lebanon and its conflict with Iran.
Netanyahu has highlighted what he describes as Israel's military achievements. His opponents blame him for failing to prevent the attack and demand an independent inquiry.
Other major issues include mandatory military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men, the high cost of living and government efforts to increase political influence over the judiciary.
Netanyahu's corruption trial also overshadows the campaign. He denies all charges. ■

DUBAI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption could boost annual economic growth in the Middle East and Central Asia by 0.1 to 0.6 percentage points over the medium term, depending on countries' digital readiness and their ability to integrate the technology into productive activities, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said Thursday.

The adoption of AI offers economies in the Middle East and Central Asia a unique opportunity to raise productivity and strengthen medium-term growth, the report said, adding that several Gulf Cooperation Council countries, including the United Arab Emirates (UAE), are making substantial investments to position themselves as global AI hubs.
The IMF raised its forecast for the UAE's economic growth in 2027 to 7.7 percent, up 2.4 percentage points from its April projection, with AI investment estimated to add around 0.5 percentage points to the country's annual economic growth.
The fund stressed the importance of continued investment in digital infrastructure, education, skills development and innovation to improve productivity and support economic diversification, according to the report.
In tandem with its policy guidance, the IMF noted that it had provided approximately 48 billion U.S. dollars in financing to countries in the Middle East and Central Asia since 2020 and implemented 437 technical assistance and capacity development projects across 31 countries during fiscal year 2026. ■

The UN humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said severe rainfall deficits are deepening humanitarian needs, especially in Darfur and Kordofan. There is an urgent need for food and nutrition assistance, clean water, sanitation and health services, as well as support for smallholder farmers ahead of the winter planting season.
The United Nations and humanitarian partners said they are preparing to scale up life-saving assistance in the most affected areas of Darfur and Kordofan over the next six months. However, severe funding shortages threaten the ability to respond to growing needs.
Brown warned that without urgent additional funding, humanitarian food and nutrition stocks are expected to run out by early next year, leaving vulnerable families without critical assistance.

"With less than three months remaining in the year, Sudan's humanitarian response plan is just over 46 percent funded, with 1.32 billion U.S. dollars received against the nearly 2.9 billion required," the office said. ■

5.0-magnitude quake hits 153 km S of Kokopo, Papua New Guinea -- USGS

US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:25:14 UTC
07:25:14 KST

US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award
The prize comes less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump announced sanctions against the court.
The European Union has awarded the International Criminal Court (ICC) its top human rights award, two weeks after US President Donald Trump vowed to dismantle the court through new sanctions.
Thursday’s Sakharov Prize is the second international recognition for the war crimes tribunal this month, with former ICC Judge Navi Pillay awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work to promote peace and international law.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for the honour “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of Trump, whose campaign against it has escalated since the court announced in 2024 arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.
‘Brick by brick’
The Trump administration has promised to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, recently announcing sanctions aimed at crippling its day-to-day operations. The ICC tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a video posted on social media when the sanctions were announced.
Washington has also sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, as well as a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court.
EU backs ICC
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions, which are due to come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can continue functioning.
“The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.
Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but according to EU officials is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington.

Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:21:08 UTC
07:21:08 KST

In case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.
Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3.
The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's mega-cap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home.
Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion.
"If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."
Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."
The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said.
"There were many driving factors that led the board and special committee to approve the Class C shares, and it would be misleading to attribute it to any single reason," Meta told CNBC in a statement.
The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure.
In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.
Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.
Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said, "I don't want California to end up in the same place."
Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking, with a net worth of $185 billion.
Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure, recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared with 43% who oppose it.
Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs, which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang.
"The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.
Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."
Instead, the new stock incentive will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.
WATCH: 'Fast Money' traders react to Meta's Q3 results as stock climbs in extended trading.

Türkiye's economy grows 5.5% on average over 23 years despite crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:19:14 UTC
07:19:14 KST

Gökhan Çeliker
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Türkiye averaged annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 5.5% over the past 23 years under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's tenure, despite geopolitical crises in the surrounding region, Necmeddin Bilal Erdogan, chair of the Dissemination of Knowledge Society, said on Friday.
Speaking at the 19th edition of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum kicked off in Istanbul on Thursday, he said Türkiye is taking center stage to outline its growing global responsibilities in seeking a more peaceful and equitable international order.
“I think Türkiye found a path that could benefit the world, as we move towards a multipolar order, but right now, we’re experiencing some growing pains adapting to a new world order,” he said.
Erdogan noted that Ankara will play a key role in shaping the new world order moving forward under its “Century of Türkiye” vision, as Türkiye grows its capabilities and seizes its unique potential in managing conflicts, responding to challenges and persevering under difficult conditions.
He recalled that Türkiye ranks first worldwide in humanitarian aid per capita, referring to the country’s culture of solidarity and Ankara’s belief in sharing global wealth rather than allowing it to accumulate in the hands of a select few.
“Türkiye continues to strive for a more peaceful world and has undertaken certain responsibilities in this endeavor, with Istanbul becoming one of the most suitable hubs for global conferences, as all countries can come to these meetings in the megacity, while in the past, many cities that traditionally hosted such events are now facing hardship allowing certain countries or representatives in — the fact that we’re gathered here today shows that Türkiye has much more to contribute to building a better world in the 21st century,” he said.
Erdogan also mentioned that Europe should not rely solely on the US when it comes to issues concerning sovereignty and that Türkiye can step in to assume greater responsibility in the region.
“Türkiye, under its counterterrorism initiative, is addressing this issue not only because of domestic difficulties that persisted for nearly 50 years, but also because it is in the region’s best interest,” he noted.
He added that Türkiye has been mediating and finding common ground on geopolitical issues in its immediate vicinity, engaging with all parties, and has shown commitment to ending conflicts and building stronger ties as part of the nation’s broader goal of building a better future for future generations.
Erdogan stated that the recently inked Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a pact between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, showed that medium-sized powers are ready to ensure regional security.
The Mecca Pact requires the three countries to treat an attack against one of the signatories as an attack on all three.
Erdogan noted that economic inequalities and disparities between the Global North and the Global South are widening, while prejudices and double standards exist in many areas, making it difficult to establish and maintain dialogue.
As with Moscow over the Russia-Ukraine war, Erdogan said Palestinian people have long been subjected to sanctions.
“Despite the ongoing genocide, there are no hopes for sanctions to be imposed on Israel at a level comparable to those of the EU’s on Russia,” he said. “We’re seeing some limited steps by the UK and Canada but these double standards continue to erode trust in Europe.”

Trump asks Musk to lift Ukraine Starlink restrictions: WSJ
US President Donald Trump called billionaire SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starlink, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 22, citing US officials.
Trump later told reporters that Musk had restored access, but declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to Musk about the matter.
Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Starlink system was working more normally on Oct 22, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, according to US and Ukrainian officials cited by the Journal.
Trump backs attack ad featuring Democrat’s estranged mother
US President Donald Trump on Oct 22 backed Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, over an attack ad featuring his Democratic rival’s estranged mother, whose husband was charged with raping the candidate as a child.
Ramaswamy faced a firestorm of criticism over the ad featuring the mother of Amy Acton, who remained married to the man who the candidate says sexually abused her for years.
But Trump on his Truth Social network defended the “very powerful” advertisement and accused the media of a “well coordinated attack” aimed at getting Ramaswamy, a former presidential hopeful, to stop running it.
Monet’s Iris fetches €50 million at Paris auction
Iris, a monumental painting by Impressionist Claude Monet, sold for €50 million (S$70 million) including buyer fees in Paris on Oct 22, becoming the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.
The 1.60m high and 1.8m wide work had never left the billionaire Schlumberger family’s mansion in Paris and was known only through a black-and-white photograph.
It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889–1983), according to Thomas Bompard, co-head of the Modern and Contemporary Art Department at Sotheby’s France.
Actor Tom Skerritt, star of Alien and Top Gun, dies at 93
Versatile actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Hollywood megahits including the sci-fi classic Alien, the war comedy M*A*S*H, and the action drama Top Gun, has died at the age of 93, his manager confirmed.
Skerritt, a Detroit native whose Hollywood career spanned from the 1960s to the 2020s, died on Oct 21 of natural causes, said ABC7, citing a statement from his family.
Known for his rugged good looks and ability to shine in a variety of genres, Skerritt delivered memorable performances in leading and supporting roles in film and television.
Sixteen authors try to write novel on one-day train ride
Sixteen writers – half French-speaking and half Japanese – boarded a luxury train in Kyoto on Oct 22, faced with the unusual task of collectively writing a novel in under 24 hours.
The authors, who include Muriel Barbery, are taking part in a project by “L’ecriture en mouvement” – Writing in Motion – a French association that promotes literary exchanges.
By the time the “Mizukaze” – their striking, bottle-green train in the Art Deco style – pulls into the western city of Matsue on the morning of Oct 23, they hope to have completed a 200-page story.

Ecuador opposition leader Luisa Gonzalez arrested in campaign finance probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:09:38 UTC
07:09:38 KST

Ecuador opposition leader Luisa Gonzalez arrested in campaign finance probe
Gonzalez’s Citizen Revolution Movement has denounced the arrest as politically motivated, calling for her release.
Ecuadorian opposition leader Luisa Gonzalez has been arrested as part of an investigation into alleged irregularities in the financing of her 2023 presidential campaign.
Local media reported on Thursday that Gonzalez, a prominent left-wing politician and ally of former President Rafael Correa, was detained in Canuto, a rural town in western Ecuador.
She lost presidential elections to right-wing President Daniel Noboa in both 2023 and 2025.
In a statement on social media, Ecuador’s Attorney General’s Office said it had executed arrest warrants against three people suspected of money laundering.
Seven people are under investigation over “inconsistencies in the contributions and the lawful source of the funds” during the 2023 presidential campaign.
Investigators are examining the use of a network of entities to channel approximately $500,000 for campaign advertising between May and August 2023.
The attorney general’s office has alleged that the money may have been transferred improperly, without disclosing the sources of the money or the identities of contributors.
The investigation, known as the Laberinto case, follows an earlier probe into alleged irregular campaign financing. Authorities have previously investigated claims that money brought from Venezuela was used to finance Gonzalez’s 2023 presidential bid. Gonzalez has denied wrongdoing.
Gonzalez described the accusations as “absurd” in a post on the social media platform X, comparing her situation to that of a political prisoner.
She also called on her supporters to unite in pursuit of democracy in the face of the “Noboa dictatorship”.
“I will respond with the dignity of Ecuadorians who owe nothing and who are committed to achieving freedom for Ecuador and a better future for the country,” she wrote of her arrest.
Gabriela Rivadeneira — the president of the Citizen Revolution Movement, of which Gonzalez is a member — also denounced the arrest as political persecution. She demanded Gonzalez’s immediate release.
Correa, who served as president from 2007 to 2017, also rejected the allegations, calling the case persecution.
“Luisa Gonzalez has been arrested. ENOUGH IS ENOUGH!!!!” Correa wrote on X.
Gonzalez, a lawyer and former member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, fought a notably acrimonious presidential race against Noboa. The two candidates faced each other in a run-off race in April 2025, resulting in Noboa winning with more than 55 percent of the vote.
But Gonzalez rejected the results as fraudulent and demanded a recount. Noboa’s government, meanwhile, accused her political movement of conspiring with criminal groups to plot attacks against the right-wing leader.
Noboa, a close ally of United States President Donald Trump, has cracked down on the opposition since winning re-election last year.
In March, the Citizen Revolution Movement was suspended from participating in upcoming local elections. The local elections are scheduled for November 29.
