England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:27:02 UTC
05:27:02 KST

Sri Lanka has chased down a total of 430 in a one day international against England after Harry Brook scored a blistering double-century off just 114 deliveries.
Brook's 202 is now the highest individual ODI score for an Englishman and is also the fastest double century of all time.
Pavan Rathnayake scored 130 in Sri Lanka's runchase before Janith Liyanage sealed the win with a six off the penultimate delivery of the match.
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.
Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.
Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.
Loading Twitter content
The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.
Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.
He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.
The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.
"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.
"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.
"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.
"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."
Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.
Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.
Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.
England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."
Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.
Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."
"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.
"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.
Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."
"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.
Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.
Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.
But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."
Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.
Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.
Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."
"My mother is not well," Acton said.
Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.
"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."
Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.
"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."
— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election

Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election
The student movement aims to end Vucic’s 14 years of rule at Sunday’s vote, as he holds a rival rally across town.
Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia’s student-led opposition movement have gathered in central Belgrade for their final rally ahead of a parliamentary election in which they hope to oust veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic’s party.
The crowds filled the capital on Thursday, as Vucic held a rival rally at a sports hall across town.
Waving “students are winning” flags and blowing whistles, the marchers converged on Slavija Square, the site of some of the movement’s biggest protests.
Sunday’s vote is seen as a chance to end Vucic’s longtime rule.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible,” said Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, who said young people had given her hope of “a normal country“.
The vote follows nearly two years of student-led protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at a newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is seeking to unseat Vucic’s right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has been in power for more than 14 years.
It is running 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, many of them academics or political outsiders, on a platform centred on fighting corruption.
“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of the candidates on the Student List, told the crowd in Belgrade, who chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
The railway disaster, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest demonstrations since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, and demands for transparency grew into calls for an early election.
Over the week, students marched for days across the country, including rural areas that are Vucic’s strongholds.
Vucic, who resigned the presidency in September to run for prime minister, called the snap election last month. He has accused the movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he told supporters on Thursday.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling. But political scientist Dusan Vucicevic told the AFP news agency he expected the students to win more than 40 percent of the vote, far more than any opposition list since the SNS took power in 2012.
The Associated Press news agency reported that polls suggested a close race between the two sides, raising fears of incidents if both claim victory.
Twenty-four Serbian civil society groups warned this week that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking, and a monitoring group cited more than 100 violent incidents during the campaign.
On Wednesday, prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.

'Received with bewilderment, Netanyahu chose to engage in provocation,’ Russia slams Israeli PM saying it ran antisemitic online campaign
Unknown

- i24NEWS

- 'Received with bewilderment,' Russia rejects Netanyahu claim it ran antisemitic online campaign
'Received with bewilderment,' Russia rejects Netanyahu claim it ran antisemitic online campaign
Netanyahu said he remains in occasional contact with Putin and suggested Putin does not want Iran to acquire nuclear weapons
Russia’s Foreign Ministry rejected accusations by PM Benjamin Netanyahu that Moscow was involved in an antisemitic online campaign, calling them entirely unsubstantiated and saying it received them “with bewilderment,” in a statement reported by TASS.
“We have received with bewilderment these entirely unsubstantiated accusations against our country, voiced publicly by the Prime Minister of Israel, a state with which Russia shares a rich, common history,” the ministry said. It argued that attributing an antisemitic campaign to Russia appears “particularly absurd.”
The ministry cited what it called a fact well known to the Israeli side and repeatedly acknowledged by it, that thanks to the policies of Russia’s leadership, manifestations of antisemitism in the country are virtually non-existent.
The ministry also noted the timing. “It is particularly disappointing that such statements were made on October 18, the very day that Russia and Israel marked the 35th anniversary of the full restoration of diplomatic relations,” it said.
Addressing Netanyahu’s references to so-called “bot farms,” the ministry said Russia proposed as early as 2018 that Israel enter a bilateral agreement on cooperation in information security, and received no response. The ministry concluded that Netanyahu had “chosen to engage in media-driven provocations” ahead of Israel’s parliamentary elections, rather than fostering a dialogue between cybersecurity experts.
Netanyahu made the accusations in response to a question from i24NEWS. He accused Russia of aiding Iran and of using artificial intelligence to operate antisemitic bot networks targeting Israel and Jews worldwide.
The prime minister leveled unusually sharp criticism at Moscow while acknowledging that Israel and Russia share some interests despite their differences.
Netanyahu said Israel and Moscow have conflicting interests, but that he remains in occasional contact with Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking with him when necessary. He also suggested Putin does not want Iran to acquire nuclear weapons, arguing that a nuclear-armed Tehran could threaten Russia’s own interests.
Among the potential risks, he said, was the possibility that Iran could recruit Muslim groups within Russia to act on its behalf.
The remarks marked a shift in tone from Netanyahu’s longstanding portrayal of his relationship with Putin as an important asset in Israel’s foreign and security policy. His public accusations highlighted tensions between the two countries.

Why has the Libya-Turkiye maritime deal stirred controversy?
Some countries in the region say it infringes on their rights.

Damascus has repeatedly condemned Israeli incursions as violations of its sovereignty and called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Syrian territory.

Federal politics: Taylor ramps up criticism of energy minister over Snowy 2.0 cost blowout — as it happened

'I'm going around for another lap of the field': Bowen to run at next election
Chris Bowen has declared he's "still got more juice in the tank" and will run again at the next election.
The energy minister has been in parliament since 2004 and told News 24 he had no plans of stepping aside.
"I'm running again," he said.
"I'm still a relatively young man … some will be shocked to hear. I'm 53. I've got more juice in the tank yet. So yep, I'm going around for another lap of the field. Absolutely."
Libs also responsible for Snowy 2.0 blowouts: Bowen
Energy Minister Chris Bowen has rejected criticism the model adopted for Snowy 2.0 was responsible for the billions in cost blowouts.
Back in 2023, the contracts between Snowy Hyrdo and the lead contractor were renegotiated. The original fixed-price contract was scrapped, with both Snowy Hydro and Future Generation sharing the cost of completing the project, which is now expected to total $12 billion.
The Coalition has argued the change of contract is responsible for the cost increases, something Bowen dismissed when asked by News 24.
"If [Shadow Energy Minister] Dan Tehan was fair dinkum, he'd acknowledge that, yes, this is a cost blowout. Yes, feel free to criticise us, but he'd acknowledge that the Liberal Party has some culpability here," he says.
"Obviously we wish the project was being delivered more cheaply. But it's a geological and engineering fact that it is just impossible to deliver it any more cheaply than it's being delivered."
Canavan won't say if he'll make a run for lower house seat
Nationals leader Matt Canavan won't say if he'll make a run for the lower house.
The retirement of Michelle Landry in the central Queensland seat of Capricornia has paved the way for the current senator to seek preselection.
But Canavan says he'll make an announcement on that in due course.
"I'm sad because it is an end of an era and also I sleep better at night if I have great members like Michelle running again," he says.
Landry denies she was pushed to vacate North Qld to make way for Canavan
Nationals MP Michelle Landry has rejected speculation she was pushed to retie so leader Matt Canavan could make a run for her seat.
"Some people out there have told me I need to stand aside and resign so they can come in," she said.
"That's certainly not Matt [Canavan]."
Landry says she's sure many people will "put their hat in the ring" for preselection but stopped short of endorsing Canavan, who was standing next to her.
What is she going to do with her free time when she retires? Landry wants to spend some time in her "neglected" orchid house and reconnect with friends.
Michelle Landry to retire from politics
Nationals MP Michelle Landry has announced she will retire from federal politics at the next election.
Landry called it an "exciting" decision for her, saying it's the right time to step aside after representing the seat of Capricornia since 2013.
The Nationals chief whip will stick around until the federal election.
Taylor coy on speculation Canavan could run in Capricornia
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor was also asked about Michelle Landry, who will announce her retirement at a press conference shortly.
Taylor told reporters he didn't want to pre-empt her press conference (which is due in about 20 minutes) and he'll have more to say afterwards.
Asked about the speculation Matt Canavan could seek preselection in Landry's seat of Capricornia, Taylor declined to engage.
"What I will say is Matt Canavan is an extraordinary colleague. He's fighting every day for our plan and our vision for our great country and it's the right vision in the face of a government that won't accept responsibility for its failures," he says.
Taylor blames Labor for Snowy 2.0 cost blowouts
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he's not to blame for the Snowy 2.0 cost blowout.
The project has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes.
Taylor funded and green-lit the project when he was energy minister. Asked if he should take some responsibility for increased costs he, responded: "No, not under me."
"I'll tell you what happened. Chris Bowen took over and everything that bloke touches turns to custard," he says.
Taylor repeatedly sidestepped when asked if the project should be scrapped.
Wells shuts office temporarily after police charge woman for minor disturbance
A 47-year-old woman has been charged with public nuisance following reports of a minor disturbance at Communications Minister Anika Wells's office.
Queensland Police were called to her office in the Brisbane suburb of Nundah about 10:20am on Wednesday.
In a statement, Wells said the decision was made to close the office temporarily.
"Our staff deserve to feel safe at work and this kind of behaviour is unacceptable. We will reopen as soon as possible and continue to be accessible to the community and contactable while this temporary closure is in place."
The woman will appear in court next month.
Tehan on the defensive over Coalition's Snowy 2.0 estimates
Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan has rejected suggestions the Coalition is partially responsible for the latest Snowy 2.0 cost blowout.
A report released today found the hydropower project could cost 12 times the original price. Snowy 2.0 boss Dennis Barnes this morning told the ABC the project wasn't fully designed, nor were the complexities understood, when it was initiated.
Tehan defended opposition leader Angus Taylor, who funded and green-lit the project when he was energy minister.
"Angus Taylor did the due diligence and he had the right approach," he says.
Instead, he says it is Energy Minister Chris Bowen who should apologise and resign over the blowout.
"If he won't, the prime minister should do the right thing and sack him," he says.
"We still do not know what the final cost of Snowy Hydro 2.0 will be.
"It needs to release all the costings around this project so that everyone can look at it and understand what is occurring here."
Will the government give Snowy 2.0 a cash injection?
Industry Minister Tim Ayres won't say if the government is considering stumping the cash to cover the latest Snowy 2.0 blowout.
The hydropower energy project had an initial budget of $2 billion and was estimated to come online in 2021. It's now expected to cost up to $25 billion and not be delivered until 2029.
Ayres says questions of funding should be directed to Energy Minister Chris Bowen.
"It'll be dealt with in the context of the budget in the normal way," he says.
Questioned if the project was value for money, Ayres says it was important for Australia's energy security.
"We have got a job to do for Australia to modernise our electricity system to provide new electricity generation and transmission at the volumes that's required to deliver a future made in Australia, which will be electricity intensive for heavy industry. That's what this is all about," he says.
Government submits offer to European Space Agency to send Australian of Year into space
The federal government has submitted an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send Australian of the Year Katherine Bennell-Pegg to the International Space Station, federal Science Minister Tim Ayres has confirmed.
If ESA agrees to Australia's offer, Bennell-Pegg will be required to attend training at the European Space Agency's astronaut training centre in Cologne, Germany.
"We have submitted a final bid to our friends in the European Space Agency," Ayres says.
"We are grateful for the opportunity to apply for this important project. It is an important opportunity. It does require careful fiscal management and making sure that we are balancing the fiscal pressures appropriately."
Marles pressed on if government weighing up bolstering MP safety
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles has been out and about today, where he was asked about bolstering safety for MPs.
It comes amid reports the government is weighing up options to address MP concerns following the attack on Helen Haines.
Marles says the government will act in accordance to advice provided by security agencies.
He has pointed to the extra funding allocated in the May budget. The AFP received a little over half a billion dollars in the 2024-25 financial year to protect politicians and sensitive facilities.
But he has declined to go into the specifics of what measures have been adopted.
"What we do is get the advice from the agencies about what the threat environment is, about what can make a difference to that in terms of providing security measures for members of parliament, and then we act accordingly," he says.
Batteries lower evening peak prices
Continued from previous post
Violette Mouchaileh, AEMO's executive general manager of policy and executive affairs, said it was a milestone.
"Batteries continue to shift record amounts of renewable energy into the higher-demand evening period, when households and businesses typically need more power," Mouchaileh said.
"Increased battery charging and discharging contributed to significantly lower evening peak prices, with batteries setting prices in almost half of dispatch intervals, up from 18 per cent a year ago."
AEMO said the east gas market was relatively subdued during the third quarter, with prices averaging $10.77 a gigajoule, up slightly from the same time last year.
Demand was marginally lower, as declining demand from gas-fired generators was offset by an increase in exports from Queensland producers.
On the other side of the Nullarbor, demand went up by 1.6 per cent amid lower temperatures and greater heating needs.
Gas-fired plants surged 27 per cent year-on-year to meet those needs on the back of lower wind output and coal plant outages.
Prices, meanwhile, soared to uncomfortable levels in the west, where they were 30 per cent higher at an average of $117 a megawatt hour, a new record.
Once other system costs were taken into account, they averaged a painful $175 a megawatt-hour.
Power prices continue to drop as batteries flex their muscles
The latest troubles to hit Snowy 2.0 come amid profound changes in the national grid.
In its latest snapshot of the national electricity system, the Australian Energy Market Operator noted that demand for power was surging even while wholesale spot prices were easing.
So-called underlying demand, which includes the consumption households meet themselves through rooftop solar, jumped 1.3 per cent to an average of more than 25,000 megawatts in the three months to September 30 compared with the previous corresponding period.
According to AEMO, Victoria accounted for most of the growth, which was driven by the switch to electrification, high industrial demand, and the rise of power-hungry data centres.
As well as this, the market operator noted renewable energy was meeting an ever-greater share of the market.
Generation from renewable sources increased from 41.8 per cent to 44.3 per cent of demand during the quarter, which included winter months typically associated with relatively low output from wind farms and solar panels.
Leading the way was the unstoppable growth of rooftop solar, which surged 13 per cent to an average of 3,200 megawatts, followed by rises in grid-scale solar and hydropower output.
And, in a major shift, AEMO noted that batteries for the first time eclipsed the contribution of gas-fired power plants during peak hours in the evening.
Grid-scale batteries, the agency said, met 8 per cent of total generation during those hours compared with 5 per cent of gas plants as the amount of storage installed tripled over the course of the year.
Australia applies sanctions targeting North Korea's fraudulent IT worker network
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has confirmed sanctions have been slapped on two individuals and entities involved in financing North Korea's unlawful weapons program.
Wong says the entities and individuals facilitate North Korea's use of fraudulent IT workers to raise revenue for the regime's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
"These workers obtain remote employment while posing as nationals of other countries, constituting a violation of UN Security Council resolutions that prohibit North Korea's export of labour," the statement says.
The government says the sanctions reinforce Australia's efforts to disrupt North Korea's revenue-generating networks and increase pressure on the regime to comply with international obligations.
"We are taking this action in coordination with international partners, including the European Union," Wong said.
"We call on North Korea to comply fully with UN Security Council resolutions and to take concrete steps towards complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearisation."
Chalmers declares optimism about business investment despite domestic gloom
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says business investment is on track to grow nearly twice as fast as was forecast in May.

The Google Home Speaker Has Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:05:51 UTC
05:05:51 KST

If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess 3 terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini–powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.
While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the past 10 days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.
Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices and that it has rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”
Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the past week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the past week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.
If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for which device could be at fault.
How to Check Your Device Usage
You have a couple of options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.
There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router, and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:
- Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in.
- Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour).
- You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab.
- You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone.
Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:
- Open the Deco or Tether app.
- Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage.
- What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information.
Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter, you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface. (It usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app.) If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.
But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the past seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or over the past three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home.
But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.
Why Should You Check?
It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the 2 terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a 3-terabyte bug slowing your whole network.

Epstein, Iran and ‘drain the swamp’: Have Republicans shifted before vote?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:05:22 UTC
05:05:22 KST

Epstein, Iran and ‘drain the swamp’: Have Republicans shifted before vote?
Some of the core issues that drove Trump’s US supporters and the MAGA movement are no longer Republican talking points.
United States President Donald Trump has long touted himself as a political outsider, someone who would expose the elites’ abuse of power and shift government focus from far-off conflicts to problems at home. Phrases like “drain the swamp” and “America first” have proved to be powerful rallying cries, sparking a whole cadre of “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) Republicans.
Halfway through his final term as president, though, Trump has backpedalled on many of those ideas, cosying up to the ultra-wealthy, sidelining investigations into convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, and launching an ongoing war with Iran.
That about-face appears to be having a real impact on Republicans running in the US midterm elections in November, said Rina Shah, a geopolitical adviser and strategist and a former senior GOP congressional aide.
“In competitive races, some are quietly distancing,” Shah said, adding that they are “talking about gas prices, local issues, or [saying] ‘I’m focused on my district’ – because the Iran war and the Epstein drip are already showing up in attack ads and soft polling.”
Here’s what you need to know about whether the Republican Party has softened its stance on these issues.
Which Republicans have broken with Trump over the Epstein files?
During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump said he would declassify troves of files kept by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) about Epstein and his global network of contacts. Trump’s future cabinet members, too, were enthusiastic about this, with Kash Patel, now head of the FBI, saying it was time to “put on your big boy pants and let us know who the pedophiles are”.
Yet a few months after taking office, Trump began dragging his feet, sparking a backlash from influential MAGA figures. Trump began calling the entire issue a “hoax” and saying Republicans were being duped by Democrats into calling for an investigation into Epstein’s network.
Congress did eventually force the release of the files, with help from a handful of Republicans who broke with Trump. The Trump administration has released batches of the heavily redacted files, but has continued to withhold some. Meanwhile, all the Republican lawmakers who voted to mandate releases have paid a price for their insubordination, with three even losing their offices.
US Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene left her Georgia seat in January 2026, after publicly clashing with Trump over Epstein. Nancy Mace, a Republican from South Carolina, lost her bid to become the party’s candidate in her home state after Trump refused to endorse her. Colorado’s Lauren Boebert barely won the primary in her own contest after angering Trump by supporting calls for transparency from Thomas Massie, another Republican bent on exposing what the files held. Massie, of Kentucky, also drew Trump’s ire, which likely cost him the primary.
No more foreign wars
Trump had long said he would be reducing foreign military involvement, breaking with the interventionist tendencies of other recent Republican presidents. Now he and his party face tough questions about the US-Israel war on Iran, which influential figures in the MAGA movement like political commentator Tucker Carlson have called a mistake, saying, “This is Israel’s war. This is not the United States’ war.”
Amongst disgruntled MAGA supporters, a narrative has emerged of Trump using the war to also distract from the Epstein issue. Massie, the former congressman, summed up the sentiment by saying, “Bombing a country on the other side of the globe won’t make the Epstein files go away.”
Trump has tried to downplay the war’s impact, but voters, even in the Republican Party, think he broke his own promise, driving the overall approval rating for the ratings-obsessed president down to record lows. “Seven months into an open-ended campaign with shifting goals,” said Shah, “that promise looks different to a lot of his voters.”
Few Republicans, however, have responded to that public sentiment with their votes in Congress, where Democrats have tried repeatedly to curtail Trump’s war on Iran by passing resolutions pointing out he failed to get the body’s approval.
In September, just seven Republican House members joined Democrats to pass an anti-war bill. In the Senate, similar efforts have been supported by just a handful of Republicans. Trump called the Republican lawmakers supporting the anti-war bills “unpatriotic,” and said, “They should be ashamed of themselves.”
As with the Epstein files, Trump took action against rebellious Republicans over the Iran war, for instance backing a rival of Senator Bill Cassidy, who voted in favour of the anti-war bill, in a primary in Louisiana that the Republican senator ended up losing.
What happened to Trump’s promise to ‘drain the swamp’?
One of Trump’s most appealing promises had been to purge the government of a “deep state” establishment he says is running the country without being accountable to the public on social issues, and fiscal and foreign policy.
In a way, Trump did keep that promise. An entire federal government division – the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) – forced tens of thousands of federal workers out of their jobs and dismantled institutions like the US Agency for International Development (USAID). The military threw out notions of racial, gender, and economic diversity. Everything from universities to the Smithsonian Institution was subjected to a campaign against an unqualified, diversity-obsessed elitist class.
But lobbying groups, including some supporting foreign governments, have been given a free hand, and ethics rules and watchdogs who would tackle political corruption have been weakened, said Shah, the Republican strategist.
At his presidential inauguration, Trump literally surrounded himself with the wealthiest people in the world, some of whom have gone on to play some part in his administration.

Race and gender are linked to how Americans protest and campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:00:24 UTC
05:00:24 KST

When Americans feel angry about the state of the country, their gender and racial identities appear to shape whether they channel that emotion into formal campaigns or street protests. A recent study reveals that angry Black women and white women participate across a wider variety of political avenues than their male counterparts. The research was published in Public Opinion Quarterly.
Political scientists study emotion to understand what drives people to become politically active. Anger often acts as a catalyst. It encourages individuals to take action against perceived threats by volunteering for campaigns, donating money, or attending demonstrations. Emotion bridges the gap between holding an opinion and actually doing something about it.
However, people only turn to formal electoral politics if they believe the system will respond to their voices. Political scientists refer to this belief as political efficacy. Historical barriers, ongoing discrimination, and unequal access to resources mean that different demographic groups experience distinct levels of political efficacy. As a result, groups view the available pathways for political change in fundamentally different ways.
Past research established a gap between how white and Black Americans express political anger. Those earlier studies found that white Americans generally channel their anger into electoral participation, such as campaigning. In contrast, Black Americans often turn toward non-electoral participation, like protesting, largely because of historical exclusion and lower trust in the formal political system.
Sara Morell, a political scientist at The College of New Jersey, and Marzia Oceno, a political scientist at Florida International University, suspected this racial divide missed a piece of the puzzle. They wanted to see how gender overlaps with race to shape political behavior.
Feminist movements and civil rights movements have distinct histories of using protests, boycotts, and campaigns to push for change. Because Black women and white women possess different historical relationships with the political establishment than men, the researchers expected to find distinct patterns in how these groups act when provoked by political events.
To test these expectations, the researchers analyzed data from a large survey conducted around the 2020 presidential election. The sample included 6,661 adults who identified as white or Black and male or female. The survey asked respondents how angry, outraged, or irritated they felt about how things were going in the country. The researchers controlled for factors like age, education, and household income.
The 2020 survey then measured electoral participation. Respondents reported whether they tried to persuade others to vote a certain way, attended online or in-person rallies, or wore political buttons. They also noted if they had worked for a campaign or donated money to a political group. Finally, the survey tracked self-reported voter turnout for the November election.
The researchers found distinct differences in how anger predicted campaign involvement across the four groups. As expected, white men who reported high levels of anger were much more likely to engage in formal electoral activities. They focused on persuading voters, attending online rallies, and donating money. Black men largely did not show increased electoral participation when angry, and were actually less likely to report working for a campaign.
The patterns looked entirely different for women. Both white women and Black women showed higher levels of electoral participation when they felt angry. This suggests that women utilize a broad set of formal political tools when they feel threatened or upset by national conditions.
Black women, in particular, reported the highest average levels of anger in 2020. This intense emotion translated directly into the largest measured increase in campaign engagement among all four groups. Angry Black women were highly mobilized to persuade others, wear political buttons, and work for campaigns. The results point to Black women’s central role as active organizers in modern electoral politics.
For both white men and white women, anger did not predict whether they actually cast a ballot. The researchers suggest this is because voting is a baseline expectation for many politically active people. Anger instead motivates individuals to take on political activities that require more time and effort than the standard act of voting, such as volunteering or donating.
Next, the researchers analyzed a separate large panel survey to measure non-electoral participation. This study tracked 3,529 adults across two periods. The first wave occurred immediately after the 2020 election, and the second wave occurred after the 2022 midterm elections.
This second survey focused on activities outside of formal campaigns. Respondents reported whether they had attended a protest or a political rally. They also indicated if they had signed an online petition, posted a political message online, or boycotted a product for political reasons over the previous year.
Once again, white men followed expected historical patterns. Their anger did not lead to higher rates of non-electoral participation in either 2020 or 2022, aside from a slight increase in boycotting during the 2022 wave. White men typically rely on the formal electoral system, rather than outside pressure, to express their grievances.
Black men showed a delayed response in their non-electoral participation. In 2020, their anger was not statistically significant in predicting protest or petition activity. By 2022, however, angry Black men were substantially more likely to engage in non-electoral activities, primarily by signing petitions and posting political messages online.
Women again showed much broader avenues of engagement. White women were highly likely to translate their anger into non-electoral action during both 2020 and 2022. They frequently signed petitions and boycotted products. During the 2022 wave, which followed the Supreme Court decision overturning federal abortion protections, white women reported the highest levels of anger among all groups and maintained their high rate of non-electoral activity.
For Black women, anger was consistently linked to one specific form of non-electoral action. In both 2020 and 2022, angry Black women were uniquely motivated to attend protests. They were the only group to show a persistent link between anger and physical protesting across both survey waves. This finding aligns with the historical centrality of Black women in civil rights and social justice demonstrations.
The researchers note a few limitations to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The surveys asked respondents about their general anger toward the state of the country, rather than asking them to identify the specific issues making them angry. Because the data lacks this specificity, it is impossible to know exactly which policies or events drove different demographic groups to the streets or the campaign trail.
The lack of issue specificity makes it difficult to explain some unexpected results, such as why Black men’s anger did not lead to higher protest attendance in 2020. That year featured massive nationwide protests against police brutality, an issue with profound relevance to Black men. The researchers suspect that for some groups, anger might need to combine with other psychological factors to trigger physical action. A strong sense of community fate or intense personal interest might be necessary to push an angry individual to join a physical protest.
Future research should investigate whether specific sources of anger change how people choose to participate. The researchers also recommend expanding this intersectional approach to include Hispanic and Asian American populations. Understanding how overlapping identities influence political emotion helps reveal the diverse ways Americans fight for their political interests.
The study, “The Intersectional Anger Gap: How Race and Gender Condition the Impact of Anger on Participation,” was authored by Sara Morell and Marzia Oceno.

Autex Acoustics panels “place sound at the heart” of Manchester’s Bar Shrimp
Acoustic brand Autex Acoustics has equipped Manchester’s Bar Shrimp with sound-enhancing acoustic panels, creating an “immersive and energetic space” dedicated to music listening.
Bar Shrimp is a seafood-serving music destination designed to provide a high-quality music experience within a relaxed environment.
The bar’s interior combines luxury acoustic panels, layered textures, rich red tones, and atmospheric lighting to create an intimate space that can switch from a relaxed dining setting to a vibrant late-night venue.
The bar’s walls were furnished with Autex Acoustics’ Mirage finish, a lightweight acoustic panel made from PET, customised using a precision laser etching technique to create a distinctive textured aesthetic.
The finish softens reverberation from the bar’s concrete floors, while its textured, soft appearance adds to the venue’s relaxed visual identity.
According to Autex Acoustics, Mirage also controls background chatter and balances music played throughout the space, which, according to Bar Shimp’s co-founder Richard Cossins, was one of the key parts of the bar’s design.
“Our mission at Bar Shrimp is to place sound at the heart of the venue, treating it as an integral part of the experience,” said Cossins. “The goal is to deliver an immersive sonic identity, detailed and balanced within the space.”
Above the bar, an Autex Acoustics’ Frontier Axis system was also added for its striking grid-like appearance and additional sound-absorbing qualities.
Autex Acoustics products are made in the UK from at least 80 per cent recycled content.
According to Cossins, the project was built on a shared understanding of how sound and acoustics can shape people’s experience of a venue, whilst also aligning on sustainability values.
“In hospitality, sound panelling is often an afterthought,” said director at Autex Acoustics UK and EU, Daniel Senior.
“But what we’ve learned with the team at Bar Shrimp is that acoustics can actually elevate the design and be an integral part of it.”
Bar Shrimp was named “Manchester’s new best thing ever” by Guardian food critic Grace Dent, and it is the third collaboration between Cossins and Autex Acoustics.
Autex Acoustics crafts acoustic products that combine decades of expertise with innovative solutions that aim to enhance both the visual and acoustic experience of interior spaces.
The brand has recently launched Raft, the latest addition to the Frontier range, which combines sculptural acoustic design with “significantly reduced embodied carbon and material use”.
To learn more about Autex Acoustics, visit its website.

EXPLAINER – Brazil faces political crossroads as Lula, Bolsonaro head to runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:58:38 UTC
04:58:38 KST

As Brazil heads to Sunday's runoff to elect its next leader, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, are offering contrasting visions for the country's future, with economic policy, social welfare, public security and corruption among the main issues dividing voters.
Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, received 47.03% of valid votes in the Oct. 4 first round, compared with 45.16% for Lula.
Neither candidate secured an outright majority, setting up a decisive contest for the leadership of Latin America's largest economy.
The final weeks of the campaign have featured rival rallies, televised debates and accusations over corruption and foreign interference.
Lula has emphasized workers' rights and social programs, while Flavio has focused on public security, fiscal restraint and closer ties with the United States.
How does Brazil's runoff work?
Brazil elects its President through a two-round system. A candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes in the first round to win outright, excluding blank and null ballots.
Since neither candidate crossed that threshold on Oct. 4, Lula and Flavio advanced to the runoff.
The winner will serve a four-year presidential term beginning in January 2027.
Brazil, where voting is compulsory for literate citizens aged 18 to 70, uses electronic voting machines, allowing results to be counted rapidly after polls close.
The presidential contest is not the only race taking place on Oct. 25. Runoffs for governor will also be held in six states and the Federal District, covering seven federative units.
Regional contests will determine who governs Acre, Amazonas, Espirito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Norte, Tocantins and the Federal District.
Their results could influence relations between the next president and state governments, which play an important role in areas such as public security, health and education.
Who are the candidates?
Lula, a veteran leader of the left-wing Workers' Party, returned to the presidency in January 2023 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
He previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, when economic growth and social programs helped establish his political legacy.
His current campaign emphasizes income distribution, workers' rights, public investment and protection for lower-income households. Lula argues that government spending and social programs can support economic growth while reducing inequality.
Flavio Bolsonaro is a senator from the Liberal Party and the political heir to his father's conservative movement.
His campaign seeks to turn dissatisfaction with the current government into support for changes to economic management, stricter law enforcement and closer cooperation with Washington.
His candidacy also tests whether the political movement built around Jair Bolsonaro can retain its national influence under a new leader.
Flavio's campaign draws on his father's conservative base while presenting him as an alternative to Lula's economic and social policies.
Allegations of foreign interference
Allegations of foreign influence have emerged in Brazil's presidential campaign, focusing on US-linked political accounts and social media platforms.
Brazilian media reported that accounts on US social media platform X, some associated with President Donald Trump's political movement, published paid posts promoting Flavio Bolsonaro and prediction market Polymarket.
Brazilian electoral law prohibits third parties from paying to promote candidates and bars donations from foreign entities. Flavio's campaign said it had no knowledge of the advertisements, according to media reports.
Lula's campaign has also accused Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, of influencing the election through political advertising and the distribution of campaign content. Meta denied political bias, attributing reported disruptions to technical problems.
The allegations have raised questions about foreign-linked political advertising and the role of technology companies in elections, although no direct interference by a foreign government has been established.
Social programs and public security
Among the major issues of the election, social welfare has been central to Lula's platform.
Programs such as Bolsa Familia provide cash transfers to low-income households, while Minha Casa, Minha Vida supports access to housing. Flavio Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has emphasized fiscal discipline and more efficient public spending.
Public security is another major issue, with organized crime, armed groups and violent offenses remaining prominent concerns across Brazil.
The candidates have proposed different approaches to combating criminal organizations and improving law enforcement.
Flavio has promised tougher measures against organized crime, vowing to classify major gangs and militias as narcoterrorist groups. He has also advocated expanding prison capacity and increasing the use of surveillance cameras and facial-recognition technology.
Lula, meanwhile, has called for greater federal coordination of security policy with states and municipalities.
He has proposed establishing a Ministry of Public Security to strengthen cooperation and support local law enforcement efforts.
While Flavio emphasizes tougher punishment and expanded policing powers, Lula favors a more coordinated approach involving different levels of government.
Why has corruption become central to the race?
Corruption allegations have featured prominently in the campaign, drawing relatives of both candidates into the dispute.
Lula's past corruption convictions were annulled by Brazil's Supreme Court in 2021 on procedural grounds. He has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.
Flavio has also faced scrutiny over alleged financial misconduct and connections to businessman Daniel Vorcaro, associated with the collapsed Banco Master.
Investigators have examined an investment he reportedly sought from Vorcaro to finance a film about Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio denies wrongdoing.
Lula's son Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, known as Lulinha, has also faced investigations involving alleged influence peddling and pension-related fraud. He also denies wrongdoing.
During an Oct. 18 televised debate, Lula challenged Flavio to authorize the release of their financial records.
On Oct. 20, Lula's campaign submitted an authorization to the Superior Electoral Court covering eight years of his bank, tax and telephone records, as well as those of his wife and five children.
Lula made the disclosure conditional on Flavio releasing comparable records for himself and his relatives. Flavio had not agreed to the proposal at the time of the filing.
What lies ahead?
Polls published over the past week show a close race, though Flavio has retained his narrow lead.
RealTime Big Data and PoderData put him at 52% of valid votes against Lula's 48%, while AtlasIntel/Bloomberg showed 51.1% to 48.9% and BTG/Nexus 50.3% to 49.7%.
The surveys had margins of error ranging from one to two percentage points, underscoring the importance of turnout in the final days.
The next president will face pressure to address household debt, public security and demands for better public services while managing public finances.
Lula is asking voters to endorse his record on social programs, wages and public investment, while Flavio promises tougher security policies and a different approach to public spending and foreign relations.
The election also comes amid a broader rightward shift across Latin America, following victories by conservative and center-right candidates in Chile, Colombia, Peru and Bolivia, alongside governments in Argentina and Ecuador.
As Latin America's largest country and a massive diplomatic player, Brazil could significantly influence the region's political direction.
Flavio has advocated closer alignment with US President Donald Trump, while Lula has emphasized maintaining independent relations with Washington, Beijing and other global powers.

The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:56:32 UTC
04:56:32 KST

I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”
Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”
That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.
They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?
Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”
Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …
Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.
There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”
Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.
How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees?
Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.
Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.
Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”
Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”
You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?
Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.
Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?
Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.
One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?
When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.
I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.
Berger: The economic value piece is really important, because women have long suffered from being stuck at home as domestic laborers, because we weren't seen as economically valuable in the marketplace, right? So the idea behind Aged Intelligence Society is that if anyone needs to optimize their time, it's women.
In some ways, AI is the new washing machine or the new laundry or whatever it is. It's giving women many, many hours of the day back by offering them automation.
The reason we narrowed the aperture to people 40-plus is that we feel like the product-market fit for women who are over 40 is so spot on. One, because we have very discerning taste after many decades of honing it. We know how to ask really sharp questions. We have very strong bullshit meters, so we're not going to take just the first answer. We're going to keep probing and pushing.
And so we feel like in some ways this tool was built for people who have a certain level of intelligence and accrued experience. It's not really built for young people. It's not built for people who have not already gone through the failure and the friction of life and learned for themselves what makes for a good question.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

What Is Nobody Wants This’ Sasha-Morgan Endgame?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:52:00 UTC
04:52:00 KST

This article discusses the full third season of Nobody Wants This.
Joanne and Noah are going to make it. Two seasons of so many highs and lows, will-theys and won’t-theys, makeups and breakups had gotten a bit repetitive. So it comes as a relief that Season 3 of the Netflix romantic comedy Nobody Wants This all but guarantees us Kristen Bell’s formerly secular sex podcaster and Adam Brody’s hot rabbi will live happily ever after. With Joanne taking conversion classes, the couple checks off commitment milestones in quick succession: cohabitation, then engagement, and, in the finale, an unplanned exchange of wedding vows after the bride emerges, officially Jewish, from an ocean mikvah. It’s a lovely, duly earned culmination of their interfaith courtship. But it raises the question of where the show can go from here.
The season’s other main storyline—and sole substantive source of conflict—suggests that creator Erin Foster and her co-showrunners, Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan, are staking its future on the relationship between Joanne’s erratic, underachieving sister, Morgan (Justine Lupe), and Noah’s eccentric, underachieving brother, Sasha (Timothy Simons). Morgan is fresh off her latest ill-advised romance, an ethically dubious relationship with her ex-therapist (Arian Moayed) that imploded at their engagement party. Sasha is separating from his wife, Jackie Tohn’s Esther. (This is her choice, probably because writers remain sensitive following complaints about the portrayal of Jewish women in the first season and wanted to avoid making hot, blonde Morgan the cause of the split.) And so the best buddies, who’ve been flirting since Season 1, are finally single at the same time. But is it actually a good idea for the show to bring them together, as it briefly does in the second half of this season? I’m of two minds about that.
What the Morgan-Sasha romance has going for it is the unlikely, off-kilter yet undeniable chemistry between Lupe and Simons, which has somehow surpassed even the electric connection of Bell and Brody’s soulmates. (Let’s take a second to appreciate the versatility of Simons, whose other great performance was as Veep’s toxic West Wing staffer Jonah, a character who would never be attractive to anyone.) Morgan is a brash, blunt, benignly self-absorbed icon in her own mind who also, in her darker moments, fears she’ll never get her life together. Awkward, self-deprecating Sasha is genuinely dazzled by her. For a guy who sacrificed his youth to marriage and fatherhood, she represents all the fun he never got to have. And because they’ve never seemed like viable partners for each other, they have a better rapport than either could manage on a date with someone who’s more their type. “Act the way you act with me,” Morgan advises Sasha as he apprehensively delves into the apps. “You should pretend that you’re talking to me every time you talk to anyone, because I bring out the most charming side of you.” She’s conceited, as usual, but she also happens to be right.
The most refreshing aspect of their friendship is their mutual honesty. So it was clever of Foster, Konner, and Kaplan to make that the driver of their storyline this season. When Sasha fills in for Joanne on the sisters’ podcast, his banter with Morgan is, of course, gold. He explains how he has used the Let Them theory to make peace with professional setbacks—then she calls B.S., and goes on to improvise her own Make Them theory, a pure expression of her aggressive approach to getting what she wants. The episode goes viral. Morgan starts to see a future for herself as a self-help author. Sasha is there to encourage her to dig deeper when her early attempts at writing fall flat. And she can be counted on to inform him that his “lucky shirt” is not exactly the chick magnet he imagines it to be. Yet they also frequently build each other up.
Each faces more disappointment as the season goes on. Morgan blows a meeting with a publisher (Poorna Jagannathan, in her third of four high-profile TV role this year. Hey, I’m not mad about it). Sasha tries to force a connection with a woman who gets confused when he mentions the social contract. So they’re both in a tender place when Morgan impulsively invites him to accompany her to New York, where she’s been booked to talk Make Them with Andy Cohen on Watch What Happens Live. The season’s seventh episode is almost entirely devoted to the trip. That it is such a pleasure to, er, watch what happens between them is a testament to the power of great characters to reinvigorate old genre tropes. From the shopping montage where Sasha buys Morgan a dress, Pretty Woman style, to her earnest speech as they walk the High Line, to the false starts that end with them in bed, familiar rom-com beats feel exciting because of the affection we have for these two. Morgan’s epiphany that, “When I was younger, I always fell for people I wanted to be seen with. And now I think I just wanna be with someone who sees me,” could be a Carrie Bradshaw koan. It hits, though, because it’s so true to her character arc.
But what’s the endgame for Sasha and Morgan? Presumably in order to save some material for Season 4, Nobody Wants This pulls them apart just hours after their hookup. Sasha awakens to a note that says Morgan has hopped on an earlier flight home. There, she crashes out in bed, resigned to the impossibility of a long-term relationship with her future brother-in-law. When it dawns on Joanne that her sister is serious about Sasha, she gives Morgan her blessing. Yet by the time Morgan tracks him down and delivers another big monologue (“I don’t wanna half-ass you”), he’s decided he can’t endure her avoidance so soon after Esther left him. Then he sleeps with Esther, who’s dating a rich guy a full generation her senior (Steven Weber), laying the groundwork for an absolutely disastrous encounter between Joanne’s and Noah’s families at the mikvah.
No end to the season could have been more apt than Joanne and Noah pledging their eternal love while, in a gorgeous beachfront rental just steps away, their parents and siblings tear each other apart. And, again, the scenes Sasha and Morgan share have become some of the most exhilarating of the show. But Nobody Wants This has always been better with isolated situations and screwball dialogue than it is with big-picture plot. With that in mind, I worry it’s written itself into another corner with this relationship. A Season 4 love triangle, with Sasha forced to choose between Esther and Morgan, could only lead back to the same old referendum on Jewish women. If the two Jewish brothers did both end up with the two gentile sisters, that would make its own, somewhat discouraging statement on the latter issue.
Even if you can get past those implications, it’s hard to imagine Morgan and Sasha’s long-term romance arc going anywhere worthwhile, narratively speaking. We’ve already seen the culture clash, the parental pushback, the conversion drama. Are we going to do the same thing all over again, with the same abrasive mother-in-law, brief breakups, and tearful reunions—except with lower stakes because Sasha isn’t a rabbi? I’m not saying nobody wants this. I just need to be convinced.

Households asked to prepare for three days of disruption
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:51:37 BST
04:51:37 KST

Households across Britain are being asked to keep enough supplies to manage three days of disruption to power, water, phones and the internet, under a campaign launched today that forms the first stage of a three-year programme, according to the government.
The Be Ready campaign is run by the Cabinet Office and published alongside a campaign website and a downloadable checklist. More than five hundred organisations across the United Kingdom have signed up to share the materials.
Dan Jarvis, the Security Minister, said: “Those who can follow this advice should follow this advice.” He said the campaign would bring Britain into line with European counterparts where such advice is part of everyday life, and added: “This is just the sort of community-focused campaign the UK needs to improve our resilience as a nation.”
The three-day figure matches the guidance used in France, Ireland and the Netherlands.
The checklist covers nine categories, and on water it asks for bottled water for three days at three litres per person per day for drinking, noting more would be needed for cooking and washing. On food it asks for non-perishable items with a long shelf life that need no refrigeration or cooking, such as tinned meat, fish or vegetables, dried fruit and nuts, and advises buying food people would usually eat.
Other categories cover hygiene products, a torch with spare batteries, blankets, sleeping bags and warm clothing, a battery or wind-up FM radio and a charged power bank, cash in a mix of coins and notes alongside cards, copies of identity documents, important phone numbers including regular medication and doses, a first aid kit, essential medication, baby formula and nappies, and pet food.
On formula the checklist specifies ready-made or ready-to-feed products, because households may not be able to boil water safely to make up powdered formula.
The guidance tells people to check cupboards first, build the kit gradually during regular shopping trips to spread the cost, set a reminder every six months to check expiry dates, and talk to neighbours about what support they could share during an outage. It also suggests donating spare items to others who might not have the means to prepare, or printing documents for them.
Laura Scott, British Red Cross Director for UK Resilience, said: “We can’t control when emergencies happen, but we can all take some simple steps to be prepared.” She said local people know their communities best and want to play a part when a crisis happens, and that clear and trusted advice, especially for those more at risk, could reduce the impact of crises and save lives.
The campaign also directs people to the Priority Services Register, a free scheme that helps utility companies identify customers who may need extra support during an outage, and to Met Office weather warnings. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own versions of the advice. Social media and radio advertising over the coming weeks and months will target families with young children and older people.
The campaign arrives alongside a substantial body of government work on resilience, and ministers confirmed this month that a Defence Readiness Bill will be brought forward before the end of this Parliament to give government the powers it needs to respond during escalation towards war, and that government messaging on defence and security will continue to build ahead of Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW, a major British home defence exercise, and NATO’s Crisis Management Exercise in spring 2027.
