German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Thursday that Montenegro is on track to join the European Union soon.
Speaking after a Berlin Process summit hosted by Montenegro, Merz stressed that the Western Balkans’ route into the EU must become irreversible. He described enlargement as a geopolitical imperative so the region does not turn into an arena where major powers compete for influence.
“Montenegro is on the best path to join the EU soon. Others must and will follow,” Merz said. He linked the urgency to Russia’s war against Ukraine, noting that only a shared perspective inside the European single market and the institutions of the EU can deliver lasting stability.
Regarding open bilateral issues between EU member Croatia and candidate country Montenegro that still affect two remaining negotiating chapters, Merz said the matters had been discussed at the EU summit in Brussels the previous Thursday. He added that he had also spoken directly with Croatia’s prime minister about the issues.
“I know that there is a very intensive and constructive discussion between Montenegro and Croatia on these two remaining topics,” Merz said. “Montenegro has already taken very concrete decisions in this regard, paving the way forward. I am very confident that the final reservations held by Croatia can be resolved. I do not consider them significant enough to stand in the way of Montenegro’s membership in the EU,” he said adding that this assessment was shared by both prime ministers.

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation
Another five children and young people have been successfully brought back from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: Under occupation, the children were forced to accept Russian passports and sing the Russian national anthem at school, Bring Kids Back UA reported.
When the full-scale invasion began, brothers Ihor, Andrii and Dmytro (names changed) and their mother were living in their hometown, which was soon occupied by Russian forces. From then on the family lived under constant pressure and restrictions from the occupation authorities.
Andrii attended a kindergarten under occupation, while Dmytro was in the sixth grade at a local school. Their mother said the children were forced to sing the Russian national anthem there, and the curriculum contained Russian propaganda.
The family also faced forced "passportisation", with the occupation authorities demanding that the parents obtain Russian documents.
Experts from the Ukrainian Child Rights Network, working with The Humanity Funds, helped get the family out safely.
The boys and their mother are now in Ukrainian-controlled territory. They will be helped through the adaptation and reintegration processes and will return to the Ukrainian education system.
Two young people, Albina and Viacheslav, were brought back with the assistance of a team from Helping to Leave.
Albina lived in the temporarily occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast and decided to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory on her own. She planned her route herself and got as far as the Mokrany-Domanove checkpoint between Belarus and Ukraine, but she could not cross the border because she did not have a Ukrainian passport.
It was then that she contacted Helping to Leave. Volunteers advised her on the documents she needed and helped coordinate her onward route.
In Minsk, Albina obtained a certificate enabling her to return to Ukraine and was able to continue her journey. She is now with relatives in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Viacheslav found out about Helping to Leave from a friend whom the team had previously helped leave the occupation. After he reached out, volunteers helped him plan his route and supported him during his departure.
On the way, Viacheslav also helped a friend by taking two of her cats with him. Upon arrival in Ukraine, Viacheslav was met by a team from Helping to Leave who helped him find temporary accommodation.
He is currently obtaining new documents and planning his future in Ukraine. The cats have been reunited with their owner too.
Background: Previously, we reported on how 23 children and teenagers who had endured constant pressure, threats and fear were brought back from occupation to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Yemen’s government forces carried out 780 strikes against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, neutralizing approximately 512 fighters and destroying or damaging more than 330 military vehicles, a military spokesman said Thursday, Anadolu reports.
Majed Abdullah al-Nuzayli, spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a statement that the operations were conducted as part of the ongoing “Operation Dawn of Yemen.”

READ: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since August as fighting escalates: UNHCR
The spokesman vowed to continue targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with international humanitarian law.

The announcement comes amid intensified fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Houthis across several Yemeni provinces.
Earlier Thursday, Yemeni state television reported airstrikes targeting Houthi missile launchers, radar systems, military communications equipment and weapons depots in Taiz.

Libya central bank raided hours after governor's exit
Libya's central bank on Thursday said unidentified individuals raided its headquarters in Tripoli, hours after parliament said it had accepted a request from its governor to resign.
The incident comes more than two months after bank governor Naji Issa first announced his resignation, which the parliament rejected at the time.
Beset by instability since the 2011 overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya is divided between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Earlier this month, a new speaker took the helm of parliament, which sits in the eastern city of Benghazi under Haftar control.
The legislature said on Thursday it had belatedly accepted Issa's resignation "in principle" and appointed central bank board member Fauzi Abokhzam to be interim governor pending a final decision.
The central bank said the raid on its headquarters took place while Issa was away, adding that it held responsible for the incident "all parties that participated in this act".
It singled out "the defence ministry, which is tasked with protecting the bank's headquarters", without providing further details on its involvement.
The government in Tripoli did not issue a comment on the reported raid.
Issa's 2024 appointment by parliament as central bank chief had followed a political standoff that saw a halt in oil production amid a deep financial crisis.
It remains unclear why he had presented his resignation in August of this year.

Powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes China's Tibet region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck southwestern China's Tibet region late Thursday, the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) reported, with the tremor recorded at 10:33 p.m. local time (2:33 p.m. GMT).
Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicenter showing cracks, the state broadcaster said. The quake is the strongest to hit China since January 2024.
The epicenter was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 10 km (6.2 miles). The average elevation within 5 km of the epicenter is about 4,864 meters (15,960 feet), CENC data showed.
Videos released by local officially run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street. One resident reported being awakened by the strong quake and heard the house squeaking in the tremor.
The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicenter was around 400 km from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa.
Local fire and rescue teams have mobilized and are heading to the affected region, state media said.
A string of smaller tremors of around magnitude 3 and 4 have been recorded in surrounding regions following the magnitude 7 quake, CENC data showed.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck Yushu in neighboring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.

Yaxel Lendeborg has only played one NBA game, yet he has already started a feisty feud with Luka Doncic.
The Golden State Warriors rookie began his career on Wednesday by refusing to back down from the reigning NBA scoring champion, who punctuated their prolonged on-court exchange of trash talk by making a spectacular half-court shot in Lendeborg’s face at the halftime buzzer.
Doncic also won this fight decisively on the scoreboard when the Los Angeles Lakers blew out Lendeborg and the Warriors 127-105, with Doncic scoring 28 points in just three quarters.
Photo: AFP
Yet Lendeborg somehow was not finished talking: He called out the six-time All-Star as a complainer and a free-throw merchant during his post-game news conference.
“I lost all respect [for Doncic], man,” Lendeborg said. “That was awful... A lot of flopping, a lot of foul-baiting, a lot of praying to the ref, man. Interesting first game for me, for sure.”
The Warriors’ 24-year-old rookie first-round pick said he sparred with Doncic on the court because of the Slovenian superstar’s constant complaining to the officials — admittedly a common feature of most games in Doncic’s nine-year career.
Photo: AP
Lendeborg, who won an NCAA title with Michigan last season, said he enjoyed watching highlights of Doncic’s electric scoring performances in the past — but he has a more jaded perspective on Doncic’s skills now.
“Me getting frustrated, it’s not about the foul being called,” Lendeborg said. “It’s about him complaining the entire game, and then you get the foul call, and congratulations, bro. And then you talk to me like you did something great? Bro, come on. That’s just weak, you know? It kind of threw me off for a little while, because like I said, I had so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.”
Lendeborg and Doncic exchanged insults for much of the second quarter, with Lendeborg being whistled for a technical foul after saying something so loud and profane it caught the officials’ attention.
“I was telling him he sucks,” Lendeborg said with a smile. “‘You can’t score on me.’ I said it the whole game. I said a couple of cuss words, obviously. That’s why I got the technical and all that, but I was letting him know, because he was laughing and talking, all this because of that one foul call.”
Doncic mostly laughed off Lendeborg’s provocations, but the Lakers star obviously thrives amid confrontation. He was whistled for 16 technical fouls last season, earning a one-game suspension for exceeding the single-season limit.
“He was talking crazy, but I wasn’t trying to talk back this season,” Doncic said of Lendeborg. “Not trying to get techs. For the first time, that was not a double tech, because I didn’t say nothing, so I’m working on it. As you see, I think it worked great.”
Doncic got the ultimate victory at the final buzzer — but his halftime win was incredibly sweet as well.
“I knew that was going in before I got it in my hands,” Doncic said with a grin. “I work on those.”
He got the ball near the scorer’s table and let it fly with nearly three seconds left on the clock. When it banked through and set off pandemonium in the Lakers’ downtown arena, Doncic gleefully pointed at the fuming Lendeborg, who was not impressed.
“His only bucket on me was a banker from half court,” Lendeborg said. “I know it’s a team sport. He had 28 on us as a team. Me, I took my matchup personally. Tried not to get called on the fouls. Tried my best. I was thinking about playing him with my hands behind my back to see if that worked. Probably would have still got a foul call. But interesting.”

Rom-com or  sib-com?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

It is a truth universally acknowledged, as somebody once wrote, that a Jane Austen novel is a precursor to the modern rom-com.
And so we find ourselves, in a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, rooting for one thing: a kiss. A simple kiss, to break through the miscues and misunderstandings and finally release all that romantic tension.
Of course, we get it. Elinor locks lips with her Edward, out there in the grassy Devon fields, just as Bridget Jones did with Mark Darcy, in the snowy London streets. It’s a lovely kiss, and worth the wait.
Photo: AP
But then … we get something better: A hug, between sisters, even more joyful. And that’s what we remember as the credits roll.
Sisters. They’re not exactly “doing it for themselves” in this new version directed by Georgia Oakley — we’re still in 18th-century England, after all, and young women need to find husbands.
But Oakley, seeking a 21st-century approach to the Austen classic, finds a way to subtly shift the weight from romantic chemistry to the more profound chemistry between no-nonsense Elinor (Edgar-Jones, in the “sense” role) and turbulent Marianne (Esme Creed-Miles, in the “sensibility” role.) And this alone — well, and two killer dance scenes — seems reason enough to revisit the story, three decades since Ang Lee’s (李安) 1995 version won Emma Thompson a screenplay Oscar.
Oakley also brings a welcome naturalistic feel to a script by Diana Reid, with a strong sense of nature itself but also the reality of economic hardship — or what stands for economic hardship in an Austen novel. When Elinor and her mother (Caitriona Balfe) and sisters are relegated to a small cottage upon their father’s death, they’re hardly starving — they still have a servant, after all. But they share clothes, their hair is unkempt, they perform country chores. Their dresses are even stained.
We begin with some bad news. Marianne is lying in the grass, with the caterpillars, waiting for the day’s letters. Soon, the Dashwoods are in tears. Their father has left his wealth to a son from a previous marriage, meaning John Dashwood and his insufferable wife Fanny (Stacy Martin, amusing) will be moving into their sprawling country estate.
Mom and sisters soon decamp to a much smaller cottage — only one servant — in Devon, thanks to the help of Mrs. Jennings, “mother of your mother’s cousin’s cousin’s wife,” as she announces herself (a delightful Fiona Shaw).
But not before Elinor has fallen in love with Edward Ferrars (George MacKay), Fanny’s handsome and upstanding brother, during a family visit.
It seems these two are perfect for each other, both honorable and sensible but also just a little sexy underneath — Edgar-Jones and MacKay are well-matched here.
Complications arise, though — duh, this is an Austen novel! Ferrars is, well, otherwise engaged, literally. Elinor learns this on a trip to London, from the fiancee herself. It will take the rest of the movie for this to be ironed out. Meanwhile, Marianne is going through her own romantic journey.
There’s no need to count the times Marianne is tasked with explaining here that she’s the passionate one, more in touch with her turbulent emotions, and expects the same from a partner. A few too many, anyway.
But Creed-Miles, whose mother, Samantha Morton, is having a scene-stealing moment herself in The Odyssey, gives an exhilarating turn as the sister who, yes, seems to wear it all on her sleeve, making it totally believable when she screams into the rain or laughs with delirium. Or falls head-over-heels with Willoughby, a handsome rake (deliciously played by Frank Dillane) who swoops in to save her when she turns her ankle on a beach.
These two, also, seem perfect for each other — especially when dancing. Kudos to choreographer Holly Blakey, who makes the most of two social dance scenes: the exuberant “hop” in the countryside (what fun the actors seem to be having), and the more refined but still creative London ball.
But Willoughby, as Austen’s readers know, will prove an even more elusive catch than Ferrars. Meanwhile, waiting in the wings is a man of few words — and initially, few feelings, or so thinks Marianne — the steadfast Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum).
Will he find a way to her heart? It’s hardly a spoiler to reveal the end of a novel published centuries ago, but more importantly, we know how all rom-coms end — with the “rom” part working out, somehow.
We’re happy for the sisters, of course. They landed a couple of nice guys.
But most of all? We’re happy they have each other.

Laid out on bamboo racks by the Keya River (客雅溪), freshly made noodles dried in the wind without compromising their quality or texture. The ideal conditions, it was once said, were 70 percent wind and 30 percent sun. France’s unrest lays bare the ‘slow agony’ of Macron’s final months in office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:34 UTC
01:44:34 KST

France’s worst bout of civil unrest in years has plunged French President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office deeper into turmoil, exposing the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger with little money to spend, scant political capital and an increasingly fragile grip on public order.
The rioting that swept across France on Saturday last week, leaving a trail of looted shops, torched buildings and defaced public institutions, presents Macron with perhaps the most explosive challenge of his twilight presidency: A country demanding more from a state that can no longer afford to give much.
Macron came to power almost a decade ago promising to upend France’s sclerotic political class, turbocharge economic reforms and restore authority through a more assertive presidency.
Instead, with just six months left in office, he finds himself effectively a lame-duck head of state presiding over a country mired in political paralysis, facing acute financial pressures and grappling with unrest that has exposed the limits of state authority.
Unlike during the yellow vest uprising of 2018 to 2019, when Macron sought to defuse public anger with billions of euros in concessions, France’s strained public finances and fractured parliament leave him with precious few levers to pull.
Even former allies are openly scathing, tracing the country’s current impasse to Macron’s decision to call a snap parliamentary election in 2024 that weakened his authority.
“The end of this term is a slow agony,” said Loic Kervran, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp. “The president paralyzed the country with his absurd decision to dissolve parliament in 2024. Arguably the worst decision in the history of the Fifth Republic.”
The turmoil might benefit far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in next year’s presidential race and stands to gain from the anger over declining living standards and the fears over law and order unleashed by the weekend’s violence.
“Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign,” said Jean-Baptiste Moreau, another former Macron lawmaker. “It’s not just a clear path ahead of her — it’s a six-lane highway.”
Le Pen delivered her own message to the nation in a video statement on Sunday, portraying Macron’s administration as a crumbling power and casting herself as the figure capable of restoring order.
When Macron later addressed the country, he offered little concrete action, stopping short of declaring a state of emergency. As he spoke, looting was continuing for a second consecutive night, including in affluent Paris districts, prompting Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to announce local curfews on Monday.
Opponents and one-time allies alike were underwhelmed. His former prime minister, Edouard Philippe, preparing his own presidential run, was unsparing in his criticism.
“Mr President, I listened to you last night,” Philippe said on X. “I would have preferred, like millions of French people, decisions and initiatives to restore order.”
“Our country needs to be commanded,” he added.
However, even Philippe is struggling to shake off his past association with Macron, and most recent polls show far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon edging ahead of him in the race to qualify for the second-round runoff vote. That outcome would all but guarantee a Le Pen victory, the opinion polls show.
Macron’s office on Monday announced that he had refused his interior minister’s resignation and ordered a review into apparent failures in intelligence gathering and police preparedness — deepening the impression of a government struggling to regain control.
Investors also took fright. Market analysts say the violence adds another layer of political risk at a time when France is already under scrutiny over its swelling debt burden and struggle to reduce one of the euro zone’s largest budget deficits.
The president finds himself trapped between bond markets demanding spending restraint and protesters demanding the opposite.
Despite calls from opponents to remain in France, Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday on a Gulf tour he says would help secure fuel supplies and ease some of the economic pressures that have helped swell the ranks of the protesters.
The trip carries risks, reinforcing perceptions of a president disconnected from the public mood. Images of Macron attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte on Friday last week, hours before the unrest erupted, prompted ridicule on social media and became an easy symbol for critics seeking to portray him as detached from events.
In a sign of the depth of disenchantment in parts of his political camp, some former allies have begun openly discussing whether he should leave office before the end of his term. Moreau, who spoke to Macron on Sunday, said he urged him to prepare an orderly early departure to break the political deadlock and avoid another six months of drift.
“He doesn’t want to give up, that’s not his character. But that’s what he should do for the country,” he said.

Micron announces a new profit-sharing program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:33 UTC
01:44:33 KST

Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) yesterday unveiled a new profit-sharing program and structural wage hikes as part of its efforts to build a predictable and transparent compensation framework in response to feedback from unions.
The memorychip maker, a subsidiary of US-based Micron Technology Inc, announced the major compensation structural overhaul during an online news conference following a milestone agreement with the union representing more than 10,000 workers at its Taichung facility.
Under the new framework, quarterly profit-sharing bonuses would supplement payments under the Incentive Pay Plan (IPP), the company said.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
The IPP formula has also been substantially enhanced, it said.
“Profit-sharing mechanisms are common among Asian companies, but they are rarely seen among American technology firms,” Micron Memory Taiwan chairman Donghui Lu (盧東暉) told the news conference. “This approach offers transparency and, to a certain degree, predictability.”
The new mechanism is to take effect in fiscal 2027 and apply to eligible employees in Micron Technology’s global workforce.
Quarterly net income minus forecast capital expenditure for the following quarter would be the basis for calculating profit-sharing bonuses, the company said.
The payout will be distributed equally between stock — subject to one-year vesting — and cash, it said.
Following its annual wage adjustments, Micron Memory Taiwan is to implement another structural payroll increase in an extensive way to avoid salary inversion.
Previously, Micron Memory Taiwan’s wage hikes primarily targeted entry-level personnel and newcomers.
The company hopes to implement the adjustments by Lunar New Year next year, it said.
Micron Memory Taiwan also plans to increase shift differential pay from December. The monthly allowance for day shifts would triple to NT$4,500 (US$138.43), while the allowance for evening shifts would increase to 15 percent of their regular pay, and night shift workers would receive a 20 percent shift differential, it said.
After the adjustments, the conditional top-end compensation for an entry-level engineer would be nearly NT$4 million in fiscal 2027, up from NT$1.45 million in fiscal 2025, while the amount for mid-to-senior-tier engineers is projected at NT$6 million, up from more than NT$2 million, the Taichung union said.
The projections include stock awards and employer retirement contributions.
Micron Memory Taiwan said it would increase its employer pension contribution rate to 10 percent of workers’ regular pay from 8 percent to retain talent.
Representatives of the company’s Taoyuan union yesterday held a one-day strike over accusations that company management had failed to disclose its profit-sharing ratio.
The Taoyuan union is demanding that the allocation be set at 15 percent of Micron Technology’s global operating profit.
Micron Memory Taiwan and a union representing workers at its Taichung operations today said they had signed a labor-management agreement covering multiple issues, prompting both sides to withdraw from mediation scheduled for tomorrow. The joint statement did not disclose the terms of the agreement, saying the company and the union would separately communicate details to affected employees in the coming days. Idaho-based Micron, the world's third-largest memory chipmaker, employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan, a key manufacturing base where it produces DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) servers. Any disruption to Micron's Taiwan operations could affect already strained global

Four financial firms approve merger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:28 UTC
01:44:28 KST

Four state-owned financial holding companies yesterday approved a plan to merge their investment trust subsidiaries into a larger, more competitive asset manager, aiming to cut operating costs, broaden product offerings and improve Taiwan’s position as a regional asset management hub.
The planned merger aims to achieve economies of scale by pooling resources, technology and distribution networks, allowing the combined company to improve operating efficiency and compete more effectively, executives said.
First Financial Holding Co (第一金控), Mega Financial Holding Co (兆豐金控), Taiwan Cooperative Financial Holding Co (合庫金控) and Hua Nan Financial Holdings Co (華南金控) said their boards and those of their investment trust subsidiaries had approved the deal.
Photo: CNA
First Securities Investment Trust Co (第一金投信) would be the surviving entity because of its larger asset base and stronger operating performance, they said.
The merger, which requires regulatory approval, is planned for Jan. 1, 2028.
First Securities Investment Trust would absorb Mega International Investment Trust Co (兆豐國際投信), Taiwan Cooperative Securities Investment Trust Co (合作金庫投信) and Hua Nan Investment Trust Co (華南永昌投信), with all of the approximately 370 employees to have the option to stay on.
The parent companies would hold stakes of 50.3 percent, 30.4 percent, 9.8 percent and 9.5 percent respectively in the combined firm.
The transaction would be conducted through a share swap, with First Securities Investment Trust issuing about 59.3 million new common shares.
The new company would retain the First Securities Investment Trust name, with First Financial controlling appointments to its top management positions, First Financial Holding president Frank Fang (方螢基) said.
The combined company is expected to benefit from lower operating costs and more effective use of the four groups’ distribution networks, Fang said, adding that a broader range of investment products should help improve profitability and shareholder returns.
First Securities Investment Trust president Richard Kao (高子敬) said that the entity’s assets under management would total about NT$500 billion (US$15.38 billion), including publicly offered funds and discretionary investment mandates.
The company aims to increase assets in publicly offered funds by 15 percent annually and those in discretionary investment mandates by 10 percent, Kao said.
To achieve those targets, it plans to develop products focused on retirement planning, sustainable investment, overseas asset allocation and wealthy clients, he said, adding that it intends to pursue opportunities arising from the government’s push to establish Taiwan as an Asian asset management hub.
The combined publicly offered fund assets of the four merging firms would rank about 12th among Taiwan’s investment trust firms and the merged entity would aim to break into the top 10, he said.
The merged company would have seven directors and two supervisors.
First Financial would appoint four directors and one supervisor, while each of the other three financial holding companies would appoint one director.
Mega Financial would appoint one supervisor.
The four merging companies pledged to protect employee and customer rights during the integration.
First Securities Investment Trust would assume responsibility for existing customers, whose rights would remain protected under applicable regulations.

Millions of hacking attempts amid rush to patch PHP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:27 UTC
01:44:27 KST

Companies and governments worldwide yesterday rushed to patch critical flaws in the widely used PHP programming language, as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.
The push came after governments in Europe and elsewhere took Web sites offline as a precaution on Wednesday while Web site operators scrambled to secure systems running the software.
The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki showed how much public and corporate systems rely on the software, and how hard it is to fix such flaws quickly once they are made public.
Photo: Reuters
“It was a long day and a long night, I know for all the IT [information technology] and security folks ... I’ve not seen anything like this in a long, long time,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at a company event in Cologne, Germany, yesterday.
The episode underscored the importance of building digital systems that can be maintained securely, he said.
PHP developers on Wednesday released urgent fixes for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using artificial intelligence (AI), urging users to “update immediately.”
“Details of these flaws became public before fixes were ready, and attacks have since been reported,” said Madeline Lawrence, cofounder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security. “So companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them.”
As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended sites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, cloud services firm Cloudflare said.
“In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince wrote on X late on Wednesday. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”
Japanese companies including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway yesterday said they were temporarily suspending some Internet services as part of emergency measures.
Insurer Tokio Marine Holdings said it had suspended the site of a group company.
The Japanese Ministry of Finance and Japan Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan’s National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service.
The precautionary shutdowns underscore growing concerns over cybersecurity in Japan, which recorded more cyberincidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, TrendAI data showed.
French telecom Orange said it had temporarily suspended access to certain PHP-based Web sites and applications across several subsidiaries as a precaution.
South Korea yesterday raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks.
Tencent Cloud (騰訊雲), one of China’s largest cloud-computing providers, urged clients to install updated PHP versions, but stopped short of calling for widespread Web site shutdowns.
Finland’s state IT services provider Valtori said it had continued installing PHP security patches overnight and was gradually lifting precautionary service blocks after shutting down government public Web services a day earlier.
“Restoring services can take days or even weeks, as in addition to updates, the systems need to be carefully tested,” Valtori director-general Hannu Naumanen said in a statement.
The outages were not caused by exploitation of the vulnerabilities or by a breach, Valtori said, adding that it was not aware of any active exploitation of the flaws.
The Chinese Ministry of Industry and Information Technology yesterday urged organizations and users to inspect systems immediately and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP.
It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary.

Wu is a prolific public commentator and owner of My-Formosa.com, an online outlet focusing on political news.
The Hsinchu County Prosecutors’ Office said it launched an inquiry into a man surnamed Wu over alleged breaches of the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法).
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
The office did not disclose further information.
Sources familiar with the matter said police had questioned Wu, and searched his residence and offices.
Cheng, the mayor of Jhubei City (竹北), had filed a criminal complaint accusing Wu of distributing libelous materials with the intent of preventing his election, they said.
Wu allegedly spread two tranches of defamatory pamphlets, which bore Wu’s signature, among Hsinchu voters over the past two months, sources cited the Cheng campaign’s lawyers as saying in the complaint.
The material falsely accused Cheng of illegal profiteering and unlawful lobbying tied to Chih Shan Manor (至善莊園) and Shencyu Village (神去) development projects in Jhudong Township (竹東), the sources said.
The pamphlets falsely claimed Cheng’s brother had ordered gangsters to break into a home in a bid to intimidate a whistleblower, they cited the document as saying.
Wu has repeated these claims on his talk show, acknowledged his authorship of the pamphlets and said he printed 500,000 copies of similar material for distribution, they added.
Cheng’s lawyers consider the pundit’s actions to constitute the crime of preventing the election of a candidate and aggravated defamation, the sources said.
Wu’s digital platform in a statement called the investigation an attack on freedom and said Wu is carrying out a hunger strike in protest.
Wu would refuse to pay bail if ordered to do so, it added.

Photo: AFP
The Portugal midfielder suggested that Nico Paz’s early strike for Como had a damaging effect on the visitors, leaving them struggling to impose themselves.

“Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat,” Fernandes said. “It’s difficult to get out of that, trying to be brave, to have the ball and make something happen.”
“If we are not able to do that, it is going to be very difficult to get out of this situation,” he added.
Fernandes also highlighted United’s passive approach out of possession, saying Como were allowed too much time and space to dictate play.
Asked whether those comments amounted to criticism of Carrick’s tactics, Fernandes said: “That’s on the manager and staff to see, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.”

Transport services disrupted by storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:25 UTC
01:44:25 KST

Airlines, ferry services, railways and national parks announced cancelations and closures yesterday, as Typhoon Champi bore down on Taiwan.
The Central Weather Administration yesterday issued land warnings for most of Taiwan proper, as Champi is forecast to come closest to the nation today.
Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) has canceled all express trains on its western and eastern trunk lines today, while the high-speed rail system would continue to operate normally.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
For non-reserved TRC services, trains on the Coast Line, Chengzhui Line, Yilan Line and North Link Line are fully suspended.
Services between Hualien and Taitung counties, as well as other unsuspended routes, would operate dynamically based on weather conditions, the TRC said.
The Alishan Forest Railway has also suspended its main line services between Chiayi and Alishan (阿里山) for today and tomorrow.
Conversely, the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp announced that all of its trains would run on their regular schedules today to meet passenger demand.
Maritime and aviation transport face widespread disruptions.
Ferry services between Kaohsiung’s Gushan (鼓山) and Cijin (旗津) districts were suspended at midnight last night, while ferries between Pingtung County and Siaoliouciou (小琉球) would be completely suspended tomorrow and on Sunday.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Hualien Branch
Meanwhile, China Airlines and Tigerair Taiwan have canceled or rescheduled flights to and from Okinawa.
Mandarin Airlines and UNI Air have partially canceled domestic flights connecting Taiwan proper to Penghu, Kinmen and Lienchiang counties.
Mandarin Airlines said it would continue adjusting schedules according to weather conditions and urged passengers to check its Web site or app for updates.
Authorities also announced closures of forest recreation areas and tourist attractions.
Yushan National Park banned entry and activities from 11:30pm on Wednesday.
Yilan County’s Taipingshan National Forest Recreation Area closed as a precaution from noon yesterday, and Gueishan Island (龜山島) is closed for three days from yesterday.
Forest recreation areas, forestry cultural parks and lowland forest parks in Hualien County closed from 1pm yesterday.
The North Dawu Mountain Trail, Jingu Valley Cabin, Kenting National Forest Recreation Area and Shuangliu National Forest Recreation Area in Pingtung County also closed from 1pm.
Alishan National Forest Recreation Area is to close from 8am today. The Alishan Forest Railway is also suspending services today, except for the Jhushan Line’s early-morning sunrise trains.
Aowanda and Hehuanshan national forest recreation areas, along with Tianchi Lodge on the Nenggao Cross-Ridge Historic Trail, are scheduled to close from today.

Taipei defends the removal of ‘political’ sticker from bulletin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:24 UTC
01:44:24 KST

Taipei officials yesterday defended their decision to ask Our Theatre (阮劇團) to remove stickers supporting Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈柏楊) from a public bulletin at Taipei’s Wellspring Theater, sparking controversy over freedom of speech.
The Chiayi-based troupe is using the city-run venue to perform the play Louder! (噪音風暴).
Our Theatre said it contacted Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs Commissioner Tsai Shih-ping (蔡詩萍) after the venue’s managers requested that the stickers be removed.
Photo courtesy of Our Theatre
Removing the stickers would be inappropriate, the group told Tsai, who they said voiced concern to protect the troupe from political strife.
“We understand the position of the department and appreciate the commissioner’s concern for and protection of the troupe,” Our Theater said.
“From the troupe’s perspective, the bulletin is a free space for the audience to exchange their opinions, and we respect each audience member’s right to express their views,” it added.
Shen yesterday said the incident is a replay of a previous controversy in which officials asked street vendors to refrain from displaying political messages or slogans at their stands.
“Administrative neutrality applies only to civil servants and public venues, not vendors or theater groups,” he said, adding that the city “may have misinterpreted the law.”
Tsai defended the venue managers’ decision at a news conference, saying that partisan messages are forbidden in publicly owned venues, per municipal regulations.
“Administrative neutrality applies not only to civil servants, but also to public venues and groups utilizing the venues to keep cultural spaces pure and professional,” he said, adding that the department “does not attack freedom of speech.”
The department would have handled the incident exactly the same had the campaign stickers voiced support for Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), Tsai said.
“Taipei’s municipal venues have followed the same rules governing neutrality for many years and I remind Shen that he should learn about these rules and have some knowledge in civics, as a citizen and politician should,” Tsai added.

Fourth Strategic Dialogue between the State of Qatar and the Republic of France
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:44:22 CEST
01:44:22 KST

Fourth Strategic Dialogue between the State of Qatar and the Republic of France Qatar Relation bilatérale Joint statement On : October 21st 2026 On the sidelines of the State Visit of H.E. Emmanuel Macon, President of the French Republic to the State of Qatar, the Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the State of Qatar, H.E. Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, and the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs of the French Republic, Mr. Jean-Noël Barrot, co-chaired the fourth annual Qatar-France Strategic Dialogue in Doha, Qatar on 21 October 2026, reaffirming the deep and historic ties between the two countries Both Ministers reviewed areas of collaboration between the two countries since the third Strategic Dialogue held in June 2025. They reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral relations and expanding their strategic partnership across shared priorities. They welcomed the progress achieved through sustained high-level engagement including on regional security, defense and military cooperation, security and counterterrorism cooperation, trade and investment, innovation, education and higher education, culture and the arts, and humanitarian assistance and development. Political and Diplomatic Cooperation: Qatar and France reaffirmed their strategic partnership and commitment to addressing shared regional and global challenges. Both sides exchanged views on the latest regional and global developments, including on Gulf Security, the ongoing Iran conflict, the means to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, peace efforts in the Middle East and in Africa, and developments in Syria and Lebanon. Prime Minister Al-Thani and Minister Barrot condemned the attacks carried out by the Houthi against civilian facilities and energy infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as well as its attacks that threaten maritime security in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They emphasized the need to halt these attacks and ensure the security of international waterways and freedom of navigation therein. Both sides stressed the importance of diplomacy, dialogue, and coordinated international efforts to advance de-escalation and preserve regional stability. Minister Barrot commended Qatar’s leading role in international mediation and its continued efforts to foster dialogue, de-escalate tensions, and advance diplomatic solutions in the Gulf, the Middle East, Africa and beyond. Economy, Trade, and Investments: Qatar and France reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening economic, trade, and investment ties, with bilateral trade exceeding €1.52 billion in 2025. The Ministers highlighted the importance of Qatari investments in France spanning across a range of sectors including consumer and luxury goods, telecommunications, real estate, industry, healthcare, and financial services contributing to economic growth, job creation, and innovation, and expressed interest in exploring new opportunities, particularly in quantum technologies and artificial intelligence. Both sides agreed to enhance cooperation through seminars and workshops on public-private partnerships, central bank reserve management, and monetary policy, and welcomed in that regard, the signing of a Letter of Intent on cooperation in the field of communications and information technology. Both Ministers stressed on the need of deepening collaboration in intellectual property, food security, digital technologies, and the circular economy. Both sides also explored ways to further develop their trade and investment partnership, through a Roadmap focused on strategic areas in alignment with the framework of the economic diversification goals stated by Qatar’s National Vision 2030 and in accordance with the economic plan “France 2030.”, both Ministers exchanged views on the economic implications of regional conflicts and highlighted opportunities for French companies to support Qatar’s infrastructure priorities and strategic development projects. Defense, Security, and Counterterrorism: Qatar and France emphasized the importance of their strong and long-standing defense and security partnership, welcoming increased high-level exchanges and close coordination on regional security challenges. France reiterated its commitment to Qatar’s security and stability. Minister Barrot reiterated France’s commitment, as a trusted strategic and defense partner, to supporting Qatar’s security and stability. The two sides welcomed the close coordination between their authorities during the crisis and reaffirmed their determination to further strengthen defense cooperation, joint training, operational coordination, and information sharing in support of regional security and stability.The Ministers also welcomed the agreement signed during the 27th High Military Committee, the implementation of the Letter of Intent on strengthening military cooperation and coordination between the two countries signed on 11 January 2026, and Qatar’s participation in Exercise ORION 2026 in France, underscoring their commitment to enhanced military interoperability and readiness. Both sides highlighted their extensive security cooperation, particularly in major event security, crisis management, aviation security, cybersecurity, and capacity-building, both sides agreed to work towards a new ministerial action plan for 2027–2030 to further strengthen cooperation across these areas. They also welcomed the strengthening of their partnership in the field of civil protection, including in disaster response, wildfire management, document fraud prevention, maritime security, and professional training. Both sides also highlighted their joint efforts in support for the Syrian Civil Defense. Qatar and France reaffirmed their commitment to combating terrorism, violent extremism, and illicit financial flows and stressed the need to enhance international cooperation to fight terrorism and its financing, Humanitarian and Development Cooperation: Qatar and France reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening humanitarian and development cooperation through joint initiatives supporting crisis-affected populations, particularly in Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Africa. Both sides welcomed ongoing cooperation between the Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD), the French Development Agency Group (AFD Group), and the French Crisis and Support Centre (CDCS). Education, Health and Sports: Qatar and France reaffirmed their commitment to expanding cooperation in education, healthcare, and sports, emphasizing academic exchanges, student mobility, and joint programs. In education, both sides welcomed progress in French language teaching, DELF certification, teacher training, and university partnerships. They reaffirmed their commitment to signing the Eighth Executive Program for Cooperation in Education and strengthening collaboration in scientific research and innovation. In healthcare, both countries agreed to enhance medical education and professional training, including facilitating opportunities for Qatari physicians and healthcare professionals to undertake specialized training and residency programs in France. In sports and youth, both sides emphasized strengthening people-to-people ties through youth exchanges, community sports, anti-doping cooperation, and the exchange of expertise in sports policies, logistics, and major sporting events. Nantou’s elevated woodland sanctuary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:22 UTC
01:44:22 KST

Tucked away within a deep, undulating valley, Xitou Nature Education Area’s (溪頭自然教育園區) misty high-altitude realm spans approximately 25 square kilometers and sits at 1,150 meters above sea level.
Its untamed beauty unfolds across a mosaic of emerald and chartreuse treetops, slick, pendulous fronds, imposing conifers and boundless bamboo groves.
Xitou, in Nantou County, is Taiwan’s most popular forest park, attracting over 2 million visitors each year in search of both sylvan exploration and respite from oppressive urban humidity.
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
Parking is terraced up a gentle hillside, with two lots found close to the Visitor Center and ticketing area 1. Another smaller parking lot sits adjacent to the main entrance and ticketing area 2.
Maps are presented on arrival, detailing the 14 trails of varying length. Many crisscross or link up with others, and there’s a map legend attributing levels of difficulty to each.
Preparedness is essential and should reflect the individual’s level of fitness and experience. For a full day of activity, consider trekking poles and hydration backpacks.
For those underprepared or simply exhausted, comfortable electric shuttle cars resembling elongated golf carts are provided at designated pick-up zones.
THE TRAILS
The various circuitous trails are flanked by dense, towering greenery, at times connecting as a lattice overhead; the air is always cool, tinged with earthy scents.
University Pond Trail (大學池步道) and Sacred Tree Trail (神木步道) are the reserves most popular trails. Both offer a paved option for a much smoother trek, with an easy ascent making it ideal for those with strollers or mobility concerns.
The former culminates at an idyllic algae-spotted pond and footbridge adjacent to waterways and a well-appointed restaurant and dining area.
The latter concludes at its 2,800-year-old namesake. No longer standing, it’s still an incredible sight, its immense, horizontal mass clearly discernible from the viewing platform.
The Bird Watching Trail (賞鳥步道) and the Mountaineering Trail (登山步道) offer much more of a challenge with a dramatic incline and plenty of steps.
THE SIGHTS
Visitors will find a wealth of fascinating landmarks scattered throughout the area, as depicted on the illustrated map, from a ginkgo grove to a pavilion, a bamboo cottage, various bridges, arboretums and a plant nursery.
Particularly notable sights include the Phoenix Mountain Astronomical Observatory (溪頭天文台), which stands at 1,800 meters above sea level, making it the park’s highest accessible point.
And to the east, the Sky Walk (空中走廊) is perched 23 meters above the forest floor, allowing visitors exceptional views amid the outstretched branches of the forest canopy.
Nature buffs often seek out the elusive wildlife here, like the Taiwan Serow or Formosan Giant Flying Squirrel.
Most, however, may have to settle for the sudden darting movements of pallas’s squirrels, found scampering throughout the various picnic areas.
Occasional encounters with a Formosan rock macaque (台灣獼猴) have also been known to happen. Bright-eyed and brazen, they are opportunistic creatures, and visitors must remember not to feed them.
The Han Kuang exercises in August simulated the repelling of attackers from the People’s Republic of China (PRC). One scenario saw the PRC seizing Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) in a daring helicopter assault. The airport is a key military operations center, and its seizure or destruction in a PRC invasion would be inevitable. Yet that is hardly the only conflict involving Songshan. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) recent, surprising suggestion that the airport be converted to an AI park is just the latest variation on an old theme. Replacing Songshan airport with some kind of green or park space
Oct. 19 to Oct 25 For many in Hsinchu, the cold, dry October winds bring uncomfortable weather. But in the past, rice noodle makers waited all year for these winds. Laid out on bamboo racks by the Keya River (客雅溪), freshly made noodles dried in the wind without compromising their quality or texture. The ideal conditions, it was once said, were 70 percent wind and 30 percent sun. Most producers were concentrated in the Nanshih (南勢) area, which became known as Mifenliao (米粉寮, literally “rice noodle shed”). SOUTH KOREA
Freed shark returns
A shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a Busan canal returned hours after being coaxed out, authorities said yesterday, prompting another attempt to guide it back to the sea. Workers had herded the 3m-long female dusky shark, nicknamed “Bukhangi,” out of the canal the day before, after weeks of trial and error, but after lingering in nearby waters for hours, the shark swam beneath an outer barrier net installed on the platform that night and re-entered the waterway. “The shark is now between the outer net and an inner net installed 30m to 40m ... further inside the canal,” a Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries official said. A fresh attempt began yesterday morning, with authorities raising the outer net to allow Bukhangi to move from the canal, she said. There were no signs that the shark had been feeding regularly during its month-long stay in the canal, and falling water temperatures could pose additional health risks, officials said.
Photo: AP
AUSTRALIA
Man threatens lawmaker
Police yesterday said they had charged a man over threatening behavior at a lawmaker’s office, days after an attack on a parliamentarian that has put a spotlight on the security of elected officials. The 56-year-old was arrested on Wednesday after he allegedly made threats and brandished a pair of nunchucks, Western Australian Police said. The man has been charged with making threats as well as possession of cannabis and was to face court yesterday, police said. It comes days after lawmaker Helen Haines was struck by a car outside her office in the rural town of Wangaratta.
EUROPEAN UNION
ICC wins rights prize
Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court (ICC) was yesterday awarded the EU’s prestigious Sakharov Prize, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said. “The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” Metsola told lawmakers in Strasbourg. An awards ceremony for the rights prize is to be held in December. The ICC was named among three finalists, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government. The US announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

Actor Tom Cruise, known for movies from Risky Business to Top Gun, is to receive the American Film Institute’s (AFI) Life Achievement Award at a Hollywood ceremony in April, organizers said on Wednesday. The nonprofit dedicated to preserving and promoting movies has bestowed the honor annually since 1973. Previous recipients include Bette Davis, Gene Kelley, Elizabeth Taylor and Tom Hanks. Grassroots voices for guiding governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

On Sunday last week, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said that, if elected, he would hold soapbox sessions called “Mayor, I can’t do it anymore” (市長，我不想幹了) to listen to frontline civil servants and teachers talk about the difficulties they face at work.
The idea draws from his campaign trail soapbox events and platform on Line called “Mayor, listen to me” (市長，你給我聽好了), which allows users to leave messages regarding their municipal concerns.
The idea is good. A city government is about more than packing political achievements, and public messaging should not be allowed to drown out grassroots voices. Good governance is not measured by the scale of construction projects or how impressive the numbers look, but by whether public services meet people’s needs and whether frontline workers receive adequate support.
Taipei’s promotion of smart-city initiatives, digital services and performance management systems should be improving efficiency. However, if digital systems effectively double certain work requirements, or if performance assessments leave personnel exhausted from having to prepare reports and working overtime to fulfill their regular duties, reform becomes a burden.
Administrative streamlining should involve reviewing departmental procedures, performance assessments and staffing arrangements, eliminating ineffective tasks and allowing civil servants to focus on serving the public rather than endlessly filling out forms. Public sector workers’ time and energy should not be squandered to manufacture the appearance of strong performance.
In addition to teaching and counseling students, teachers must handle administrative reporting and communicate with parents. When the Ministry of Education demands results and evaluations without simplifying procedures or providing sufficient staff, the burden is shifted onto frontline workers.
Before promoting bilingual education and digital learning, the government should ensure that teachers, teaching materials and supporting measures are in place. Otherwise, teachers would be left to contend with a constant stream of open demonstration lessons, project evaluations and training sessions on top of their already onerous teaching workloads. Reforms that focus on results while neglecting necessary supporting measures undermine not only teachers’ professional expertise, but also the quality of students’ education.
The value of Shen’s proposal is not just that it provides an outlet for the frustrations of frontline public servants and teachers, but also that it turns their responses into a basis for institutional reform. The government should distinguish between issues that can be addressed immediately and those that require changes to regulations or budgets. It should assign responsibility to specific departments, set implementation deadlines and establish monitoring mechanisms to ensure tangible progress in reducing administrative workloads, supporting education and improving staffing.
Shen deserves commendation for his willingness to give frontline workers a voice. Genuine results are not about talking up achievements, but about enabling civil servants to serve the public and teachers to teach with peace of mind. When frontline workers sound the alarm, those in power should confront systemic problems rather than defend the appearance of success. That is the true measure of a Taipei mayor’s governing ability.
Yeh Yu-cheng is a secretary at the Pingtung County Public Health Bureau.

It was packing maximum sustained winds of 173kph and gusts of up to 198kph, with a storm radius of 320km, the agency said.
The storm’s radius remained broad, and as the Pacific high-pressure system weakens, Champi’s movement is expected to slow down today and tomorrow, CWA Weather Forecast Center Deputy Director Wu Wan-hua (伍婉華) said.
Photo: CNA
The typhoon could move erratically as it interacts with Taiwan’s terrain, with its center projected to pass within 80km of the coast, although landfall remains possible, Wu said.
The storm’s outer band is expected to blanket the entire nation this morning, with the center coming closest between tonight and early tomorrow morning, she said.
The storm circle is forecast to leave Taiwan proper by tomorrow evening, and Champi is expected to weaken after moving into waters east of Hualien County, Wu said, adding that the land warning might be expanded to include Penghu and Lienchiang (Matsu) counties.
Coastal winds are to intensify early this morning, with waves of more than 10m possible through tomorrow afternoon, she said.
Rainfall was to increase from last night, with the heaviest downpours expected from today through tomorrow morning, she added.
Mountainous areas in northern and northeastern Taiwan could receive 600mm to 900mm of rain through tomorrow, the CWA said.
The agency forecast continuous, widespread showers for northern and northeastern regions today, warning of localized heavy or extremely heavy rain, particularly in northern mountainous areas.
Central and eastern regions are to see localized brief showers, with heavy rain possible in the mountains of Taichung and Hualien County, while the south and southeast could expect sporadic showers, it said.
Widespread showers and localized heavy rain are to persist in the north tomorrow, with brief localized showers in the east and central mountains, the agency said.
More than 23,000 military personnel are on standby to help with rescue efforts, while more than 150 domestic and international flights were canceled yesterday ahead of the storm.
As tomorrow is the start of a three-day Retrocession Day weekend, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) yesterday urged the public to stay away from creeks, beaches and mountainous areas, even after Champi has left Taiwan.
National Fire Agency Chief Secretary Cheng Chih-chiang (鄭志強) said the agency had asked the Hualien County Government to evacuate residents living downstream of the Wanli Creek (萬里溪) landslide dam.
As of yesterday morning, the landslide dam was holding 5 million tonnes of water, posing a potential disaster risk, Cho said earlier at a Cabinet meeting.
Earlier yesterday, a free diver in his 20s died after apparently being swept out to sea by a strong rip current off Siaoliouciou Island (小琉球) in Pingtung County, the Coast Guard Administration said.
At 2:25pm, more than two hours after the search began, divers aboard a recreational boat found the diver drifting off Beauty Cave (美人洞).
Champi is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbo-charged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.
The UN on Wednesday said that the El Nino system gripping the planet is heading off the charts, and that countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.
El Nino is expected to peak in December, but the human impact is set to last into next year and beyond.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate human-caused global warming.

Musk might affect SpaceX-Tesla talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:17 UTC
01:44:17 KST

Elon Musk’s public endorsement this week of a potential US$3.5 trillion merger between SpaceX and Tesla has rattled some insiders involved in the discussions, who worry his comments could invite shareholder scrutiny and delay the process by several weeks, a person with direct knowledge of the talks said.
The disclosure created a “mess” for the process, as it could lead to questions about how well Tesla shareholders’ interests would be represented, the person said.
The concerns reflect similarities some participants see with Tesla’s 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which sparked years of litigation over Musk’s role in the deal.
Photo: AFP
Musk, who serves as chief executive officer of SpaceX and Tesla, and owns significant stakes in each company, this week told investors that the two companies were examining what would be the largest corporate transaction in history and revealed that both had formed special committees to evaluate it.
The parties have hired advisers, but discussions are at an early stage, three sources familiar with the matter said.
SpaceX approached Tesla in recent weeks and the companies have been discussing a range of transaction structures, including a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla or a merger under a newly formed holding company, the person familiar with the matter said.
They are weighing different forms of merger consideration, including an all-stock deal, the person said.
In related-party transactions such as a SpaceX-Tesla merger, independent board members typically oversee the process to safeguard public shareholders’ interests.
That issue loomed large in Tesla’s 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which triggered years of litigation after shareholders alleged the world’s richest man had influenced the process to bail out his investment in the struggling rooftop solar company.
At the time, Musk owned about 22 percent of both Tesla and SolarCity, which was founded by his cousins.
Shareholders argued that Musk’s involvement and public support undermined the deal’s fairness.
Central to the case were claims that despite his minority stake, Musk was a controlling shareholder of Tesla due to his ties to board members and domineering style.
The Delaware Supreme Court later said that plaintiffs’ contention of the absence of an independent committee, together with “certain other facts concerning Musk’s involvement in and public support for the transaction,” warranted the finding of unfair dealing.
The courts ultimately upheld the acquisition as fair, although it took several years for the case to be resolved and Tesla directors settled allegations for US$60 million.
Musk owns nearly one-fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.
On Tuesday’s call with investors, Musk said that as a conflicted party, he cannot be part of the discussions of the special committees.
Advisers are also in contact with his lawyers to ensure Musk is recused from the merger discussions, the source familiar with the talks said.

China escalating election interference efforts, NSB says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:15 UTC
01:44:15 KST

China is shifting its election interference efforts in Taiwan toward specific groups, National Security Bureau (NSB) Director-General Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥) said yesterday.
For example, Beijing is mobilizing airlines to offer discounted tickets to certain Taiwanese living in China to return home to vote in next month’s local government elections, Tsai said.
In addition, the bureau believes China is providing illicit funding to candidates and political groups it supports, he told reporters ahead of a meeting of the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee, where he reported on the NSB’s intelligence work so far in the second half of this year.
Photo: Fabian Hamacher, Reuters
The bureau and other intelligence agencies are investigating suspected interference cases and have identified several key tactics used by China, including suspected bribery of voters by offering cheap sightseeing tours to China, Tsai said.
Another suspected tactic is spreading disinformation and controversial content, operating illegal betting pools and hacking specific people to steal election-related intelligence for targeted interference, he said.
The bureau is using artificial intelligence tools to trace the sources of disinformation and related content, he said.
It is collecting evidence of suspected election interference and hopes to hand it over to judicial authorities for investigation before the Nov. 28 elections, he added.
In his report to the committee, Tsai said the Government Service Network was dealing with an average of about 2.58 million cyberintrusion attempts per day as of last month, a sharp increase from June.
The NSB does not rule out that the increased activity was linked to preparations for interference in the local government elections, he said.
Asked by reporters about an incident in which comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), who is known for making fun of Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), was injured in an allegedly staged traffic accident, Tsai said it had crossed a serious line in Taiwan’s democratic and rule-of-law society.
Prosecutors in New Taipei City suspect that the incident was instigated by China to stop Huang from performing.
Several people, including a Chinese national identified only as “K” who allegedly planned the attack, were indicted on Wednesday.
China’s transnational repression is intensifying, with its tactics shifting from surveillance and violent intimidation to other forms of harassment intended to evade Taiwan’s laws, including the alleged staging of traffic accidents, Tsai said.
The priority in that case is to protect the victim and to ensure that those responsible face severe punishment, he added.
Local networks that cooperate in incidents such as the attack on Huang are mostly criminal gangs or private investigation firms linked to organized crime, Tsai said.
“The NSB is concerned with whether anyone behind them has been directed and funded by the Chinese Communist Party. How to dismantle the entire criminal group and network is a key focus for us,” he said.
Taiwan might need to amend its laws to better deal with China’s activities, he added.
The Supreme Prosecutors’ Office in a separate statement yesterday said people should be more vigilant and never assist hostile foreign forces or allow themselves to be exploited as local collaborators.
Separately, China Coast Guard activities to the east of Taiwan are becoming more routine, and often involve research vessels, Tsai said.
He said he was particularly concerned with the appearance of Chinese militia boats to Taiwan’s east and southwest.
“Generally speaking, militia fishing boats are more commonly seen in the South China Sea, so the emergence of this situation around Taiwan is significant,” Tsai said.

After three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

Israel’s general election is fast approaching, with little clarity about who might win. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is more likely to lose in Tuesday’s vote. His polling is poor, and the fractious opposition parties might yet find a way to form the next government.
What would such a government do? Most of the Zionist opposition parties, the frontrunners to lead such a coalition, have offered bromides about good governance and unifying the country. Others have focused on more specific plans to establish a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures around the attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, and end the exemption from military service enjoyed by most ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.
However, if a new government truly plans to build a better future, Israel needs more profound changes. Simply ousting Netanyahu would not be enough.
Illustration: Mountain People
The two issues the opposition has highlighted are understandably important to Israelis. For so many citizens, the disaster of Oct. 7 and subsequent two-year hostage crisis became a crisis of faith in the state itself. Without accountability through an independent inquiry, society cannot move on. And even staunch supporters of peace cannot tolerate the rank injustice of some citizens serving and dying in wars while others are systematically let off the hook.
Israel’s war in response to Oct. 7 has continued to devastate Palestinian society. The past few years have damaged Israel internally as well.
Social solidarity in Israel is abysmal. Hundreds of thousands of reservists have served for months, interrupting their studies, family life and income. Up to 30,000 people have been wounded, Israel’s Ministry of Defense said.
Meanwhile, the government has slashed social service budgets in favor of defense spending. The psychological toll is immense, yet Israel had a shortage of psychiatrists even prior to the war.
“The mental health situation is catastrophic, and so are the social systems that are supposed to support mental health, like outpatient clinics and Kupot Holim [Israel’s state-mandated health funds],” youth and child psychiatrist Graciela Cors said.
These problems are urgent, but addressing them would amount to damage limitation. Without deeper change, better-funded services and greater conscription would do little more than help Israel cope with the next round of seemingly endless wars.
Israel desperately needs to confront the factors that brought the country to this point to begin with.
Before Hamas’s attack, 2023 was already the year these long-festering problems burst into full view. Society was torn apart by two unreconciled, deeply interconnected questions: What kind of democracy should Israel be, and what is the future for the Palestinians?
Historically, Israel has demonstrated a flawed, ambiguous commitment to democracy. It avoided writing a constitution, and has no law that explicitly guarantees equality to all citizens. However, over the past 15 years, that ambiguity has given way to a full-blown assault on democratic institutions. Attacks on the judiciary came from top governing officials, culminating in the Netanyahu government’s plans in 2023 to drastically weaken judicial independence.
That top-down assault fell on fertile ground because of a deeper problem: the erosion of democratic values, shaped in part by education. Or Kashti, the former longtime education correspondent for Haaretz (where I also write), told me that the seeds of the judicial assault are found in the new civics textbook adopted in 2016. He has traced a shift from vague treatment of democracy in earlier decades, to what he describes as “indoctrination,” with greater emphasis on Jewish identity and state power. This is a thin and misguided view of democracy, one that risks elevating the will of the majority above all other democratic values.
The curriculum can also be alarmingly parochial. Kashti said that history matriculation exams focus on World War II and the Holocaust, the wars of modern Israeli history and the establishment of the Zionist movement.
“All other topics in history of the world are marginal,” he said, adding that religion infiltrates unrelated subjects.
“In geography or weather lessons, children are told to learn the prayer for rain. What’s the connection between prayer for rain and a lesson on geography and climate change?” he asked.
This narrow conception of democracy helps explain how, in 2022, half the country elected parties that sought to hobble judicial institutions as part of the coalition government’s program. And when education gives barely any attention to human rights, civil liberties and the equality of all citizens — it becomes easy to see why Palestinian self-determination has dropped off the Israeli agenda entirely.
For decades, Israeli society has increasingly acted on the assumption that Palestinians could be contained through military force or control. In the years before Oct. 7, most Israelis saw no contradiction between democracy at home and their active military occupation regime effectively ruling over all Palestinians, without giving them rights or representation.
Netanyahu’s government has pursued the logical end of occupation — permanent annexation, ever-expanding settlements and ethnic cleansing. To do that, the government had to destroy the final guardrails on its power. The 2023 assault on the judiciary finally galvanized many Israelis, who feared that their own liberties were under threat. Massive protests followed, plunging the country into prolonged social turmoil.
No Israeli government can offer a different future without fundamental and comprehensive change on these deepest issues. What is needed is a fundamental reassessment of the country’s entire social ethos.
The good news is that such change is absolutely possible. Education curriculums can be rewritten to embrace the principles of a modern liberal democracy. Teachers, politicians and even religious leaders can embrace human and civil liberties, minority rights, checks and balances, good governance and the universal values that too many Israelis disdain today. Societies and people can change.
In such a society, it would be the occupation, rather than democracy, that would become an unsustainable affront to the values of Israel.
This is a long way off; the opposition leaders demonstrate no vision leading to such an outcome, and change is needed much more urgently. Israel’s right wing and many ordinary citizens, shaped by years of fear, would fight any change favoring Palestinian independence. However, without embarking on the path, the country would never get there; needless to say, Palestinians would never be free.
None of this would transpire if Netanyahu wins or if Israel’s elections yield a stalemate, but an opposition victory should be the day when the hardest, yet most hopeful, work will begin.
Dahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analyst and author of The Crooked Timber of Democracy in Israel.

Gazing fearlessly into the abyss of Scorpio season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:12 UTC
