As autumn reaches its peak, the intense energy of Scorpio forces us to confront the ugly, buried truths that have been festering in the dark for far too long.
The formidable hunter Orion was extremely arrogant, boldly proclaiming that he could kill every animal on Earth. Mother Earth, wanting to put an end to this threat to nature, sent forth a giant scorpion. Quietly emerging from beneath the earth, the scorpion struck with precision, stinging Orion on the heel and ending his arrogance. Eventually, the scorpion was elevated into the night sky, becoming the constellation of Scorpio.
INTENSE MONTH
Illustration: Morin K.Y.
Scorpio falls at the point in the Earth’s seasonal transition, when autumn reaches its fullest intensity and its energy becomes most concentrated. Oct. 24 to Nov. 22 marks the peak of autumn’s energy. This energy carries the force of bringing things buried deep beneath the earth to the surface, drawing hidden truths and that which is concealed in darkness into the light. Much like the ambition lurking beneath Orion’s arrogance and his disrespect for all living things, the world contains countless hidden ugly and dark truths. During this month, when Scorpio energy is at its most intense, all these hidden truths will be exposed.
Like a wound on the Earth itself, the more it is covered up and the more the truth is concealed, the less chance the wound has to form a scab and heal. The very purpose of sending forth the scorpion is to eliminate, as much as possible, the harm caused by those with arrogant ambitions and excessive pride, the pain of the sting forcing them to reflect on their actions in the hope that they will grow from the experience.
THE UGLY SIDE OF SCORPIO SEASON
During Scorpio season, the world will reveal more of its ugly and filthy sides, causing even those who are much admired to fall from grace. During this month, the darker sides of our inner worlds will be more likely to surface. Yet Scorpio season is precisely when we should devote time and attention gazing deep into the abyss because it is there where we can reflect more clearly.
The energy of this month is particularly well suited to revisiting unresolved problems, tracing them back to their roots, finding appropriate solutions and ultimately reaching reconciliation. Those facing legal difficulties who did not receive justice, may go through a more painful struggle this month because the parties involved may all share deeply entangled karmic ties that cannot easily be severed.
Additionally, during Scorpio season, those in intimate relationships should not shy away from engaging in honest and meaningful discussions about commitments or the division of assets. This could be a make-or-break conversation, so give the opportunity presented by this month the respect it deserves.
SCORPIO AND INVESTING
Meanwhile, the stock market may undergo some rather dramatic changes this month. Stable markets may be the domain of other zodiac seasons, but the investment world becomes a high-risk arena during Scorpio season. For those of you who trade using leverage, pay close attention to the information you rely on and how quickly you make your decisions.
As for the energy affecting individual zodiac signs: Cancer, if you have plans to conceive this month, there may be good news ahead. Maintaining a positive state of mind and making sure your body receives the nutrients it needs will be especially important. If you are not planning to conceive, be sure to practice safe sex.
Aquarius, you may experience quite noticeable emotional fluctuations. Do not worry; there is nothing wrong with you. By allowing certain emotions to surface and be released, you may actually find clarity on questions that have left you confused for quite some time. Make the most of this opportunity.
Finally, may everyone who has been hurt by ugly truths concealed in the shadows find genuine peace and tranquility during this Scorpio season, a month in which the truth is brought to light.

NTUH, Adata Tech unveil medical AI sanitation robot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:09 UTC
01:44:09 KST

National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) and Adata Technology on Tuesday unveiled a jointly developed artificial intelligence (AI)-piloted medical-grade sanitization robot in a potential breakthrough for public health.
The sanitation robot, which comprises a mobile platform, algorithmic visual recognition system and an innovative robotic arm, has been used to sterilize operating and endoscopy rooms at the hospital, NTUH superintendent Yu Chung-jen (余忠仁) told a news conference.
Each feature is necessary for the robot to navigate through spaces cluttered with medical equipment, recognize objects that require sterilization and perform cleaning procedures with dexterity, he said.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
The robot’s AI also keeps records of the object, location, time and result of sterilization procedures for review, Yu said.
The hospital recognized the need for an advanced sanitization robot during the COVID-19 pandemic, as keeping the hospital sterile was time-consuming and required many personnel, he said.
The risk of exposing sanitization personnel to the virus was another factor for automating the process, he said.
Adata supplied the technology and the hospital provided a test venue and feedback, he said.
The NTUH uses the second-generation model of the robot, which has reduced the number of night shift staff needed by four people, NTUH deputy superintendent Tan Ching-ting (譚慶鼎) said.
The third-generation robot can be programmed for specific routes and sterilization missions appropriate to the working space, including patient rooms, clinics and public areas, he said.
Adata executive vice president Ivan Lin (林昭陽), who is also chairman of Adata AI Technology, said the robot design emphasizes adaptability to the environment and meeting real-world needs.

Police bust illegal plastic disposal ring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:08 UTC
01:44:08 KST

Environmental authorities collaborated with prosecutors and police to bust an illegal plastic waste disposal ring in Miaoli County that involved illicit gains of more than NT$70 million (US$2.2 million).
The Environmental Management Administration’s Central Center of Environmental Management found that a plastic recycling company used non-compliant raw materials to make solid recovered fuels.
It further identified an environmental engineering company that falsely claimed to be a certified plastic waste disposal operator.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
The center worked on the case with the Miaoli County Environmental Protection Bureau and the Miaoli District Prosecutors’ Office.
A task force was set up and led by prosecutor Wu Chia-wei (吳珈維) in collaboration with the Seventh Special Police Corps and the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation Bureau.
The administration on Tuesday said that the fake plastic waste disposal operator collected massive amounts of mixed waste plastics at high disposal fees from plastic packaging production plants in different administrative areas.
The operator then transferred the plastic waste mixtures to two plastic recycling companies, which left the waste piled up in rented industrial buildings, it said.
The task force found that the “waste mountains” contained not only plastics, but also other business waste such as rubber and wooden pallets, it said, adding that the volume amounted to 4,287cm2.
The two companies claimed that they piled up the waste plastics for reuse, it said.
However, the waste was a mixture of various materials instead of a single type of plastics, the administration said, adding the two plastic recycling companies did not have a permit for handling such mixed waste.
The two companies generated illicit proceeds of about NT$24.18 million and NT$2.92 million respectively, while the fake plastic waste disposal operator earned more than NT$44.51 million, it said.
The prosecutors’ office has applied to the court for confiscation of all illicit gains and instruments of the crime, including two excavators and two plastic shredders, it said.
It has also indicted six people allegedly involved in the case and the three companies in accordance with Article 46 of the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), the administration said.
Those who dispose of waste without a permit could be sentenced to one to seven years in jail, with a fine of up to NT$15 million, it said.

Australia and East Timor sign deal to boost security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:07 UTC
01:44:07 KST

Australia and East Timor yesterday signed a defense deal boost cyber and maritime security as Canberra seeks to curb China’s influence among its island neighbors.
Australia is East Timor’s largest defense and security partner and the agreement will significantly increase defense exercises, Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles told reporters.
“This is a time to double down on friendship, to double down on family,” he said in East Timor’s capital, Dili.
Photo: Reuters
Australia will provide A$62 million (US$43.5 million) for cyber security, maritime security, infrastructure, disaster relief and training, under the defense framework signed yesterday by Marles and East Timorese Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao, a statement from Canberra said.
East Timor, about 700km northwest of Australia, gained independence from Indonesia in 2002.
Australia has expressed concerns over the rapid expansion of China’s navy and the presence of Chinese police in several Pacific island countries.
As part of yesterday’s agreement, Australia would also give East Timor three additional police vessels, Marles said.
Gusmao told reporters the agreement would help East Timor fight organized crime and illegal fishing.
Australian National Security College expert associate Euan Graham said that Canberra is facing difficulty “matching its recent cut-through in the Pacific” in South East Asia.
East Timor is situated close to the northern city of Darwin, which hosts a rotating force of US Marines, and is “a key location for the security of Australia’s northern approaches,” Graham said.
“It is vital for Canberra to ensure that Dili, at very least, does not provide strategic access to China,” he said.
Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun (董軍) met with East Timor’s leaders in Dili and offered to “take military-to-military relations to a new level,” Beijing said in August.
East Timorese Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation Bendito dos Santos Freitas visited Moscow for talks this month.
Australia has struck a series of defense and economic agreements with Pacific islands including Vanuatu, Fiji and Papua New Guinea, designed to limit China’s security role.
The A$500 million Vanuatu agreement states that no foreign military base or infrastructure can be built there and Australia is the archipelago’s main policing partner.
However, Vanuatu’s police minister on Wednesday rejected that the deal would require Chinese police to be “phased out,” and Vanuatu’s police force published images on social media of Chinese police training officers to use surveillance drones.

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi yesterday said he spoke to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris wrote on Facebook.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, Burmese authorities say, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Photo: AFP
Agence France-Presse could not immediately reach Aris — who lives in the UK — and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.
However, he posted images accompanying his Facebook post that appeared to show him standing outside the Burmese embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
The Burmese military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.
However, in the past few months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.
Authorities on Monday said she received a package from King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.
Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, Burmese authorities said, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing — who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup — was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he might be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

Executive Yuan approves draft tax incentives for TISAs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:04 UTC
01:44:04 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday approved draft tax incentives for the Taiwan Individual Savings Account (TISA) program, allowing annual deductions of up to NT$24,000 (US$738.30) to encourage long-term investment and retirement savings.
TISAs are government-backed, long-term savings accounts launched in July last year to help people prepare for retirement.
The government hopes TISA could become a “third pillar” of Taiwan’s retirement system, alongside labor insurance benefits and employer-funded labor pensions, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said.
Photo: CNA
Under the revisions, taxpayers could deduct up to NT$24,000 a year per person from their gross consolidated income for TISA contributions made for themselves, their spouses and their dependent minor children.
Withdrawals would also be tax-exempt for account holders aged 60 or older, or those who have held a dedicated account for at least 30 years.
Special provisions would cover death, serious illness and other major life events, the Cabinet said.
The measures require a legislative amendment before they can take effect.
The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) is to draft revisions to the Securities Investment Trust and Consulting Act (證券投資信託及顧問法) for Cabinet review, with the government aiming to complete the legislative process next year and apply the incentives to income tax filings in 2028.
Since its launch, TISA’s total assets have exceeded NT$21.64 billion, FSC Deputy Chairman Chuang Hsiu-yuan (莊琇媛) said.
The first phase included 53 funds with dedicated TISA share classes, while funds previously included in the “I Really Want to Retire” initiative brought the total to 84.
More than 270,000 TISA accounts have been opened since the program launched, Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) quoted Cho as saying.
TISA was introduced by the FSC and the Taiwan Depository and Clearing Corp (台灣集中保管結算所) to encourage regular, long-term investment. It offers access to selected mutual funds with reduced management fees and no subscription fees, with monthly investments starting at NT$1,000.
The first phase offers no tax incentives, but would continue operating alongside the proposed TISA 2.0.
Existing account holders could retain their current accounts or open separate accounts to qualify for the new tax benefits, officials said.
Whether the incentives would apply retroactively remains under discussion.

The fake commute: How China’s unemployed save face
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:01 UTC
01:44:01 KST

A photo of a home-cooked lunch almost exposed Coco Li’s secret.
The 32-year-old, a former employee of a Chinese state-owned property firm, had been about to share it in her family group chat before catching herself. Her mother might ask why she wasn’t at work.
Li is one of many unemployed Chinese hiding their joblessness from relatives, wary of the concern and pressure that often follow in a labor market where finding work has become increasingly difficult.
Photo: AFP
“She would fall into an endless cycle of anxiety and eventually pass that anxiety on to me,” said Li, who quit more than six months ago, citing high workload and little recognition. Her mother’s concern “couldn’t really solve my problem,” she added.
PRETENDING TO BE EMPLOYED MAY EASE SOCIAL TENSIONS
The scale of online engagement suggests pretending to have a job is widespread.
Posts advising where to spend the day, how to dodge relatives’ questions about work, and chronicling the experiences of pretend-workers have drawn more than 70 million views on the Instagram-like RedNote app and 610 million views on Douyin, China’s TikTok. On X-like Weibo, related hashtags have drawn up to 320 million views.
Analysts say the phenomenon is a stark reflection of a weakening job market in an economy increasingly reliant on roaring exports. As Monday’s third-quarter data showed, manufacturers are battling fierce competition by slashing prices and payrolls while piling heavier workloads onto remaining staff.
A prolonged property market crisis and tight local government finances have also hurt jobs and incomes, along with automation and rapid AI adoption.
Diana Fu, an associate professor of Chinese politics at Cornell University, says pretending to go to work allows people to save face and potentially defuse collective discontent.
This helps preserve social stability as Beijing pushes ahead with automation and its tech race against the US, she said.
“Pretend-workers are helping the Chinese government to stave off the hard choice between leaping ahead in automation and protecting job security, which is so essential to the social contract,” she said.
LURKING IN PARKS, MALLS, LIBRARIES
Most social media posts share tips on how to spend the day away from home, drifting through parks, libraries, cafes and shopping malls, in scenes reminiscent of salarymen who hid their joblessness in South Korea and Japan during the Asian financial crisis in the 1990s.
Li follows similar routines when her parents visit.
“I never would have believed the library would be completely full on a weekday,” said Zhang, 36, a visual effects producer who lost her job in AI-driven redundancies in August. She gave only her surname.
In other posts, users wonder if the people around them are in a similar predicament, or — echoing Li — explain why they hide and how it makes them feel.
Some posts are daily journals. In one titled “Day 30 of unemployment: a month pretending to work,” a user recounts 80 failed job applications.
Susan Sun, 28, has concealed her layoff from an Internet company since late last year. The balancing act became more complicated in May when her mother and stepfather moved in with her in the megacity of Chongqing from their smaller hometown to look for work.
This forces her to leave home before 9am and return after 6pm.
Sun lives on 1,864 yuan (US$278) per month in unemployment benefits and what remains of her severance package. She says she is happy living on little and not working. Her only pressure comes from her parents.
“They pass their anxiety on to me, through subtle, insistent expressions and tone of voice,” she said, especially when they advise her to save money because “the economy is bad.”
Yige Dong, an assistant professor of sociology at the University at Buffalo, says China’s relatively thin social safety net, compared with those in Japan and South Korea during the 1990s, could eventually make it harder for the unemployed to keep up the pretense.
At some point, “individuals would probably be more concerned with pooling resources from all available sources, including borrowing from family members and relatives,” Dong said.

EDITORIAL: Beware of money-pit legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

As the nine-in-one local elections draw nearer, the opposition-dominated legislature have proposed and passed a slew of amendments critics described as “money-pit” legislation that would not only create a fiscal imbalance, but also endanger Taiwan’s democracy.
On Friday last week, the opposition Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party voted through an amendment to Article 22 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), which stipulates that the central government shall fully subsidize National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for people aged 65 or older whose annual comprehensive income does not meet the tax-filing threshold or whose income tax rate is less than 20 percent.
The amendment would increase the central government’s annual expenditure by at least NT$40 billion (US$1.23 million) and reach more than NT$62 billion by 2049.
KMT legislators also proposed and directly forwarded to committee review an amendment to the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act (兒童及少年福利與權益保障法), which stipulates that the central government must provide a non-means-tested subsidy covering all NHI premiums for children younger than six. The proposal is projected to increase annual government expenditure by another NT$8.8 billion.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare has warned that the amendments would drain the government’s medical and welfare budgets, and shrink the subsidy budget allocated for disadvantaged nationals.
The Cabinet has approved the allocation of NT$235.7 billion in excess tax revenue to fund a universal cash handout of NT$10,000 next year. Not to be outdone, KMT legislators last week passed a special act to increase the amount to NT$20,000. That has directly been sent to a second reading and cross-party negotiations.
The KMT Central Standing Committee is resolved to push the act through before the local elections on Nov. 28, with KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (?) saying party legislators would strive to complete legislation and distribution by the end of the year.
However, the Ministry of Finance said that as the opposition-controlled legislature had amended the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法) — transferring a significantly larger share of revenues to local governments — the KMT proposal would cost more than the NT$250 billion left to the central government, which would force it to issue debt to fund the cash distribution.
Experts also warned that the proposal would contravene the Public Debt Act (公共債務法) and the Budget Act (預算法), which stipulate that government borrowing and public debt should only be used for capital expenditures, not for recurring expenditures, such as funding general cash handouts.
While advocates of cash handouts say it would boost domestic consumption and the economy, Academia Sinica research show that previous cash distributions — NT$6,000 in 2023 and NT$10,000 in March this year — showed that the marginal propensity to consume only reached 0.15 and 0.16 respectively, far below the expected standard of 1. That means the handouts had a very limited effect on stimulating public consumption and expanding demand.
The IMF has warned that indiscriminate cash handouts incur extremely high fiscal and budgetary costs, and are less efficient than targeting those who need the money when it comes to maximizing the economic multiplier effect while maintaining fiscal discipline.
As it is, the legislature has already incurred the public’s ire with its dismal record, including repeatedly extending the legislative session, failing to review urgent bills in time and delaying passage of the fiscal 2026 budget by more than 350 days. Opposition lawmakers’ promotion of “money-pit” bills without careful financial planning has further tarnished the reputation of the legislature, which has not only overstepped the Executive Yuan’s constitutional right of drafting the government budget, but also sabotaged national fiscal discipline and stability.
The working and taxpaying population has continued to decline due to a low birthrate, and legislation that waste tax revenue would only saddle the younger generation with a heavier financial burden.
The hasty passage of such bills before the elections has also triggered concerns about “vote buying” and partisan political interests. Legislation that squanders public resources and leverages taxpayer dollars to buy votes would ultimately stain Taiwan’s democracy. Regardless of whichever party takes power in the future, the country and its people would bear and pass down to future generations a depleted treasury and a legacy of debt. The public must use their right to vote wisely to stop populist policies, safeguard the country’s democracy and protect the future of young Taiwanese.

Lai outlines climate resilience plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday outlined two strategies to prepare Taiwan for a forecasted “super El Nino” later this year and the growing threat of extreme weather.
The first strategy focuses on expanding urban forests to reduce heat and strengthen the nation’s ability to adapt to climate change, while the second aims to improve the resilience of transportation networks by accelerating the transition to greener transport, Lai told the ninth meeting of the National Climate Change Committee.
The government has held more than 30 public information sessions nationwide, drawing more than 4,000 participants, Lai said, adding that the government plans to incorporate the suggestions into a national urban forest plan, which it aims to submit for approval by the end of the year.
Photo from the Presidential Office YouTube
Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun (鄭麗君) is overseeing efforts to draft special legislation for the initiative, he said.
Urban forests can reduce heat and provide shade, absorb air pollution, store carbon and reduce surface runoff, while also providing habitats for wildlife, improving urban landscapes and supporting public health, he said.
The initiative builds on a climate-adaptation plan to expand tree cover proposed in April.
The government aims to connect urban green spaces, community tree belts and natural forests to create a broader network that bolsters the nation’s resilience to climate change.
Promoting urban forests is about protecting human life, as trees serve as an important defense against extreme heat, Lai said.
Taiwan is an island nation with a high concentration of people and industries, making it essential to strengthen the resilience of critical infrastructure, as well as improve system integration to ensure emergency rescue operations, essential supplies and key supply chains remain functional when disaster strikes, he said.
Regarding the second strategy, electric buses account for more than 40 percent of buses operating in urban areas, he said.
The government will encourage private investment in green transportation infrastructure and create an environment conducive to vehicle electrification, Lai said.
The next step is to better integrate urban cooling measures with transport networks to create routes that offer shade, comfort and safety, encouraging people to walk, cycle or use public transportation, he added.
The government will also continue developing sustainable aviation fuel and green ports to help related industries align with international standards and seize opportunities arising from the transition to net zero emissions, he said.
The two strategies complement each other by addressing people’s everyday needs while supporting the nation’s broader economic and transportation goals, Lai said.
Climate governance requires cooperation among central and local governments and the private sector to ensure that Taiwan remains safe, resilient and competitive as it pursues a sustainable future, he added.

Ride-hailing firms face new rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:56 UTC
01:43:56 KST

The government has proposed amendments allowing stricter regulation of online ride-hailing platforms and lifting the “one vehicle, one fleet” restriction, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) said yesterday.
The ministry said that it has proposed amendments to the Regulations Governing the Application to Operate a Taxi Transportation Service Business (計程車客運服務業申請核准經營辦法) in response to growing demand for online ride-hailing services in the past few years.
The aim is to increase platform operators’ accountability and regulatory oversight while giving taxi drivers greater flexibility in accepting bookings from multiple taxi firms, it said.
Photo: David Chang, EPA
The amendments would require online ride-hailing platform operators to obtain commercial licenses for taxi services within one year after regulations take effect, the ministry said.
Those who fail to do so could face a maximum fine of NT$25 million (US$769,000) as well as having their business suspended.
Meanwhile, platform operators would be held responsible for maintaining service quality, providing professional training for drivers, ensuring that drivers have third-party liability insurance, and settling disputes between drivers and passengers, the ministry said.
The amendments would include supplementary measures to protect consumers and drivers, the ministry said.
The service fees charged to drivers by taxi companies and platform operators must be approved in advance by the Highway Bureau, it said.
Information about taxi drivers and their vehicles must be properly disclosed when consumers book the services online, the ministry said.
Once a booking is confirmed, drivers must not terminate services without a legitimate reason, it added.
Taxi firms and platform operators must also state in their business plans how they would protect consumer data, respond to service disruptions and defend the ride-hailing systems against cybersecurity threats, the ministry said.
As supplementary measures, the amendments would require taxi firms and platform operators to provide at least three hours of safety and service quality training to drivers every six months.
Taxi firms and platform operators should recall drivers for additional safety training if drivers commit traffic-related offenses twice in six months, the ministry said, adding that drivers can accept bookings again only after they complete the training.
The ministry said taxi drivers would be able to appeal decisions by dispatch service providers to suspend or revoke their right to accept bookings from passengers under the amendments.
The Taiwan Digital Platform Ride-Hailing Workers’ Trade Union and Taipei City Taxi Drivers’ Occupational Union thanked the ministry for the amendments.
“Ride-hailing platforms reap profits, but let drivers and taxi fleets they work with take full responsibility wherever there are traffic accidents or disputes with customers. The amendments clearly state their share of responsibilities,” the associations said in a joint statement.
Local governments should be prepared to implement the new regulations, which could take effect at the end of next month or at the beginning of December, they said.
“They should begin by helping taxi companies and platform operators provide educational training to drivers, listing terms that should be included in the standardized contract between them and drivers, setting up arbitration committees and capping the commission taxi fleets can receive,” the associations said.
Uber said in a statement that while it supports reasonable government oversight, the new regulations should be open to public input for two months, rather than two weeks.
“Before allowing drivers to accept bookings from multiple taxi firms and platform operators, several issues should be resolved first, including responsibilities for suspending drivers across multiple taxi fleets, passenger safety, accident handling and customer complaints,” it said.

Media important for accountability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:55 UTC
01:43:55 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Tuesday gave an exclusive interview on Face News (新聞面對面) — a nightly political talk show hosted by lawyer and TV presenter Arthur Hsieh (謝震武) — where he discussed a number of his administration’s achievements.
However, when asked if he would serve out a full second term as mayor, he avoided giving a direct answer, repeatedly emphasizing only that he would do a good job as mayor. It was not until reporters pressed him again the following day that he said he would complete the next four-year term.
In Chinese, there is only a one-word difference between “doing something well” (zuo hao, 做好) and “completing something” (zuo man, 做滿); however, in this context, their political implications are entirely different. The former expresses an attitude toward governance, while the latter represents a concrete and verifiable commitment to his tenure. Chiang’s statement the following day underscores that the question left unanswered during the interview still needed to be addressed.
Chiang’s responses about his administration’s achievements demonstrated similar gaps. Hsieh asked why Chiang, despite believing he has a good track record, has failed to convince the public of his performance. Chiang then cited as examples the first 30 minutes of YouBike rentals being free and the removal of motorcycles from sidewalks, saying the policies have become part of people’s daily lives.
However, Hsieh was not asking for another list of achievements — he was asking why those achievements had not translated into public support. He also pressed Chiang on whether his response had actually addressed the question.
Asked how Chiang would persuade the central government to support his proposal to relocate Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport), the mayor focused on the economic and transportation benefits it would bring. Those benefits could be reasons to support the move, but do not explain how he would negotiate with the central government, overcome institutional barriers and build cross-party consensus.
However, Chiang did not fail to answer every question. Asked whether a recent poll’s results surprised him, he responded directly. The criticism is not that politicians must always accept the premises of media questions — if they disagree, they can explain why, outline the constraints they face or state why they cannot make a commitment.
The issue exposed by Tuesday’s interview was not that politicians have too little to say, but that even the lengthiest of responses can leave crucial questions unaddressed. Chiang’s pledge on Wednesday to serve out his full term gives voters a clear benchmark to hold him accountable and underscores the need for the media to keep pressing for answers.
What a democracy needs most is not politicians who always have an answer, but those who do not evade questions.
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.

Committee seeks to tighten labeling for kids’ food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:55 UTC
01:43:55 KST

The legislature’s Social Welfare and Environmental Hygiene Committee yesterday advanced draft amendments to prevent snacks from being misleadingly marketed as suitable for infants and toddlers.
Revisions to Article 28 of the Act Governing Food Safety and Sanitation (食品安全衛生管理法) would ban foods that do not meet safety and nutritional standards for infants from being advertised or labeled in ways that imply they are suitable for young children.
It would also grant the government the authority to mandate warning labels and nutritional disclosures on foods that could lead to chronic diseases or are unsuitable for long-term consumption by children.
Photo: CNA
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Wang Yu-min (王育敏) said some snacks contain high levels of sugar, sodium or saturated fats, but companies often use deceptive slogans such as “loved by adults and kids” or “for the whole family,” which can mislead caregivers into feeding them to babies.
Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Lin Ching-yi (林靜儀) said infant foods are already subject to stricter regulations regarding nutrients and heavy metals.
The amendment aims to close a loophole whereby common foods implicitly target infants through advertising, she said.
The ministry would draft regulations setting thresholds for sugar, sodium and saturated fat content, Lin said, adding that products exceeding these limits would require explicit warning labels so parents can identify them at a glance.
Food and Drug Administration Director-General Chiang Chih-kang (姜至剛) said that rules already restrict the marketing of unhealthy snacks, candies and sugary drinks to children, including a ban on toy giveaways or claims that the snacks can replace regular meals.

TSMC seeks factory-equipment alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:55 UTC
01:43:55 KST

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) is exploring alternatives to rare earth components in factory equipment, three people familiar with the matter said, aiming to reduce the risk that Beijing’s export controls could disrupt operations at plants that make the world’s most advanced chips.
The move underscores how China’s grip on rare earths has become a vulnerability for the global semiconductor industry after the country last year put some rare earth materials, magnets and related processing technology under export controls, requiring licences.
Rare earth magnets are commonly used in motors that power moving parts in industrial equipment, including machinery in highly automated factories such as those operated by TSMC.
Photo: AP
A shortage of such specialized parts could disrupt chip production for customers in smartphone, artificial intelligence system, data center and defense supply chains.
TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has surveyed suppliers on using rare earth-free motors in factory-automation equipment, three industry executives briefed by the company on its plans said.
One of the people said the effort was driven by concerns about potential supply disruptions from China.
The discussions remain in the early stages and have not yet resulted in a broad rollout of rare earth-free equipment, two of the people said.
The Taiwanese company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
TSMC’s efforts follow statements from Taiwan and the US that they would begin looking for ways to reduce their reliance on Chinese rare earth and critical-mineral supply chains.
In June, American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene said that the US is working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) in February said that the government would support the Industrial Technology Research Institute (工研院) to develop rare earth technologies, with plans to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet an estimated 50 percent of the nation’s domestic demand.

Manila exploring cables cooperation with Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

The Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing “gray zone” activity, despite Manila’s “one China” policy, a Philippine diplomat said on Wednesday.
The Philippines and Taiwan have repeatedly complained about Chinese activities designed to pressure the countries without direct confrontation.
Felipe F. Carino III, deputy chief of mission at the Philippine embassy in Washington, told a seminar that this “pragmatic and practical approach” with Taiwan was necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Speaking at Washington’s Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name.
Security of undersea cables was vital, given that they carried nearly all intercontinental data flows “and that 60 to 67 percent of cyber incidents happen in our region,” he said.
“These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.”
Taiwan and the Philippines are exploring “practical and more pragmatic approaches in cooperation, including knowledge-sharing and capacity building,” he said.
“We see this cooperation leading toward ... addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world,” he added.
Asked if the cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but added: “I’m sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition.”
Taipei has stepped up efforts to protect undersea communications links, which are vital to the nation’s connections to the rest of the world, after several incidents involving cables and China-linked vessels.
This month, the Philippine coast guard said it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes near undersea cable corridors.
At the same seminar, Deputy Representative to the US Andrea Yang (楊懿珊) referred to the jailing in Taiwan of a Chinese ship captain over damage to an undersea cable.
Taiwan will put more resources into developing uncrewed systems to improve maritime surveillance, Yang said.
Interference with undersea cables is an issue that should be taken up by the UN, which should consider mechanisms to prevent “bad behavior,” she added.
In Beijing, China warned the Philippines that it should “strictly adhere to the one China principle with real actions” and sent Taiwan a similar message, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning (毛寧) said yesterday.

Endurance athlete makes historic swim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:50 UTC
01:43:50 KST

Ultra-endurance athlete Catherine Breed this week became the first person to swim California’s entire 1,448 km coastline, completing the journey from Oregon to Mexico in less than four months.
Breed, 33, a San Francisco Bay Area native, confronted treacherous currents, storms, sharks and sewage as she swam a steady crawl stroke for up to five hours a day during her 111-day journey, according to organizers of the Swim California expedition.
She was flanked throughout the swim by a motorized dinghy and her team’s sailboat, the Catalyst, carrying observers who kept watch on her, tracked her coordinates and filmed her progress.
Photo: AP
Swimming 4km to 8km offshore, she averaged about 16.6km a day, and spent 18 days out of the water on scheduled rest stops and breaks forced by inclement weather, spokesperson William Rinehart told reporters on Wednesday.
Breed set out from Pacific waters off the California-Oregon border on July 1 and reached the finish line at the US-Mexico maritime boundary on Monday.
Her support crew hastened Breed out of the water on several occasions when sharks were spotted. Perhaps her biggest physical challenges were heavy ocean currents running northward directly against her off northern California, intensified by super El Nino conditions prevailing in the eastern Pacific.
Barely able to make headway against the powerful current, Breed adopted a strategy in which she reversed course and backtracked north along some stretches to make up for southbound segments that became nearly impassable, Rinehart said.
To stay nourished, Breed consumed more than 6,000 calories a day, well more than required to stay fit under normal circumstances. Near the end of her journey, she took prophylactic antibiotics to ward off infections from raw sewage known to pollute waters off the California-Mexico border.
Through it all, Breed remained healthy and avoided jellyfish stings or other injuries, Rinehart said.
Breed has touted a lifelong passion for the sea and said she undertook her record-making expedition to raise awareness of the fragile ocean ecosystem and marine conservation issues.
She has already logged a number of extreme-endurance swimming accomplishments, including nine open-water records, and holds the fastest swimming time across Lake Tahoe, straddling California and Nevada.
In a YouTube video message recorded at the start of her expedition, Breed said: “I want to tell the story of how the ocean has changed my life, and I want people to protect this coastline.”

Police banned protests in parts of Paris yesterday, while Lyon banned all protests tomorrow as France braced for more demonstrations just days after student and other rallies degenerated into some of the worst street unrest in years.
Wednesday’s announcement came after French President Emmanuel Macron took an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump for exploiting the riots for political advantage in the US midterm election battle.
The Paris ban was to last from 8am to 8pm and apply to key landmarks in the French capital, including the Elysee Palace, both houses of parliament and tourist havens such as the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees.
Photo: AFP
Rallies were also prohibited in the Bastille and Republique squares, and the Chatelet-Les Halles shopping area, which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend.
Lyon officials yesterday said that given the violence that unfolded in the city on Saturday last week, it would ban “all protests” in Lyon tomorrow.
France has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted over the weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalized public buildings.
As his government struggled to contain a crisis that has damaged France’s image abroad and rattled financial markets six months before presidential elections, Macron implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also fighting an election campaign, made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain.
“There are people who campaign at France’s expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha.
Trump has sought to link the unrest to “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the US on his anti-immigration messaging.
Trump on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies.
Le Pen late on Wednesday branded Macron’s remarks as “conspiratorial” in a post on X.
“The images we saw last Saturday are not generated by artificial intelligence: they show the sad reality of what France has become after 10 years of Macronist rule,” added Le Pen, who is leading in the polls for next year’s presidential election.
The unrest overshadowed weekend demonstrations in which more than 500,000 people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France.
Since the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of fresh cost-of-living demonstrations planned for tomorrow, Macron’s government has warned it would brook no further violence.
Fresh demonstrations planned by high-school and university students were similarly struck down in Paris and Lyon.
Following a meeting on Wednesday with French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, Confederation of Labor secretary-general Sophie Binet called for a “new phase” of protests, with strikes early next month.
French Minister of Justice Gerald Darmanin on Wednesday said that, of the 2,500 people taken into custody during and after the protests, 174 had been jailed, while another 917 had been formally prosecuted.

Best fries competition heats up potato-mad Belgium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:47 UTC
01:43:47 KST

Thick or thin, greasy or crispy, with samurai sauce or a more traditional mayo dip? A TV show has been on a quest to find the best fries in potato-mad Belgium.
For four years running “La Meilleure Friterie” (“The Best Fries Shop”), a lighthearted culinary competition aired by broadcaster RTL-TVI, has been seeking out perfection among fry peddlers in the country’s French-speaking region.
Watching it is a “sacred Thursday night ritual,” host David Antoine said.
Photo: AFP
Crowning a winner among a dozen contestants is no picnic.
“There’s sometimes friction among the judges, but we always find that famous Belgian compromise” over a portion of fries, Antoine joked, referencing the country’s penchant for lengthy political negotiations.
Fried potatoes are a national dish and symbol of pride in Belgium, home to about 4,600 diners specializing in the dish known as friteries in French or frituren in Flemish.
That number “has remained stable for many years,” said Bernard Lefevre of the National Chip Shop Union, an industry group, adding that the “market is doing well.”
Each has its own flair. To Lefevre, a good chip is preferably cut from a Belgian potato of the Bintje variety and double fried in beef fat.
Size is paramount.
“Anything under 9mm is too thin and anything over 14 is too thick,” he said.
At Hill’s Burger, a diner in Brussels, chef Massimo Sefa has gone for a “size twelve” — that is “a 2mm crust and 10mm of creamy flesh,” he said.
The 23-year-old smiled nervously when the TV show’s judges entered his joint and the cameras started rolling.
The stress is worth it, he said, as the broadcast would shine a spotlight on his friterie and a win would likely send sales skyrocketing.
Sefa opened up shop with his two younger brothers, Lorenzo and Marco Sefa. For them fries are a family matter: Their grandfather ran about 10 fries shops in Brussels.
“Wow, delicious, crispy, and peeled by hand,” Fabienne De Corte, one of the judges, raved upon tasting the goods.
“Fries in Belgium are our gold,” added her husband, Patrick De Corte, who is also on the judging panel. “Every little detail makes a difference.”
The show has a devout following, including some who tag along for filming sometimes dressed as fry cones and chanting: “We’ve got the fries, we’ve got the potatoes.”
It has also had its share of controversies, particularly on the hot topic of sauces.
A technical glitch caused trouble during public voting in the first season and some grumbled the winner had bamboozled jurors with dazzling sauces, while the fries were not to everyone’s taste.
Still the show has established itself in the French-speaking Belgian media landscape at a time when fries are sometimes changing along with Belgian society.
“There are halal, vegetarian and vegan fry shops — that’s perfectly normal; society is evolving. We’re not a museum of bygone folklore,” Lefevre said.

Canada holds together — against Donald Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:45 UTC
01:43:45 KST

Canadians are proving to be a voice of sanity. In roundly rejecting the idea of separating from Canada, voters in the oil and gas-rich province of Alberta sensibly backed the nation-building strategy of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. He has put Alberta at the center of his plan to make Canada an energy superpower that is “much less dependent on the United States.”
US President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st US state were a fillip for Carney in Alberta, a landlocked western province where liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. The stakes were high: A successful separatist campaign would have handed Trump leverage over Canada’s resource belt. The result instead lets Carney cast Alberta’s mineral wealth as a national asset, rather than allow separatists to define it as a regional grievance.
Albertans were not offered a binding secession vote. They rejected the idea of beginning the process toward such a vote. The early result — about 75 percent against 25 percent — looks emphatic. For all the separatists’ talk of “success,” Albertans did not buy their tactical argument: that voting for a referendum would strengthen the province’s hand against Ottawa.
However, the sense of alienation in the province is profound: Polls show that Albertans think most of the country does not respect the region.
Addressing that alienation has come at a worrying cost, politically and environmentally. Carney, who was raised in Alberta’s capital, Edmonton, made a series of pacts with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith. He agreed to back a new 1 million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline and tear up environmental rules. Carney has to deliver tangible gains, or else the sizable faction that supports separatism within Smith’s United Conservative party would entrench itself and look for future opportunities to act.
Whatever replaces the “Let Alberta decide” movement would have an uphill struggle. In his book The Republic of Alberta, the journalist Tyler Dawson wrote that it has “no charismatic leader like Rene Levesque, the suave, smoke-wreathed Quebec separatist who took his province to its 1980 secession referendum. There is no culturally entrenched canon of nationalist literature to fill Alberta bookshelves. The province has no unique language or race or faith that binds its residents together.”
Yet victory this month for the Levesque-founded Parti Quebecois in provincial elections reveals that separatists can win power despite their raison d’etre being unpopular.
To those who witnessed the Brexit referendum, the Albertan poll offered a depressing rerun of nationalist gripes and political fantasy. The easy assurance that sovereignty can be recovered painlessly is wearily familiar.
Keith Wilson, an architect of Alberta’s separatist movement, calling the task of founding a country “super easy” would prompt a sense of deja vu. Perhaps most importantly, Blackfoot leaders saying that separatists regarded treaty nations as a “speed bump” is a sign that the sovereigntists have not caught up with the fact that First Nations’ rights are belatedly being recognized as a critical part of Canada’s constitutional makeup.
Canada’s unity is a political achievement that is continually negotiated among regional interests, Quebecois nationhood, indigenous people’s rights, new arrivals and the continental pull of the US.
Paradoxically, the insecurity that characterizes Canadians keeps them in check — and holds the nation together. Or as one of the country’s most famous novelists put it: Canada is “not a country you love, it is a country you worry about.”

Ministry seeks NT$6bn in smart farm upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:44 UTC
01:43:44 KST

The Ministry of Agriculture yesterday at a Cabinet meeting proposed a NT$6 billion (US$185 million) budget over four years to develop smart and resilient agricultural facilities.
The Cabinet on Aug. 31 approved the ministry’s agricultural machinery development program, with a budget of NT$9.2 billion over four years.
Combined with the NT$6 billion budget, a total of NT$15.2 billion would be allocated to support the ministry’s efforts in upgrading greenhouse agriculture and strengthening production resilience, the Cabinet said.
Photo: CNA
The NT$6 billion budget was planned under the ministry’s smart and resilient agricultural facility development program, which would run form next year to 2030, Agriculture and Food Agency Deputy Director-General Chen Chi-jung (陳啟榮) said at a post-Cabinet meeting news conference.
The program aims to promote domestic agriculture’s smart transition, disaster resilience, production stability, energy saving and carbon reduction by upgrading four key agricultural technologies, he said.
First, more enhanced greenhouses or net houses would be built with subsidy rates ranging from 50 to 65 percent, Chen said.
Second, smart environmental control equipment powered by artificial intelligence of things — such as hypochlorous acid water disinfection systems — would be introduced to enhance greenhouse microclimate management, he said.
Third, nutrient solution management and subsurface drainage systems would be adopted for precision fertilization and water drainage, thereby accelerating farmland rehabilitation, Chen said.
Fourth, modular vertical farming methods would be used to increase land use efficiency as well as crop resilience, he said.
Regarding the NT$9.2 billion program, the ministry said it aims to address the aging workforce and labor shortage in agriculture by developing a farming machinery assistance system.
Chen said that the ministry would subsidize the purchase of 65,000 agricultural machines to save 1.2 million days of labor.
The existing machinery sharing system would be expanded, doubling the total service area, he said.
The ministry said the number of machinery farming service groups would be increased to 130 from 59, making high-efficiency machinery farming services affordable to smaller farmers.
Chen said that the NT$9.2 billion budget would also be used to build sites for agricultural machinery inspections and operation safety training.
The goal is to inspect at least 300 machines and organize up to 400 training sessions, he said.
To boost the nation’s food security, low-temperature grain silos would be bought to extend the shelf life of stock paddy by two years, Chen said.
Citing Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰), Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said that stabilizing agricultural production and stepping up agricultural transition have become imperative amid climate change and an aging farm population.
The ministry in 2017 launched a scheme for the construction of enhanced greenhouses and net houses, Cho was cited as saying.
As of last year, the scheme has extended to 2,912 hectares of farmland nationwide and reached a stable annual fruit and vegetable supply at about 150,000 tonnes, drawing a total of 5,824 young farmers to agriculture, he said.
Analyses of post-Typhoon Danas agricultural losses showed that only 17 percent of the subsidized steel-framed greenhouses or net houses were damaged, showing that such enhanced facilities have outstanding disaster resilience, Cho said.
Agricultural labor shortage also dropped from 6.9 percent in 2019 to 5.3 percent in 2024 after the ministry expanded its farming machinery subsidy scheme in 2019, he said.

Differing views on foreign talent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

Only 107,812 babies were born in Taiwan last year, barely half the number recorded in 2016. The nation is now a super-aged society, with more than one-fifth of its population aged 65 or older.
The National Development Council forecast that the population could fall from an estimated 23.2 million this year to just 12.1 million in 2075.
The decline in the working-age population would be even more severe. The number of people aged 15 to 64 is projected to plunge from an estimated 15.8 million this year to 5.1 million by 2075, a reduction of about 67 percent. By then, people aged 65 or older could constitute 52.9 percent of the population.
Taiwan is beginning to recognize something that many governments still hesitate to say openly: Family subsidies alone cannot repair a labor shortage that has already been determined by births that did not happen 20 or 30 years ago.
Its answer is an increasingly deliberate, although still incomplete, attempt to attract and retain foreigners.
Amendments to the Act for the Recruitment and Employment of Foreign Professionals (外國專業人才延攬及僱用法) took effect this year. They extended digital nomad visas to as long as two years, made it easier for foreign graduates of local universities to remain and work in Taiwan, expanded access to employment insurance and labor pensions, and shortened permanent-residence pathways for some highly skilled professionals.
The message is significant. Taiwan is no longer looking only for temporary employees. It is cautiously competing for taxpayers, engineers, entrepreneurs and graduates who might build their lives in the nation.
Taiwan already has more than 800,000 foreign workers, representing about 7 percent of its workforce, roughly twice that of Japan. Workers from Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand have become indispensable to local factories, construction sites, hospitals and long-term care system. However, Taiwan’s policy remains divided between welcoming internationally mobile professionals and controlling the lower-paid migrant workers on whom much of its economy depends.
Under the National Immigration Agency’s Alien Permanent Resident Certificate (APRC) criteria, applicants using the salary route must demonstrate average monthly income exceeding twice Taiwan’s minimum wage, which is something out of reach for blue-collar employees.
Taiwan nevertheless appears to be moving toward the idea that selected foreigners should be encouraged not only to work, but also to settle.
Japan is moving in a more cautious direction.
Its demographic arithmetic is equally unforgiving. Japan recorded 671,236 births last year, a fall of 2.2 percent from the previous year. Its total fertility rate declined to 1.14, while deaths exceeded births by 918,253.
Japan’s population is projected to decrease from 126.1 million in 2020 to about 87 million in 2070. Its working-age population could shrink from about 74.2 million in 2022 to 45.4 million over the same period.
Japan is not, as is sometimes claimed, closing its borders. It had a record 2.57 million foreign workers in October last year, an increase of 11.7 percent in a single year. The number of foreign residents exceeded 4.1 million by the end of last year.
Companies need the workers, and the government has continued expanding employment programs to obtain them. The country would struggle to operate its factories, hotels, restaurants, farms, construction projects and care facilities without foreign workers. Yet Japan is drawing a sharper distinction between allowing foreigners to work and allowing them to stay permanently.
Under revised permanent-residence guidelines, Japan is introducing tougher expectations covering household income, pension and tax compliance, language ability and family integration. In principle, applicants might be expected to demonstrate Japanese proficiency equivalent to the B1 (intermediate) level, although exemptions apply to certain highly skilled professionals and other categories. The permanent-residence application fee also rose from ￥10,000 to ￥200,000 (US$64 to US$1,273), while other residence-renewal and status-change fees increased sharply.
None of these measures ends immigration. However, taken together they suggest a country that wants foreign workers while remaining reluctant to convert that labor into permanent membership of Japanese society.
That is the emerging difference between the two East Asian economies.
Taiwan is trying to turn at least part of its foreign workforce into long-term residents. Japan is admitting foreign workers in record numbers while placing higher barriers around permanent settlement. Taiwan’s system says, imperfectly, that more foreigners should be persuaded to remain. Japan’s increasingly says that foreigners might be needed, but continued residence must be more selectively earned.
Both approaches contain political and economic risks.
Taiwan’s liberalization remains focused heavily on professionals and investors. If migrant caregivers and factory workers remain locked into a separate, temporary system with limited mobility and settlement opportunities, Taiwan would have created a hierarchy of desirable and disposable foreigners.
Japan faces the opposite danger. A country can raise entry numbers without becoming more attractive as a permanent destination. Foreign workers compare salaries, currencies, living costs, workplace treatment and the possibility of bringing their families. They are not simply a reserve labor force waiting for Japan to select them.
Higher barriers might be politically popular, but they could make recruitment more difficult as Japan competes with Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, Europe and the Gulf states for a shrinking pool of internationally mobile workers.
Neither country can solve its demographic crisis through immigration alone. Automation, later retirement, higher female employment and support for families will all remain necessary. However, migration is one of the few policies capable of affecting labor supply in the near term.
The real choice is therefore not between immigration and no immigration. Taiwan and Japan are already immigration economies, whether their political systems acknowledge it or not. The choice is whether foreign workers are treated primarily as temporary inputs or as potential long-term members of society.
Taiwan has started, cautiously and inconsistently, to place a greater bet on the second model. Japan is expanding the first while making the second more demanding.
As their populations age and their workforces contract, the results of those opposing bets will matter far beyond immigration policy. They will help determine which economy can keep its factories operating, care for its older people and remain competitive in an Asia where workers, not jobs, are becoming a scarce resource.
Taiwan has time to turn demographic necessity into a competitive advantage over its neighboring countries. It can offer foreign workers what many aging societies hesitate to provide: a realistic opportunity to become permanent residents, raise families and participate in national life.
Doing so would require fairer residency standards, stronger labor protections and pathways that extend beyond highly paid professionals. Immigration will not reverse Taiwan’s low birthrate or replace broader economic reform, but it can slow the contraction and give society more time to adapt.
The countries that attract workers will survive demographically. Those that persuade them to stay will be the ones that prosper.
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduran journalist based in Taipei. His work on Taiwan-China-Latin America relations has been published in Nikkei Asia, The Diplomat and the Taipei Times.

Agency announces critical patches for cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

The Administration for Cybersecurity yesterday urged government agencies and businesses to immediately install security updates for PHP, Node.js and Go after developers disclosed vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to remotely execute code or intercept digital certificates.
All three are open-source software: PHP is a server-side scripting language, Node.js is a JavaScript runtime environment and Go is a programming language.
Emergency safety updates for PHP and Node.js were issued on Wednesday, while updated versions for Go were issued on Monday, the agency said.
Photo: EPA
The PHP safety team identified two security loopholes, with the vulnerabilities rated 9.2 out of 10 under the CVSS v4.0 scoring system, it added.
PHP is used extensively for Web sites, content management systems and administrative interfaces, the agency said, adding that the loopholes could allow hackers to remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication.
Systems such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento also rely on PHP, it added.
In response to the potential threat, the agency said it has notified concerned organizations through cybersecurity alerts, the National Information Sharing and Analysis Center, and the Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center.
Government agencies and businesses are advised to scrutinize all PHP-based systems and related packages, check their versions and apply patches in accordance with vendor advisories, it said.
After updating, they should review system logs and unusual access, and verify the security of involved accounts and credentials if suspicious activity is detected, it added.
Node.js issued three updated versions after patching 10 loopholes, four of which were rated as high-risk vulnerabilities.
The main security loophole affects the Brotli decoder and involves an out-of-bound write that could cause memory corruption and potentially lead to remote code execution, it said.
Other issues addressed included TLS certificate validation bypasses, DNS resolution errors and permission model bypasses, the agency said.
“We urge organizations to check their servers and docker image, and upgrade to secure versions as soon as possible,” it said.
Go offered two updated versions following a recent security incident in an Indian intermediate certificate authority, which exposed eight known private keys.
The stolen keys could be used by hackers to launch man-in-the-middle attacks, the agency said.
The new Go versions add the affected intermediate certificates to a blocklist to reduce the risk of abuse of the certificate trust chain, it said.
Developers using the programming language must recompile and redeploy applications after updating the Go toolchain for the certificate-blocking mechanism to take effect, the agency said, adding that updating only the development or runtime environment is not sufficient.

Malaysia concerned over Waze data falling into Israeli hands

Malaysia concerned over Waze data falling into Israeli hands
Malaysia’s government has urged users of the navigation app Waze to uninstall the platform amid concerns that personal and movement data could fall under Israeli jurisdiction.
Malaysia, which does not have diplomatic relations with Israel and has consistently supported Palestinian rights, has also encouraged motorists to switch to TuJu, a locally developed navigation app, as an alternative.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim ordered a ban on civil servants using Waze for official duties, citing the need “to protect government information and users' personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime,” his office said in a statement.
The restriction applies to civil servants using the app for official purposes, amid warnings that location data collected through the platform could be misused and pose risks to personal and national security.
However, Malaysia’s National Security Council director-general for National Security, Raja Datuk Nushirwan Zainal Abidin, stressed that the government had stopped short of imposing a blanket ban, seeking to balance security concerns with fundamental rights, freedom of expression and individual choice.
“We always need to strike a balance between security and human rights consideration and freedom of expression, freedom to choose,” Nushirwan said during a press briefing.
He added that the concerns extended beyond technology to the legal framework governing the collection and use of personal data.
Nushirwan pointed to Waze Mobile Ltd’s terms of use, which reportedly stipulate that the agreement is governed by Israeli law.
On Thursday, Waze rejected Malaysia’s claims, saying allegations that the platform collected sensitive information or allowed any entity to exploit users’ personal data were entirely false.
“Waze operates under strict privacy policies that protect user data and comply with global legal data protection standards,” a company spokesperson said.
Founded in Israel, Waze uses satellite signals and crowdsourced data from drivers to provide real-time traffic information.
Google’s parent company, Alphabet, acquired the platform in 2013.
The latest developments follow Iraq’s announcement earlier this month that it would ban Waze from next year because the app was developed in Israel.
Iraq, like Malaysia, does not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Malaysia has consistently opposed normalisation with Israel and has previously restricted engagement with companies perceived to support the Israeli government.
Amid the genocide in Gaza and ongoing Israeli military operations and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, Kuala Lumpur has continued to advocate for Palestinian statehood and criticise Israeli policies.

MIAMI - A federal judge on Oct 22 ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec 11 in his US$10 billion (S$12.7 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC, which has accused the US president of stalling to avoid answering questions under oath, the Associated Press reported.
Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for at least US$10 billion over a misleadingly edited clip of a speech.
The case is one of several Trump has privately filed against the news media as part of wider pressure campaign against coverage he dislikes.
US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ordered Trump to take questions from the BBC’s lawyers under oath in a ruling from the bench at a court hearing on Oct 22, according to a spokesman for Trump’s personal legal team.
Trump cancelled a deposition in October, citing conflicts with his presidential duties.
The Trump spokesman said the lawsuit is aimed at holding the BBC accountable for defamation and “reckless election interference.”
The BBC declined to comment. It previously admitted the edits were misleading and apologised to Trump, though it denies being liable for defamation.
Trump’s lawsuit filed in December in Florida federal court accuses the BBC of intentionally misleading viewers into thinking he directed supporters to storm the US Capitol by splicing together different parts of a Jan 6, 2021 speech.
In court filings, the broadcaster has accused Trump and his lawyers of dragging their feet in response to their requests for records and other information that is exchanged between parties in a process known as discovery.
The BBC is seeking financial records from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club and the web of business entities associated with him, saying the information is necessary to defend against Trump’s damages claims.
Trump’s lawyers say the requests are too broad and irrelevant to the case. They have also denied in court filings that Trump is avoiding a deposition, saying Trump’s duties and security needs must take precedence.
The edited speech appeared in a BBC Panorama documentary show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, which Trump won.
