Inside Israel's deepening ties with Bosnia's Serb separatists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:39:32 UTC
01:39:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside Israel's deepening ties with Bosnia's Serb separatists
“I think that everything that Israel has done since the 7th of October is justified. Israel should not suffer.”
These words were spoken last month by Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH).
This statement was hardly surprising. In recent years, Dodik has been outspoken in his support for Israel and its genocidal war on Gaza at a time in which relations between Republika Srpska and Israel are growing.
From high-level political endorsements and the opening of an Israeli Chamber of Commerce office in Banja Luka to increasingly explicit expressions of mutual solidarity. Such growing alignment speaks to how both leaderships are seeking to bolster their international legitimacy amid mounting political pressures.
For Dodik, deep relations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could strengthen his access to Washington and bolster his long-standing ambitions to expand the Bosnian-Serb entity’s autonomy, while Israel may see the relationship as an opportunity to cultivate new allies and increase its diplomatic leverage in Europe.
The implications, however, extend beyond bilateral cooperation. In BiH, where the fragile constitutional order rests on the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, the growing alignment raises questions about the international legitimisation of separatism, the resurgence of ethnic and religious nationalist narratives, and Brussels’ ability to preserve stability in Europe’s “Inner Courtyard.”
Political calculations
Republika Srpska’s mounting tensions with some Western European governments and international institutions provide some of the necessary context for understanding the significance of Israel’s growing engagement with the Bosnian-Serb entity.
According to Dr Asim Mujkić, an associate professor of philosophy at the University of Sarajevo, the sharp decline in international support for Israel’s government has made Tel Aviv more open to unconventional partnerships.
By engaging with Dodik publicly, Israel demonstrates its ability to maintain existing partnerships while forging new ones. At the same time, Israel’s ties to the Republika Srpska government may provide Tel Aviv with greater leverage in its dealings with European powers.
“I would say the ever-growing lack of international support for [Netanyahu’s] government, the rise of criticism and even boycott by traditionally amicable countries and organisations made Netanyahu open to political adventurism of this kind. For [the] domestic public it is surely advantageous to be able to show that some political leaders in fact visit Israel,” he told The New Arab.
Giorgio Fruscione, a research fellow at the Milan-based Italian Institute for International Political Studies, sees a related but broader set of motivations. He holds that Netanyahu’s government seeks international legitimacy via relationships with political actors that have strong connections to Washington and Moscow.
Fruscione also understands disputes over the interpretation of the Srebrenica genocide as part of the political context shaping Israel-Republika Srpska relations.
Viewed at a regional level, the expansion of Israel’s partnerships with actors in the Balkans serves to counter the influence of Iran, Turkey, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, which have their own networks in southeastern Europe.
Put simply, while Israeli officials will frequently stress the importance of commercial cooperation, trade, and investment with Republika Srpska, Albania, and other players in the Balkans, there is no denying that the significance of these partnerships goes beyond stated economic objectives.
Dodik’s search for political leverage
Above all these considerations, Dodik’s main motivation for establishing closer ties with Israel seems to be his desire to enhance his access to Washington.
Although Dodik was officially removed from the Republika Srpska presidency last year, he remains the de facto leader in Banja Luka, and the Bosnian-Serb strongman is determined to continue advancing his political agenda at the expense of BiH’s fragile stability. International support, therefore, remains valuable to Dodik as he pursues his political ambitions, even if full independence is not necessarily his ultimate goal.
In terms of cultivating deeper ties with the Trump administration, Dodik has relied on conventional lobbying. But that alone might not suffice for the Bosnian-Serb leader, who can probably count on Netanyahu as a key intermediary in Washington.
Support, or at least accommodation, from the United States and Russia has benefited Dodik’s political position. With an Israeli Chamber of Commerce office opening in Banja Luka and officials from Republika Srpska and Israel increasing their public engagement, Dodik has an easier time presenting his leadership as globally connected instead of isolated.
At the heart of Dodik’s desire to bolster ties with the United States, Russia, and Israel is his interest in obtaining greater bargaining power when dealing with other actors in BiH and internationally. By invoking independence without necessarily attempting to establish Republika Srpska as an independent state (a process that would be extremely challenging and messy in practice), Dodik can gain such leverage.
There are important economic and security dimensions to Israel and Republika Srpska’s deepening ties. Dodik wants greater cooperation with Israel in technology and investment, while Netanyahu’s government is focused on energy and security as key areas of this bilateral relationship.
Yet, given the lack of concrete details available to the general public, the scale and scope of this envisioned economic cooperation remain unclear.
Nonetheless, with Republika Srpska under financial pressure, it is understandable that the leadership in Banja Luka would welcome Israeli capital alongside any political advantages that could come from this growing partnership.
Belgrade's role
Republika Srpska’s growing ties with Israel should be understood in the context of Belgrade’s relationship with Tel Aviv, given Serbia’s influence in Banja Luka. Particularly in the area of defence, Serbia has strengthened its relationship with Israel, underscored by the establishment of a drone assembly plant involving Israeli defence company Elbit Systems and Belgrade’s arms exports to Tel Aviv.
Fruscione holds that Republika Srpska’s foreign policy is not entirely independent and that Banja Luka’s international relationships remain closely connected to Serbia’s priorities on the international stage.
“Republika Srpska does not have an autonomous foreign policy. Although it may appear so, it is aligned with, if not even piloted by Belgrade. Therefore, relations between Israel and Republika Srpska must be understood within this framework,” he explained to The New Arab.
This perspective places Republika Srpska’s growing partnership with Tel Aviv within a broader network of political and economic relationships linking its leadership with Belgrade, Moscow, and Washington.
These relationships reflect overlapping, and at times competing, efforts to secure external support and advance political interests. The relationship with Israel also intersects with political cooperation between Milorad Dodik’s Alliance of Independent Social Democrats and the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, BiH’s principal Croat nationalist party.
Both parties have sought changes to aspects of BiH’s political arrangements, particularly those affecting entity autonomy, political representation, and the distribution of power, although their objectives and interests are not identical.
According to Dr Mujkić, the Netanyahu government’s engagement with Serb and Croat nationalist leaders risks reinforcing political forces that challenge BiH’s Daytonian balance. Taken together, these relationships could increase pressure on the institutions in Sarajevo and complicate efforts to develop a coordinated Bosnian foreign policy.
They also create a regional dynamic in which developments involving Tel Aviv become increasingly intertwined with Belgrade’s ambitions, internal divisions within BiH, and competing US and Russian interests amid an era of intensifying great-power competition.
"Netanyahu’s government has supported [the Croat nationalist hard-liners of the] ethnic party in Bosnia, HDZ, even economically through the presence of Amir Kabiri, [an] Israeli businessman who not only supported Croat nationalism but also distorted [the representation of the] Bosnian Jewish community. It has supported Serb nationalist hard-liners as well, so of course, such a policy [threatens the] Dayton equilibrium,” he told The New Arab.
According to Dr Mujkić, both nationalist movements have increasingly incorporated Christian nationalism and claims of an “Islamist danger” posed by Bosniaks into their political rhetoric.
The irony of history is that contemporary Croat nationalism is heir to the ideology of the Nazi-allied Independent State of Croatia, which sought to exterminate local Jews. Meanwhile, contemporary Serb nationalism draws on a radical nationalist tradition that, under Milan Nedić’s collaborationist regime in 1941, proudly declared Serbia the first Judenrein country in the ‘new Europe’
"Yet today, these are - and not, for example, [the] Jewish Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina - [who] are the ‘allies’ of [Netanyahu],” Dr Mujkić told The New Arab.
The Dayton order and Bosnia's fragile stability
Republika Srpska’s strengthening relationship with Israel stands to reinforce a political environment in which there is greater acceptance of serious challenges to BiH’s territorial dignity.
This development, as Dr Mujkić explains, fits into a wider geopolitical pattern in which Moscow’s support for local nationalist movements and shifts in Washington’s foreign policy during the Trump 2.0 era risk weakening the European Union’s capacity to respond to instability in the Western Balkans.
As Fruscione told The New Arab, Israeli support is not creating a new secessionist dynamic in BiH. Yet, it might accelerate one already underway, particularly as the EU’s internal divisions serve to complicate Brussels’ engagement with the Balkan country.
The challenges surrounding the appointment of a new High Representative, whose office provides a critical international safeguard for the Dayton framework, highlight the serious issues facing the existing system of oversight.
However, the eventual consequences of the strengthening Republika Srpska-Israel relationship remain uncertain. Tel Aviv’s growing engagement may help Dodik bolster his international standing and bargaining power, but how far Washington or Tel Aviv would go to support him remains unclear.

Aral Sea's forest shield: Over 56 million saxaul seedlings planted on dry seabed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:36:40 UTC
01:36:40 KST

Aral Sea's forest shield: Over 56 million saxaul seedlings planted on dry seabed
More than 56 million saxaul seedlings have been planted across 1.1 million hectares of the dried Aral Seabed over six years, Qazinform News Agency cites Kazakhstan's Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
The drying of the Aral Sea remains one of Central Asia’s gravest environmental disasters, leaving behind vast expanses of highly saline land. Strong winds sweep salt and dust from the exposed seabed, carrying harmful particulates across the region and far beyond.
One of the ways to mitigate the impact is to plant saxaul (Haloxylon). The shrub thrives in arid climates and highly saline soils. The plant's deep root system binds loose sands, reduces soil erosion, and suppresses salt and dust storms.
In 2021, the Head of State directed officials to expand saxaul plantations on the dried Aral Seabed to 1–1.1 million hectares.
Since the campaign began, annual land reclamation covered 101,100 ha in 2021, 250,000 ha in 2022, 193,400 ha in 2023, and 127,000 ha in 2024.
Annual coverage reached 330,000 ha in 2025, followed by 116,000 ha in 2026.
Total reclamation area now stands at 1.117 million hectares. Alongside seedling cultivation, workers have sown more than 3,440 tons of saxaul and halophyte seeds into the seabed.
Beyond targets, plant survival remains a priority. The dry seabed conditions are severe: saline soil, low moisture, high winds, and scorching summer heat.
To supply high-quality stock for ongoing reclamation, authorities constructed a 33-hectare forest nursery designed to cultivate up to 3 million seedlings a year.
Work is also underway on a second nursery located on the dried seabed. At the site, there are now modular container units and a newly drilled 500-meter well. Producing 9 liters per second, the well supplies warm, near-fresh water.
This will enable saxaul cultivation directly under Aral Sea region conditions, yielding seedlings that are better adapted to the local climate and improving survival rates after transplantation.
Scientific oversight is central to the project's execution. To guide reclamation efforts, the Kazakh Research Institute of Forestry and Agroforestry established a local branch. Two researchers work at the dried seabed.
Restoring vegetation across the former sea floor is a long-term process. Even under favorable conditions, saxaul requires years to mature into stable, self-sustaining stands.
However, these plants are vital for stabilizing the arid landscape. By anchoring loose sands and reducing wind exposure, saxaul helps halt further desertification.
Officials emphasized that the ultimate goal extends beyond initial planting numbers to establishing resilient, long-lasting green belts that could protect the region for decades.
Reforestation and reclamation efforts across the dried seabed are continuing.
As previously reported, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s environmental achievements at the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan.

Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan, head of Damascus's Fourth Criminal Court, said on Thursday that the rulings had been referred to the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol), Syria's official SANA news agency reported.
Al-Aryan explained that the in absentia judgments were not final and would be annulled if the defendants were arrested or surrendered voluntarily, allowing their trials to begin again in their presence.
He said the ruling against Bashar al-Assad was based on evidence that the court said established his responsibility for violations through the chain of command and orders issued, rather than simply his position as president.
The court is currently examining around 61 cases involving serious abuses, having already ruled on four, according to al-Aryan.
He stressed that the Fourth Criminal Court operates under Syria's Supreme Judicial Council and applies Syrian law, rather than functioning as a special or exceptional tribunal.
The court has issued rulings against several prominent figures from the former regime, including Bashar and Maher al-Assad, senior military and security commanders, and former political and religious officials.
The sentences include the death penalty and life imprisonment. Judgments were issued against defendants who were presnet for their trials, including Assad's cousins Atef Najib and Wassim al-Assad and former mufti Ahmad Hassoun.
Al-Aryan accused the Assad regime of systematically concealing evidence and information about detainees before its collapse, complicating efforts to determine the fate of thousands of missing Syrians, whose families still have no definitive proof of their fate.
Assets confiscated to compensate victims
As part of efforts to secure justice for victims, the court has ordered the confiscation of convicted individuals' assets, with the proceeds to be deposited into a designated account pending the establishment of a compensation fund.
Al-Aryan said the measure was intended to protect the rights of victims who had been unable to appear before the court or submit personal compensation claims.
He added that the court had introduced measures to protect witnesses and evidence, including witnesses called by both victims and defendants.
The judge cited the case of Atef Najib, who was previously sentenced to death, saying the court had agreed to his request to hear testimony from protected witnesses identified only by confidential numbers.
Al-Aryan insisted that Syria's transitional justice process would continue, with authorities pursuing those implicated in abuses during the country's brutal conflict.
Russia refuses to extradite Assad
The chances of Bashar al-Assad appearing before a Syrian court today appear quite low.
The former dictation has been living in Russia, where he fled following the collapse of his regime in December 2024.
On 14 October, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko reiterated Moscow's refusal to extradite Assad, declaring that its decision to grant him political asylum on humanitarian grounds was "irreversible".
Borisenko added that Syria's current authorities understood Moscow's position.
Russia has repeatedly ruled out handing over its longtime ally.
In April 2025, Russia's ambassador to Iraq, Elbrus Kutrashev, said Assad's extradition was not an option, describing such a possibility as unacceptable under any agreement.
The latest court rulings form part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to hold former regime officials accountable for abuses committed during the country's years of conflict and repression.
However, the transitional justice process continues to face significant challenges, including documenting violations, uncovering the fate of missing and detained Syrians, pursuing suspects living abroad and ensuring victims receive justice and compensation.

Finland licenses world's first permanent nuclear waste repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:27:00 UTC
01:27:00 KST

Finland has approved the operation of the world's first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel, marking a major milestone in radioactive waste management more than two decades after construction began, operator Posiva said Thursday.
Blasted into 1.9 billion-year-old stable bedrock in Eurajoki in southwestern Finland, the geological repository will house spent nuclear fuel in holes drilled into the bedrock, where it will remain harmfully radioactive for thousands of years.
"This is a great and historic day for both Posiva and Finland," Posiva chief executive Ilkka Poikolainen said in a statement.
The site, dubbed Onkalo, which means "cave" in Finnish, is expected to start operations soon, but Posiva said no exact date had been decided yet.
"No detailed schedule is given at this point for the start-up," it said.
"Before final disposal begins, Posiva will finalize the commissioning stage, carrying out the necessary tests and inspections which STUK (the Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority) also needs to verify and approve."
With space for 6,500 tons of uranium, Onkalo will provide permanent storage for spent fuel from Finland's five nuclear reactors.
The fuel will be encapsulated in copper canisters that are highly resistant to corrosion, then lowered into holes drilled in tunnels in the bedrock, which will be filled with bentonite clay and finally sealed with a steel-reinforced concrete plug.
The fuel will be highly radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After about 100,000 years, the levels will be about the same as the uranium ore of which the fuel is made, according to Posiva.
Countries have been wrestling with what to do with dangerous nuclear by-products since the first plants were built in the 1950s. Currently, most of it is in temporary storage.
Final repositories are being built in other countries, including neighbouring Sweden and in France, but Finland is expected to be first to open its underground storage facility.
The cost of the Onkalo site has been estimated at $1.16 billion.

====================================================================================================

Can Netanyahu legally launch a war against Iran before elections? Here's what the law says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:26:04 UTC
01:26:04 KST

Israel is set to hold its first elections on their legally scheduled date in 38 years next week, while a public and legal debate unfolds over a question that has never been fully tested: Can a prime minister whose Knesset has already been dissolved, and who heads a caretaker government, lead Israel into a major military campaign against Iran?
Behind the legal question lies concern about possible political motives: that a war, whether it breaks out before the elections, in the days between the vote and the swearing-in of the 26th Knesset, or in the weeks afterward, could be used to influence the election results, the composition of the next government or even the formation of an emergency government.
There is no public evidence of such an intention, and these concerns remain assessments and suspicions raised by critics and commentators. But the debate itself exposes how unclear the legal boundaries governing caretaker governments become when national security is involved.
The starting point is Section 40 of Israel's Basic Law: The Government, which stipulates that launching a war, or undertaking significant military action that is almost certain to lead to war, requires a decision by the government or the security cabinet.
The provision makes no distinction between a regular government and a caretaker government, nor does past practice. Former Cabinet Secretary Oved Yehezkel explains that the assertion that a caretaker government cannot go to war is overly sweeping and does not reflect the legal reality. According to him, restrictions on caretaker governments focus primarily on appointments and budgetary decisions, while they retain considerable freedom of action in defense and foreign affairs.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid, who served as caretaker prime minister during Operation Breaking Dawn in August 2022, emphasizes a basic principle: "A caretaker government must not take steps that fundamentally change reality. That's what a caretaker government is." Lapid himself qualifies that statement, however, saying it is "a question for legal experts."
The two precedents cited in the debate point in different directions.
During Operation Guardian of the Walls, Israel was governed by a caretaker government, but the military campaign followed Hamas rocket fire toward Jerusalem. In other words, it was a response rather than an initiative.
Operation Breaking Dawn was launched by decision of Lapid and then-Defense Minister Benny Gantz, without convening the security cabinet and with the approval of Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara. Some 25,000 reservists were called up during the operation. It was a limited military campaign launched in response to a specific intelligence warning, rather than a full-scale war. Nevertheless, it demonstrated that a caretaker government can initiate military action.
The fundamental distinction, as opposition officials describe it, lies between responding to an immediate intelligence warning and launching a war that has been "manufactured" to influence an election. Even without manufacturing a war, however, a government can argue that a particular threat is too urgent to be postponed.
It is worth listening carefully to what Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said just Wednesday at an officers' graduation ceremony at the IDF's Officer Training School:
"Mojtaba - that's the name of the current dictator, Khamenei's son, Mojtaba - has decided to follow in his father's footsteps. He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death. Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies."
In other words, Netanyahu appears to be laying the groundwork for a possible imminent war with Iran and establishing a justification for it.
The defense establishment, incidentally, is divided over the accuracy of his statements. Some senior officials ynet spoke with on Thursday said Netanyahu's assessment was accurate. Others said they had no idea what he was referring to and expressed concern that his remarks, combined with his actions, including sending dozens of fighter jets on a flight approaching the Iranian border, were intended to create a situation of "miscalculation."
According to this concern, Iran might launch a preemptive attack on Israel in the belief that Israel was about to strike, thereby providing Israel with justification for attacking Iran.
Scenario one: War before Israel's elections
Only five days remain for this scenario to materialize, a period during which the government remains fully subject to the attorney general's guidelines requiring restraint during an election campaign. The central concern here is not formal legality but the possibility that a war could affect whether the elections take place on schedule.
Such a postponement is not a decision the government can make on its own. Under Basic Law: The Knesset, extending the Knesset's term, including postponing elections, requires a majority of 80 lawmakers and exceptional circumstances. That was how the elections were postponed in 1973 because of the Yom Kippur War.
In other words, even a war would not allow Netanyahu to postpone the elections without the opposition's consent.
A former senior government official argues that a war cannot be launched for electoral reasons and that any such decision would have to be made by the government as a whole, rather than on the prime minister's initiative alone. 
According to him, judicial review cannot prevent such a decision in advance, and even the High Court of Justice would not issue an injunction against going to war. "People will be held accountable by history," he says.
Scenario two: War between the elections and the swearing-in of the Knesset
This scenario is different because the election results would already be broadly known, but the government, potentially the outgoing government, would remain in office. Under the normal legal timetable, the new Knesset would be sworn in approximately two weeks after Election Day, around November 10. The president would then begin consultations on whom to task with forming a government.
During this window, concerns arise that a war could influence the composition of the next government and create pressure to establish an emergency or national unity government. There are precedents for such developments: the national unity government formed on the eve of the Six-Day War and the emergency government established in October 2023.
From a legal standpoint, Yehezkel sees no substantial difference in the government's formal authority across the three scenarios. The distinction, he says, lies primarily in the expectation of restraint and the burden of justification: The less representative a government is of the public, the stronger the justification required for a dramatic decision.
Scenario three: After Knesset is sworn in, but before permanent government formed
During this period, parliamentary oversight is particularly weak.
Although the new Knesset has convened, its committees, including the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, generally have not yet been established. Meanwhile, the mandate to form a government is held either by Netanyahu or by whoever receives it. This creates a period in which the prime minister retains full authority while facing very limited oversight.
Here, too, the formal legal position remains the same: If the security cabinet or the government convenes and orders military action, the army may present objections, but ultimately it must carry out the decision.
This brings us to the question of institutional checks and balances, which lies at the heart of the debate. According to Netanyahu's critics, very few independent gatekeepers remain. IDF Chief of Staff Zamir and Attorney General Baharav-Miara, who may argue that a caretaker government's authority to declare war is more limited, are among the last senior figures who were not directly appointed by Netanyahu.
There are also indications that the military opposes launching an attack at this time. Mossad Director Roman Gofman and Shin Bet chief David Zini were appointed by Netanyahu, and critics argue that they owe their positions to him.
These are allegations made by Netanyahu's critics. The counterargument is that appointments by the prime minister are the standard arrangement under Israeli law and do not, in themselves, indicate a lack of independence.
The regional situation and the American dimension add further weight to the discussion. The current war against Iran began on February 28, 2026, when Zamir announced a "significant, fateful and unprecedented" military campaign coordinated with American strikes.
Another round of fighting followed in June. In late September, Israeli media reported that President Donald Trump had set a deadline: The war with Iran would end immediately after the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
Some commentators have suggested that Netanyahu is betting on a swift American strike against Iran before the midterms, which would effectively give Israel a green light and allow him to use the war as a campaign issue.
These are assessments, not established facts, and the available time is already running out. Nevertheless, they explain why October 27, November 3 and the swearing-in of the Knesset are being considered together: a period of several weeks in which two election campaigns, one Israeli and one American, overlap with decisions about whether, and how, to fight Iran.
The bottom line is that Israeli law does not prohibit a caretaker government from going to war, but neither does it give that government unlimited authority. The central legal requirement is that the decision be made by the government or security cabinet, rather than by the prime minister acting alone. Beyond that, oversight is primarily public, political and parliamentary rather than judicial.
As Yehezkel put it, it is difficult to imagine a court intervening in real time in a security decision to launch military action against Iran. The principal checks would therefore come from public opinion, Netanyahu's political rivals and the media.
That is precisely the gap between the formal legal framework and the realities of government: The law sets a relatively low threshold, while limits on the exercise of power depend largely on the restraint of those who hold it and the willingness of institutional gatekeepers, however few remain, to say no.

Two Syrian security officers killed in raid on ISIL cell near Damascus
The Syrian Interior Ministry says five suspected fighters killed and six arrested outside of Damascus.
Two members of Syria’s internal security forces have been killed and five wounded in clashes with a suspected ISIL (ISIS) cell during a raid on the outskirts of Damascus, the Interior Ministry reported.
The fighting began on Thursday morning, when security forces launched an operation against the cell in the town of Rankous in the western Damascus countryside. The operation is the latest in a series of raids as the government tries to dismantle ISIL networks and prevent attacks.
The ministry said the suspects refused to surrender and opened fire, triggering the clashes. Five alleged ISIL members were killed and six arrested, and weapons and explosive belts were seized.
Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from Syria, said residents told her the clashes began around 6am (03:00 GMT) and lasted two to three hours. Some of the wounded security personnel were seriously hurt, she said.
Residents said the group was about nine people – smaller than what officials reported – with two members killed, another two escaping, and an unknown number injured.
Residents told the local outlet Syria Now that security forces imposed a curfew and arrested several people.
Series of operations
The ministry also reportedly foiled an ISIL plot in the Damascus countryside and dismantled an ISIL cell in the Houla area of Homs earlier this month. The plots involved attacking places of worship and security patrols, according to Syria Now.
On October 6, the ministry announced the arrest of Khaled Raed Birouni, also known as Abu Hassan Dushka, in the town of Hujaira in the Damascus countryside. Authorities say he was the group’s top military commander for Homs.
They accused him of planning several attacks there, including the December 2025 bombing of a mosque in the city’s Wadi al-Dhahab neighbourhood during Friday prayers, which killed eight people and wounded 18, according to Syria’s Health Ministry.
ISIL has repeatedly attacked Syrian security forces, usually targeting buses and vehicles carrying personnel, Pett said, along with a few attacks on civilians.
Syria joined the 90-member international coalition against ISIL in November, six years after Syrian Kurdish-led forces led the territorial defeat of ISIL strongholds in the country’s northeast.

Pentagon creates agency for technological sabotage in foreign countries — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:24:20 UTC
01:24:20 KST

WASHINGTON, October 22. /TASS/. An agency tasked with technological sabotage in foreign countries has been created within the US Department of Defense, the Politico newspaper wrote.
"The Pentagon has spent months quietly building an elite new tech agency to help covertly disrupt and sabotage foreign technology programs considered threats to American military superiority," the report says.
The agency was created in April, but neither US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth nor any of the department’s key officials have made a public announcement.
It was named Technology Support Office (TSO) and is mentioned in some of the Pentagon’s internal documents, but any information about its activities is classified.
Sources told the newspaper that the agency was established on Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg’s initiative, with active participation of his senior adviser Tom Rakusan, who is a longtime veteran of the CIA’s clandestine service.
Hegseth and Feinberg shaped the new agency "by reorganizing two classified Pentagon intelligence programs that have conducted similar clandestine tech-sabotage efforts at a smaller scale since 2023."
By creating the agency, the Pentagon "is signaling its intent to ramp up a range of aggressive covert activities abroad - potentially including cyberattacks, supply chain disruptions and disinformation operations."
Sources said that one of its objectives was to obstruct research in AI technologies and unmanned systems. A Pentagon spokesperson, however, denied the information outlined in the article.
The Washington Post newspaper wrote earlier, citing sources, that the Pentagon was looking to build a more robust deep-cover spying program to conduct economic warfare against China and other US competitors. This new spy program is also being overseen by Tom Rakusan.

US to provide up to $389M for semiconductor research, development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:22:21 UTC
01:22:21 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The US Commerce Department said Thursday it plans to provide up to $389 million in research and development funding to four companies working on power semiconductors and critical materials, including technologies designed to support fusion energy and advanced data centers.
The awards, announced through letters of intent under the CHIPS and Science Act, aim to strengthen domestic production capabilities and reduce reliance on overseas suppliers for components essential to the country's energy infrastructure, it said.
“The Trump Administration is accelerating American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. “These investments expand domestic research, secure critical supply chains, and create high-paying American jobs.”
Fusion energy companies Helion and Commonwealth Fusion Systems are among the intended recipients.
Helion could receive up to $175 million to develop high-voltage semiconductors and power modules for fusion generators, while Commonwealth Fusion Systems is set to receive up to $85 million for technologies used in plasma heating, fusion diagnostics and radiation-resistant electronics.
Vertical Semiconductor could receive up to $73 million to advance gallium nitride power semiconductors for advanced computing, including a demonstration project targeting a 2.5-megawatt data center rack.
Materials supplier Sibelco is slated for up to $56 million to develop purification technologies for ultra-high-purity quartz used in semiconductor manufacturing.
The agency said improved power electronics could increase energy efficiency, strengthen grid stability and reduce heat losses, supporting growing electricity demand from data centers and other critical infrastructure.
Bill Frauenhofer, the agency’s executive director of semiconductor investment and innovation, said the awards would help advance technologies for the grid, defense systems and emerging fusion energy.

UN expert urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump's Gaza board
Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories told Reuters on Thursday.
The "Board of Peace," of which Indonesia is a key troop-contributing member, was unveiled by Trump in January to address global conflicts typically handled by the United Nations. The world's largest Muslim-majority nation has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilisation force.
Francesca Albanese, a prominent human rights lawyer known for her vocal criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause, but joining the board was dangerous.
Indonesia's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position.
Albanese has drawn the ire of a number of Western capitals. The US has imposed sanctions on her, and others, including her own native Italy, have called for her resignation.
"I understand (Indonesia's) good intentions. I still think that it's very dangerous, because it risks to normalise a very abnormal mechanism," she said.
Albanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians.
Rights experts have criticised the board for not including a Palestinian representative even though it is meant to supervise the temporary governance of a Palestinian territory.
The Board of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside US business hours.
Indonesia, which backs a two-state solution and has repeatedly condemned Israeli violence, has drawn criticism from domestic Muslim groups for agreeing to join the board, which also counts Israel as a member.
President Prabowo Subianto has vowed to quit if it does not bring benefits to Palestinians, his office has previously said, adding that joining the board would allow Indonesia to push for cessation of violence.
Albanese said Indonesia risked compromising its close ties with Palestinians. "It's very risky to do so when the rules are set by Israel," she said.
Albanese recommended Jakarta join the Hague Group of countries, which includes South Africa and Indonesia's neighbour Malaysia and seeks to uphold international law and processes, including in the International Criminal Court over Israel's actions.
Trump's Gaza plan has stalled. A 2025 ceasefire secured the release of the remaining captives held by Hamas and hundreds of Palestinian detainees, but efforts to disarm Hamas and secure an Israeli withdrawal have faltered, while Israeli forces continue near-daily attacks in Gaza.

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:17:10 CEST
01:17:10 KST

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
As part of the County Pairings Programme, which matched each of Ireland's 26 counties with an EU member state, the north-western County Donegal, a home to just over 161,000 people, was paired with Poland until the end of December.
Thanks to the initiative of the Irish authorities and the efforts of the Polish Embassy in Dublin, the pairing has helped raise awareness in Ireland of Pawel Strzelecki, a largely forgotten Polish hero of the Great Irish Famine. The unveiling of a commemorative plaque at a school in Donegal brought the achievements of the Polish explorer, geographer and philanthropist to the attention of local residents for the first time in 178 years.
In Poland, Strzelecki is best known for naming Australia's highest mountain Mount Kosciuszko in 1840, in honour of the Polish national hero Tadeusz Kosciuszko, whom he admired throughout his life. Strzelecki was the first Pole to undertake a scientific expedition around the world, travelling through both the Americas, the Pacific region, Australia and Tasmania. He also played a remarkable role in Irish history.
During the Great Irish Famine, Strzelecki worked on the island as a volunteer for a British humanitarian organisation. By introducing an innovative food distribution system centred on schools, he helped save the lives of as many as 200,000 children, both Catholic and Protestant.
The Polish explorer and philanthropist visited famine-stricken Ireland twice, working without pay out of a deep sense of compassion and duty. His efforts focused on three counties: Donegal, Mayo and Sligo.
Remembering Strzelecki sheds light on a different chapter in Ireland's history, highlighting the compassion and dedication of a Polish volunteer who devoted himself to helping Irish families through one of the darkest periods in the country's past. His legacy stands as a powerful testament to the solidarity that can transcend national, religious and political divides. (PAP)

22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Sudanese army announced Thursday that it had regained control of two strategic areas in southeastern Blue Nile state and shot down a drone that it said had entered the country from Ethiopia.
The army’s 4th Infantry Division said in a statement that its forces had recaptured the Bakouri and Akleili areas following military operations that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on opposing forces.
The division said its troops were continuing operations to pursue rival forces, secure the two areas and consolidate control.
Akleili holds strategic importance because of its location along the road connecting Kurmuk to Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile state.
Control of the area allows forces to influence military movements along the Kurmuk, Geissan and Bakouri fronts.

On Aug. 28, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), announced that they had seized Bakouri. It remains unclear when the allied forces took control of Akleili.
In a separate statement, Sudanese army spokesman Asim Awad said air defenses had shot down a “hostile strategic drone” near Bakouri on Thursday morning.
Awad said the military had tracked the aircraft since it crossed into Sudan from Ethiopia, without identifying the party operating it.
On Monday and Tuesday, the army announced that it had repelled attacks by the RSF and allied SPLM-N forces on the Al-Baraka and Sali areas in Blue Nile state.
The state has witnessed escalating clashes in recent weeks between the army and the allied forces.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023 over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary group into the military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million others, according to UN and international estimates.

Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes hours after U.S. prisoner release
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of using cluster munitions overnight as it renewed strikes on Kyiv and multiple other locations.
At least four people were killed, according to Ukraine's foreign ministry. Another 34 people were injured, including five children, Zelenskyy said Thursday, hours after Russia released American Stephen Hubbard and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and called him a humanitarian.
"Last night, the Russians used, among other weapons against Kyiv, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday. "The distinguishing feature of these missiles is that they detonate in the air as they approach the target, striking everything within a 400-meter diameter."
More than 100 countries have banned the use of cluster bombs under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, an international treaty that was adopted in 2008. The munitions spread smaller "bomblets" over a wide area that can hit civilian locations indiscriminately.
Russia, like the United States, did not sign on to the treaty.
Russia's Defense Ministry said, meanwhile, that air defenses downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that two people were reported injured, The Associated Press reported. More than 600 drones were fired toward Moscow between late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.
The developments came after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
"Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack," Zelenskyy said. "This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening."
Twelve regions came under attack from Russia overnight, according to Zelenskyy, who said one attack hit Pechersk, Kyiv's historic center, and damaged monastery buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.
Since Oct. 11, there have been 170 strikes on energy infrastructure sites across Ukraine, the Ukrainian president said.
Zelenskyy said earlier this week that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."

Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid US backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:07:39 UTC
01:07:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid increasing US unpopularity
The powerful pro-Israel lobby AIPAC has announced it will stop directly funding and endorsing US congressional candidates, marking a major shift in its electoral strategy amid growing public opposition to Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) announced the decision on Wednesday, saying it would end formal candidate endorsements and direct contributions through its political action committee while continuing to spend heavily on elections through its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP).
The move comes as AIPAC faces growing criticism, particularly among Democratic voters, with a leading Palestinian advocacy figure telling The New Arab that the decision amounts to an admission that the lobby's support has become politically toxic.
"They're admitting themselves that their endorsement is a net negative for anyone that they would endorse," Hamid Bendaas, communications director at the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project said.
The decision marks a significant change for one of Washington's most influential lobbying organisations, which established its political action committee and super PAC in 2021, expanding its electoral involvement.
In a letter to members, AIPAC said it would concentrate on mobilising individual donors and developing new fundraising methods, while insisting its objectives remained unchanged.
"Our mission and strategy remain the same," AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said.
Federal Election Commission filings show that AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees through September, while UDP spent more than $53 million on independent electoral expenditures.
Unlike traditional political action committees, super PACs can spend unlimited amounts supporting or opposing candidates, provided they do not coordinate directly with campaigns.
The announcement comes amid sharply deteriorating American attitudes towards Israel following its genocide in Gaza and wider military actions across the Middle East.
An April 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 60 percent of Americans held an unfavourable view of Israel, including 80 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents.
Polling published by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs in October found that American favourability towards Israel had fallen to its lowest level since the organisation began measuring attitudes towards the country in 1978.
The changing political climate has complicated AIPAC's efforts to support candidates, particularly in Democratic primaries.
In Michigan, AIPAC's super PAC spent heavily attempting to defeat Abdul El-Sayed, a critic of Israel, during the Democratic Senate primary.
El-Sayed nevertheless secured the nomination against Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who received substantial backing from pro-Israel interests.
UDP has subsequently intervened against El-Sayed in the Senate election campaign, where he faces Republican Mike Rogers, departing from AIPAC's traditional emphasis on maintaining bipartisan support.
Bendaas said the intervention was particularly significant given AIPAC's longstanding preference for influencing primaries rather than general elections.
"They usually stick to primaries, and they stay out of general elections because they want to stay bipartisan," he said.
Such interventions risk alienating Democratic voters whose overriding priority is defeating Republican candidates, regardless of their views on Israel.
Nevertheless, AIPAC's withdrawal from endorsements does not mean it is abandoning its ability to influence elections.
Its super PAC will continue operating, while supporters will still be encouraged to contribute to candidates backing its policy objectives.
Bendaas described the decision as a survival strategy intended to preserve AIPAC's financial influence while distancing candidates from an increasingly unpopular association.
"This is a move that's going to ensure that AIPAC stays relevant and continues to have an influence because they're going to continue to spend money through their SuperPAC," he said.
He also argued that AIPAC could increasingly rely on less transparent electoral spending, including committees whose financial backers may not become publicly apparent until after voting.
The restructuring comes as growing numbers of Democratic candidates reject AIPAC's support, challenging an organisation that has historically enjoyed considerable influence over both major parties.
For Bendaas, the most consequential aspect of the decision may be the loss of AIPAC's formerly privileged position in American politics.
"AIPAC is now just kind of one of those lobbies. But they're still a powerful one," he said, comparing the organisation to other wealthy lobbying groups seeking to influence elections.
"That kind of sheen and that feeling of no one should try to challenge us I think is gone probably forever."

Prices of other goods have gone up, but many people can’t afford to stock up. Others are simply exhausted and have lost hope. I’m one of them.”

The most valuable lot was a Legendary Collection master set featuring a rare Charizard card, which fetched £130,000, including buyer's fees.

He discovered their potential value only after reading a newspaper report about a single Pokemon card selling for more than £6,000.
Ewbank's described the sale as the most valuable trading-card auction in UK history and suggested it could also be a European record.
James Spooner, head of trading cards at Ewbank's, said advance bids had already reached £825,000 the day before the sale.
Andrew Ewbank, who conducted the auction, described the international interest as exceptional.

Italy and Spain lift border controls after months of tension over Ceuta
More than 70,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in late July, triggering border security concerns in the EU bloc.
Italy and Spain have agreed to lift border controls on each other’s citizens, ending a three-month standoff triggered after a mass surge of migrants and asylum seekers entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
The Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and his Spanish counterpart Fernando Grande-Marlaska spoke on the phone and agreed not to extend their suspension of the European Union’s open-border Schengen arrangements, an Italian statement said on Thursday.
“The decision, reached after a careful assessment of the situation, will be accompanied by enhanced information-sharing measures to ensure the full security of the common Schengen area,” the ministry added.
The decision followed a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on the sidelines of a European Council meeting.
Italy’s right-wing government first suspended its open-border arrangements with Spain on July 31, saying it wanted to make sure no migrants entering the North African enclave of Ceuta could travel to Italian territory.
Madrid responded by taking similar action against Rome, describing the Italian measures as “unjust, contrary to European Union interests, and discriminatory to the population of Spain”.
Ceuta migrant surge
The tit-for-tat border closures happened after upwards of 70,000 people swam around barricades and entered Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31, fuelling tension in the Spanish territory.
Most returned to Morocco within hours, but thousands, including unaccompanied minors, have remained for weeks in often dire conditions.
“We thought our government was going to do something in the short or medium term, but we’ve been here for two months, and these people haven’t been sent back,” Ceuta resident Ruben Gonzalez said.
The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing of migrants into Ceuta has complicated Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s bid for re-election in November.
Sanchez was already facing criticism for his government’s decision to open a path to legal status for hundreds of thousands of undocumented foreign residents.
After the Ceuta incident, Far-right Vox and centre-right PP parties accused him of being soft on immigration and put the issue at the centre of their campaigns in the run-up to next month’s elections.

Pentagon, Lockheed Agree on 10-Year Framework for Buying F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:02:40 UTC
01:02:40 KST

The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin on Oct. 22 announced a framework agreement to buy F-35 Joint Strike Fighters for the next 10 years.
But the deal, touted by the Pentagon as “landmark” and a first of its kind, depends on Congress granting the military authority to enter into such a multiyear agreement.
Under the deal, Lockheed will build 156 of the fifth-generation jets per year for both the U.S. and international customers, across lots 21 through 30. The U.S. military will buy at least 850 of those 1,560 aircraft over the decade covering the agreement, as well as procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, the Pentagon and Lockheed said in statements. The deal also covers sustainment of the global F-35 fleet.
Details such as pricing and schedules have yet to be hammered out. It’s also unclear how many of each F-35 variant will be produced, and how many will go to individual services like the Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps.
“We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in the Pentagon’s statement. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.”
Lockheed Martin has also agreed to invest at least $7 billion of its own money into projects to support the F-35 program.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” Lockheed President and CEO Jim Taiclet said in the company’s statement. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.”
While the Defense Department touted the agreement’s ability to create “a stable, long-term procurement signal to modernize and expand” the F-35, it also noted in its statement that actually executing the agreement “remains subject to congressional authorization and appropriations.”
Congress is currently considering granting the Pentagon the authority to enter into multiyear procurement contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX fighters as part of its work on the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers have also yet to pass a budget for fiscal 2027, leaving the agreement unfunded at the moment.
With all that legislation still pending, the Oct. 22 announcement is only a framework and not finalized.
Lockheed said if Congress does grant the multiyear procurement authority and the necessary appropriations in the next few months, it will work with the F-35 Joint Program Office to finalize the contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal award.
Lockheed said having predictable, multiyear procurement plans for the F-35 would save billions of dollars “through long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” And the agreement will allow the program to combine data from a variety of sources into integrated analytics, that will provide more visibility into parts inventory and readiness metrics and allow “transparent, data-driven decision making.”
The deal will also allow Lockheed to enter into long-term contracts with suppliers to buy raw materials and critical parts in bulk, which the company predicted would improve F-35 mission-capable rates. Currently, those deals are made on an annual basis, which Lockheed said “has historically strained the industrial base.”
In an earnings call with investors Oct. 22, Taiclet said at least 60 percent of an F-35’s content comes from its suppliers, including major suppliers such as Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, which make the center and aft sections of the jets’ bodies, respectively.
“We want them to have production stability, just as we would like to have it,” Taiclet said.
Taiclet said one of Lockheed’s biggest costs comes from suppliers providing components late, or at poor quality, and he predicted this agreement will help correct those problems.
Taiclet told investors that Lockheed and its suppliers will be under a fixed-price escalation contract, in which set prices increase under certain economic conditions.
“We’ll all collectively—if we do well and perform well, and those investments pay off that we make—we will get to retain those profits under the fixed-price-with-escalator concept,” Taiclet said. “Before, we would have to give back, with price and operating profit, any improvements we invested in internally. So that is going to apply to the production system. Even if it stays at 156, it’ll be a much healthier production system for industry, and a more predictable production system for government.”
And combining aircraft production with the purchase of spare parts and modification kits in the same contract will also yield volume savings and cost predictability, Lockheed said.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President OJ Sanchez said in the company’s statement. “This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission-capable rates and a more resilient supply chain—critical capabilities the warfighter needs to meet today’s mission and prepare for tomorrow’s threats.”
During the earnings call, Taiclet reiterated Lockheed’s desire—first voiced in April 2025, after the company lost the Air Force’s F-47 contract to Boeing—to add sixth-generation technologies into the F-35, which he previously referred to as making a “Ferrari” F-35. Taiclet said this could achieve 80 percent of a bespoke sixth-generation aircraft’s capabilities, at half the cost.
Lockheed’s primary F-35 factory is in Fort Worth, Texas.

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:52 UTC
01:01:52 KST

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
The US-Israeli war on Iran has caused an “unprecedented” shock to global energy markets, removing some 3 billion barrels of oil supply, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser has warned.
The war launched in February effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial oil and LNG artery, sending crude prices up roughly 50%. Despite Gulf exports recovering to a reported 80% of pre-war levels, renewed attacks on vessels have kept markets on edge, with Brent hitting a five-month high above $112 this week. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping have compounded the crisis, threatening another vital trade chokepoint, the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In an interview with Al Arabiya Business aired on Thursday, Nasser said the nearly eight-month crisis had deprived global markets of an estimated 3 billion barrels of oil.
“The impact of this crisis on energy markets is unprecedented,” he said. “We have lost around 3 billion barrels since it began. And bear in mind that the Gulf accounts for roughly 20% of global oil demand.”
The figure is equivalent to nearly a month of global oil consumption and reflects cumulative supply losses caused by disrupted shipping, reduced production and logistical bottlenecks.
With global oil inventories already below their five-year average when the war erupted, prices could have soared past $200 a barrel, Nasser warned. He credited emergency reserve releases, China’s sharp cut in seaborne oil imports and Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline, which bypasses Hormuz, with averting an even more severe price shock.
Nasser warned, however, that even an end to the crisis could bring fresh pressure on oil markets, as recovering consumption and a rush to replenish depleted reserves will likely fuel another demand surge.
“Once things return to normal, we expect additional demand of around 3 million barrels per day – about 2 million from consumption growth and another 1 million just to replenish the reserves countries have drawn down during the crisis,” he said, noting that the added demand could keep markets under strain long after shipping routes reopen.
Fresh escalation fears
Meanwhile, fears of another escalation are growing as US-Iran talks remain deadlocked. Reports on Wednesday claimed Washington was quietly pulling troops from bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, evacuating some diplomats and their families from Saudi Arabia and preparing similar withdrawals elsewhere. Similar precautions were taken ahead of the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
The moves follow US President Donald Trump’s rejection last month of Tehran’s proposal to reopen Hormuz in exchange for lifting the US blockade of Iranian ports, easing oil export restrictions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending regional hostilities, including Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Washington and Israel have since reportedly discussed another major offensive, potentially soon after the November 3 US midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also openly threatened fresh strikes on Iran, even without US backing.

Shas rabbi warns voters backing rival parties will have 'no place in the afterlife'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:09 UTC
01:01:09 KST

A senior rabbi in the ultra-Orthodox Shas party has warned that Jews who vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud or another political party will have no place in the afterlife, escalating a fierce battle for religious voters ahead of next week's national election.
Rabbi Moshe Maya, the oldest member of Shas' Council of Torah Sages and a former lawmaker who served in the Knesset in the 1990s, made the declaration as the party sought to prevent supporters from defecting to other parties on the political right.
"Anyone who votes for Likud or another party has no share in the world to come," Maya said, invoking the Jewish religious concept of Olam HaBa, or the world to come, commonly associated with the afterlife and spiritual reward.
The remarks underscored the increasingly heated rhetoric among the ultra-Orthodox parties as they compete for votes with Likud and other right-wing factions.
Shas, which primarily represents Sephardic and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox Jews, has traditionally relied on the authority of prominent rabbis to mobilize its electorate. Religious endorsements and rulings play a significant role in the party's election campaigns, particularly among voters who regard rabbinical guidance as binding.
Former chief rabbi renews attack on Ben-Gvir
In a separate speech in Jerusalem, former Sephardic Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, another influential Shas religious leader, warned that a victory by the opposition bloc would bring severe restrictions on the ultra-Orthodox community.
"If the left comes to power, it will create difficulties," Yosef said. "What we have now will be nothing by comparison. It will be many times worse. You cannot imagine the decrees that will come."
Yosef claimed that an opposition leader had proposed expanding compulsory military service to include religious women, in addition to ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students.
"One of the leaders of the left said, 'We are not finished. We will also introduce the conscription of women, not just yeshiva students, but women into the army,'" he said.
"That is something one must die rather than transgress," Yosef added, invoking a principle in Jewish religious law under which certain prohibitions must not be violated even at the cost of one's life.
Military conscription has long been one of the most contentious issues in Israeli politics. Most ultra-Orthodox men have historically received exemptions or deferments while studying in religious seminaries, an arrangement that has faced growing legal and political challenges.
The issue has become especially divisive amid the military's manpower needs and demands for a more equal distribution of the burden of national service.
Yosef also reiterated a religious ruling he issued earlier this week prohibiting his followers from voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose far-right political movement competes with Shas for support among religious and nationalist voters.
"It is forbidden to vote for him," Yosef said. "Anyone who votes for him is as though he himself ascended the Temple Mount. A person's agent is considered equivalent to the person himself."
The Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, is the holiest site in Judaism and the third-holiest in Islam. While Ben-Gvir has advocated Jewish prayer rights at the site, many leading ultra-Orthodox rabbis prohibit Jews from entering the compound because of religious restrictions concerning ritual purity and the location of the ancient Jewish temples.
Yosef's remarks reflected that longstanding religious disagreement with Ben-Gvir, whose visits to the site have repeatedly generated controversy.
The former chief rabbi also accused Ben-Gvir of failing to intervene against police violence toward ultra-Orthodox demonstrators.
"Look at how the police beat the ultra-Orthodox," Yosef said. "He is the minister responsible for the police. Has he said a word?"
Yosef alleged that Ben-Gvir benefited politically from confrontations between police and ultra-Orthodox protesters because they could weaken support for Shas representatives.
"He is happy about it because people will get angry with our representatives and his support will rise," Yosef said.
He further questioned Ben-Gvir's contributions to ultra-Orthodox religious institutions.
"Has he established a single religious school? A ritual bath? A synagogue?" Yosef asked.
Addressing young religious voters, particularly Sephardic yeshiva students considering supporting Ben-Gvir, he added: "How is that even a consideration?"
Ultra-Orthodox parties devise new voter-tracking system
Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, the other major ultra-Orthodox party, is preparing an alternative voter-monitoring operation following a Supreme Court ruling barring polling station committee representatives from transmitting real-time information about voter turnout to party campaign headquarters.
The practice has been a central component of ultra-Orthodox election campaigns, particularly in tightly knit religious communities where parties use turnout information to identify supporters who have not yet voted and encourage them to cast ballots.
The court's restrictions prevent party representatives serving on official polling station committees from digitally transmitting such information in real time.
United Torah Judaism is now preparing a separate monitoring operation designed to collect information outside the official election administration system.
Under the plan, a registration booth will be placed at the entrance to each polling station, outside the restricted area reserved for election officials and voters. Workers will record the identities of people entering to vote, with the information subsequently transferred to party headquarters without passing through the official polling station committee.
Agudat Yisrael, a Hasidic faction within United Torah Judaism, is preparing an additional system.
Party officials said they would establish dedicated tents at clusters of polling stations, staffed by married yeshiva students engaged in full-time religious study.
After casting their ballots, voters will be asked to visit the tents and report that they have voted using a designated digital platform.
To encourage participation, the faction has launched a campaign under the slogan, "If you voted but didn't report it, you didn't vote."
The initiative is being led by Jerusalem Deputy Mayor Tzachi Brim.
The arrangements are intended to preserve the parties' ability to monitor turnout and mobilize supporters despite the court-imposed restrictions on information sharing by official polling station representatives.

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
October 22, 2026
Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.
The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
France's protests grow
More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
Weapons made for war?
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.
Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.
"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.
Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?
The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.
"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.
"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Confrontation vs. de-escalation
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.
"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."
When can police officers use force?
According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.
"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark
The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.
Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."
