Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission.
And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.
ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.
Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021.
The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.
Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.
Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.
An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.
About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.
There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees.
This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.
For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.
Disney's different options
Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.
Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.
Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts" of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").
Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"-themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.
The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.
Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.
"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."
Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.
"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."
Affiliate board involvement
This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).
It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.
The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.
Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.
"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."
The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

German AfD party asks government about UFOs, aerial phenomena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:30 UTC
01:00:30 KST

Ayhan Simsek
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Germany’s right-wing AfD party has asked the government whether public institutions are reporting incidents of unidentified aerial phenomena, and whether any findings exist on the topic.
The parliamentary question, signed by the party’s co-chairs Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, follows recent US Pentagon reports, congressional hearings involving pilots and officials, and scientific work by NASA.
In the inquiry, lawmakers asked which ministries or offices are responsible for receiving and evaluating reports of unidentified aerial phenomena and since when records have been kept. They also inquired whether specific terms and definitions such as “UAP” or “UFO” are used and whether standardized federal guidelines exist for public officials.
The Defense Ministry replied to the parliamentary question on behalf of the government, and the response was published on the parliament’s website this week. “There is no information available regarding unidentified aerial phenomena,” the ministry said, adding that the government uses no specific terms or definitions such as “UFO,” “UAP” or “unidentifiable contacts.”
The ministry said monitoring of German airspace is handled by the interior, transport and defense ministries, while tracking objects near Earth in space is the job of the research, technology and space and defense ministries. Officials added that there are no special reporting channels for pilots, air traffic controllers and other personnel to report sightings of unidentified objects in the air or space.

Higher progesterone is linked to blurrier brain signals for emotional control, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:22 UTC
01:00:22 KST

Young women with higher natural levels of the hormone progesterone tend to show less distinct brain activity patterns when they must override their automatic emotional impulses, according to a new neuroimaging study published in Psychological Medicine. The findings suggest that progesterone may blur the neural signals that help the brain regulate emotional actions. Reduced precision in a frontal brain region also accounted for an indirect statistical pathway linking higher progesterone to worse recent mood.
In everyday life, people naturally gravitate toward positive or rewarding things and pull away from threats or unpleasant situations. Psychologists refer to this automatic habit as approach-avoidance behavior. Overriding these instincts, such as stepping toward an angry person or walking away from something appealing, requires active emotional control.
This regulatory process relies heavily on the lateral frontal pole, a brain structure located at the very front of the cerebral cortex just behind the forehead. A 2020 neuroimaging study indicated that the lateral frontal pole plays a key role in overriding automatic impulses when people have to make these kinds of emotional choices. When this region fails to properly guide behavior, people tend to struggle with emotional regulation, as seen in a 2023 study covered by PsyPost showing that highly anxious individuals have difficulty recruiting the lateral frontal pole and must rely on other brain regions instead.
Scientists have also found that sex hormones can influence these exact brain circuits. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that high levels of the hormone testosterone are associated with reduced activity in the anterior prefrontal cortex during emotional control in adulthood. Far less is known about how the female ovarian hormones estradiol and progesterone shape these regulatory networks.
“Historically, neuroscience research has disproportionately focused on men, partly because hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle were considered a source of unwanted variability,” study author Macià Buades-Rotger, an associate professor of clinical psychology and psychobiology at the University of Barcelona, told PsyPost. “As a result, we still know surprisingly little about how naturally occurring changes in ovarian hormones influence the brain and behavior.”
“At the same time, the relationship between female hormones and emotions is surrounded by sexist stereotypes and assumptions that often have little scientific basis,” Buades-Rotger added. “I was interested in moving beyond these simplistic narratives to investigate what hormones actually do in the brain, particularly how they might influence the mechanisms that allow us to control our automatic emotional responses.”
Both estradiol and progesterone fluctuate naturally throughout the menstrual cycle, and shifts in these hormones are frequently tied to changes in emotional well-being. The authors of a 2020 review argued that progesterone can act like a double-edged sword: one of its chemical byproducts has proven useful for treating depression after childbirth, yet the hormone may trigger negative symptoms in women with premenstrual syndrome or premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a severe form of premenstrual mood disturbance. Meanwhile, a 2019 neuroimaging study of naturally cycling women found that during the cycle phase when progesterone is high, frontal and striatal regions tended to be more active during mental tasks.
Most earlier brain imaging studies looked only at whether entire brain regions became more or less active overall in response to hormones. Buades-Rotger and his colleagues wanted to look deeper by examining whether estradiol and progesterone relate to fine-grained patterns of brain activity during emotional control, and whether those patterns connect to recent mood.
To investigate this in a preregistered study, the researchers recruited 116 healthy, naturally cycling women between the ages of 18 and 35. None of the participants were using hormonal contraceptives or had a history of neurological, hormonal, or recent psychiatric disorders. Before entering the brain scanner, each participant provided a saliva sample (stimulated by chewing gum) so the researchers could measure their current levels of estradiol and progesterone.
Participants also completed questionnaires measuring their typical emotion regulation habits and their mood over the preceding seven days. The mood survey assessed feelings of friendliness, vigor, fatigue, anger, tension, and depression, which the researchers combined into a single overall mood score. All testing sessions took place between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. to minimize natural daily fluctuations in hormone levels.
Inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner, which tracks brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow, the women completed a 240-trial approach-avoidance task. During the task, they viewed photographs of actors displaying happy or angry facial expressions. Depending on the instructions for each block of trials, participants pressed buttons to either “approach” a face, which made the image grow larger as if looming closer, or “avoid” a face, which made the image shrink as if receding.
In half of the trials, the instructions matched natural human instincts: approaching happy faces and avoiding angry ones. In the other half, the instructions went against those instincts, requiring participants to approach angry faces and avoid happy ones. After excluding six participants with unusually high error rates, the researchers analyzed the behavioral responses of 110 women.
As expected, overriding automatic emotional tendencies took more effort. When participants had to approach angry faces, their average reaction time was 0.782 seconds with an error rate of 1.52 percent, compared to 0.663 seconds and a 0.55 percent error rate when approaching happy faces. Similarly, avoiding happy faces took an average of 0.762 seconds with a 1.36 percent error rate, compared to 0.684 seconds and a 0.64 percent error rate when avoiding angry faces.
Next, the researchers examined the brain scans of 106 participants, after excluding four additional women who moved too much in the scanner. Instead of just measuring overall blood flow in a given brain area, the team used a machine learning technique called multivoxel pattern analysis. A voxel is a tiny three-dimensional unit of brain tissue, similar to a three-dimensional pixel.
The computer algorithm looked at the detailed grid of activity across thousands of voxels during odd-numbered trials and tried to predict which task condition the participant was performing during even-numbered trials. If the computer could accurately tell whether a participant was overriding their instincts or following them based on a region’s activity pattern, it meant that brain area was distinctly encoding the rules of emotional control.
The algorithm had to sort each trial into one of the four task conditions, so guessing would be right 25 percent of the time. Activity patterns in several regions allowed it to beat that chance level, including the lateral frontal pole, the striatum (a cluster of neurons deep beneath the cortex that helps manage movement and reward), the central insula (a region involved in processing internal bodily states and emotions), the primary visual cortex, the cerebellum, and the periaqueductal gray (a brainstem area involved in threat responses). The amygdala, a threat-processing region the researchers had planned in advance to examine, did not distinguish between the conditions. The algorithm mainly succeeded at telling instinct-opposing trials apart from instinct-matching ones, while often confusing the two conditions within each type.
When the researchers combined the brain data, hormone levels, and mood scores for the 101 participants who had complete data across all measures, they found a consistent link with progesterone. Women with higher concentrations of salivary progesterone showed lower classification accuracy in both the lateral frontal pole (r = −0.25) and the striatum (r = −0.26). In other words, in women with higher progesterone, the brain activity patterns representing emotional control in these two regions were less distinct and harder for the algorithm to tell apart.
“In everyday life, we constantly encounter situations in which our automatic emotional reactions conflict with what we actually need to do,” Buades-Rotger explained. “Imagine needing to ask a grumpy colleague for help: your instinct might be to avoid them, but achieving your goal requires approaching them instead. Our findings suggest that higher progesterone levels may make the brain’s representation of these competing emotional demands less clear, potentially making it harder to distinguish when to follow an instinctive reaction and when to override it. This could be one way in which natural hormonal fluctuations subtly influence how we navigate emotionally challenging situations.”
Sharper activity patterns in the lateral frontal pole were also associated with better mood over the past week (r = 0.26). Even without a direct correlation between progesterone and mood reported in the study, a preregistered mediation analysis found a small indirect pathway: higher progesterone was linked to less distinct frontal patterns, which were in turn linked to worse recent mood. The model explained 7.1 percent of the variation in mood scores, and a reversed version that swapped the roles of progesterone and the brain patterns produced a weaker effect that was not statistically significant.
Contrary to the researchers’ initial expectations, estradiol levels were not linked to brain decoding accuracy or to mood. In addition, neither estradiol nor progesterone correlated with how quickly or accurately participants pressed the buttons during the behavioral task. When the researchers divided participants into early and late stages of the menstrual cycle based on self-reported cycle length, they found higher progesterone in the late phase as expected, but cycle phase by itself was not linked to differences in mood, task performance, or brain decoding accuracy.
“What surprised me most was the absence of comparable effects for estradiol,” Buades-Rotger noted. “Both estradiol and progesterone are known to influence brain function, and we had good reasons to expect that either hormone might be associated with how emotional control is represented in the brain. Instead, the associations we identified were specific to progesterone. This does not mean that estradiol has no role in emotional regulation, but it suggests that the two hormones may influence these processes through different mechanisms.”
The authors suggest that progesterone may make brain activity patterns more diffuse across frontal and striatal circuits. While this blurring of emotional signals might make it harder to actively regulate mood and impulses, the researchers note that a slight blunting of emotional representations could be helpful in other ways, such as reducing sensitivity to physical pain during the second half of the menstrual cycle.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because the researchers collected only a single saliva sample and brain scan from each woman at one point in time, the study cannot prove that higher progesterone directly causes changes in brain patterns or mood. In addition, the 101 participants included in the correlation analyses fell short of the preregistered target of 120, leaving the study with 71 percent statistical power to detect effects of the observed size. Tracking the same individuals across multiple days of their menstrual cycles in future studies will be necessary to separate temporary hormonal states from stable personal traits.
“One important misconception would be that higher progesterone necessarily makes women more emotional or less capable of controlling their behavior,” Buades-Rotger emphasized. “That is not what our study shows. We examined statistical associations between naturally occurring hormone levels, patterns of brain activity, and mood in healthy young women; we did not experimentally manipulate progesterone or demonstrate that these neural differences cause changes in emotional behavior. It is also important to remember that hormonal effects vary considerably between individuals, and many women experience little or no noticeable mood changes across the menstrual cycle.”
Methodological factors may have also introduced measurement noise that masked potential effects of estradiol. The researchers used chewing gum to help participants produce saliva, which is known to alter measured concentrations of steroid hormones, and salivary estradiol is a poor marker of menstrual cycle phase. In this sample, estradiol did not differ between the early and late phases of the cycle, while progesterone did. Finally, the pathway linking progesterone, frontal brain patterns, and mood accounted for just over 7 percent of the variation in mood among participants, meaning most of the differences in how participants felt were explained by other factors.
“The associations we observed were relatively modest, which is unsurprising given that mood and emotional regulation depend on many interacting biological, psychological, and environmental factors,” Buades-Rotger said. “Progesterone is certainly not a master switch that determines how someone feels or behaves. The significance of our findings lies primarily in identifying a potential brain mechanism linking hormonal variation to mood, rather than demonstrating a large or immediately noticeable effect on everyday behavior.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to test these hormonal pathways more directly over time. “An important next step would be to follow the same women across different phases of the menstrual cycle to determine whether changes in progesterone are accompanied by corresponding changes in neural representations of emotion control,” Buades-Rotger said. “Pharmacological studies that experimentally manipulate progesterone levels or the activity of its neuroactive metabolites would provide a more direct test of causality. Ultimately, understanding these mechanisms could help explain why some women are particularly sensitive to hormonal fluctuations, including those who experience premenstrual dysphoria, and potentially inform future approaches to treatment.”
“I think our findings also illustrate the value of looking beyond conventional measures of brain activation,” Buades-Rotger concluded. “This allowed us to investigate how information about emotional control is represented in the brain. More broadly, the study highlights why hormonal state should be taken seriously as a meaningful source of variation in neuroscience, rather than simply treated as a nuisance variable.”
The study, “Endogenous progesterone blurs frontostriatal representations of emotion control in healthy young women,” was authored by Macià Buades-Rotger, Rosamunde Hendricks, Beatrice Roncarati, Marta Calderón-García, Kaja Bergmann, and Francisco José Pérez-Cano.

The One Question AI Could Not Answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

The One Question AI Could Not Answer
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Why Children Need More Than Screens to Master the Future
Hong Kong is moving decisively into the age of artificial intelligence in education. The government has committed significant funding to digital education, supporting schools in purchasing AI tools, digital resources and related training. The message from policymakers is clear: our children must learn to master technology.
They are right. But true mastery requires much more than screen time.
To master AI, children must first master something far older, subtler and more profound themselves.
Artificial intelligence can calculate, translate, summarise, generate images and simulate conversation at astonishing speed. Used well, it can support learning and open new possibilities. But AI cannot replace the experiences through which children become grounded, confident, imaginative and fully human.
This is why, at Garden House Waldorf School, our approach to education begins not with the screen, but with the child.
The Senses Are Not Optional
Children do not become fully human through information alone. They become human through experience.
The evidence on screen time is alarming. Studies tracking children aged two to five have found that as screen time increases, so does emotional fragility, irritability, difficulty calming down, and an inability to complete tasks. These patterns persist across age groups from six to seventeen. Children with high screen exposure struggle to remain calm when faced with challenges. Their curiosity declines. The risks of anxiety and depression escalate.
These behaviours are not signs of dysfunction. They are signals of confusion — of a child who has lost their internal compass. The problem is not merely the screen itself. It is everything that screen time displaces: physical activity, imaginative play, face-to-face interaction, and the rich sensory engagement that builds resilience.
For those of us living in cities, there is another urgent concern. A landmark study involving over 300,000 children found that for every additional hour of daily screen time, the risk of myopia increases. At four hours per day, the risk roughly doubles. In parts of Asia, myopia rates have surged from modest levels in the 1970s to 80 or even 90 percent today. The eye is designed for flexibility — alternating between distant horizons and nearby objects. Locked onto screens for hours, it loses that adaptability.
The Sensory Imbalance of the Digital Age
Consider the online meetings that have become part of our daily lives. They engage at most two senses: vision and hearing. The sense of warmth — that tangible experience of human presence — is entirely absent.
This is the deeper risk of the AI era. A mode of perception dominated by vision and hearing will only intensify, leaving the lower senses — touch, smell, taste, life sense, balance and movement — chronically underdeveloped. AI excels at recognising words. But it operates on a dangerous assumption: that understanding words is equivalent to understanding thought, and that understanding thought is equivalent to understanding another human being. Everything becomes confined to the literal, with no warmth to complete the circuit.
There are people who "know" each other through social media, yet find themselves completely lost when meeting in real life. They possess information about one another, but they lack the sensory experience of one another. Their sensory pathway is incomplete.
Wisdom Cannot Be Downloaded
None of this means that technology is bad, nor that AI should be kept out of education forever. Children must eventually learn to understand it, question it and use it wisely.
But the key word is wisely.
The question for our age is not whether children will use AI. They will. The question is whether they will bring to it a fully developed humanity — bodies that are awake, senses that are alive, hearts that can feel, and minds that can judge.
That is the one question AI could not answer. It can only be answered by how we choose to educate our children.

Navy drone project kept quiet to protect advantage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:00:07 BST
01:00:07 KST

Project HORUS is supporting an urgent operational requirement, and the Ministry of Defence will not specify the platforms involved, the length of the contract or the timing of a procurement decision in order to protect operational advantage, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, tabled three questions on the project, asking what platforms are being used by the Royal Navy under Project HORUS, what the length is of the contract for the capability provided, and by when a procurement decision will be made to replace the capability currently under contract.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, gave the same answer to all three: “Project HORUS is supporting an urgent operational requirement and so the MoD would not wish to specify specific platforms or procurement decisions at this stage, so as to protect operational advantage.”
An urgent operational requirement is the mechanism Britain’s forces use to buy equipment outside the normal procurement cycle when an operation needs a capability quickly, and it carries its own funding route and an abbreviated approvals process. Equipment bought that way is usually in service within months, and the mechanism was used heavily during Iraq and Afghanistan for protected vehicles, counter-explosive equipment and surveillance systems.

Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.

PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said Thursday.
The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to change drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements.
Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.
Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC.
Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.
The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

India to Upgrade Four Outdated Ships With BrahMos Supersonic Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:49:52 UTC
00:49:52 KST

The Indian Navy is modernizing two destroyers and two missile corvettes of Soviet design by equipping them with BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles.
This was reported by Naval News.
The agreement, worth 6.615 billion rupees (about $68 million), was signed on October 6. It provides for the procurement of ship-based launchers and fire control systems. The share of Indian-manufactured components is to exceed 68%.
The new weapons will be installed on two Ranvir-class destroyers (Project 61ME) and two Veer-class corvettes (Project 1241RE). The specific ships have not been officially named.
Between 1980 and 1987, the Indian Navy received five Project 61ME destroyers from the Soviet Union. Currently, three remain in service: INS Rana, INS Ranvir, and INS Ranvijay.
The latter two already have eight-cell BrahMos vertical launch systems at the stern, but they still carry four inclined launchers for the obsolete P-15 Termit anti-ship missiles at the bow.
It is these ships that are most likely to receive additional armament to replace the Soviet systems. In that case, the total warhead load for each ship could increase to 16 missiles, as on modern Indian destroyers of the Kolkata and Visakhapatnam classes.
In addition to the destroyers, the rearmament will include the Veer-class corvettes, which are an Indian modification of the Soviet Project 1241 Molniya missile boats. New Delhi initially purchased five such ships from the USSR and later built eight more under license at its own shipyards.
The INS Vidyut previously underwent a similar modernization, receiving two twin launchers from the decommissioned destroyer INS Rajput. According to the publication’s speculation, the new contract may involve the INS Prabal and the INS Pralaya, which are currently armed with 16 Kh-35E anti-ship missiles.
Due to their displacement of less than 500 metric tons and the BrahMos’s substantial dimensions, their warhead load will likely be limited to four missiles weighing about three metric tons each. This will make the ships among the smallest carriers of such weapons.
At the same time, India is already preparing to replace its aging corvettes. Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on September 18, 2026, the first new-generation NGMV missile ship was laid down at Cochin Shipyard Ltd. A total of six vessels with a displacement of about 1,500 metric tons are planned for construction, each of which will carry four BrahMos missiles.
In addition to modernizing its own fleet, New Delhi is expanding exports of this weaponry abroad. In particular, Vietnam plans to purchase Indian missile systems, as well as patrol ships and boats.

UK plans tougher penalties for damage to undersea cables, pipelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:48:47 UTC
00:48:47 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The UK government has proposed tougher prison sentences and unlimited fines for those who intentionally damage critical undersea infrastructure, citing growing security threats, including suspicious Russian activity in British waters.
A White Paper published on Thursday outlines plans to modernize legislation dating back 140 years to strengthen the protection of undersea telecommunications cables, energy pipelines and electricity interconnectors.
Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical undersea energy and telecommunications infrastructure could face prison sentences of up to 14 years, alongside tougher financial penalties.
The plans would also introduce new security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications companies, obliging them to identify and manage risks to their networks.
The government would gain additional powers to direct telecommunications providers to take protective measures against threats such as sabotage and espionage. The proposals also include safeguards for fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but may pose national security risks if sensitive data is compromised.
“Undersea cables are the hidden backbone of modern Britain, carrying the data we rely on every day to message friends and family, do our banking, and run our businesses,” Telecoms Minister Ian Murray said in a statement.
He added: “We intend to modernise those laws with tougher penalties, stronger requirements on industry and new powers to protect our national security, making sure the UK’s critical infrastructure is fit for the threats of today and tomorrow.”
According to the government, undersea fibre-optic cables carry around 99% of the UK’s international data, while subsea pipelines provide 74% of its gas supply. Electricity cables also support energy imports from Europe and connections to offshore wind farms.
Energy Minister Michael Shanks also said the legislation would strengthen deterrence and help prevent, detect and respond to threats against the country’s energy supply.
The publication of the White Paper marks the start of a 12-week public consultation seeking views from industry, experts and the public.

CEC impeachment: Speaker Om Birla says fresh motion against Gyanesh Kumar will be examined as per rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:48:45 UTC
00:48:45 KST

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said if the opposition brings any fresh impeachment motion against the country's top poll officer, it will be examined according to rules and procedures.
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.
“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum after The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.
If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.

Japanese troops test-fire air defense missiles at New Mexico range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:47:27 UTC
00:47:27 KST

- Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been conducting live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at Shizunai, Rokkasho and other ranges in Japan.
- At McGregor Range in New Mexico, its Type 03 medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units.
Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been carrying out live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at ranges in northern Japan and in the United States, where its medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot batteries at McGregor Range in New Mexico.
The Ground Self-Defense Force, Japan’s army, said on X that units at home are firing at the Shizunai range in Hokkaido, the Rokkasho range in Aomori Prefecture and other sites. The training covers the force’s layered short-range air defense weapons: the Type 81 short-range surface-to-air missile, the Type 93 close-range surface-to-air missile and the Type 87 self-propelled anti-aircraft gun.
Those systems cover the lowest and closest layers of Japan’s ground-based air defense.
The Type 93 mounts short-range missiles on a light utility vehicle, while the tracked Type 87 carries twin 35 mm cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters and other low-flying targets at close range.
In New Mexico, the Ground Self-Defense Force is firing the Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile, known in Japan as Chu-SAM, in coordination with Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units. Built by Mitsubishi Electric, the Type 03 replaced the U.S.-designed HAWK missiles Japan had used since 1965 and has a range of about 50 km (31 miles), with the system designed to hit aircraft, air-to-surface missiles and cruise missiles directly.
The Type 03 has a long history at the New Mexico range. Japanese forces fired it in a live training exercise for the first time at McGregor Range in late 2006, after six earlier test launches at nearby White Sands Missile Range.
McGregor Range, part of the Fort Bliss training complex, offers the open airspace and distances needed for live missile firings that are difficult to arrange in Japan. The Air Self-Defense Force has held annual Patriot live-fire training there since 1963, and recent iterations have included combined live firing with Ground Self-Defense Force anti-aircraft units, bilateral firing with U.S. Army Patriot units and, in 2025, counter-drone training.
Pairing the two services lets Japan’s army and air force practice defending against air threats as a single network, with the medium-range Type 03 and the longer-range Patriot covering different layers of the airspace.
The Ground Self-Defense Force said it will continue firing training at home and abroad to further strengthen its air defense capabilities.

France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots
- French courts are using fast-track justice after weekend riots, handing out swift jail terms and suspended sentences to restore order.
- Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 2,500 were arrested and 917 prosecuted, calling the response a sign of “great firmness”.
- Lawyers say the process is rushed and harsh, with one calling it “state repression” and warning judges face pressure for tougher penalties.
AI generated
PARIS – French courts have swiftly handed out verdicts, including orders to serve jail time, in fast-track justice for defendants accused over the rioting that erupted on the sidelines of protests at the weekend.
The government says the accelerated legal processes are needed to restore order after some of the worst urban violence in recent years on Oct 17.
But courts are also overwhelmed, while some lawyers say the scale of the hearings reeks of state repression.
Mathilde B, a student, 19, and 20-year-old Francois D, who said he wants to be a mountain guide, had come to Paris on Oct 17 from Auxerre, a city south-east of the capital.
But police found a knuckleduster and flick knife in the young man’s bag and discovered the pair had discussed “guerrilla warfare” and “beating up riot police” on social media.
Mathilde B received a five-month suspended prison sentence; but Francois D was sent to jail immediately as part of an eight-month sentence, with two months to be served in custody.
Tristan Lawless, a lawyer at the bar in Melun south of Paris, said he was defending a client for whom prosecutors had demanded a five-month sentence with immediate custody.
He said the trial was taking place “on the basis of a 50-page case file that, in my view, was put together in haste, with reports that are often vague and lacking detail”, and alleged his client had been beaten in custody.
‘Pressure on judges’
Speaking on Oct 21 in the southern city of Marseille, which saw some of the worst violence, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said that out of some 2,500 people arrested nationwide at the weekend, 917 were being prosecuted, a number he hailed as a “truly impressive figure”.
“The holding cells are full,” he said, referring to the units where people are held ahead of trial, adding this was proof of “our great firmness”.
One of the most longstanding and hyperactive members of the government, Darmanin, a former interior minister, is taking a high profile as Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s Cabinet seeks to show it is in control.
Once seen as having presidential ambitions himself, he is a leading supporter of former centre-right premier Edouard Philippe, who is seen as one of the few candidates capable of defeating far-right front runner Marine Le Pen in 2027 elections.
“We’re here to firmly oppose what we see as an attempt by Gerald Darmanin to make the justice system more punitive,” said Paris lawyer Romain Ruiz, a member of the “Colere noire” (Black anger) collective, which is highly critical of the judicial system.
He accused Darmanin of “putting pressure on judges in pursuit of harsher penalties” and “publicly celebrating the imprisonment of young people”.
“We will never accept that the justice system should become an arm of repression.”
‘Perhaps unprecedented’
Manuel, a 21-year-old cook from central France with no prior criminal record, said he had come to Paris “on a whim” to celebrate his birthday with a friend.
But police who stopped him on Oct 17 close to the starting point of a demonstration found several glass bottles, some rags, and a lighter – what the prosecutor described as “the perfect kit” for a Molotov cocktail. He was sentenced to two months in prison and another six suspended.
Souleymane, a 19-year-old from Ivory Coast without valid residency in France, was arrested in northern Paris while allegedly trying to steal a scooter after storming a corner shop. Convicted three times previously, he was sentenced to eight months in prison and taken into custody.
Julien M, 27, a video artist from south-east France, is accused of hurling a traffic cone which just missed a policeman. He vowed that the protest would be his last and the court set him free under judicial control until a trial at the end of November.
In comments on Oct 20 in the northern city of Lille, also badly hit by rioting, Darmanin said 150 people had already been sent to prison, a colossal figure in a country where short sentences are often served outside of prison with electronic tags.
“People with no previous criminal record are being sent to prison. This is extremely unusual, perhaps even unprecedented, for offences involving damage to property,” he added. AFP

US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:45 UTC
00:40:45 KST

US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move "deliberately reckless."
In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own "aggressive military space ambitions."
The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved "dangerously" near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE.
The Russian satellite came "exceptionally close" -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.
"This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."
ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence.
Kosmos-2612 "exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite," Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. "These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."
"The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless," he said.
Russia's representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.
"We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said.
He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch.
Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink's comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action" -- caused a jolt among policy experts.
Other longtime space watchers, however, said, the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.
"The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities," wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. "An arms race in space has been under way for years."

U.S. orders 60,000 attack drones from nine companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:05 UTC
00:40:05 KST

- The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the Drone Dominance Program’s Gauntlet II.
- Perennial Autonomy and Neros topped the Deep Strike and Close Quarters Battle categories, each receiving the maximum initial order of 8,000 drones.
The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the second round of its Drone Dominance Program, with Perennial Autonomy and Neros each set to receive the maximum initial order of 8,000 units.
The Defense Innovation Unit, which runs the program with the Test Resource Management Center, said orders are now in the works following Gauntlet II, a month-long flyoff held in August 2026 at Fort Carson, Colorado. Perennial Autonomy took the top spot in the Deep Strike mission area with 80.1 points, while Neros led the Close Quarters Battle category with 88.1 points, according to the program’s published leaderboard.
“Congratulations to all the winners. Now, it’s time to deliver,” the Defense Innovation Unit wrote in announcing the results.
The orders are split evenly between the two mission areas, with 30,000 drones in each, and scale with each company’s ranking. In Deep Strike, Hyperscale placed second and is in line for 7,000 drones, followed by Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In Close Quarters Battle, ORQA US placed second with 7,000, followed by XTEND with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000. Neros is the only company to place in both categories, bringing its combined allocation to 14,000 drones, and final quantities will be set when contracts are awarded.
Gauntlet II tested the drones on a find-fix-finish mission, meaning locating a target, confirming it and striking it. Deep Strike lanes required drones to hit targets from 15 km (9.3 miles) away, while Close Quarters Battle lanes tested performance in confined spaces such as buildings, with part of the testing repeated at night. Additional lanes evaluated controlled strikes and electronic warfare performance, with the drones flown against counter-drone systems designed to jam or defeat them.
Companies were scored on more than flight results. The final rankings combined Gauntlet II performance with evaluations from military operators who flew the systems and an assessment of each company’s ability to produce drones at scale and secure its supply chain.
The second round raised the bar considerably on range. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, in February and March 2026, sent 25 companies through testing that included strikes at about 10 km (6.2 miles), and the Defense Innovation Unit said only 24% of drones in that round reached 10 km. That first round produced orders for about 30,000 one-way attack drones worth roughly $150 million, with London-based Skycutter topping the leaderboard and Neros in second place.
The program grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s July 2025 memo on military drone dominance, which called for every U.S. Army squad to be armed with small one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. The Department of War plans to spend about $1.1 billion across four phases of the program, which is designed to build a U.S.-based industrial base for low-cost expendable drones. Officials said in testimony earlier this year that Phase II would exclude systems using motors or batteries from so-called covered countries, a requirement aimed at Chinese components.
Several of the Gauntlet II winners have already shared details of their orders. Vector said it received orders for up to 5,000 drone systems along with its high-voltage electronic safe and arm device, which lets operators arm drones with different munitions, and XTEND said it delivered 120 STRIKER systems for testing, as The Defence Blog reported when the Close Quarters Battle scores were released.
Officials plan to follow Gauntlet II with Gauntlet 2.5, focused on bomber drones that drop munitions, and Gauntlet 3 is scheduled to begin about six months after Gauntlet II.

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:39:37 UTC
00:39:37 KST

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
According to the company’s official guidance, locked conversations disappear from regular chat history, pinned chats and standard conversation searches.
“This can help keep sensitive conversations out of view when you share your screen or use a shared device,” OpenAI said.
Users can access protected conversations through Projects > Locked chats by entering a four-digit account PIN. Supported mobile devices also offer Face ID, Touch ID or device unlock.
To protect an existing conversation, users select “Lock chat” from its options menu and create or enter their PIN.
The feature is rolling out across Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans, although some conversation types are ineligible.
Locking a conversation does not add end-to-end encryption or change data retention and model-training settings.
OpenAI also cautions that resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes locked conversations and content protected solely by that PIN. Changing a known PIN preserves them.

Lockheed lines up deal for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:32:33 UTC
00:32:33 KST

- The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin agreed on a framework for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years, covering Lots 21 through 30.
- The deal keeps production at 156 aircraft a year and moves to a formal contract once Congress grants multiyear authority and funding.
The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin have agreed on a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal that covers 850 aircraft for the United States, along with spare parts, modification kits and international orders across production Lots 21 through 30.
The framework keeps F-35 production at 156 aircraft a year and folds three things that have traditionally been bought separately into one long-term plan: new jets with their initial spares, a decade of modification kits, and fleet sustainment. The next step runs through Congress: once multiyear authority and the associated funding are granted, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will finalize contract terms, pricing and delivery schedules in a formal contract award.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain. That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.”
The 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years work out to an average of 85 jets a year for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, with the remainder of the 156-a-year production rate going to international partners and foreign customers. The United States plans to buy a total of 2,456 F-35s across its three services.
Until now, the F-35 has been bought in lot-by-lot contracts that often took years to negotiate. The most recent deal, covering Lots 18 and 19, was finalized on Sept. 29, 2025, after a handshake agreement the previous December, and covers 296 aircraft worth about $24.3 billion. Long-lead funding for parts for Lot 20 and Lot 21 aircraft has already been awarded, and Lot 21 is now the first lot included in the new framework.
A multiyear arrangement lets Lockheed Martin and its suppliers commit to larger, longer orders for raw materials and parts. The company says that approach will produce volume discounts, lower unit prices and savings for taxpayers estimated in the billions of dollars over the life of the program, while giving the government more predictable costs.
Readiness is a central part of the plan. The framework links aircraft production with purchases of spare and modification parts and adds integrated analytics that tie budget decisions to readiness results and give real-time visibility into parts inventories. Lockheed Martin says replacing the annual contracting cycle with long-term supplier contracts will cut turnaround times for parts and repairs and raise mission capable rates, the share of the fleet ready to fly its assigned missions.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The company estimates the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate about $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. International customers would share in the benefits through economies of scale across the global fleet and its shared sustainment network.
More than 1,375 F-35s are now in service around the world, operating from 42 bases, including in 13 countries that fly the jet from home soil, and the fleet has passed 1 million flight hours. Lockheed Martin delivered a record 191 F-35s in 2025.
The F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will move to a formal contract award for Lots 21 through 30 once Congress grants multiyear authority and the associated appropriations, which the companies expect in the coming months.

Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:30:31 UTC
00:30:31 KST

Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.
It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.
Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.
Older but Still Capable
The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.
Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.
If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 22 octobre 2026.
PROJETS DE LOI
ACCORD ENTRE LA FRANCE ET LES FIDJI CONCERNANT LA COOPERATION EN MATIERE DE DEFENSE ET LE STATUT DES FORCES
Le ministre de l’Europe et des affaires étrangères a présenté un projet de loi autorisant l’approbation de l’accord entre le Gouvernement de la République française et le Gouvernement de la République des Fidji concernant la coopération en matière de défense et le statut des forces.
Cet accord, signé à Nouméa le 6 décembre 2023 par le ministre des armées de la République française et le ministre des affaires intérieures et de l’immigration de la République des Fidji, instaure entre les deux pays une coopération structurée dans le domaine de la défense et régit le statut des forces françaises aux Fidji et inversement celui des forces fidjiennes en France en cas de séjour ou de transit. Cet accord fixe un cadre juridique solide et pérenne à la coopération entre les deux pays en matière de défense dans des domaines tels que l’armement, la formation et la fourniture d’aide humanitaire.
Cet accord s’inscrit ainsi dans la stratégie française dans l’Indopacifique et participe au renforcement de notre relation bilatérale avec la République des Fidji, pays avec lequel la France entretient notamment une coopération en matière de maintien de la paix et de réponse aux catastrophes naturelles à travers les forces françaises déployées dans le Pacifique.
CONVENTION DE PARTENARIAT ENTRE LA FRANCE ET L’ORGANISATION INTERNATIONALE DE POLICE CRIMINELLE – INTERPOL (OIPC-INTERPOL) RELATIVE AUX MODALITES DE REALISATION DU PROGRAMME IMMOBILIER GLOBAL DU SIEGE D’INTERPOL A LYON ET AUX ENGAGEMENTS ET RESPONSABILITES DU GOUVERNEMENT FRANÇAIS ET D’INTERPOL
Le ministre de l’Europe et des affaires étrangères a présenté un projet de loi autorisant l’approbation de la convention de partenariat entre le Gouvernement de la République française et l’Organisation internationale de police criminelle – INTERPOL (OIPC-INTERPOL) relative aux modalités de réalisation du Programme Immobilier Global du siège d’INTERPOL à Lyon et aux engagements et responsabilités du Gouvernement de la République française et d’INTERPOL, signée à Marrakech le 27 novembre 2025 et à Lyon le 15 décembre 2025.
INTERPOL a établi son siège à la cité internationale à Lyon en 1989. A la suite d’une croissance continue des effectifs et des activités d’INTERPOL, le siège existant nécessite une opération immobilière d’envergure.
La convention de partenariat définit ainsi le cadre juridique, opérationnel et financier d’un programme immobilier global, répondant aux besoins fonctionnels et opérationnels d’INTERPOL, et des engagements et responsabilités respectifs des Parties. Ce programme comprend des travaux de rénovation du siège existant, financés par INTERPOL, et des travaux d’extension et de restructuration, financés par la France à hauteur de 61,2 millions d’euros, dont 43,2 millions d’euros de l’Etat. La convention de partenariat permettra de pérenniser l’implantation du siège d’INTERPOL à Lyon en créant des conditions de travail modernisées et adaptées à l’ensemble des agents d’INTERPOL, avec une ouverture des nouveaux locaux prévue en 2031.
Elle renforce l’attractivité du territoire national pour l’installation d’organisations internationales.

The situation across the occupied West Bank has deteriorated beyond control as escalating attacks seek to drive Palestinian communities from their land, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday, Anadolu reports.
“In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land,” Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is “simply out of control” as occupiers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the UN chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains “severely restricted” ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program “urgently” requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
‘El Nino of war’ and economic strain
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.

He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. “War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them,” Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Regional diplomacy, Sudan, and Yemen
Turning to Yemen, Guterres described continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as “totally unacceptable,” urging restraint amid mounting displacement in Yemen.
Guterres said he will travel to Egypt to advance regional de-escalation, underscoring Egypt’s essential diplomatic role as a mediator in the war between the US and Iran, alongside its neighboring stakes in the wars in Sudan and Libya.

Herzog warns political rhetoric can kill, rules out pardon for Rabin assassin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:26:15 UTC
00:26:15 KST

President Isaac Herzog warned Thursday that inflammatory political rhetoric can lead to deadly violence and declared that the assassin of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin must never be released from prison, as Israel marked 31 years since the killing of the leader who pursued peace with the Palestinians.
Speaking at a state memorial ceremony at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, Herzog appealed to politicians, commentators and voters to exercise restraint ahead of national elections scheduled in five days, invoking Rabin's final warning about the dangers of political violence.
"I stand here and warn that words kill," Herzog said. "Candidates, leaders, opinion leaders and commentators — all of you — be careful with your words."
Addressing candidates from across the political spectrum, Herzog urged Israelis to remember Rabin's final public remarks, delivered shortly before his assassination at a peace rally in Tel Aviv on Nov. 4, 1995.
"Violence erodes the foundations of Israeli democracy," Herzog said, quoting Rabin. "Debate must be respected. Violence must be rejected. Elections are not a civil war."
The ceremony commemorated the 31st anniversary of Rabin's assassination and the 26th anniversary of the death of his wife, Leah Rabin.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not attend. The government was represented by Minister Gila Gamliel.
Other attendees included Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit, military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet security agency chief David Zini, former President Reuven Rivlin and political figures Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Golan.
Herzog: Rabin's assassin must die in prison
Earlier Thursday, Herzog delivered an equally forceful message at the annual "Candle for Yitzhak" state memorial ceremony at the President's Residence in Jerusalem, rejecting any possibility of clemency for Yigal Amir, the Jewish extremist convicted of murdering Rabin.
"The despicable murderer aimed his weapon not only at Yitzhak Rabin, but at the heart of the nation," Herzog said. "We lost our leader, and we nearly lost ourselves."
Herzog recounted recently seeing a billboard along Highway 1, the main road connecting Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, calling for Amir's release.
"The very possibility that such a call could appear in public and be met with a shrug should keep us awake at night," Herzog said. "We must not dismiss it as just another provocation."
He warned that calls for Amir's release risk undermining the fundamental principle that political assassination must remain an absolute red line in Israeli society.
"Behind the call to release the murderer lies the horrifying possibility that Israeli society will cease to regard his despicable act as absolutely forbidden, that, God forbid, it will stop treating it as a red line that must never be crossed," Herzog said.
"Thirty-one years are not a cooling-off period for the murder of a prime minister. And the passage of time does not diminish the gravity of the crime."
Herzog said the message passed down to future generations must be unequivocal.
"The murderer must never be released. He must end his life in prison. He must never receive any leniency or pardon whatsoever. There can be no questioning this under any circumstances," the president declared.
Amir, a right-wing Jewish extremist opposed to Rabin's peace efforts with the Palestinians, shot the prime minister after a peace rally in Tel Aviv in 1995. The assassination remains one of the most traumatic events in Israel's political history, exposing deep divisions over the Oslo peace process and the country's democratic institutions.
Rabin's grandson: His legacy belongs to all Israelis
At the Mount Herzl ceremony, Rabin's grandson, Yonatan Ben-Artzi, called for his grandfather's legacy to be remembered beyond partisan divisions.
"The memory of Yitzhak Rabin should not belong to one political camp," Ben-Artzi said. "His diplomatic legacy can be a matter of disagreement, and his actions deserve to be studied, appreciated and also criticized."
Ben-Artzi said the assassination was not merely a personal tragedy but an assault on democratic decision-making.
"The murder was not only a personal loss. It was a successful attempt to settle with bullets a disagreement that should have been resolved among citizens, in the Knesset and at the ballot box," he said.
He described Rabin as a leader defined by responsibility, hard work and difficult decisions rather than political slogans.
"He understood that leadership is measured not only by the ability to lead when everyone agrees, but also by the willingness to make difficult decisions and bear their consequences," Ben-Artzi said.
Rabin, who served as IDF chief of staff during the 1967 Six-Day War before entering politics, understood the human cost of armed conflict, his grandson said.
"He knew war firsthand. He understood its cost, the bereavement, the loss, the moral obligation to secure the release of prisoners of war and the heavy responsibility borne by those who send young people to fight on behalf of the state," Ben-Artzi said.
"He was first and foremost a fighter who struggled for the Jewish state, but he also had the vision and courage to fight for its democratic character."
Ben-Artzi said Rabin was neither naive nor under any illusion that Israel's enemies would necessarily become its friends.
"He understood that courageous decisions could provoke fierce opposition, both in combat and in the diplomatic arena," he said. "He saw and understood that Israeli society was divided over questions concerning its future, but he believed in his path and, above all, in his people."
Recalling remarks Rabin made minutes before his assassination, Ben-Artzi said his grandfather had emphasized that disagreements were legitimate in a democracy, but that political decisions must ultimately be settled through elections.
"It was as though he foresaw his fate and wanted us to remember, for the sake of our own future, that democracy does not require us to agree with one another," Ben-Artzi said.
"It allows us to disagree, argue, protest, criticize the government and try to persuade others. It requires all of us to agree on the fundamental principles of this place: Only free elections are the means by which the public grants its leaders the authority to govern. And once elections have been held, their results must be accepted."
Rabin's daughter: Israel is still struggling with the wounds of war
At the earlier ceremony at the President's Residence, Rabin's daughter, Dalia Rabin, described a country still grappling with the consequences of war and deep political divisions.
"Given what is happening in the State of Israel, this ceremony is not something we can take for granted," she said.
She recalled that the annual memorial had been especially important to her mother, Leah, who died in 2000.
"Thirty-one years, and we are in a difficult, painful and complicated period, on the eve of elections, licking the wounds of a war that has not ended," she said. "A country suffering from post-traumatic stress, with an uncertain future."
Dalia Rabin emphasized that her father's killing was a politically motivated assassination.
"He was murdered in a political assassination. A religious Jew wearing a skullcap emerged from the darkness and fired three shots into his back to stop a diplomatic process," she said.
With elections approaching and divisions in Israeli society at their peak, she said she felt a responsibility to preserve the nonpartisan character of the ceremony.
"The elections are in the air and the divisions in society are at their peak, and I, his daughter, am expected to maintain balance rather than speak candidly," she said. "So I accept the obligation of this house to preserve the dignity of the state and its institutions, as I have always done."
She said the memorial center established in her father's name was dedicated to democracy, tolerance and reducing political violence.
"We have not boycotted or disqualified any person or group," she said. "We have extended a hand to every segment of Israeli society."
Dalia Rabin also reflected on the qualities she hoped younger generations would remember about her father.
She said young visitors, tourists and Israelis frequently ask what she most wants them to take away from his legacy.
"Two elements were always there: an unwavering insistence on details before setting out, and an uncompromising demand for a serious and thorough investigation, because only through that can we learn lessons and do better," she said.
She added that learning from mistakes must go hand in hand with accepting responsibility.
"Yitzhak Rabin knew how to take responsibility for every action he regarded as falling within his authority, without compromise or exceptions," she said.
"That is also how he raised and educated us from an early age: to admit failure, learn lessons and take responsibility."
The ceremonies came as Israel prepared for another national election amid heightened political tensions.
For Herzog, the anniversary served as a warning that the country's democratic institutions depend not only on the outcome of elections, but also on the willingness of political leaders and citizens to reject violence and accept the legitimacy of their opponents.
His message was particularly stark in light of renewed public calls for Amir's release: The passage of three decades, he insisted, must not weaken the country's condemnation of political assassination.
