Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:24:21 UTC
00:24:21 KST

- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.

Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
The Chief of the General Staff, General Sir Roly Walker's speech at the official opening of Telford Gun Hall.
Secretary of State, ladies and gentlemen, it is an absolute privilege to be here at Telford today. This marks the return of large-calibre gun barrel manufacturing to the United Kingdom. This is a capability that sadly has been absent from these shores for decades.
I say sadly because Great Britain has a proud history of producing its own artillery. For centuries the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich was synonymous with excellence in this technology, and it produced artillery that shaped the outcomes of conflicts from the Napoleonic Wars through the World Wars and into the Cold War.
That arc of history reminds us that whilst armies, navies and air forces can win the battles, it takes nations to come together to win wars. The world today has brought that lesson sharply back into focus. Modern warfare consumes equipment and ammunition at extraordinary rates. In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day. And that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate.
So, to be ready to defend against attack, we must be prepared to replace and repair those fighting systems at the rate of their consumption. But industrial capacity cannot be conjured in a crisis. It must be built before the conflict.
And this facility represents an important step, a really important step in that direction. It supports the modernisation of our land forces whilst also rebuilding the skills and industrial capacity on which our future fighting power depends. It is also an incredibly strong signal of intent, a commitment to the partnership between governments, industry, and the armed forces to build the national arsenal that underwrites our national security and allows the nation’s soldiers to protect all that we hold dear.
So, in many ways, this is for them, for those soldiers, and on their behalf, today’s and tomorrow’s that I say thank you for doing what you’ve done.

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
The world’s first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus has been reported in France, where a hospitalized patient later died, according to the health authorities.
The insect-borne disease, which has circulated among livestock for decades, was previously believed to be incapable of infecting humans.
In a joint statement on Thursday, the French Health and Agriculture Ministries confirmed that the patient, who had a severely weakened immune system, died in early October after being hospitalized in Lyon.
“Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans,” the ministries said, according to AFP. They described the infection as the first confirmed detection of the pathogen in a person.
The patient developed severe neurological complications that the authorities believe were linked to the infection. However, investigators have still not established conclusively whether the virus was responsible for the death.
Officials suspect that the patient contracted the virus through the bite of an infected midge in eastern France, where the pathogen has recently been detected in cattle. The circumstances of the infection remain under investigation.
Despite the unprecedented case, the French authorities said there is currently no indication of a wider threat to public health. They stressed that the patient was severely immunocompromised and that no other human infections have been identified.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the orthobunyavirus group and was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s. It is transmitted by tiny biting insects known as Culicoides midges and has been detected in livestock in Africa and Asia.
The virus has recently emerged among European cattle, triggering concern among the veterinary authorities. In France, infections have been reported across dozens of departments, with affected animals suffering fever, diarrhea, weakness, and falling milk production, according to the French agricultural authorities.
Other viruses that have crossed from animals to humans include HIV, Ebola, and bird flu. The Covid-19 pandemic was caused by a virus widely believed to have originated in bats.
The European Center for Disease Prevention and Control has confirmed the unprecedented human case and is working with the French authorities to assess its implications.
Health officials are continuing epidemiological and laboratory investigations to determine how the patient became infected and whether other cases may have gone undetected.

Türkiye aims to strengthen energy, climate diplomacy through next month's COP31 UN Climage Change Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:52 UTC
00:22:52 KST

Gulsen Cagatay and Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
As Türkiye prepares to host next month's 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31 or COP31 Türkiye), it aims to strengthen its role in energy and climate diplomacy, help turn global climate targets into concrete action and harness its renewable energy potential through international partnerships.
COP31, scheduled for Nov. 9-20 in Antalya, will provide an opportunity to highlight Türkiye's diplomatic capabilities, position in the energy transition and climate policies on the international stage.
Türkiye will hold the COP31 Presidency and lead the Action Agenda, while Australia will serve as President of Negotiations.
Türkiye's approach to the summit focuses on turning existing climate commitments into achievable and measurable outcomes through dialogue, consensus and action.
Priority areas include electrification, the clean energy transition, green industrialization, the circular economy, climate-resilient cities and climate finance.
The COP31 Presidency has announced initiatives aimed at increasing electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, reducing energy intensity in buildings by at least 25% and cutting the rate of growth in global waste generation by half.
Turning climate commitments into bankable and investment-ready projects is also a central part of the agenda.
 
Renewable energy potential supports cooperation
Türkiye's solar and wind energy potential provides a foundation for partnerships that could emerge from COP31.
Expanding renewable energy capacity, strengthening electricity grids and accelerating electrification are among the country's energy transition priorities.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar has announced that Türkiye aims to increase its installed renewable energy capacity to 120 gigawatts by 2035, with work underway on more ambitious targets for 2040.
COP31 is therefore expected to offer opportunities to advance Türkiye's clean energy investments through international financing, technology transfer and partnerships.
 
Geographic location enables regional energy cooperation
Situated at the crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Türkiye is strategically positioned to connect energy sources with consumer markets, creating opportunities for cooperation in climate diplomacy.
Its location along international trade and energy routes allows the country to develop regional partnerships in electricity interconnections, renewable energy investment, energy efficiency and low-carbon industry.
Making better use of this potential to meet climate targets will require increasing the share of renewables in the energy system, upgrading electricity grids and accelerating the transformation of energy infrastructure.
 
International partnerships, green industry gain prominence
Global Energy Association President Murat Dilek told Anadolu that expanding Türkiye's manufacturing capacity for renewable energy equipment, particularly wind turbines and solar panels, offers significant opportunities for green industrialization and for strengthening the country's role in energy and climate diplomacy.
Increasing domestic manufacturing capacity would support renewable energy investment, while Türkiye's strategic position connecting Europe, the Middle East and Asia could help the country play a greater role in regional supply chains, Dilek said.
He added that these developments would improve Türkiye's competitiveness in the global clean energy market.
"Türkiye's diplomatic success in this process will be measured not only by the establishment of dialogue between countries, but also by the transformation of the targets set out in Antalya into concrete partnerships and viable projects," Dilek said.
"To turn this potential into lasting gains, Türkiye needs to implement its national climate targets, accelerate clean energy investments and facilitate access to climate finance," he said, adding: "By boosting domestic manufacturing and technological capabilities, reducing environmental impacts and strengthening international partnerships, Türkiye can demonstrate its potential not only as a diplomatic actor in the COP31 process, but also as a manufacturing and technology hub contributing to the global green transition."

====================================================================================================

Michael Wynne, Fired as SECAF Alongside CSAF Moseley, Dead at 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:21:43 UTC
00:21:43 KST

Michael Wynne, the 21st Secretary of the Air Force died Oct. 17. He was 82 years old.
Wynne was Secretary from 2005 to 2008, a stretch of time when the U.S. military was struggling to quell insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Army was struggling to simultaneously man occupation forces in two theaters. Roadside bombs and insurgent attacks were killing U.S. troops, and the Air Force was under intense pressure to support its sister service with increased intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage and manpower and force cuts to ease the Army’s burden.
The Air Force was also fighting to protect its modernization efforts at the time, especially the F-22 Raptor program, which was less than halfway to its objective of 750 planes, new tankers (which would ultimately become the KC-46), and a future bomber (which would eventually yield the B-21).
In 2006, an Air Force B-52 took off from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and flew to Barksdale Air Force Base, La., its crew unknowingly carrying nuclear weapons on board, a so-called “bent spear” incident. The discovery kicked off an investigation, recriminations, self-examination, and subsequent organizational, procedural, and cultural changes across the nuclear community.
The incident added to the tension between the Air Force and then-Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, who saw the service and particularly then-Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael “Buzz” Moseley as recalcitrant in their pushback over budget, manning, and modernization. Seeing Wynne and Moseley as a close knit tandem, Gates fired both in June 2008, beheading the service—the first-ever simultaneous removal of a service chief and secretary.
Military Roots
Wynne hailed from a military family and followed his father’s footsteps to attend the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, graduating at the height of the Vietnam War. Among his 578 classmates, 30 died in Vietnam and about 100 others were wounded in fighting in Southeast Asia.
Instead of joining the Army, however, Wynne followed his older brother into the Air Force, reporting for Active Duty in August 1966.
“The day I reported for Active Duty, the report of my brother being shot down was announced,” Wynn recalled in a 2005 interview with the Washington Post. Maj. Patrick Wynne, a 1963 graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, had trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the 555th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Thailand. After only four months in country, his F-4C Phantom was shot down over Vietnam on Aug. 8, 1966. He was declared missing in action, and remained so until 1977, when his remains were identified and later returned to the United States. He is buried at the Air Force Academy.
The younger Wynne served seven years in the Air Force, his final tour as an assistant professor of astronautics at the Air Force Academy.
Wynne then went to work for General Dynamics. For the next 26 years, he worked as an executive there, save for a three-year stint with Lockheed Martin after Lockheed acquired GD’s Space Systems Division. His work during in those years spanned General Dynamics’ F-16 and M1A2 tank divisions as well as space systems, including work on the Atlas, Titan, and Centaur launch vehicles.
In 2001, Wynne joined Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s Pentagon leadership team. Following the election of President George W. Bush, Wynne was confirmed as Principal Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics, the start of a seven-year run in public service. In 2003, he was made Acting Undersecretary and he remained in that role until June 2005. Among his tasks at the time were leading the Pentagon’s preparations for the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure plan, which sought to “rationalize” the Defense Department’s far-flung bases and increase cross-service cooperation.
The 2005 BRAC results proved disappointing. Projected to save the Pentagon more than $25 billion annually by 2011, the plans failed to deliver due to higher-than anticipated construction costs, inflation, and incorrect assumptions. Instead of savings, the changes yielded a net cost increase, even when spread out over 20 years.
As Air Force Secretary, Wynne opposed efforts to consolidate and adopt joint basing, having come to embrace the Air Force’s explanation that many of its units operate and fight from their home bases rather than deploy to forward theaters.
“The Air Force has a very different concept of operations,” he would tell Air Force Magazine in 2008, weeks after his departure. Putting Air Force bases under the control of other services would undermine combat effectiveness, he said, adding, “I’d probably get fired again over my objection to the way the joint basing is happening.”
More than that, Wynne was a visionary, said Richard Andres, a professor at the National War College worked with Wynne in government. Wynne’s ideas presaged numerous future defense initiatives, Andres said: “His vision of linking sensors and weapons across military domains anticipated today’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control. He was first to champion cyberspace as a warfighting domain and brought data transparency and decision dashboards into Air Force management. He understood early that America’s military advantage would depend as much on connecting information and people as on building superior weapons.”
Wynne also butted heads with Gates over the F-22. While Gates suggested the Air Force could give up the “exquisite” F-22 because the then-fledgling F-35 was scheduled to join the fleet in 2014, Wynne disagreed.
“The notion of the F-22 [is] … similar to the F-35—we need to get rid of that,” Wynne said in his 2008 debrief with Air Force Magazine. The F-35, rather, “complements the F-22, but the F-22 is clearly an air superiority and air dominance weapon. The F-35 is a multinational, multirole, [air-to-ground] versatile airplane.”
When Gates dismissed concerns about future conflict as “next-war-itis,” Wynne didn’t give in. “He was willing to put his position on the line. He understood that the demands of the wars we were fighting could not excuse neglecting the wars we might have to fight next.”
In the months leading up to his dismissal, Wynne and Andres spoke weekly, including about the possibility that Gates would fire him, Andres recalled. “He understood the risk,” Andres said. “He cared more about what the nation needed than about keeping his job.”
Gates took over as Secretary about a year after Wynne had been moved to the Air Force. At the time, USAF was bearing a heavy burden for the Army. In a 2006 C-SPAN interview, Wynne tried to justify a planned cut of 40,000 Airman, suggesting that technological advancement made it possible to do “trimming in advance of new systems coming on and planning for the future right now.” But he acknowledged that having 5,000 Airmen doing Army jobs in Iraq was not sustainable.
“At some point in the future, it doesn’t work in the math—the Army has to pick up combat service support,” he said.
The Air Force’s pursuit of a new tanker aircraft, a protracted and contentious effort that preceded him and would continue to drag on for years, was another challenge during Wynne’s tenure. As Secretary, he pressed for a single tanker aircraft rather than splitting the order between Boeing and Airbus platforms, as some urged. But after departing the Pentagon, he reconsidered, seeing value in it. He also came to regret not requiring that tankers become network nodes, an extra role for which they might have been well-suited.
And while many in the Pentagon failed to appreciate the Air Force’s contributions to the war in Iraq, Wynne became a strong advocate, noting that the 2007 “surge” of forces in Iraq was not merely an Army ground operation. “We surged 400 percent in the number of sorties and 1,000 percent in the pounds of ordnance dropped,” he said in a press conference on his final day in office. “What happened? I would tell you that what happened was the realization that we could get connectivity between the ground commanders and the air component—that there was true situational awareness available.”
Still, on June 5, 2008, Gates decided he wasn’t getting what he wanted out of Air Force leadership. Wynne and Moseley were en route to a Corona meeting of Air Force leaders at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, when Gates dropped the bombshell, dismissing both.
The stated reason was the failures of Air Force leadership to safely steward the security of nuclear weapons, but it was no secret Gates and the Air Force were at odds on a range of issues, and few believed the public explanation. From the number of “orbits” flown by surveillance drones over Iraq and Afghanistan to support troops operating on the ground to Gates objections to “next-war-itis” and the Air Force’s focus on high-end stealth fighters and the threats of a rising China in the Pacific, the two sides were out of sync.
Moseley, in an interview, recalled his close working relationship with Wynne as “a privilege and a gift.” The two tried to meet daily and they shared a perspective both in terms of their duty and vision for the service. They also became friends.
“Mike Wynne and I had the best relationship of any that I’ve seen with 13-plus secretaries I worked with,” Moseley said. Wynne was well versed in the workings of the Pentagon hierarchy, the needs of each of the services, and how to get things done, the former chief said. “But he also understood the theater logistics, the technology to address the new world, and he understood the acquisition process better than anybody.”
Together, they worked to lay out and explain their priorities, the need for increased resources—estimated then to be $20 billion annually to modernize, in order:
- Tankers
- Search and rescue
- Satellites that could be protected from cyber and maneuver attack
- F-35s to replace the F-16
- A new bomber
They laid out that plan shortly before the firing in a Pentagon meeting with Gates and other officials. Mosely recalled that afterward Wynne declared the presentation a success.
“I think that meeting went well,” Wynne told him, draping an arm around Moseley’s shoulder as they walked the Pentagon hallway. “But I think we’re both dead.”
Wynne may have been the only one who saw it coming.
When the decision came down to fire them, both were at Scott Air Force Base, en route to Dayton for a planned Corona meeting of Air Force leadership at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Moseley was ordered back to Washington, where Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen delivered the news. In Dayton, Wynne was told to stand by for an unscheduled visit from Deputy Secretary of Defense Gordon England, who was flying in. No reason was given. Was England coming to discuss Moseley’s successor, someone wondered. “No,” Wynne said. “He’s coming for me.”
As the Corona meeting unfolded, Moseley called Wynne from Washington to say he was being relieved. Reporters began to call before England even arrived, adding to Wynne’s convictions. CNN might have been first to report the firings. Defense News Editor Vago Muradian, a rare press gallery guest at the Corona gathering, got his story out online on Defense News and Air Force Times. At the Pentagon, frustrated reporters gathered outside the press secretary’s office looking for answers; inside, staff was still trying to piece together what happened.
Two weeks later, Wynne departed the Pentagon at an official ceremony presided over by Gates, with Moseley at his side. What had been a very public firing was glossed over for public consumption as Gates pinned a medal on Wynne’s chest. Having Gates preside was Wynne’s idea, said retired Maj. Gen. Daryl Burke, Wynne’s military aide at the time. It was a challenge: Gates would either have to refuse or honor Wynne for his public service.
At the ceremony, Wynne expressed love for the service. “But it is the people of the Air Force that make the Air Force,” he added, “so in loving the Air Force, we love the people.”
Burke recalled how Wynne advised him to stand away as they awaited England’s arrival. Burke insisted he would stand with Wynne regardless, but Wynne was trying to ensure that Burke wouldn’t be damaged by association in the future by being seen as too closely associated with a politically unpopular boss. Wynne subsequently worked behind the scenes to find Burke a next assignment that would keep his career on track. In doing so, Wynne demonstrated both caring for his Airman and a savvy hand on the tiller for navigating Pentagon politics.
Lt. Gen. David Deptula, now dean of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, was on the Air Staff at the time, recalling that Wynne kept working on the issues he believed in up to the very end—in particular, his opposition to joint basing.
“Secretary Wynne was a leader of uncommon integrity, genuine kindness, and extraordinary loyalty,” Deptula said. “He never confused holding a position of authority with the responsibility to do what was right. I witnessed his character firsthand when, even after learning he would be removed as Secretary of the Air Force, he continued working tirelessly to strengthen the service he loved. He put principle above position, loyalty above personal ambition, and the nation’s security above all else. In a famous action, when SECDEF Gates told Secretary Wynne to fire Chief of Staff, Buzz Moseley… Wynne refused. So, Gates fired both. The Air Force and our nation are better for his service, and I am better for having known him. He will be greatly missed.”
Robbin Laird, a military analyst and prolific writer who worked for Wynne during his Pentagon tenure, wrote admiringly of the former secretary in a remembrance, citing what he called the Wynne Doctrine: “If you are ever involved in a fair fight, it is the result of poor planning.”
“It is easy to hear it as swagger. It was the opposite,” Laird wrote. “A fair fight is one whose outcome is in doubt. When the outcome is in doubt, young Americans pay for that doubt with their lives. Mike believed a leader’s first duty was to make sure it never happens. That meant technology, organization, the unglamorous work of logistics and sustainment, and the discipline to think years ahead of the adversary.”
Michael Walter Wynne was born in Clearwater, Fla. He is survived by his wife Barbara and four married daughters.

The vulnerabilities, identified with the assistance of artificial intelligence and disclosed on Wednesday, have prompted governments and businesses worldwide to temporarily suspend websites and online services amid concerns that the flaws could be exploited in cyberattacks.
The PHP development team announced that it had identified two major vulnerabilities by the early hours of Wednesday and released security patches to address them. ■

Interview: China rowing coach hails athletes after eight-medal haul in Qingdao
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:15:27 CST
00:15:27 KST

QINGDAO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's Italian head coach Francesco Cattaneo credited teamwork, mutual trust and his athletes' determination for the country's success at the 2026 World Rowing Beach Sprint Finals in Qingdao, where the host nation won four gold, three silver and one bronze medal.
"When a foreign coach arrives in a new country, it is not always easy for everyone to embrace new ideas immediately," Cattaneo told Xinhua. "But in China, the athletes and coaching staff trusted the changes we introduced, and I believe that made a difference."
Known as Franco, Cattaneo is a former elite rower who won several medals at the World Rowing Championships before moving into coaching. He spent 12 years in a senior technical role with Italy's national rowing team and oversaw the country's beach sprint program from 2020 to 2024.
Cattaneo joined China's national team earlier this year, with the squad beginning preparations in late January. Training camps in Italy and Portugal formed part of a nearly 10-month buildup to the Qingdao championships.
Beach sprint rowing, which will make its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028, combines running on sand with high-speed rowing in open water. Athletes sprint from the beach, board their boats, navigate around buoys and return to shore before racing across the finish line.
Unlike traditional flat-water rowing, where races typically last around six minutes, beach sprint events demand explosive efforts lasting just two and a half to three minutes.
"Being a good flat-water rower is not enough," Cattaneo said. "Athletes must also learn to run, jump into boats, navigate waves and make turns under pressure."
He said the months of preparation had helped China's athletes develop the physical and technical skills needed to compete at the highest level.
Those preparations were tested in Qingdao, where rough seas and changing weather conditions disrupted the competition schedule and forced organizers to squeeze much of the racing into two days.
"The athletes have followed our advice on how to deal with different situations," Cattaneo said. "I am very pleased with how they responded to the challenges."
Although he acknowledged that competing on familiar waters had given China an advantage, Cattaneo said the team's eight-medal haul had exceeded expectations.
"It confirms that we are on the right path," he said.
However, the Italian warned that success on home waters was no guarantee of Olympic glory, insisting that China still had considerable work to do before the Los Angeles Games.
"We can celebrate these medals for a few days, but then we must put them away and get straight back to work," he said. "The level we have reached will certainly not be enough in Los Angeles."
Cattaneo identified aerobic and anaerobic fitness, explosive power, boat handling and navigation as key areas for improvement, while stressing the importance of adapting to different sea conditions.
He noted that the relatively calm waters expected in Los Angeles could present a different challenge from the rough seas encountered in Qingdao.
"We must be able to make the boat go fast even when there are few waves," he said.
Beyond China's Olympic ambitions, Cattaneo hopes the discipline's inclusion in the Games will inspire more young people to take up the sport.
"It is a beautiful, exciting and very young discipline," he said. "Whether you come from traditional rowing or not, if you have speed, power and the ability to handle the sea, I would encourage you to give it a try." ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China-Europe freight train trips top 140,000 as land corridor gains ground
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:15:08 CST
00:15:08 KST

A freight train loaded with containers departs from Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Oct. 22, 2026. A China-Europe freight train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, at around 11:30 a.m. Thursday, bringing the service's cumulative trips to top 140,000 and transporting goods worth over 560 billion U.S. dollars since 2011. Within China, 96 scheduled routes for trains traveling at 120 km per hour link 132 cities along the western, central and eastern corridors, while overseas the network now runs on three lines: northern, central and southern. Together they reach 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering most parts of Eurasia, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway), the national rail operator. The southern route is now operating on regular basis, running 746 trains in the first nine months of 2026, up 125 percent year on year. (Xinhua/Pan Yulong)
SHENYANG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The China-Europe freight train service passed 140,000 cumulative trips on Thursday, a milestone that underscores its role as a reliable logistics corridor for Eurasian trade, especially as geopolitical tensions and disruptions to traditional shipping routes challenge global supply chains.
The milestone was marked as a train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, at around 11:30 a.m. Thursday. The value of goods transported by the China-Europe freight train service has exceeded 560 billion U.S. dollars since 2011.
The figures reflect that Eurasia's overland corridor has shifted from a niche alternative to a mainstay of regional logistics. This shift is seen not merely in the number of trains, but in what they carry, their destinations, and the reliability of their arrivals.
The growth has been steady rather than sudden. Annual trips rose from 1,702 in 2016 to 20,022 in 2025, an average annual increase of more than 30 percent, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC).
As a flagship project and a landmark brand of the Belt and Road Initiative, the China-Europe freight train service, also referred to as the "steel camel caravans," has established a comprehensive logistics network across Eurasia.
The expansion has come as geopolitical tensions, disruptions to maritime routes and high air freight costs pushed more trade firms to look for stable and efficient transport channels. Rail freight costs roughly one-fifth of air transport and takes about one-quarter of the time of sea transport, and it is less exposed to weather and to disruption on traditional maritime routes, according to the NDRC.
The network has broadened in step. Within China, 96 scheduled routes for trains traveling at 120 km per hour link 132 cities along the western, central and eastern corridors, while overseas the network runs on three lines: northern, central and southern.
The overseas routes now reach 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering most parts of Eurasia, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway), the national rail operator.
The southern route shows where that demand is going. Operating on a regular basis, it ran 746 trains in the first nine months of 2026, up 125 percent year on year, far faster than the network as a whole. Regular service linking the Chinese city of Xi'an with Baku, capital of Azerbaijan, began in July 2024, and one such service traverses Central Asia and crosses the Caspian Sea before continuing to Europe either via the overland railway network or by crossing the Black Sea.
The reach extends outward as much as inward. Shuai Bin, a professor at the School of Transportation and Logistics at Southwest Jiaotong University, said the service "has drawn global resources and production factors further into inland regions, while fostering a new pattern of opening up featuring highly-coordinated development between coastal ports and inland hubs."
On the European side, Duisburg alone handles about 30 percent of China-Europe rail freight volume, according to Markus Teuber, the German city's China affairs commissioner.
The range of goods that move along those lines has expanded even faster. Goods now span 53 categories and more than 50,000 items. In the first quarter of 2026, mechanical equipment remained the largest category on outbound trips, followed by automobiles and auto parts. Exports of automobiles and auto parts rose 46 percent year on year, while inbound grains, wood pulp and rubber products climbed 87 percent, 64 percent and 24 percent respectively, data released by China Railway in April showed.
According to the operator, the loaded container rate on the return leg had held at 100 percent for 49 consecutive months as of September.
"The rising share of return services shows the China-Europe freight trains are shifting from one-way exports to a healthier, two-way trade corridor, helping make Eurasian trade more balanced and sustainable," Sun Zhang, a professor at Tongji University, was quoted by the Global Times as saying.
Carrying that cargo reliably is harder than finding it, and reliability rather than speed has now become a primary gauge of the service. Trains running on fixed timetables, with designated numbers, routes and crossing times agreed across borders, cut transit time by about a quarter, and the journey from Xi'an to Duisburg takes as little as 11 days, down from 15. Some 22 such services now link nine Chinese and six European cities, and the average value of a single container is 41 percent higher than on regular trains, according to the NDRC.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for upgrading the service, and the NDRC has said it will improve transport organization, open more alternative routes and deepen coordination with countries along the corridor.
An official with the logistics center of China Railway said the operator has been advancing infrastructure connectivity and the alignment of standards and rules to build a smooth, efficient, multi-directional network that connects rails with sea routes. ■
A freight train loaded with containers departs from Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Oct. 22, 2026.(Xinhua/Pan Yulong)

From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:13:34 UTC
00:13:34 KST

From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.
It all began on the streets.
A student-led movement has emerged as the most serious challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader, Aleksandar Vucic, ahead of Sunday’s election.
Over the past two years, many citizens, teachers, professors and other experts have joined the students, a protest group that has evolved into a political movement: “Student List–Students Win” (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeđuju).
The catalyst came after the collapse of a concrete canopy at the renovated Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024. Sixteen people were killed in the tragedy, which triggered public outrage over alleged corruption and raised questions about construction safety, the quality of renovation work, and government oversight. Students who led protests have sought a fundamental overhaul of a system they deem rotten.
‘Serbia belongs to people, not to criminals’
Kosta Golubovic, a law student at the University of Novi Sad, has been involved since day one.
“Change is clearly necessary. The state must belong to its people, not to the mafia and criminals,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The way they treat the judiciary, the catastrophic conditions at the local level, mayors resorting to violence, dying villages – along with dubious privatisations, money laundering, the erosion of every single institution, police being replaced by thugs, and an education system vanishing before our eyes… these are some of the reasons why change is needed,” said Golubovic.
Demonstrations transformed into the biggest protest movement in Serbia in years, joined by tens of thousands.
The students have not called for the overthrow of Vucic. But their persistence created one of the biggest threats to the president’s long grip on power.
Vucic became prime minister in 2014. In 2017, he was elected president, a traditionally ceremonial role that he has bolstered by maintaining influence over his SNS party.
‘Vucic is afraid of us’
Opposition parties and rights watchdogs accuse Vucic and his SNS party of bribing voters, stifling media freedom, violence against opponents, and ties with organised crime.
Vucic and his allies deny these allegations. But Serbia’s rating on Transparency International’s global corruption index has worsened gradually in recent years.
“Vucic is clearly afraid of us – it’s obvious. He knows that, for the first time in 16 years, the SNS is no longer the most popular political option in the country,” Golubovic said.
The students’ efficiency is down in part to its structure.
The old student parliament at the University of Belgrade has been replaced with plenums – daily assemblies where each group votes on its course of action. Working groups focus on strategy, donations, and security. Universities in different cities coordinate so demands remain broadly aligned.
This is why the students say they do things differently. One rule is to be leaderless, making it harder for authorities to disrupt the protests. Also, demonstrations must be peaceful, and any debris has to be cleaned up. Third, all decisions must be made democratically during hour-long plenary sessions in their university faculties.
“Even though the authorities mobilised criminal groups against the students and citizens participating in the protests, the students have remained focused on their goal: to oust a government they view as authoritarian and deeply corrupt,” said Natasa Kandic, a Serbian peace activist, sociologist, and founder of the Humanitarian Law Center (HLC) in Belgrade.
“For the first time in Serbia, they have managed to lead protests entirely without violence,” she said. “The video clips we see daily represent a new culture – one defined by irony, laughter, and the deliberate disregard for primitivism and political depravity.”
‘Serious and comprehensive plan’
State-affiliated media have maligned the students. Some Serbian authorities claimed that the group has no programme, and Vucic labelled them as “terrorists”. But their leaders, experts from different fields, claim that they have a plan.
The platform is officially titled the “Student Plan” and is divided into three sections. There are 11 points.
Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and the lead candidate and ballot holder for the Student List, explained that the platform deliberately avoids setting fixed, precise deadlines for the proposed changes. He argued that such timelines can only be determined once contributors have gained insight into the “full current state of affairs”.
“[We plan] many things – too many to list – but the goal is to change the system,” said Srdanovic in a brief call to Al Jazeera.
During debates, the establishment of a special prosecutorial police unit, a law on the origin of assets, transitional justice and the renovation of rural medical clinics are some frequent themes.
Could this be implemented in the case of a victory? Kandic is sceptical.
“The student movement doesn’t possess a transformative potential – the capacity to drive social change, break with the past, and alter a political climate where convicted war criminals are celebrated, Kosovo is treated as part of Serbia, and politicians from neighboring countries are branded as enemies,” he said.

Gaza could face another famine as Israeli restrictions on incoming goods leave residents struggling to obtain food, with flour shortages threatening bread production, a Geneva-based human rights group warned Thursday, Anadolu reports.
Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor said its teams observed increasingly empty markets and soaring food prices, accusing Israel of “deliberately depriving” Palestinians of adequate nutrition as part of an ongoing genocide.
According to the rights group, after Israeli authorities suspended commercial goods deliveries to Gaza on Oct. 13, it announced on Oct. 19 that some imports would be allowed to resume. However, the group said the decision brought little relief, as shipments remained heavily restricted and fresh fruits and vegetables were still denied entry.
It added that residents and traders face further uncertainty when crossings close on Fridays and Saturdays, with no assurance that deliveries will resume on Sundays. Such interruptions risk exhausting already scarce supplies and pushing food prices further beyond residents’ reach.
READ: Gaza Health Ministry warns hospital generators may shut down
The organization reported that several bakeries had recently stopped operating because they lacked flour and fuel, including two major facilities in Gaza City.
It cited the head of Gaza’s Bakery Owners Association as warning that seven other bakeries receiving World Food Program (WFP) support might cease operations within 48 hours.
According to the group, deliveries allowed into Gaza currently cover no more than 37% of residents’ requirements, while fresh produce remains severely restricted.
The warning follows the WFP’s Monday announcement that funding shortages had forced it to reduce food assistance, affecting approximately half a million Palestinians.
Euro-Med urged Israel to remove restrictions on essential goods and called on international donors to increase food assistance and help bakeries resume operations.

Romanian prosecutors send hard-right lawmaker to trial for suspected hate speech
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romanian prosecutors on Thursday sent one of the country's most prominent hard-right politicians, AUR vice-president and lawmaker Dan Tanasa, to trial on charges of inciting hate speech and discrimination against foreign workers.
Tanasa is a senior figure in the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians (AUR), Romania's second-largest party, which currently leads opinion polls.
Prosecutors said Tanasa urged followers in an August 2025 social media post to refuse deliveries made by foreign workers.
"Refuse the order if it is not delivered by a Romanian," Tanasa wrote. "Do not encourage the import of unqualified labourers from Asia and Africa."
He also said he did not want Romania to follow the same path as other Western nations which he said were "drowning under the Islamic wave".
Prosecutors said the statements incited discrimination and could damage relations between citizens by undermining mutual respect. Romanian lawmakers have parliamentary immunity for political views which prosecutors said did not extend to the current case.
Days after the post, a South Asian delivery worker was assaulted in the capital Bucharest and required medical treatment. Tanasa rejected accusations that his comments had encouraged the attack. A second delivery worker was attacked near Bucharest several months later.
Like other countries in central and eastern Europe, European Union member Romania relies on non-EU workers, many from South Asia, to fill labour shortages in sectors including hospitality and construction.
Tanasa was not available for comment. AUR called the prosecution an attack on free speech.
"If simply opposing immigration policy can become a crime then the problem is not Dan Tanasa," it said in a statement.
AUR, which has been critical of the European Union, military aid to Ukraine and defence spending plans, is polling at around 40%, making it Romania's most popular political party. REUTERS

Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over civilian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over attacks on civilians
Syrian authorities have arrested a former brigadier general accused of ordering attacks on civilians under Bashar al-Assad's regime, alongside five other suspects, as the country's new government continues efforts to prosecute those implicated in atrocities during the civil war.
Brigadier General Abdul Hakim Wanous, former chief of staff of the 35th Special Forces Regiment, was detained by military police in the central province of Hama on Wednesday, according to local judicial authorities.
Wanous is accused of ordering artillery attacks, carrying out arbitrary arrests and participating in military raids and operations targeting civilian areas in the Damascus countryside and the Ghab Plain in Hama province.
Ahmed al-Sheikh Khalil, head of the transitional justice prosecution office in Hama, said the former officer was suspected of involvement in serious violations and crimes against humanity committed during the Syrian uprising.
The five other detainees, whose identities have not been disclosed, are also suspected of involvement in abuses against civilians under the former government.
Judicial authorities said preliminary investigations were continuing before the suspects are referred to Hama's specialised transitional justice investigation chamber.
Hama's attorney general, Mohammed Ahmed al-Naasan, stressed the importance of pursuing those implicated in abuses through legal proceedings that ensure accountability, justice for victims and compensation for those affected.
The arrests come amid a broader campaign by Syria's new authorities to locate former military and intelligence personnel accused of atrocities during Assad's rule, which ended in December 2024.
In a separate operation on Wednesday, security forces reportedly detained around 12 former regime officers and personnel in the Masyaf area of Hama province.
A security source told Lebanese newspaper Al-Modon that the operation involved internal security and counterterrorism units, and targeted former regime personnel who had previously undergone security reconciliation procedures after Assad's overthrow.
The detainees are suspected of continuing to gather intelligence on behalf of Assad loyalist networks despite having formally regularised their status with the new authorities.
Al-Modon also reported the arrest of Younes Mohammed, a former prison official accused of involvement in abuses against detainees at the Balouna prison in Homs and the notorious Saydnaya prison near Damascus.
Mohammed was reportedly arrested in Qadmus, in Tartous province, after security forces tracked him to a business he was operating under his wife's name. The allegations against him have not been independently verified.
Earlier this month, Hama authorities referred 30 suspects accused of crimes including murder, kidnapping, sexual violence and extortion to the transitional justice authorities following investigations in the Salamiyah area.
The arrests form part of Syria's attempts to confront the legacy of decades of repression under the Assad family, particularly the widespread detention, torture and killing of civilians during the civil war.
Following Assad's overthrow, the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa established a National Commission for Transitional Justice in May 2025 to investigate crimes committed by the former regime, support victims and pursue accountability.
Syria began its first public trial of senior Assad-era officials in April 2026, including Atef Najib, a former intelligence chief and cousin of Bashar al-Assad, whose treatment of detained teenagers in Daraa helped ignite the 2011 uprising.
In August, a Damascus court convicted Najib and several other former regime figures, including Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher, who were tried in absentia, over crimes committed during the uprising.
However, human rights organisations have raised concerns about the capacity of Syria's judicial system to prosecute the vast number of alleged perpetrators while ensuring fair trials and protecting witnesses.
Human Rights Watch has warned that gaps in the country's legal framework, alongside questions over judicial independence and due process, could undermine accountability for crimes committed during the conflict.
The organisation has also called for investigations into abuses committed by all parties to the civil war, rather than limiting prosecutions to former government officials.

Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership
On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.
“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.
This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.
The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.
On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).
On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.
Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.
‘Launching a new era’
Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.
He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.
Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.
“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” Erdogan said.
Relations between the two countries will expand “for generations to come”, Carney said alongside Erdogan.
“Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience, and that’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both, and in Turkiye, we have an exceptional partner,” he added.
Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.
He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.
The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

Dreadnought reactor still on schedule, minister says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:11 BST
00:00:11 KST

Ministers have confirmed that good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the Rolls-Royce PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought class submarines, and that reactor components remain on course to support the first boat entering service in the early 2030s as planned, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what progress he had made on delivering the Rolls Royce PWR3 reactor for Dreadnought.
Luke Pollard replied: “Good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought Class submarines. The Ministry of Defence continues to work closely with Rolls-Royce Submarines to ensure delivery of the reactor components in time to support Dreadnought entering service in the early 2030s as planned.”
PWR3 is the first wholly new British submarine reactor design since PWR2 entered service in the Vanguard class in the 1990s, developed by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Derby with design input drawn from American practice under the Mutual Defence Agreement. The plant is intended to run for the life of the boat without refuelling, which removes the mid-life refuelling docking that Vanguard required and changes the availability arithmetic across a four boat force.
Rolls-Royce has doubled its Derby site under a contract worth around nine billion pounds covering reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and has been recruiting at a rate the company has not managed since the Cold War. Reactor components are among the longest lead items on any submarine, so they drive the build schedule at Barrow.
Dreadnought replaces the Vanguard class on continuous at-sea deterrent patrol, four boats carrying Trident D5 missiles, with the first entering service in the early 2030s after a programme the National Audit Office has repeatedly flagged for schedule and cost pressure. The Vanguards are already serving well beyond their design lives, and patrol lengths have stretched past six months as a result.

For the past week, President Donald Trump and his aides have traded accusations with Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, over who restricted Ukraine’s access to a military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network product that Ukrainian forces depend on to intercept incoming Russian projectiles and target Russian launchers.
Musk blamed Trump and the U.S. military for the decision, writing on X, “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Trump insisted that his administration did not disrupt Ukraine’s access to the network. Secretary of State Marco Rubio argued that decisions about Ukraine’s access to the network were in the hands of SpaceX and Musk and not the White House. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that the decision had been Musk’s.
On Mar. 9, 2025, Musk had promised that, whatever his disagreements with U.S. policy toward Ukraine, “Starlink will never turn off its terminals. We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.” Critics have raced to blame Musk alone, casting him as the puppeteer behind the throne, the first business titan to achieve what William Randolph Hearst, Marcus Alonzo Hanna, and J.P. Morgan only aspired to: a latter-day Cornelius Vanderbilt, who is reputed to have scoffed, “Law? What do I care about the law? Hain’t I got the power?”
That gets the story backward. Musk’s businesses are uniquely dependent on the blessings of Washington: a fifth of SpaceX’s revenue comes directly from federal agencies, its satellites require federal authorization to launch and operate, and the possible merger of Tesla and SpaceX will live or die by the decisions of federal regulators.
Confronted with a White House that appeared determined to squeeze Ukraine, whatever its public denials, Musk faced a familiar choice for anyone dependent on political patronage: capitulate, resist, or retreat into ambiguity. He chose ambiguity, revealing the limits of his power. The wealthiest man in the world still answers to someone else.
The finger-pointing creates a haze of ambiguity, giving both men plausible deniability. The apparent aim is to force Ukraine into a settlement by depriving it of the means to resist: a way to secure a quick, short-term peace and lower oil prices at the expense of Ukrainian sovereignty and international law.
But that calculation mistakes capitulation for stability. Rewarding President Vladimir Putin of Russia could encourage him to test NATO’s resolve in the Baltic states, Poland, Finland, or Sweden, raising the risk of a direct confrontation with the alliance. It would also signal to other U.S. adversaries that sufficient pressure can fold Washington’s commitments.
For now, Trump could claim to have brokered peace between Russia and Ukraine, even if the peace he delivers is the silence of a defeated country. Musk can evade responsibility by presenting himself as merely one supplier among many across the defense industry whose failures have weakened Ukraine’s defenses. He could point to weapons manufacturer RTX, whose Patriot interceptors are so scarce that Ukraine reportedly ran out of them this month, or to delays in delivering F-16s manufactured by Lockheed Martin that were promised two years earlier.
Faustian bargains
Beneath the public quarrel lies a familiar pattern: surrender political independence and retain the freedom to accumulate extraordinary wealth. The historians who have studied Putin’s Russia most closely would recognize the pattern instantly. Timothy Snyder has written that Russia’s oligarchs “were tamed, but not by a neutral state.” Rather, “Putin himself became the head oligarch, the boss of bosses.” Anne Applebaum echoed the insight and described Putin as making himself “godfather to all of the other oligarchs.”
Putin laid out the terms of that bargain on Jul. 28, 2000, when he met with 21 of Russia's richest men in the Kremlin, less than three months after his inauguration. The message was simple. The fortunes they had amassed in the chaos of the 1990s were theirs to keep, as long as they stayed out of politics entirely. Keep your distance from power, and the state would leave you alone.
Those who refused the deal faced immediate reprisals. Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky, whose television networks refused to bend the knee, were driven into exile within the year. Gusinsky’s NTV was seized by state-controlled Gazprom. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, then Russia’s richest man, funded opposition parties and lectured the Kremlin on corruption. In Oct. 2003 he was pulled off his plane at a Siberian airport and arrested. He spent a decade in prison and watched his oil company, Yukos, dismantled and its assets transferred to state-controlled companies.
Those who accepted the deal are the ones who got rich, and they have never been richer. Forbes counted a record 155 Russian billionaires this year, the fourth straight year that number has grown, with a combined fortune of $696.5 billion—up 11% from the previous year, even as Putin’s war against Ukraine entered its fifth year. Their collective wealth reportedly now exceeds the bank term deposits of the rest of Russia’s population: 155 oligarchs with fortunes greater than the savings of roughly 146 million ordinary Russians.
“Oligarchies are unstable,” Snyder has observed. “Members disappear.” For those who might have forgotten the terms of Putin’s bargain, an instructive reminder came in 2023, when Yevgeny Prigozhin, the head of the Wagner Group, did the one thing the bargain forbade: he challenged the Kremlin’s authority. Prigozhin seized a military headquarters in Rostov-on-Don and sent his forces toward Moscow. His column advanced to within 125 miles of the capital before he agreed to stand down under a deal brokered by Aleksandr Lukashenko, the Belarusian dictator.
Putin publicly called the mutiny treason, then appeared to forgive him. Two months later, on Aug. 23, 2023, Prigozhin’s private jet crashed north of Moscow, killing everyone aboard. The Kremlin denied involvement, the U.S. intelligence concluded that the plane had been blown up, and The Wall Street Journal later reported that the operation had been ordered by Putin’s Security Council chief. Putin’s eulogy, delivered the next day, described Prigozhin as a man who had “made serious mistakes in life.” No oligarch in Russia needed the rest of the sentence spelled out.
Prigozhin’s fate is only the most spectacular entry on a longer, murkier list. Since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, at least 85 Russian businessmen and officials have reportedly died in unexplained or violent circumstances, many of them figures in the energy industry. Among the dead are three Lukoil executives: board member Alexander Subbotin, who died in May 2022 after a visit to a “shaman” outside Moscow; chairman Ravil Maganov, who fell from a sixth-floor window that September; and vice president Vitaly Robertus, who was found dead in his office in March 2024.
In April 2022, two former energy and banking executives were found dead alongside their families. Vladislav Avayev, a former Gazprombank vice president, was found shot dead in his Moscow apartment with his wife and 13-year-old daughter. Sergei Protosenya, a former Novatek executive, was found hanged at a rented villa in Lloret de Mar, Spain, with his wife and daughter stabbed to death inside. Catalan police concluded that Protosenya had killed his family, then himself. His son rejected that finding, insisting that his father had been in good spirits and had no reasons to kill them and himself.
Transneft vice president Andrei Badalov fell from a 17th-floor window in July 2025. The Moscow Times has counted 18 such fatal falls from windows since 2002. Three days later, Russia’s transport minister, Roman Starovoit, was found shot dead in his car hours after Putin fired him. Another transport official died of supposedly acute heart failure the same day.
A shadow over America
Putin’s Russia offers an extreme and grotesque example of the bargain. Yet some critics see an emerging American version, in a far less violent form. Snyder and Applebaum have warned that Western billionaires risk repeating the mistakes of Russia’s oligarchs under Boris Yeltsin, believing they can manage a strongman for profit, only to discover that he is managing them.
Musk spent more than $277 million to help elect Donald Trump, took a desk in the West Wing, and ran the Department of Government Efficiency like a man who believed he was co-president. When that arrangement flamed out in May 2025, he tried to exercise independent political power by turning against Trump, calling his signature legislation, the Big Beautiful Bill, a “disgusting abomination.” Musk threatened to form a third political party and then briefly launched one. He even taunted Trump about Jeffrey Epstein, posting that the president “is in the Epstein files.”
After Trump publicly mused about terminating his contracts, Musk quickly retreated. He deleted the posts, and conceded that they “went too far.” He returned to the fold, shook Trump’s hand at Charlie Kirk’s memorial, accepted the National Medal of Science from him this month, and became the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms, giving at least $366 million to Republican groups. He has grown vastly richer in the process: SpaceX’s June IPO made him the world’s first trillionaire, while the company remains the U.S. government’s dominant launch provider, with competitors such as Blue Origin winning only a fraction of the contracts.
Musk’s retreat illustrates the bargain: surrender the freedom to oppose the president and preserve the ability to enrich yourself. By that measure, Musk’s political defeat has come with an extraordinary financial windfall. He won by losing. The throttling of Starlink in Ukraine appears to fit this pattern. Last week, after Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and Kyiv did not comply, its access to a military-grade version of Starlink was restricted and responsibility disappeared into a haze of accusation and denial.
The costs of such Faustian bargains fall on everyone excluded from them. In Russia, soldiers die at the front by the hundreds of thousands while politically compliant billionaires accumulate obscene fortunes. In Ukraine, drone operators lost contact with their interceptors in mid-flight last week while Russian missiles were in the air; the consequences of a disrupted connection are immediate and potentially fatal. Other customers face the question: can a contract with Starlink be relied upon?
In America, democratic government rests on the principle that neither political office nor private places anyone above the law. Businesses must be free to challenge a president without fearing retaliation, and their owners must remain accountable for their conduct. Those protections help distinguish America from an authoritarian dictatorship like Putin’s Russia.
The Starlink saga does not suggest that America has become Russia. But it raises a troubling question: is political obedience becoming the price of commercial success in America? Putin’s oligarchs struck that bargain in 2000 and have been collecting on it ever since. Whether Americans accept a version of it will depend on how forcefully our institutions and business leaders defend our freedom to say no.

Britain must outproduce its adversaries, says Streeting
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:57:16 BST
23:57:16 KST

Britain must be able to manufacture critical defence components at home in sufficient quantities, increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase, and sustain its armed forces through a prolonged conflict, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting was speaking at the official opening of the UK Gun Hall at Telford, the Rheinmetall facility that returns large-calibre weapon production to Britain.
He said: “But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.”
He said: “To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.”
On the balance between technology and mass, Streeting said: “Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.”
He referred to remarks made at the event by the Chief of the General Staff, saying: “As the Chief of the General Staff just said, we are making daily discoveries about the changing nature of the conflict in Ukraine. Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.”
On the facility itself, Streeting said: “And so what we’re opening the doors to here is more than a manufacturing plant. We’re opening the doors to something much greater and much more ambitious. And that is readiness and resilience. For the first time in decades, artillery gun barrels will be produced in Britain. They will be made using British steel from Forgemasters. As we’ve heard, their production will create one hundred jobs here and hundreds more across the supply chain right across the country.”
He added: “Gun Hall will also support the next generation of equipment for the British Army, helping to deliver the firepower that will make us warfighting ready by 2030.”
The Telford facility will manufacture 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including those supporting Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms, with a peak capacity of up to 245 barrels a year across both calibres and more than fifty breeches annually. Rheinmetall turned an empty building into an operational manufacturing capability in eight months, with breech production beginning in May and barrel production in June.
Streeting also set out the case for combining domestic production with allied integration, saying: “And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.”
He said: “The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.”
The Defence Committee reported this week that general munition stocks are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that the unglamorous enablers of warfighting capacity including logistics networks and ammunition stockpiles have withered through decades of underinvestment across the alliance.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that there is no current requirement to procure new 105mm barrels for the L118 Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production of that calibre. This publication has reported on the wider effort to rebuild Britain’s ability to manufacture large calibre guns.
