The European Parliament on Thursday awarded its 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought jointly to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its senior officials, recognizing their work in upholding international law and justice, Anadolu reports.
“The European Union is founded on respect for multilateralism and international institutions. By awarding the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court and its officials, Parliament recognizes the important work carried out by the Court to uphold international law and justice,” said EP President Roberta Metsola, announcing the winners to the full assembly.
The parliament highlighted the ICC investigations, prosecutions, trials, and issuance or authorization of arrest warrants for serious international crimes, including genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.

Lawmakers have repeatedly called on the European Commission to activate the EU’s blocking statute to protect ICC officials from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions and safeguard the court’s independence.
The parliament also stressed that all EU member states are parties to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC, and are obligated to implement its decisions.
Established in 1988, the Sakharov Prize recognizes individuals and organizations defending human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.
The award ceremony will take place in December in Strasbourg.

Hacking attempts surge as websites race to patch PHP issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:22:54 UTC
23:22:54 KST

In short:
Cloud services firm Cloudflare says hacking attempts surged in the hours after two vulnerabilities with PHP were made public.
PHP is a programming language used widely across the internet.
What's next?
Global agencies, including the Australian Signals Directorate, are urging websites to urgently patch their code.
Millions of hacking attempts have been made since critical vulnerabilities were discovered in a key piece of internet software used by more than two-thirds of websites.
Governments and major websites have rushed to patch two critical issues with PHP, a widely used computing language, after they were reportedly discovered by AI.
Australia's own cyber security agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, is among agencies around the world to issue urgent warnings for websites to implement a new patch.
In some instances, governments have taken websites offline as a precautionary measure.
The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand.
Cloud services firm Cloudfare said since the two vulnerabilities were made public, hacking attempts had surged into the millions.
"In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it," Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday, US time.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now."
The developers of PHP released fixes for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to "update immediately".
"I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, local time.
He said the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex.
"It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks."
Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities.
China's industry ministry urged organisations and users to inspect systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP.
It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary.
South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks.

Roche CEO slams Europe for failing to reward innovation
Roche's chief executive officer has lambasted Europe’s lack of pharmaceutical innovation and support for the industry, which he said deprive patients of access to the latest medicines.
“The US and Asia really play to win, and I feel Europe is more and more playing not to lose,” Thomas Schinecker, CEO of the Swiss drugmaker, said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. Roche will “only invest in countries in the future that are also going to reward innovation.”
The comments are some of the 51-year-old executive’s strongest to date, coming after Roche paused German investments to protest the government’s cost-cutting healthcare reform. Germany and others are “not really investing in growth,” he said Thursday, echoing recent criticism by others in the industry.
More
Pharma pushes for higher European drug prices, Trump or no Trump
The drugmaker is looking for new medicines to replenish its pipeline, striking six agreements in China since August alone. Asia accounted for half of last year’s deals and the remainder took place in the US, according to Schinecker.
Europe cutting costs
European governments are looking to cut costs to help plug ballooning deficits. US drugmaker Eli Lilly and local drugmaker Boehringer Ingelheim have said they will cancel some investments in Germany.
Roche on Thursday reported better-than-expected quarterly sales but left its outlook for the year unchanged, disappointing investors who had hoped for an upgrade.
Revenue rose 8% to CHF16.1 billion ($19.7 billion) in the quarter. The gain was helped by the older asthma and allergy drug Xolair, which faces cheaper competitors. The shares fell less than 1% in Zurich trading.
More
Drugmakers reassess Europe as Trump overhauls drug-pricing rules
Roche is betting big on multiple sclerosis and oncology, including a new breast-cancer pill it says could one day surpass its former blockbuster Herceptin. The Swiss drugmaker needs new medicines and recovering diagnostics to keep growing as sales of older treatments fade.
The company reiterated its forecast for the year, with earnings growing in the high single-digit range and revenue by a mid single-digit percentage.
Questions raised
The decision not to increase the guidance “should raise some questions about the growth trajectory into 2027,” Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, wrote in a note.
Xolair, a medicine first approved more than 20 years ago, is making a comeback to reduce the risk of dangerous reactions like anaphylaxis in people with food allergies. The drug will likely keep growing next year despite cheaper copies becoming available, the company said.
Newer blockbusters like the eye drug Vabysmo, Ocrevus for multiple sclerosis and Hemlibra for hemophilia also gained.
Investors have warmed to Roche’s efforts to deliver new medicines, with shares rising about 19% in the year to Wednesday, more than other large European pharma companies. Local rival Novartis, which faces a patent cliff and has experienced research setbacks recently, has gained 16% in the period.

Procter & Gamble earnings beat as sales rise 4%, boosted by laundry and home products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:19:40 UTC
23:19:40 KST

Procter & Gamble on Thursday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations, fueled by growing demand for its laundry detergent and home care products.
Shares of the company rose more than 5% in morning trading.
Here's what the company reported for the three-month period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $2.00 adjusted vs. $1.88 expected
- Revenue: $23.3 billion vs. $22.8 billion expected
P&G reported fiscal first-quarter net income attributable to the company of $4.73 billion, or $1.97 per share, down from $4.75 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring costs and other items, the company earned $2 per share.
Net sales rose 4% to $23.3 billion.
P&G reported volume growth of 2.4%, a strong start for its new fiscal year. Like many consumer companies, P&G has seen demand for its products weaken as shoppers have become more value-conscious.
Executives have previously said that consumers are now using every last drop of shampoo or laundry detergent, and value packs have become more popular. In fiscal 2026, P&G reported just one quarter of volume growth.
P&G is still seeing signs of a bifurcated economy, CFO Andre Schulten said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday. High-income consumers are willing to trade up to new products, even a $30 shampoo, while low-income consumers are trying to make brands like Tide and Pampers work for their tight budgets.
The company has tried to address both ends of the spectrum with promotional pricing, new pack sizes and product innovation that can command higher prices. New premium products like Pampers Amore and Pantene's Abundant & Strong haircare line have helped P&G grow market share in those categories, executives said.
Adding to P&G's challenges, the competitive environment is "intense," Schulten said on the company's quarterly earnings call.
"We are getting the balance between pricing and product improvements, package improvements, claims, communication and retail execution right," Schulten told analysts. "But it's also a very fragile balance that we want to make sure we we don't compromise on, so we will price, and we will price with innovation, not jeopardizing the top-line momentum."
P&G's top-performing division was fabric and home care, which includes brands like Tide and Febreze. The segment's volume rose 4.3% in the quarter, helped by stronger demand for laundry detergent and fabric enhancers.
The company's baby, feminine and family care segment and its beauty business both reported volume growth of more than 2%.
P&G's grooming division saw volume shrink 0.4% in the quarter. The segment includes Gillette and Venus razors.
The company's healthcare business was the laggard of the portfolio this quarter. Its volume fell 2.9% as demand for oral healthcare products, like Crest toothpaste, and personal healthcare items, like Pepto-Bismol, shrank.
The company is expecting continued "geopolitical and economic challenges," but P&G is on track to meet its guidance, CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said in a statement.
For fiscal 2027, P&G reiterated its forecast for core earnings per share in a range of $6.89 to $7.11. The company is now projecting all-in sales growth in the range of 2% to 4% compared with the prior year, up from its previous outlook of 1% to 3%. The change reflects its acquisition of supplements brand Thorne, which closed Oct. 1.

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: China's millennial porcelain hub revitalizes ancient craftsmanship with global innovations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:19:28 CST
23:19:28 KST

* The 2026 China Jingdezhen International Ceramic Expo was held from Oct. 18 to 22 in Jingdezhen, a city famed as China's "porcelain capital." The five-day event attracted more than 1,000 professional buyers from home and abroad.
* With a porcelain-making history spanning more than 1,000 years, Jingdezhen developed a sophisticated handicraft industry that connected raw materials, specialized artisans and kiln production.
* Today, the city is building on its legacy by bringing together traditional artisans, international artists and young innovators to explore how ancient skills can remain relevant in contemporary life.
NANCHANG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Glimmering in appetizing colors, a stall filled with lobsters, crabs and sea urchins stands out among the teaware and decorative pieces at the Spring and Autumn Fair in Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province.
Created by Kenyan artist Megan White, the porcelain artworks reflect the sights and culture of her coastal homeland, which she has brought to China's famed porcelain hub through the city's centuries-old craft.
"I grew up on the coast of Kenya, so I'm constantly inspired by and drawn to the sea," she said.
She has spent 20 months in Jingdezhen. Using local porcelain and techniques such as slip casting, White transforms familiar marine life into sculptural works that invite visitors to appreciate the ocean from a city far from the sea.
White's stall offers a glimpse into Jingdezhen's evolving ceramic scene, where international artists are drawing on traditional craftsmanship, while introducing new cultural perspectives and creative ideas.
With a porcelain-making history spanning more than 1,000 years, Jingdezhen has developed a sophisticated handicraft industry that connects raw materials, specialized artisans and kiln production.
On July 25, 2026, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites, representing the city's historic porcelain-making system, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Today, the city is building on this legacy by bringing together traditional artisans, international artists and young innovators, exploring how ancient skills can remain relevant in contemporary life.
TRADITIONAL TECHNIQUES REFORGED
For White, Jingdezhen's appeal lies not only in its long history but also in the dedication of its craftspeople.
"The dedication and precision associated with the local ceramic craftsmanship are very inspiring," she said, adding that local artisans encourage her to strive for the same standards in her own work.
Unlike the red clay traditionally used for pottery in Kenya, porcelain has become the primary medium for her creations in Jingdezhen. She makes molds from her own designs and produces her pieces by hand, combining her personal artistic language with techniques developed in the Chinese porcelain-making tradition.
White said she values such traditional crafts in a mass-producing era, even though they require considerable time and expertise. "Once these traditions disappear, we can't bring them back."
China is making a tremendous effort to keep traditional techniques alive, she said, adding that this is what has compelled her to learn and innovate in Jingdezhen.
For Dutch artist Antonetta Eilers, meanwhile, Jingdezhen offers room to experiment with new forms and ideas.
Working with porcelain and jewelry, Eilers draws inspiration from nature and the sea, while collaborating with a friend whose artistic concepts explore possible futures shaped by climate change and environmental transformation.
Eilers said she is struck by the local creative atmosphere, where an unexpected result does not need to be discarded but can become part of an artwork. She said the city's artist residency programs are helping visiting artists exchange ideas and develop their own styles and skills.
"Techniques evolve, and I think that evolution is actually a form of preservation in itself," she said.
The growing presence of international creators is part of a broader creative ecosystem in Jingdezhen.
According to Gao Xiaoyun, deputy mayor of the city, Jingdezhen has gathered more than 3,400 inheritors of intangible cultural heritage, over 100,000 young creative entrepreneurs, around 60,000 newcomers from other parts of China, and more than 5,000 foreign residents at peak times engaged in its ceramic community.
This mix of experienced artisans and emerging creators is helping traditional techniques find new practitioners and new applications, ensuring that heritage is not confined to workshops and exhibition halls.
TECH-INFUSED CREATIONS
While handcraft remains central to Jingdezhen's identity, technology is opening up new possibilities for ceramic production.
At a local porcelain enterprise, 65 industrial-grade ceramic 3D printers demonstrate how digital design can be translated into intricate forms. The technology enables the production of customized vases featuring complex curves, hollow structures and textures that can be difficult to achieve through conventional techniques.
"3D printing allows for a wider variety of ceramic forms and more intricate textures," said Hong Ziyu, the company's general manager. The technology, he added, has helped meet growing demand for customized decorative products.
The company's 3D-printed porcelain products have gained traction in overseas markets, generating annual sales of more than 5 million yuan (about 750,000 U.S. dollars), according to Hong.
Such developments reflect a wider transformation in Jingdezhen's ceramic industry. From 2021 to 2025, the industry's output value rose from 51.6 billion yuan to 102.7 billion yuan, while the number of major industrial enterprises above the designated size increased from 140 to 298, according to local statistics.
For young creators, the convergence of traditional craftsmanship, digital tools and commercial opportunities is also creating new career paths.
Digital modeling and advanced manufacturing can help artists test ideas and produce distinctive designs, while the city's network of workshops and specialized suppliers supports the transition and commercialization from concept to finished product, supporting a booming creative industry.
Xu Wan, manager of Chentian Ceramics company in Jingdezhen, said the firm is collaborating with numerous pop culture IPs to draw Gen-Z customers, which is boosting the firm's sales.
Xu said the company has collaborated with the hit animated film "Nobody" in launching a series of intangible cultural heritage-themed ceramic blind boxes in 2025, with the product quickly becoming a sought-after hit among young collectors after its release.
"Young consumers today are more than willing to pay for creative products highlighting emotional value," Xu said, adding that they have released dozens of innovative products beyond trendy toys, including ceramic speaker boxes and night lanterns.
SUPPORTING GLOBAL CRAFTSMANSHIP
With talented artists and a booming creative ecosystem, Jingdezhen's international appeal has extended beyond the works created within its workshops.
Japanese ceramic artist Shusaku Kanzaki, who has visited the city three times, said Jingdezhen has helped him find a larger audience for his artworks.
Drawing on historical techniques and aesthetics, some of Kanzaki's pieces use no glaze, relying instead on the effects of wood firing to create their color and texture. Such Karamono-styled creations have won the hearts of many connoisseurs during the 2026 China Jingdezhen International Ceramic Expo held from Oct. 18 to 22.
Kanzaki said that combining tradition with new ideas is essential to creating compelling works of art.
Simply reproducing old objects, he argued, is not enough to sustain the craft. The abundant ceramic inspirations and support from local friends and authorities have made Jingdezhen an appealing place for him to explore, he said.
Beyond artists, the city's experience is also attracting interest from other ceramic-producing regions, which are confronting challenges in passing on traditional skills.
During a visit to the expo, Witthayalak Samjai, a senior deputy administrator of Chiang Mai, a city in northern Thailand, said she is learning from Jingdezhen's experiences to vitalize Chiang Mai's traditional Lanna ceramic arts.
Some experienced Lanna ceramic artisans remain reluctant to depart from traditional styles, and their products are often made as decorative gifts rather than everyday objects, making it difficult to reach modern consumers, she said.
Jingdezhen's integration of tradition, contemporary design and market applications offers lessons for northern Thailand, she said.
Ilada Junjiresrassamee, vice president of the Lampang Province Chamber of Commerce in Thailand, said a local university's ceramics program in Lampang, which had run for 35 years, was suspended for three years amid waning interest among young people.
Inspired by Jingdezhen, local stakeholders plan to revive the program and introduce hands-on workshops for children, she said.
Jingdezhen has established friendly ties with more than 180 cities in 72 countries, using international exchanges to promote dialogue and cooperation in ceramic culture, according to Gao, the vice mayor.
Following the inscription of the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, the city has also called for stronger global cooperation on heritage conservation.
In concurrence, a multilateral initiative issued at the 2026 Jingdezhen Forum has called for respect for cultural diversity, the use of digital tools for preventive conservation, the integration of traditional techniques with contemporary design, and closer collaboration in talent development and research.
For a city whose porcelain once traveled across continents, its global connections now encompass not only finished products but also creative ideas, technical expertise and shared approaches to heritage protection.
In the view of Tim Winter, a professor at the National University of Singapore and president of the Association of Critical Heritage Studies, the challenge is to keep the exchanges alive, preserving the skills that give porcelain its character while allowing new generations, from Jingdezhen and beyond, to shape what the craft can become. ■

"Glaring gaps" in U.K.'s Arctic defense leave it and NATO open to Russian attacks, British lawmakers say
"Glaring gaps" in the United Kingdom's Arctic defenses are leaving it and NATO vulnerable to attacks from Russia, British lawmakers said in a parliamentary report published Thursday.
The group urged the British government to "urgently address" gaps in maritime forces, particularly with the U.S. acting "more unilaterally in the region."
"This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage," Tan Dhesi, Chair of the Commons Defense Committee, wrote.
The committee said that a "shockingly low availability" of Royal Navy submarines and warships means critical infrastructure, such as underwater cables and energy supplies, are exposed to potential Russian attacks.
"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening NATO sea lanes, U.K. critical infrastructure and the U.K.'s nuclear deterrent," the report added.
The report urged Canada and European NATO allies to "take more responsibility for defence of their interests in the High North."
Like European NATO countries, the United Kingdom lacks "some critical military capabilities that it has largely relied on the U.S. to provide, such as ballistic missile defence, long range strike and intelligence and surveillance assets, which will take considerable investment and time to replicate."
"If the U.K. is to lead an effective coalition," the report continued, "it must address glaring gaps in the availability of its current maritime forces and ensure it has an agreed plan, integrated with European allies in the region, to deter and, if necessary, defeat any aggression in the High North from 2030."
'To deter war we must be ready for it'
Former British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer warned in June that Russia could attack NATO countries by the end of the decade.
Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said that if Starmer's predictions are accurate, "time is just as important as money."
"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late," Anderson said.

Lithuanian SkyWiper Wall Interceptor Tested in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:17:17 UTC
23:17:17 KST

A Lithuanian interceptor drone, part of the SkyWiper Wall air defence system, has been tested under combat conditions in Ukraine.
Šarūnas Stanislovėnas, CEO and co-founder of VYTIS TECH, shared this with Militarnyi.
VYTIS TECH is a Lithuanian company that develops and manufactures UAVs. It is part of NT Service, known for its electronic warfare systems.
The SkyWiper Wall is a short-range air defence radar system.
It consists of:
“This is a full-fledged system that we call SkyWiper Wall. It consists of various sensors, radars, software, and the interceptor itself,” Šarūnas Stanislovėnas said.
The system can be configured as a mobile trailer or a fixed unit.
Interceptor
Radar guidance allows the interceptor to approach its target to within 100–200 meters. It then automatically attacks the target using video camera guidance.
The interceptor measures 100 × 70 × 25 cm, has a maximum takeoff weight of 4 kg, and can carry a payload of 500–700 g. Its flight endurance is 10–20 minutes, and its cruising speed ranges from 80 to 220 km/h.
The interceptor has a maximum speed of 300 km/h and a range of 25–35 km. It is equipped with a thermal imaging camera with a resolution of 640 × 480 pixels and can take off automatically at a 45-degree angle.
“It is a twin-motor electric delta-wing UAV that can reach speeds of up to 300 km/h,” Šarūnas Stanislovėnas shared.
However, this speed is insufficient to intercept jet-powered drones.
“Unfortunately, we currently cannot help you deal with jet-powered drones at altitudes of 4 and 5 km, but we are working on it. We hope to be able to aid with this issue as well in the near future,” the company representative noted.
The system can be integrated with Ukrainian radars. It is already being used in combat conditions in Ukraine.
“We have partners — the Blue/Yellow foundation — who delivered the first batch of these interceptors to Ukraine. A crowdfunding campaign to support them has also recently concluded in Lithuania,” Stanislovėnas said.
It was recently reported that Lithuanians had raised €1.3 million for anti-drone protection in Ukraine and Lithuania.
In addition, the company is developing a new interceptor equipped with a jet engine.

Smugglers Collected Up to $509M on Europe Routes in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

Smugglers netted an estimated $388 million to $509 million from sea crossings to Europe in 2025, according to new research by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). The agency estimated that between 190,000 and 209,000 people were smuggled along four major Mediterranean and Atlantic routes, with criminal networks facilitating between 57 percent and 90 percent of departures. Fees varied widely depending on the journey, ranging from $170 for crossing to Spain’s Canary Islands to more than $7,500 for routes toward Italy and Malta, according to the International Organization for Migration.
The Central Mediterranean was the busiest route, with up to 100,400 people smuggled, followed by the Eastern Mediterranean with up to 51,300, the Northwest African Atlantic route with 33,000, and the Western Mediterranean with 24,500. These estimates, according to UNODC, reflect all smuggling attempts, including journeys that ended in interception or tragedy. The routes remained deadly: 3,404 people died or went missing in 2025, while another 104,200 were intercepted at sea and returned.

Lebanon-Israel talks in US end without breakthrough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:16:41 UTC
23:16:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon-Israel talks in US end without breakthrough as attacks continue
Two days of military talks between Lebanon and Israel at the headquarters of US Central Command (CENTCOM) in Tampa, Florida, appear to have ended without a breakthrough, as Israel continues its attacks on southern Lebanon and rejects Lebanese demands for a third-party mechanism to verify the Lebanese army's operations.
Lebanese military sources told The New Arab on Thursday that no further negotiating session had been scheduled, although concluding bilateral discussions with CENTCOM could still take place.
The sources said the United States was expected to issue a statement on the talks, which have been dominated by disagreements over monitoring the Lebanese army's activities in designated pilot areas of southern Lebanon and Israel's refusal to halt its military operations.
"No breakthrough has been recorded so far. There is intransigence in Israeli positions, while the Lebanese side is holding firm to its demands that steps must be reciprocal," the sources said.
They stressed that Lebanon could not be expected to fulfil its commitments unilaterally while Israel continued its attacks, bulldozing operations, demolitions, explosions and ground incursions.
The Lebanese army has also rejected Israeli demands for direct coordination between the two militaries on the ground.
Instead, Beirut is insisting on an independent verification mechanism involving third parties, potentially including France, the United States and the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), similar to the committee established to monitor the November 2024 ceasefire agreement.
"The Lebanese army is fully carrying out its duties, and all Israeli allegations against it are false," the military sources said.
They argued that Israel's continuing attacks and violations were the main obstacles to the army's deployment and the implementation of agreements, as had been the case following the ceasefire on 27 November 2024.
Dispute over Israeli withdrawal and disarmament
Lebanon is demanding that Israel halt its military attacks and operations across the south, which continue to endanger the lives of the area's residents.
Beirut is also pressing for farmers to be allowed access to their land to harvest crops, alongside broader demands for Israel's withdrawal from Lebanese territory, the release of prisoners, the return of displaced residents and reconstruction.
Lebanese authorities are calling for a clear timetable to implement the commitments outlined in a framework agreement signed with Israel in Washington on 26 June.
The agreement is intended to advance Israel's withdrawal from Lebanese territory while the Lebanese state extends its authority across the country through its own security forces and establishes a monopoly over weapons.
However, major disagreements remain over how these commitments should be implemented.
Israel has refused to expand the pilot areas designated for Lebanese army operations beyond a single zone announced in July, which includes the towns of Srifa, Froun and western Zawtar.
Israeli authorities claim the Lebanese army has failed to disarm Hezbollah in these areas and are pushing for direct military coordination through joint operations rooms.
Lebanon has rejected this demand, insisting that any verification must be carried out through an independent mechanism rather than direct cooperation with the Israeli military.
Israel has also refused to suspend its attacks or abandon the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington, meanwhile, is attempting to narrow the differences between the two sides and maintain the negotiations, viewing the June framework agreement as the principal route towards stability and security.
Israeli attacks continue across southern Lebanon
The diplomatic deadlock coincided with another day of Israeli military escalation in southern Lebanon.
On Thursday, Israeli forces carried out two explosions in the towns of Tallouseh and Bani Hayyan in the Marjayoun district, according to reports from southern Lebanon.
Israeli aircraft also struck the outskirts of Qantara in Marjayoun and Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli tanks were seen advancing towards the Nabaa al-Khoukh area on the outskirts of Hebbariyeh in the Hasbaya district and artillery shelling tageted several towns in south Lebanon.
The attacks have continued despite diplomatic efforts to secure an Israeli withdrawal and advance arrangements for the Lebanese army's deployment in the south.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly said that the ongoing Israeli military operations are obstructing reconstruction, preventing displaced residents from returning home and exposing civilians to further danger.
Lebanese cabinet faces explosives case
Separately, Lebanon's cabinet was due to meet at Baabda Palace on Thursday afternoon under the chairmanship of President Joseph Aoun, with a politically sensitive explosives case expected to feature on the agenda.
The Justice Ministry has requested that the case involving explosives seized in Dahr al-Baydar on 5 October and in al-Qasr, in Baalbek-Hermel governorate, on 9 October be referred to the Judicial Council, Lebanon's highest court for cases involving state security.
The request also covers any other matters found by investigators to be directly or indirectly connected to the seized explosives.
According to information obtained by The New Arab, extensive political and judicial consultations have taken place, including discussions involving Lebanon's president, prime minister, and Speaker of Parliment, who represent the country's three largest religious sects, over the potential consequences of referring the case to the Judicial Council.
Approval of the request could trigger a confrontation with Hezbollah.
Some political figures have favoured delaying a decision until security and judicial investigations, which remain at an early stage, have progressed further.
However, several ministers, particularly those opposed to Hezbollah, are insisting that the case should be referred to the Judicial Council.
Sources close to Justice Minister Adel Nassar told The New Arab that the seriousness of the case required such a referral.
"The gravity of the case requires its referral to the Judicial Council. This concerns the country's national security, and there can be no leniency or complacency," the sources said.
They stressed that investigations were continuing and that the ministry was determined to pursue the case without granting special treatment to anyone.
"We are determined to move forward with the investigations, without leniency towards anyone. That era is over," they added.

Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:16:00 UTC
23:16:00 KST

Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
October 22, 2026
Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes
following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.
The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.
Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Report: Plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation
Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.
One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.
Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.
On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.
A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.
Has Iran learned from earlier attacks?
Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.
Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.
"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.
Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.
Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
How Iran prepares for new strikes?
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.
Fear of war inside Iran
An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."

Bulgaria’s Growth to Reach 3.5% in 2027, EY Forecasts
Bulgaria’s economy is expected to grow by 2.9% in 2026 and accelerate to 3.5% in 2027 before slowing to 3% in 2028, according to an October economic outlook
Bulgaria’s Road Infrastructure Agency (RIA) plans to lay off 420 employees of the National Toll Administration as part of a two-stage restructuring, while offering some the opportunity to apply for jobs at the Interior Ministry, the Customs Agency and potentially the National Revenue Agency, Confederation of Labour Podkrepa Vice President Ioannis Parteniotis said.
The plans were outlined after a meeting between RIA management and Podkrepa representatives, as agency employees staged a protest demanding job security and clarity over the proposed changes.
During the first four months of the reform, RIA is expected to adopt a new organizational structure and transfer some National Toll Administration responsibilities to other institutions.
“At the end of February, 505 positions within the National Toll Administration will be cut; 85 of these are currently vacant. In reality, 420 people will be laid off,” Parteniotis said.
According to the union representative, trade unions and National Toll Administration management will begin setting selection criteria on November 11, with human resources officials from the Interior Ministry and Customs Agency taking part. The possibility of transferring employees to the National Revenue Agency will also be considered.
The 420 employees’ contracts with RIA will be terminated, and they will receive all severance payments due to them. However, moving to another administration will not happen automatically, as each institution has different legal employment requirements. Applicants will have to meet the relevant criteria and complete the required appointment procedures.
RIA has assured employees that the restructuring will not reduce road toll revenue or weaken oversight. Oleg Asenov said digital tools would make inspections more efficient, while the National Toll Administration’s responsibilities would gradually be transferred to a unified regulatory body.
Plans also call for a new executive agency under the Ministry of Transport to take responsibility for collecting road tolls, maintaining and administering the electronic system, and processing data on risk profiles. Some current employees will move to the new agency.
Trade unions have also reported that around 85-87 employees of regional road administrations are expected to lose their jobs. The cuts will mainly affect administrative staff rather than engineering and technical specialists.
These reductions are linked to plans to centralize public procurement at RIA headquarters. Parteniotis said the cuts must be completed by the end of the year because the 2027 budget contains no funding for the affected positions. In contrast, National Toll Administration employees will have their jobs secured for the next four months, he said.
RIA employees held a protest earlier in the day, before a scheduled meeting with management, following weeks of reports about extensive layoffs and structural changes.
The Confederation of Labour Podkrepa organized the demonstration under the slogan “Job Security and Predictability at the Road Infrastructure Agency.” The union said employees had received neither formal notification nor a reasoned explanation from management about the planned organizational changes.
The protesters called for an urgent meeting with RIA’s leadership.
“Our demands are not about wages. We simply have no future prospects. We want to keep our jobs because each of us has a family,” Slavi Slavov, an inspector at the National Toll Administration, said.
Parteniotis also questioned how many current employees would keep their jobs and where National Toll Administration staff would be transferred.

The NMC guidelines do not aim to stop people from seeking treatment. Instead, they aim to ensure that patients make informed medical decisions guided by clinical expertise rather than an algorithm-driven sales pitch.
Scroll through Instagram on any given Tuesday, and you are bound to hit the "Glow Up" algorithm. With the dramatic "before-and-after" transitions, an influencer gushing over their new "glass skin" chemical peels, and local clinics promising a "100% guaranteed acne cure," cosmetic medicine has officially crossed over into pop culture.It feels less like an invasive clinical procedure and more like buying a new pair of sneakers. One click, instant gratification.In India's hyper-visual, social-media-obsessed culture, looking "filtered" in real life has created a massive boom for cosmetic clinics. But behind the glossy aesthetic lies a wild-west market where non-clinical salon technicians, short-course certificate holders, and non-core medical practitioners are offering everything from laser hair removal to dermal fillers.The reels make the procedures seem cheap and accessible, but the noise creates a great deal of confusion for potential customers and raises risk of botched procedures.To halt this commercial noise and protect patients from predatory marketing, the National Medical Commission (NMC), India's apex regulator for medical practice, has introduced a strict ethical framework.The goal? Drawing a hard line between legitimate clinical care and commercial hype.
Dermatology vs cosmetology
The biggest source of consumer confusion is the assumption that a "dermatologist" and a "cosmetologist" are the same thing. They aren't.Confusing the two can leave you with severe skin damage.A dermatologist completes a rigorous eight-and-a-half-year medical training pathway, comprising a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree followed by a three-year Doctor of Medicine (MD) or Diplomate of National Board (DNB) in Dermatology, Venereology, and Leprosy.It also includes comprehensive hands-on training in clinical pathology, complex skin diseases, dermatosurgery, and laser medicine. Similarly, a plastic surgeon undergoes specialized post-doctoral surgical training (MCh or DNB) in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery.On the flip side, "cosmetology" is not a recognized medical specialty or postgraduate qualification under the National Medical Commission (NMC) framework.In practice, the term often describes salon estheticians, technicians, or non-core operators who hold short 3- to 6-month diploma certificates from private, unaccredited institutes.Under the regulatory mandates of the NMC's ethics, non-core practitioners, non-clinical operators, and salon technicians are strictly prohibited from procedures such as laser resurfacing, deep chemical peels, hair transplants, or injectable dermal fillers.As Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora, dermatology consultant at CK Birla Hospital says, "Earlier, there was no term like 'cosmetology' in medical residency. Aesthetic procedures were an integrated part of our clinical curriculum under Dermatosurgery, complete with hands-on surgical training under senior guides.”She adds, “The challenge in India is that regulations were historically lax. Non-clinical entities like salon technicians and short-course diploma holders started performing deep chemical peels, aggressive lasers, and recommending fillers without clinical supervision."
The NMC rulebook: What changes on your feed
If your favorite clinic's social media page suddenly looks a lot quieter, blame (or thank) the NMC rules.Now, doctors cannot post promotional "before-and-after" grid shots, transition reels, or retouched result photos on public feeds. Clinical photos are strictly restricted to anonymized, scientific, or educational use. They set clear boundaries on how practitioners can advertise their services, use social media and engage with influencers.Influencer barter crackdown: Free Botox, fillers, or hair transplants given to social media influencers in exchange for "spontaneous" glowing reviews are now outright banned. Doctors cannot solicit or feature patient video testimonials or star-rating screenshots.Killing Superlatives & Guarantees: Phrases like "Best Dermatologist in Delhi," "No. 1 Plastic Surgeon," or "100% Glass Skin Guarantee" are illegal. Doctors are also prohibited from claiming non-existent qualifications (like US-style "Board Certified Plastic Surgeon" titles, which do not exist in India).AI & Pay-Per-Lead Bans: AI-generated "synthetic" patient cases, face filters, or synthetic doctor voices are prohibited without explicit disclaimers. Furthermore, clinics cannot pay marketing agencies "per-patient" commissions.As Dr Vivek Gupta, plastic & cosmetic surgery consultant at Madhukar Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Delhi views it, “In a field where social media creates unrealistic expectations, decisions must be guided by clinical suitability rather than promotional claims. Restrictions on promotional photographs and testimonials mean we must adapt our communication strategies.”He also says how he has upgraded the advertising guidelines for his own clinic. “Our clinic now focuses on expert-led public health education rather than promoting individual outcomes," he says.
Shift in strategy: Before vs after the guidelines
The daily operational shift across Indian aesthetic clinics is stark.In the earlier, largely unregulated aesthetic medicine market described in the draft, clinics relied on visuals that showcased dramatic transformations and could create the impression that similar results were achievable for everyone.Under the NMC-compliant approach, clinics shift towards educational content, such as anatomical diagrams, procedure explainers and skin-science reels.Rather than promoting individual treatment outcomes, these formats help explain medical conditions, how procedures work and what patients should understand before considering treatment.Dr. Vivek Gupta acknowledges that while digital platforms remain an important source of information for people exploring aesthetic options, restricting promotional material presents a distinct communication challenge."Restrictions on testimonials, promotional photographs, and advertising can make it harder to communicate treatment outcomes and recovery experiences," he says.However, he maintains that "the solution lies in adapting communication strategies rather than compromising ethical standards. Clearer guidance on distinguishing medical education from commercial promotion would help practitioners remain informative while complying with professional regulations."He explains that his practice uses digital platforms to discuss common cosmetic concerns, treatment options, recovery expectations, and potential risks, such as acne scars or skin aging, while strictly avoiding exaggerated claims or guaranteed results."The objective is to build credibility through scientifically accurate information and responsible communication rather than promotional testimonials," he explains.This strategic overhaul also extends to how doctors manage public interaction on digital platforms. Dr. Tanvi Gupta Arora notes that sponsored endorsements and flashing contact numbers over educational reels are now firmly off-limits."Under the guidelines, we cannot do sponsored product endorsements or flash clinic phone numbers over educational videos," she points out, "If I post an educational reel about acne, I turn off comments to prevent direct social media prescribing. We redirect inquiries through proper clinical consultations or telemedicine."In her experience, this levels the playing field for doctors who built their practice on "clinical labor rather than massive ad budgets."
Education vs covert marketing
In an era where skincare trends go viral overnight on reels and shorts, the distinction between public health awareness and disguised product placement has grown dangerously blurry.The NMC’s crackdown directly addresses this hidden marketplace by prohibiting barter deals where influencers trade shoutouts for free treatments.Dr Vivek Gupta highlights that the true test of educational content lies in its intent and presentation."The distinction lies in the information's purpose and presentation. Public health education helps people understand cosmetic concerns, treatment options, preventive measures, and potential risks," he explains, "Covert marketing uses educational content to promote a particular procedure or commercial interest. Every communication should prioritise scientific accuracy, balanced information, and patient welfare rather than encouraging people to purchase a specific service or product."When asked about using non-medical influencers, Dr Gupta reveals he has never relied on them for endorsements."Aesthetic treatments require individual assessment, and their suitability, risks, and outcomes vary from person to person. Influencers can help raise awareness about skincare, but personal experiences should never be mistaken for medical evidence," he says, adding that credibility in this field "should ultimately come from clinical expertise and responsible patient care."Instead of chasing influencer viral loops, his clinic prioritizes expert-led educational content, media interactions, and public awareness initiatives.He asserts, "Trust is also established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity. In aesthetic care, sustainable trust comes from transparent communication, professional competence and a consistent commitment to patient welfare."
Performance marketing, DMs, and tele-consult safeguards
The regulatory overhaul doesn't just stop at Instagram reels; it reshapes the entire digital sales funnel used by modern cosmetic chains.Historically, aesthetic marketing relied heavily on aggressive performance marketing campaigns. Clickbait advertisements proclaiming "Get glass skin in 3 days" or "call now for 50% off hair transplants" were explicitly designed to exploit appearance-related insecurities, feeding directly into pay-per-lead models.Under the new guidelines, performance marketing must be stripped of high-pressure sales tactics, artificial urgency, and guaranteed outcome claims.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasizes that digital visibility must remain factual and consistent with medical ethics requirements."Campaigns should avoid guaranteed outcomes, misleading claims, patient testimonials used for promotion, and messaging that exploits appearance-related insecurities," he states, adding that marketing agencies must understand these boundaries.This shift has also forced a total overhaul of digital triage and initial online consultations. In the past, prospective patients could drop a comment under a video or send a direct message (DM) detailing their skin issues, receiving direct prescriptions or treatment quotes from social media managers.Dr Gupta stresses the vital difference between general inquiries and actual consultations, noting, "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment."For tele-consultations, safeguards such as identity verification, informed consent, confidentiality, and proper documentation are essential."Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation," he warns, concluding that "convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety."
When aesthetics go wrong: The clinical and human cost
When cosmetic procedures are marketed like fast-fashion beauty products, patients pay a heavy price with their physical and financial well-being.Both dermatologists and plastic surgeons frequently find themselves functioning as corrective specialists, tasked with repairing severe damage caused by non-core practitioners or aggressive "assembly-line" cosmetic chains.For instance, in a September 30 order, the Bengaluru urban district consumer disputes redressal commission held a clinic liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman suffered second-degree facial burns during laser hair removal in April.The commission directed the clinic to refund the Rs 1,100 procedure fee with interest, pay Rs 1 lakh in damages and Rs 10,000 in litigation costs, giving it 45 days to comply.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora highlights how these botched cases unfold in daily practice, pointing out that aggressive commercial chains routinely lure vulnerable patients into spending massive sums on guaranteed outcomes."Some of these cosmetology chains, what they are doing is they are running these advertisements that 'we will just cure your pigmentation, you will be 100% free of your pigmentation.' And people, they fall into the trap and go and spend thousands or lakhs with no result," Dr Tanvi explains.When these uncalibrated procedures fail, patients are thrown back into the market with damaged skin and exhausted finances.Dr Tanvi notes that treating these complications requires extensive time and care before even touching the patient's original cosmetic concern."Sometimes the damages are irreversible. You had so much damage that you now cannot treat it," she shares, adding: "So you have to further do more procedures. Like sometimes these patients come to me with even worse pigmentation. First I have to spend two to three months correcting that issue, the skin has become thin or it has become burnt, and then we talk about the pigmentation correction."
How patients can assess practitioners in the post-hype era
The experts map out certain points that a patient could look for to assess the authenticity of the clinic or expert.Verify core medical qualifications: Patients should look for recognised postgraduate qualifications, such as an MD or DNB in dermatology or an MCh or DNB in Plastic Surgery, and verify registration details with the state medical council or NMC register.Dr Vivek Gupta stresses the importance of qualifications and competence: "Plastic surgeons and dermatologists have different areas of expertise, and the procedures offered must align with their respective training and applicable scope of practice. Non-core practitioners must not misrepresent their qualifications or undertake procedures beyond their competence. Patients should be able to verify credentials and understand who is performing a procedure."Evaluate the consultation: Consultations should offer factual information about diagnosis, risks, alternatives and realistic outcomes, without guarantees or pressure to proceed.Dr Vivek Gupta explains: "Trust is established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity.”He also cautions against relying on online reviews to judge clinical capability: "Instead of promotional testimonials, patients should focus on recognised qualifications, relevant experience, consultation quality, and transparent discussions about risks, alternatives, and recovery."Review case examples privately: Instead of public promotional posts, patients can ask to see clinical case records during a consultation to understand the likely scope and outcomes of a procedure.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora says: "Before and after photos should not be on your social media. You can put it on your website, or if somebody comes to your clinic, then any day they can come to your clinic and then you can show them the before and after pictures or whatever particular procedure they are looking for."Demand clinical assessment and safety protocols: Patients should ensure that clinics conduct appropriate assessments, use approved devices and injectables, and have emergency procedures to manage adverse reactions. Digital messages and photographs may not be sufficient to determine whether a procedure is suitable.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasises: "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment... Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation. Convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety."
Putting clinical care ahead of the sales pitch
The NMC guidelines aim to curb predatory marketing, banning influencer barter culture, and restricting invasive procedures strictly to qualified specialists.
For clinics and marketing agencies, this transition demands a total overhaul of digital strategy, swapping sensationalism, clickbait, and artificial transformation grids for transparent, expert-led public education.For patients, the rules offer much-needed protection in a market that has grown dangerously confusing. A cosmetic procedure is not an off-the-rack beauty buy; it is a medical intervention carried out on living human tissue. Ultimately, the new regulatory landscape encourages consumers to value what truly matters when choosing a doctor: prioritizing clinical expertise, authentic qualifications, and patient safety over an algorithm-driven sales pitch.

Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues. Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Energy ministry calls for billions in nuclear fusion investments to compete globally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:56 UTC
23:06:56 KST

Israel's Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure published a strategic report on Thursday detailing Israel's opportunity to enter the global nuclear fusion industry, a sector the ministry claims could become one of the world's major energy sources in the coming decades and develop into a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
Multiple countries and private companies have been looking towards nuclear fusion as the energy of the future, using reactors to generate energy by smashing hydrogen isotopes together, a process that does not emit greenhouse gases or produce the level of nuclear waste that the current system of nuclear fission used in typical nuclear power plants does.
Since 2021, over $14 billion has been invested in the nuclear fusion industry, including approximately $4.5 billion in the past year alone.
According to the report, the first commercial fusion plants could be connected to electricity grids during the 2030s, developing into a global market worth hundreds of billions of dollars between 2040 and 2050.
Major technology companies including Microsoft and Google have already signed agreements with companies to purchase electricity from future fusion plants.
Israel already home to fusion research, development
Israel's expertise in several technologies essential to the development of fusion reactors, including high-power laser systems, power electronics and radio-frequency (RF) technologies, artificial intelligence and simulations, advanced materials, and robotics, provides it with an advantage and the potential to enter the industry as a supplier of critical technologies, expertise, and components, the ministry said.
Israel is also home to the Israeli Institute for Nuclear Fusion and Hot Plasma, which supports research in the sector and which the ministry is proposing to expand through investment in scholarships, workforce training, and academic research, at an estimated cost of NIS 50 million to NIS 100 million over five years.
Additionally, multiple companies within Israel are developing related technologies, including nT-Tao, which is developing a compact fusion reactor, and FusionMantle, which focuses on developing components for fusion reactor cores.
Energy ministry poses pathways to fusion development
The ministry proposed three different options for the national development in order to increase investment and development of nuclear fusion technologies within Israel, ranging from NIS 50 million to NIS 2 billion over five to ten years.
The first focuses on expanding Israel's academic research by investing in scholarships, workforce training, and academic research at an estimated cost of NIS 50 million to NIS 100 million over five years.
The so-called 'infrastructure-focused package' involves an estimated investment of 500 million to NIS 1billion over five to seven years in areas where Israel holds a competitive advantage, and would include new funding programs through public-private partnerships and making research infrastructure accessible to academia and industry.
The ministry's final and most comprehensive package involves an investment of NIS 1 billion to NIS 2 billion over seven to ten years to develop a complete national fusion ecosystem. A national coordinating authority would be established, major research facilities would be upgraded, academic training programs would be developed, and the ministry would look towards the possibility of establishing an experimental fusion reactor in Israel through an international partnership.
According to the ministry's report, Israel must take action in the coming years, or it will miss the critical window in which global supply chains are being established, and it will be significantly harder to enter the industry.

====================================================================================================

‘We’re all in the same boat,’ Noah's Ark researcher tells ‘Post’ at Turkey’s Durupinar site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:56 UTC
23:06:56 KST

The Jerusalem Post visited the Durupinar formation last week, the boat-shaped mound in eastern Turkey that is possibly the resting place of Noah’s Ark, to see what a first round of drilling conducted by Noah’s Ark Scans (NAS) has turned up.
The Post’s visit came after the close of NAS’s most recent season of fieldwork at the site, during the week of Parashat Noah, when Jews around the world read the story of the Flood and the Ark.
But the story of the Ark does not belong exclusively to the Jewish people: It appears in the Torah, the New Testament, and the Quran, and the composition of the team working at the site reflects this.
For Adv. Ohav Cohen, that is the point: “At a time when nations and religions seem more divided than ever, this project brings together Jews, Christians, Muslims, and researchers from across the world in pursuit of a shared history,” he said.
Cohen, an Israeli lawyer and researcher working with NAS, told the Post. “Whatever we ultimately discover, there is something profoundly meaningful about people of different faiths working side by side, united by a story that belongs to all of humanity.”
“After all, if we are all descendants of Noah, then we really are all in the same boat,” he quipped.
NAS, led by Andrew Jones, documents the ongoing work at Durupinar. In May 2026, the Turkish government approved the group’s request to begin invasive study of the site, a major milestone after decades of surface-level analysis.
Working under Prof. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University’s Archaeology Department, the team began core drilling in July. When the season ended in September, samples taken from within the formation were sent to several universities, including Bar-Ilan University, for testing, with a final report expected next spring.
The man who kept coming back
For Jones, the fascination with Durupinar goes back more than 30 years. Raised in a Christian home and drawn to “anything Bible-related,” he first heard about the formation in middle school.
Sitting on the sidelines of the 8th International Symposium on Mount Ararat and Noah’s Ark at Agri Ibrahim Cecen University, Jones told the Post that his interest in the site quickly grew beyond idle fascination, leading him to reach out to explorers who had studied it, such as Ron Wyatt and David Fasold.
Jones’ first visit to Durupinar was in 1997, following a trip to Turkey with a friend while in college. “It felt abandoned. There were no trees around it at that time,” he said. “It was this very lonely boat shape on the side of the mountain.”
The visitor’s center, built in 1987, was a bare cinder-block building run by a chain-smoking Kurdish caretaker who “offered us chai and no information about Noah’s Ark, nothing,” Jones noted.
He subsequently visited the site on three additional occasions between 1997 and 2000.
After a break of 13 years, Jones returned in 2013 with a tour group and reconnected with the Kurdish guides he had met on earlier trips. They asked whether he wanted to pursue something scientific, since little was happening at the site.
“Some tourists were going there; but again, it was kind of like it was in 1997. No one cared about it,” he said.
He returned to Turkey twice in 2014. On his second trip, ERT scans conducted at the site produced “really good results.”
“That got us all excited, since the last time anything was done on the ship [was in] the late 1980s,” Jones said. “That was kind of the start of the current effort because that got everyone excited.”
Further scans in 2019, utilizing ground-penetrating radar (GPR), LiDAR data collection, and thermal cameras, win conjunction with the Science Channel, showed what Jones described as an unnatural pattern of anomalies. The COVID pandemic closed borders in 2020. Following the death of his parents, Jones decided to move to Turkey to be closer to the site and learn the bureaucracy involved in excavating it.
In 2022, NAS renovated the site’s visitor center. Today, it is paneled with wood flooring and large-scale posters showing the results of the 2014 and 2019 scans covering the walls. A 3D scale model of Durupinar built using GPR data taken from the site sits in the center of the space.
During the visit, the Post was shown several marine fossils that had been previously found at and around Durupinar.
In 2024, soil scientist William Crabtree tested 88 soil samples taken from both within and outside of the site. He found that soil from inside the formation had more organic matter, more potassium, and a pH about one unit lower than soil from the outside.
But without a Turkish university partner, NAS could do nothing more than surface-level testing until Atila, a classical archaeologist from Turkey’s Sivas University, connected with Jones online.
On behalf of NAS, Atila appealed to the Turkish Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry for permission to conduct an invasive study of the Durupinar formation, providing a detailed, multi-step outline of the planned testing.
“We had core drilling to 75 meters down, everything geophysical I could think of,” Jones said. “All these are very expensive things to do. But I just threw it all in and said, ‘Let’s see what they approve.’”
According to Jones, the only question the ministry asked was regarding the requested depth of the core drilling. The 75-meter mark, he explained, was due to the estimate that bedrock rested at 70 meters below the surface.
“We wanted to core the deepest we’re allowed to,” Jones said. “To see what we can see all the way down.”
The ministry approved the plan two weeks later, Atila told the Post, with no changes made to any of the requests and plans.
What the drills found
The partnership between Atila and Jones produced results that the team says are worth pursuing, though no one is claiming to have found proof.
During the recent season, the team drilled 12 holes inside the formation and four outside it, going as deep as some 20 meters in places. By Jones’s account, none struck bedrock, which he said would have been the sign of a natural rock formation.
“We didn’t hit any solid rock layer across the site,” he said, adding: “I think that it’s in our favor.”
Notably, Jones mentioned, the drill bit had broken after hitting an unidentified object. Before breaking, the bit had been “through rock pretty fine… if we hit a boulder or something, we go right through it, back into the soil.”
Jones affirmed that NAS would be able to drill a slightly wider hole during its next season, in order to retrieve the broken bit.
To critics claiming that the drilling hadn’t gone deep enough, Jones replied that the team is expected to continue drilling during its next season, in the summer of 2027.
Alongside core drilling and collecting soil samples, the NAS team conducted new radar scans using BakhtarRadar, a subsurface imaging system developed by engineer Khosrow Bakhtar, chief scientist at Bakhtar Research and Engineering LLC.
Preliminary findings from the scans appear to show linear features, angular intersections, layered structures, and possible voids beneath the formation. Researchers interpret these features as possible corridors, compartments, and multiple internal levels similar to the biblical description of the ark.
The radar team had come from the United States, Atila said, but due to heavy rain and other constraints, had only seven days to work on the site. He noted that the team is expected to return in 2027.
Regarding the voids beneath the formation, Atila was careful not to overstate the results.
“I don’t want to say absolutely,” he said. “It’s a corridor. Maybe it can be a geological hole.”
He explained that he is planning future fieldwork at the site, attempting to understand whether the “hole” belongs to the Ark or to a geological formation.
Pieces of what may be petrified wood were also found at the site and sent to Sivas for carbon dating and identification, Atila added. The team is now awaiting the soil analysis, final radar, and carbon-dating results.
Cohen said: “As a lawyer, I have spent years examining evidence and understanding the importance of the bigger picture. In a courtroom, no single piece of circumstantial evidence necessarily proves a case, but the cumulative weight of independent findings can become extraordinarily compelling.
“That is precisely what fascinates me about this site. If this is not Noah’s Ark, we may be looking at one of the most remarkable coincidences in history. At some point, the sheer number of converging clues demands an explanation.”
But not everyone has welcomed the work being conducted at Durupinar.
Jones told the Post that not long after beginning fieldwork at the site in July, the local governor halted the dig for nearly a week after both the governor’s office and the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry received numerous phone calls questioning the work being done.
According to Jones, the callers questioned officials over why foreigners such as NAS were allowed to work so close to the Turkish-Iranian border and warned that they might do something illegal or damaging to the site.
The pause was lifted after the governor consulted with individuals familiar with the work happening on the ground, and the team was able to carry on under their original permit.
Jones recalled Atila telling him, at the time, that he’d never seen anything like it.
“This is the first time I’ve seen people so interested in the work that they want to stop us,” Jones recalled him saying. “They all become archaeologists suddenly.”
Jones said he could only guess at the motives behind the complaints, among them jealousy from other teams searching for Noah’s Ark in other locations or a Turkish dislike of foreigners working in the area.
Scientific objections to the claim of Durupinar being the resting place of the Ark, however, are less personal and focus more on the geological appearance of the site.
Such theories include the idea that its ship-like shape was formed by mud flowing around an upright piece of bedrock, that a solid limestone boulder originating near the Iranian border was over the years shaped by glaciers and weathering, and that the formation is actually a syncline (folded rocks).
All three theories, Jones noted, depend on having solid rock underneath, of which the team’s drilling found no evidence.
“We’re not forcing the results,” Jones said. “If we core drilled and hit a rock layer across the whole site, yeah, we’d be like, okay, it’s most likely natural. But we didn’t.”
Paperwork for a second season of work has already been submitted, Jones said.
While the initial permit presented by Atila and approved by the Turkish government covered far more than the team is currently able to undertake, there are several methods Jones wants to seek additional approval for, such as seismic imaging, magnetometry and microgravity, and possibly muon imaging, a technique used at the pyramids of Egypt to detect voids.
At the end of the two-year process, the team will decide on how to proceed based on the sufficiency of the data collected, Jones explained.
Digging would be the last stage of excavations, should analysis results come back positive and NAS is able to get it approved. If Durupinar is the Ark, Jones said, it would be the oldest man-made object documented by biblical chronology, making it extremely fragile, and any highly invasive work will have to be done carefully.
For Cohen, though, the case for pressing on goes beyond curiosity.
“I believe we have a moral, historical, and perhaps even spiritual obligation to investigate this site as thoroughly as possible,” he told the Post.
“We are potentially standing before something that could fundamentally change our understanding of human history.
“With every new clue, every radar scan, and every sample examined, the responsibility to pursue the truth only grows stronger. Whether this ultimately proves to be Noah’s Ark or not, walking away without exhausting every scientific possibility would be a disservice to future generations.”
For Jones and Crabtree, the discovery could mark a significant point of unification worldwide.
“If we can prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that this is Noah’s Ark, the whole world will feel it in their heart, whether they’re an atheist, a Christian, a Muslim, a Jew,” Crabtree told the Post.
Jones added, “We live in a world that’s divided, but the story itself can provide that type of unity to people, and hopefully those who want it can see it in the story, and in the site itself here.”
