Peace absent from Israel's 2026 elections as West Bank tensions continue to rise -analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:55 UTC
23:06:55 KST

There’s a short video clip that’s been circulating on Israeli social media channels in recent days showing a massive crowd of jubilant young Israelis at a music festival singing along on repeat to “The Song of Peace.”
The scene, using an anthem forever associated with assassinated prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and the peace momentum that surrounded him in the 1990s, feels ironic today. As Israelis prepare to vote on Oct. 27, peace - the idea at the heart of the song and that was once at the heart of the political debate in Israel - is strikingly absent this time around.
More than three years of war have reshaped the country, but few candidates are offering a vision for relations with the Palestinians, let alone a path toward resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, rising settler violence in the West Bank and mounting international pressure to resolve the decades-old intractable conflict with a two-state solution are making the costs of that political silence increasingly difficult to ignore.
“Objectively, this is just not the main issue in this election,” Prof. Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in a recent interview.
Future character of state, security a focus in Israel 2026 elections
In contrast to the years leading up to Rabin’s assassination in 1995 - and even those that followed - the divisions in this election have little to do with the question of peace with the Palestinians.
Rather, said Rahat, they are more about the fundamentals, the future character of the state and security. For the past four years, the government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has sought to overhaul the country’s judiciary, while a burgeoning ultra-Orthodox population has avoided compulsory military service even though Israel has been fighting a relentless war on seven different fronts.
And while there has been an attempt by Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party to frame the debate as one between right-wing and left-wing, pro-and-anti-Palestinian statehood, Rahat said this was misleading.
Most of the parties in the opposition, those seeking to oust Netanyahu and the current government, are a mix of center-right and right-wing parties. Only one Jewish party in the bloc, the Democrats, appears open to addressing the Palestinian issue.
Rahat pointed out that Hamas’s attack on Israeli civilian communities in southern Israel and at a music festival had served to harden even those who previously thought a peaceful solution with the Palestinians might be possible.
Surveys published in recent years had already shown that support for a Palestinian state, or even a process to reach some kind of solution, had been steadily decreasing even before Oct. 7.
According to Tel Aviv University’s Peace Index, which has published regular data on Israeli attitudes toward peace with the Palestinians since the first Oslo Accords were signed in September 1993, in July this year only 29% of the Jewish public in Israel now supports any form of negotiations with the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian leadership governing the Palestinians in the West Bank.
Broken down into right-wing vs. left-wing voters, the divisions on the issue of the peace process still appear to be sharp, with only 7% of those who identify as right-wing saying they support negotiations, compared to 83% of those on the left. Yet this is somewhat misleading, as overall, the percentage of people who identify with views traditionally associated with Israel’s peace camp and the left has been steadily shrinking.
After a historic low turnout for the two traditional left-wing parties, Labor and Meretz, in the 2022 election, the two factions joined forces to form The Democrats, now led by former IDF general Yair Golan. And while the Democrats believe in pursuing separation from the Palestinians through a diplomatic and regional process, Golan has refrained from talking about the position throughout the election campaign.
Additionally, former prime minister Yair Lapid, who heads the center-left Yesh Atid Party and has stated in the past that he supports a two-state solution for Israelis and Palestinians, has cooled on the idea.
He has teamed up with former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who is emphatically against the concept of two democratic states side by side, and is saying that the Hamas attack had postponed the possibility of Palestinian statehood at least for now.
“I don’t think the idea is dead. I think it will be delayed significantly because we need to find ways to secure the safety of our people,” Lapid reportedly said in an interview to a London-based Saudi Arabian newspaper in December 2023.
On the issue of settlements in the West Bank, recent surveys show that the majority of Israeli Jews support the concept. A poll published by the Israel Democracy Institute this month shows that around 55% of Israeli Jews support the policies of various governments to allow, and even encourage, the establishment of settlements. Only 32% think that settlement expansion was not correct, the research found.
While the question of peace with the Palestinians - and the possibility of a nation-state for them in Gaza or the West Bank, which many Israelis refer to by its biblical name of Judea and Samaria - is not being discussed on the political level, violent events in that contested area are becoming increasingly hard to ignore.
West Bank attacks undermine peace process
On Friday, Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with The Washington Post, was brutally attacked by masked settlers, as shown in video footage. And on Saturday, a group of European diplomats said they were similarly attacked. Both incidents took place as Palestinian farmers harvested their olive crop.
An influential rabbi associated with far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir had issued an edict that Jews were permitted to attack Palestinians and take their olives to “demonstrate our ownership of the land.”
Palestinians, Rabbi Dov Lior, the former chief rabbi of Kiryat Arba, wrote in a decree, had “stolen land in their hands,” and that it really belongs to Jews.
The phenomenon of Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians is not new, but, according to human rights organizations and the United Nations, it has increased in frequency since Oct. 7. Ben-Gvir, who oversees the Israel Police, has struggled, along with the military, to maintain law and order.
The violence has resulted in multiple deaths. Several governments imposed sanctions on individuals and organizations linked to settler violence. Netanyahu continues to insist that it is only a handful of disorderly youths who are responsible for the disorder.
The increasing violence has drawn condemnation from Netanyahu’s rivals and even some who support him.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief, whose party Yashar leads the opposition bloc, described the attacks, in a post on X, as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government.”
He said it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses.”
Avigdor Liberman, a former defense minister under Netanyahu who is now running as part of the opposition bloc, also criticized the violence, saying it was “wiping out Israel’s last bastions of support in the United States and around the world.”
“Bibi is putting out statements in English, but the defense minister and the national security minister are doing nothing to stop this madness,” Liberman wrote on X, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
“In the end, the damage is first and foremost to the State of Israel and the settlement enterprise. This just proves that Bibi doesn’t care about the country - he only cares about staying in power,” he wrote.
Israeli journalist Amit Segal, known for being pro-Netanyahu, wrote on X that the violence had caused great damage to Israel’s standing among its greatest friends.
Ilana Shpaizman, a senior lecturer in the department of political studies at Bar-Ilan University, said that the flare-up in violence was putting the Palestinian issue back in the spotlight in Israel and beyond.
“For many years or even decades Israeli policy in the West Bank was carried out quietly … It wasn’t like people didn’t know what was going on, but they tried to promote it as quietly as possible to maintain legitimacy to the settlement project,” she said, adding, “When we look at what has happened over the last couple of days, not only has the international community condemned it, but also Israeli politicians.
“People are starting to realize that this government’s support in the West Bank has become very dangerous,” Shpaizman said.
It’s not just Netanyahu, she said - the so-called “change” government that was in office between 2021 and 2022 also failed to address the Palestinian issue.
Shpaizman said Netanyahu was known for being indecisive and reluctant to address the Palestinian issue, and Bennett and Lapid’s slogan was to address only the issues they could solve and leave the tougher question of peace with the Palestinians for later, after other domestic rifts were resolved.
But she said the Palestinian issue is the most explosive and “cannot be ignored for a long period of time.”
Rahat said the rising tensions in the West Bank and the increasing international pressure, which will likely rise if Netanyahu’s government retains power, could end up forcing a solution, or at least putting the Palestinian issue back on the agenda.

Who made Gaza hospitals and homes targets? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:35 UTC
23:06:35 KST

In a Gaza neighborhood, beside a playground built with UNRWA money and flying a Hamas flag, sacks of rice and flour stamped with United Nations markings were stacked into a fighting fortification like sandbags.
Next door, according to an IDF commander who fought there, stood a Hamas training compound and a kindergarten. Inside the kindergarten, troops found weapons and photographs of small children in Hamas uniforms. A tunnel shaft had been dug into the kindergarten’s yard. When Israeli forces moved in, two Hamas gunmen emerged from that shaft and hit them with an RPG. Five soldiers were wounded.
This was the same war in which Israel stood accused, in newsrooms, at the United Nations, and in The Hague, of starving Gaza by design. In that compound, the food had arrived. Hamas used it for cover.
The scene comes from NAZA: The Real Story, the reply to NAZA, the Guardian-produced documentary by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that took the Special Jury Prize at Venice. Three Israelis made the counter-film in under two weeks with their own money: Lt.-Col. (res.) Roi Danino, attorney and reservist Ariel Averbuch, and director Hagay Gutman.
A film made that fast has rough edges. But it puts IDF soldiers and officers who fought in Gaza on camera, and it backs their accounts with footage of Hamas weapons and military infrastructure in hospitals, mosques, and schools.
I wrote here last month about how NAZA recast Israel’s lawful collateral damage calculations as something nefarious. This piece concerns the half of the story it ignores. The Guardian’s documentary asks how Israel decided whether to strike. It never asks who decided where the target would be.
The war against Hamas
The answer is on the map, where the terrorist leaders who launched these wars of choice were finally found.
On September 27, 2024, Israeli jets killed Hassan Nasrallah in Hezbollah’s headquarters, a bunker beneath apartment towers in Beirut’s Dahiyeh suburb. He chose that spot knowing what the footage of any strike on him would look like.
On May 13, 2025, an Israeli strike killed Mohammed Sinwar, Hamas’s military chief in Gaza, along with its Rafah Brigade commander, Muhammad Shabana. Troops later found the compound directly beneath the emergency room of the EU-funded European Hospital in Khan Yunis. Hamas built its command center under that ER.
Mohammed Sinwar was no bystander to his brother’s war. He helped plan the 2006 abduction of Gilad Schalit, part of the template for October 7. He was central to building the Rafah tunnel network, where Hamas hid fighters, weapons, and hostages under a city that sheltered more than a million displaced Gazans.
He spent his last months underground, under a hospital, betting Israel would not find him or strike the building above him. Israel found him and aimed at the bunker, not the wards. Gaza’s Health Ministry still reported 28 dead. It did not say who built the bunker or how many of the dead were Hamas operatives, and it never mentioned Sinwar or Shabana. Its tolls don’t distinguish its fighters from civilians.
Sinwar’s brother Yahya, the architect of the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led invasion and massacres, died on October 16, 2024, in Rafah’s Tel al-Sultan neighborhood, inside a family home whose owner had evacuated months earlier.
Nearby, seven weeks before, Hamas executed Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Carmel Gat, Eden Yerushalmi, Ori Danino, Alex Lobanov, and Almog Sarusi in a tunnel whose shaft opened inside a child’s bedroom in another family’s home, its walls painted with Snow White and Mickey Mouse.
An apartment block, a hospital, a family’s home. Each was chosen in advance by men who understood that their neighbors’ bodies were their best armor.
Hamas imprisoned its hostages with the same logic. Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov, and Shlomi Ziv were rescued in June 2024 from family apartments in Nuseirat in central Gaza. Noa Marciano, 19, was murdered by a Hamas-affiliated doctor inside Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
Sharon Aloni Cunio said she and her three-year-old twins, Emma and Yuli, were held in a Khan Yunis hospital. The bodies of Shani Louk, Amit Buskila, Itzhak Gelerenter, and Ron Benjamin were recovered from a tunnel reached through a shaft inside a house in Jabalia. Emily Damari said after her release that Hamas held her in UNRWA facilities.
Criticism of 'NAZA'
The Guardian asks viewers to trust 24 interviewees whose names and faces they never see. Everything above rests on names, dates, and addresses any reporter can check. The record of where Hamas put its leaders and captives requires no trust at all.
NAZA treats every civilian death, and even every calculation meant to avoid one, as an entry in the ledger against Israel. It never opens Hamas’s books. Who dug the shaft in the kindergarten yard? While others pushed the starvation libel, who stacked UN bags of rice into a wall? The film never asks, and a documentary that will not ask obvious questions has stopped documenting.
International law requires asking these questions. Hamas chose this war on October 7, then built its strategy around erasing the line the law of war exists to draw. That law requires fighters to distinguish themselves from civilians and treats feigning civilian status as perfidy.
Hamas fighters stored their uniforms after October 7 and fought in civilian clothes, a choice no military makes for comfort.
The law forbids using civilians to shield military targets. Hamas put shafts in kindergarten yards, weapons in schools, anti-tank missiles under a children’s rug, and a command center beneath an emergency room. Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, a hospital used for acts harmful to the other side loses its protection.
International law bars armed groups from using anyone under 18 in hostilities and makes using children under 15 a war crime. NAZA: The Real Story shows children carrying weapons to Hamas fighters in broad daylight.
The same law obliges Israel to verify its targets, estimate the civilian toll before every strike, and call off any attack whose expected harm would be excessive relative to the military gain. NAZA presents Israel’s legal compliance as confession. And the law holds the side that hides behind civilians responsible for what follows. Collateral damage requires collateral, and Hamas put it there by design.
Hamas built its war so that every Israeli strike would leave civilian bodies, and every casualty would become an indictment of Israel. But that strategy works only with media accomplices. Abraham, Szor, and the Guardian did that job, and Venice gave them a prize for it.
Micha Danzig is a contributing opinion writer for The Jerusalem Post and other Jewish publications, as well as an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former New York Police Department officer.

UK lawmakers say letters from Palantir were intended to intimidate critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:26 UTC
23:06:26 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
British lawmakers who criticized US tech firm Palantir in parliament have received letters from company executives, which they described as attempts to intimidate critics, Novara Media reported Thursday.
Former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn and Labour and Cooperative Party MP Rachael Maskell received letters from Palantir’s UK CEO Louis Mosley on June 3, detailing their parliamentary remarks about the company and offering meetings.
“I am in no doubt as to why Palantir is writing these letters to MPs to intimidate its critics into silence,” Corbyn told Novara Media, adding that the tactics would not deter him from opposing involvement in public services by the company, which faces controversy over both its co-founder’s views and its work for Israel.
Maskell, who represents York Central, said the correspondence would not change her approach toward the firm, which holds contracts with Britain’s National Health Service (NHS), the Defense Ministry, and police forces.
“Clearly there is a reason as to why Palantir has paid close attention to the scrutiny that MPs have brought to this company,” she said.
Independent MP Shockat Adam also received an email from Palantir’s UK public affairs lead following critical social media posts about the company’s involvement in the NHS and its now-ended contract with the Leicestershire Police.
Adam called on Palantir executives Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, and Louis Mosley to explain their roles before Parliament, saying the public has a right to know how the company’s software was used across public services and the armed forces.
A Palantir spokesperson said the letters aimed to correct inaccurate claims about the company, adding that it would continue responding if politicians repeated what it described as falsehoods.
Labour MP Clive Lewis separately criticized a letter from Palantir’s UK senior vice president, former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, warning that the company was monitoring his activities related to Palantir.
US-based Palantir has long been controversial in many countries, partly because co-founder Peter Thiel, a supporter of the Trump administration, has repeatedly voiced skepticism about traditional democratic systems.
The company has also faced criticism from rights groups over reports that it provided AI-enabled systems, including targeting and data-analysis support as well as critical data infrastructure, to the Israeli military for operations in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
Recently, the company and London Mayor Sadiq Khan’s office have withdrawn allegations against each other in a legal dispute over a £50 million ($65 million) police technology contract, heading off a High Court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) in June after Khan intervened to block a proposed two-year contract for the Metropolitan Police to use artificial intelligence to process intelligence in criminal investigations.
Khan’s intervention followed concerns about the company’s work with the Israeli military and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The mayor previously said Londoners wanted public money to go to companies that “share the values of our city.”
The agreement comes one month after former Labour Party deputy leader Tom Watson was hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir. The company had raised concerns that excluding it from public contracts over objections to its leadership’s values could undermine its ability to operate in the UK.

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

Tom Cruise to receive 2027 American Film Institute Life Achievement Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Hollywood star Tom Cruise will receive the 52nd American Film Institute (AFI) Life Achievement Award, the organization's highest honor for a career in cinema, AFI announced Wednesday.
The 64-year-old actor and producer will be honored at a gala ceremony at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on April 24, 2027.
"Tom Cruise is a global icon," said Kathleen Kennedy, chair of the AFI Board of Trustees.
"As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together," she added.
Cruise, whose career spans more than four decades, has starred in major Hollywood productions including, Top Gun, Mission: Impossible, Jerry Maguire, Rain Man and A Few Good Men.
His films have grossed nearly $13 billion worldwide, according to AFI, with Top Gun: Maverick remaining his highest-grossing release.
He has received four Academy Award nominations, including three for acting and one for producing Top Gun: Maverick, which was nominated for Best Picture.
Cruise also received an honorary Oscar at the Academy's Governors Awards in 2025.
The honor comes weeks after the release of Cruise's latest film, Digger, directed by two-time Oscar-winning filmmaker Alejandro G. Inarritu. The Warner Bros. satire has struggled at the box office, grossing approximately $42 million worldwide despite a reported production budget exceeding $160 million.
Established in 1973, the AFI Life Achievement Award recognizes individuals whose careers have made significant contributions to cinema.
Previous recipients include Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Nicole Kidman and Eddie Murphy, who received the honor in 2026.

Ukraine receives 252 bodies in swap with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:03:33 UTC
23:03:33 KST

Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people in an exchange of war dead with Russia.
Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War announced the repatriation on Thursday, while Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliev told the RBC news outlet that Moscow received 25 bodies in return.
The exchange of prisoners and war dead remains one of the few areas of cooperation between the two sides.
"As a result of repatriation measures, the bodies of 252 deceased have been returned to Ukraine," the Ukrainian headquarters said, adding that police and other officials would carry out identification procedures.
Police and other officials would "carry out all the necessary procedures to identify the repatriated deceased", it said.
It thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help facilitating the exchange, posting pictures on social media of several large white trailer trucks parked back to back, as workers in white, hooded jumpsuits emblazoned with the ICRC logo stood nearby.
The I Want to Live foundation, which is affiliated with Ukraine's Intelligence Directorate and involved in managing Russia's prisoners of war, meanwhile said "the remains of Russian servicemen were repatriated".
Among them was the body of a Sri Lankan citizen, the organisation said, adding that he was sent to Russia since he was considered under international law as a combatant in the Russian army.
The exchanges of remains between the two sides take place regularly.
Earlier this month, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov estimated that more than 26,000 bodies and human remains had been repatriated to Ukraine through exchange operations.
Most of them are still awaiting identification.
According to official announcements from both sides, Ukraine has received the remains of 5,300 people since the start of the year, while Russia has received fewer than 300.
The war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, has claimed tens of thousands of lives since Russia launched its military offensive in February 2022.

The US Is Losing to China in the Battle of Global Influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

Global influence is frequently a topic for conference panels, talk show pundits, and earnest think tank recommendations, but this nebulous measure of soft power has real-world impact for national security, economic strength and political power.
Today, this battle is unfolding rapidly, region by region, country by country, through security and commercial partnerships, emerging regional groupings, newly established diplomatic outposts, and academic partnerships.
As conflicts erupt and new trade and political alignments emerge, it’s clear: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete. The United States should do more than watch China’s intensive investment in building global influence – in diplomacy, in academic and cultural exchanges, in economic partnerships, and in national security pacts.
Influence is hard to gauge – and even harder to count on. Even the closest of diplomatic partners have sovereign interests and political differences. Historical relationships, either through war-hardened alliances or postcolonial reckonings, can shape perception and sway alignment. However, China’s transactional approach inherently reflects its genuine disregard for human rights, democratic aspirations, and welfare of citizens in other countries. This is China’s weak point, which the United States can leverage to regain lost ground.
Diplomacy: You Must Show up
The work of diplomacy is accomplished behind the scenes, by building connections, negotiating agreements, and advocating for businesses. The work of a diplomat is to know the government officials and trade contacts before you make an ask. This allows diplomats to build the trust required to get to agreement before a crisis happens or an ask is made.
China is succeeding at one of the first rules of diplomacy: showing up.
The Lowry Institute’s Global Diplomacy Index paints a clear picture. China has 274 diplomatic posts globally, compared with the United States’ 271. The strategic advantage is even clearer in Africa – where China has 60 to the United States’ 56 – and in East Asia, where China has 44 to the United States’ 27. While the numerical difference is small, the trend is concerning.
Beijing leverages its growing diplomatic presence as a strategic asset, populating its embassies with commercial, educational, and political professionals. It is gradually making inroads even with the United States’ longtime partners. Just this month, China’s President Xi Jinping traveled to Egypt, where Beijing and Cairo signed an array of agreements, from linking Egypt’s national development plan to China’s Belt and Road Initiative to a pledge to increase trade and investments in their own currencies, moving away from the U.S. dollar.
For the United States, the trend is going the other way, and that’s worrying. Despite a slate of recent nominations, 93 out of 196 ambassadorial slots remain vacant, according to the tracker maintained by the American Foreign Service Association. And while in many cases there are able professional diplomats serving as chargés d’affaires in these roles, a confirmed ambassador signals seriousness to host governments.
The State Department has also taken steps to close a number of smaller consulates and shrink operations at other embassies. While there is absolutely a strong case for prioritizing engagement, streamlining operations, and improving efficiencies, the narrative that the United States is retreating from the world continues to spread.
Academic opportunities and cultural exchanges are important forms of diplomacy and a path to increasing the United States’ global influence. Engaging with the next generations of global talent is a critical investment or opportunity, and China understands this.
At the 2024 Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), Xi announced 60,000 government scholarships for African students. In addition to opportunities for students, FOCAC commitments will see some 20,000 African regional and city leaders receiving training in China every year, along with African journalists sent to China.
These programs are far from boondoggles: They enmesh these emerging officials, journalists, and business leaders into Chinese institutions and professional networks. And despite warnings from the United States, China has now established over 500 Confucius Institutes around the world. These institutes are purported to facilitate Chinese education and people-to-people exchanges, but effectively serve as propaganda arms of the Chinese government.
The United States has extraordinary assets of its own, including an open and free democracy, the best universities in the world, and an innovation economy. Traditionally, U.S. government-supported exchange programs showcase all three.
From the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP), which identifies rising stars in business, government, security, and media and brings them to the United States to showcase America’s story to world-class State Department programs, including the Fulbright, Gilman, Boren, and Critical Language Scholarships, these programs engage professionals at key junctures in their professional careers.
A scholarship or an exchange isn’t simply tuition assistance. These academic and cultural programs create alumni who may become government and business leaders in their countries. According to the State Department’s own accounting, over 500 IVLP alumni alone have become heads of state or government since the program’s founding in 1940. Another 12 have won Nobel Prizes, and thousands more have served as elected officials, government ministers, and community and business leaders.
The United States can benefit from having these leaders as counterparts; they leave these programs with firsthand knowledge and appreciation of America’s economic strength, tech savvy, entrepreneurship, pluralism, and values.
These programs continue, albeit after some stutters in funding in 2025. Yet there are deep proposed reductions in the 2027 fiscal year’s budget. And there is a long-term cost to making such programs unpredictable. China is rapidly expanding its networks, while the United States is offering uncertainty into its own powerful equivalents.
Economic Strength: Building Partnerships, Not Transactions
This isn’t a new trend. Pundits have warned for more than two decades that Beijing is approaching traditional U.S. partners with something tangible to offer.
Through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), as well as smaller bilateral and regional deals, China has smartly offered financing backed by its government for desperately needed infrastructure projects linked to access to African and Western Hemisphere markets.
At the most recent FOCAC summit in 2024, Xi announced approximately $51 billion in financial support to Africa over a three-year period. At the 2025 China-Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) Forum, Xi pledged a credit line of more than $9 billion for Latin America, as well as additional bilateral infrastructure investment. According to China’s own accounting in its 2025 BRI Investment Report, agreements that are part of BRI reached over $213 billion in 2025, up 75 percent from the previous year, with about 150 countries participating.
The United States can compete. The Lobito Corridor, which links Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Angola, provides U.S. support for a critical rail and infrastructure network spanning mineral production to port facilities. Through a $533 million loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the United States both invested in these countries’ economic development and leveraged this financing with an eye to long-term regional security through employment, investment, and regional integration.
However, while the United States has (and uses) smart tools like the DFC and Millenium Challenge Corporation, it has stopped some other initiatives. Driven by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the 2025 reprioritization of foreign assistance sidelined early-stage economic development efforts, such as programs for emerging entrepreneurs, small business, and agriculture – including dedicated programs to encourage women in these fields. These and other opportunities were once administered through the now-shuttered USAID and State Department programs. The 2025 foreign assistance restructuring halted these incubator projects worldwide, ending a values-based and long-term approach to economic growth.
While reform of U.S. assistance was absolutely necessary, the geopolitical cost is clear. When the United States – with its commitment to human rights, democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption measures – withdraws from a relationship, it is often China that surges to occupy the space.
Today, faced with the immediate challenge of global leadership in artificial intelligence (AI), the United States must be more than the leader in a technology footrace with China. The U.S. global role and responsibilities will require sustained investment in innovation, talent, infrastructure and trusted partnerships so the United States can continue in setting global standards that shape how AI is developed, governed and deployed. The United States can build on its standards of openness and accountability while ensuring that these emerging technologies reflect both U.S. interests and U.S. values.
Reclaiming the High Ground
China is intensifying its investment in its initiatives, building a worldwide network of infrastructure, finance, commercial, and political relationships. The United States absolutely has best-in-class competitive alternatives, but Washington must invest in and deepen those ties.
Many countries, especially across the Global South, see benefits to relationships with both China and the United States, but U.S. strength has traditionally meant that it is the first choice for security relationships, cultural and educational exchanges, and business partnerships. China’s approach has significant and public weaknesses, including debt controversies, debates over its political influence, and allegations of exploitation and human rights abuses in partner countries.
But Washington has its own work to do to right the soft power ship. The United States possesses enormous advantages in its world-class academic institutions, technology, alliances, and the sheer love of ordinary U.S. culture. We must remember, though: the United States didn’t become a superpower by looking backward.
The United States must maintain its influence – and its values of freedom, opportunity, accountability, and compassion – by continuing to show up.

====================================================================================================

New biological marker could end trial and error in depression care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:21 UTC
23:00:21 KST

Major depressive disorder is often treated through trial and error, but a blood test may soon help doctors choose the right medication on the first try. Researchers have identified a circular RNA molecule in the blood that predicts whether a patient will respond to a common class of antidepressants. The findings were published in Molecular Psychiatry.
Millions of people globally experience major depressive disorder. Doctors frequently prescribe selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, commonly known as SSRIs, as a first line of medical defense. These drugs block the reabsorption of serotonin in the brain, leaving more of the chemical available to help transmit messages between nerve cells.
Less than half of patients experience relief from their symptoms after trying their first prescribed antidepressant. This forces patients to spend months trying different medications before finding one that works. The prolonged wait imposes a heavy burden on individuals and adds substantial costs to the healthcare system.
Medical professionals currently lack biological tests to predict which drug will work for a specific person. Genetic tests exist to show how fast a person’s body might metabolize a drug. They cannot, however, forecast if the drug will actually relieve depression symptoms.
To find a better biological indicator, a team of researchers investigated circular RNAs. These are stable, loop-shaped genetic molecules that influence how other genes operate. Because they lack exposed ends, they resist degrading enzymes in the body, giving them a much longer lifespan than standard linear RNA molecules.
Circular RNAs are highly concentrated in the brain and help regulate how neurons connect and communicate. Some of these molecules can pass through the blood-brain barrier, the semi-permeable membrane that separates circulating blood from brain fluid. Because they leak into the bloodstream in a stable form, researchers can detect brain-derived circular RNAs using a standard blood draw.
The investigation was led by scientists Grigorios Papageorgiou, Eleni T. Tzavara, and Nikolaos Mellios of Circular Genomics and various research institutes in the United States and France, along with Madhukar H. Trivedi at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. They focused on a specific circular RNA called CDR1as. This molecule is highly abundant in the brain but rarely found in other human tissues.
The researchers first analyzed baseline blood samples from patients enrolled in two independent clinical trials. They extracted RNA from the blood of patients diagnosed with major depressive disorder who were about to begin taking the SSRI sertraline. Using a technique that amplifies genetic material, the team measured the starting levels of CDR1as for each patient.
The team found that patients who did not respond to sertraline after eight weeks of treatment had notably higher baseline levels of CDR1as in their blood. Patients who experienced symptom relief had lower starting levels of the molecule. The researchers observed that unaffected control subjects also showed lower baseline levels of the molecule.
Taking advantage of the clinical trial design, the researchers also measured the patients’ blood at different intervals after they started taking sertraline. They discovered that patients who responded well to the drug experienced an increase in CDR1as levels after treatment began. Patients who did not respond to the medication saw no such increase in the molecule’s concentration.
To test if this molecule simply predicts general improvement rather than specific drug responses, the researchers looked at other treatment groups. They measured baseline blood levels in patients who were given a placebo pill. They also evaluated patients who failed to respond to sertraline and were subsequently switched to bupropion, a different type of antidepressant.
Baseline levels of CDR1as did not predict whether a patient would feel better on a placebo. The molecule also failed to predict if a patient would go on to experience remission while taking bupropion. This suggested the biomarker is specifically tied to the mechanisms of sertraline.
The research team then wanted to know if this predictive power applied to the entire SSRI drug class. They examined blood samples from patients in other clinical programs who were taking fluoxetine, citalopram, or escitalopram. They also analyzed samples from a small study of patients taking alternative medications like serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors.
The researchers observed that CDR1as levels successfully identified patients who were faring well on various SSRIs, not just sertraline. When evaluating patients taking other classes of antidepressants, the molecule’s levels did not predict symptom relief. This pointed to a specific relationship between the circular RNA and SSRI medications as a whole.
To understand exactly how the brain produces this circular RNA, the team conducted experiments on mice. They administered different chemical compounds to the animals to block specific brain receptors. They then extracted brain tissue to measure changes in Cdr1as, the mouse equivalent of the human molecule.
When the researchers blocked the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, levels of the circular RNA dropped across three different regions of the mouse brain. Blocking dopamine or glutamate receptors did not produce a similar drop in the molecule. This established a direct link between serotonin system activity and the production of the circular RNA.
The investigators conducted a final set of experiments on lab-grown human and mouse nerve cells. They treated the cells with chemicals that inhibit brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein that promotes the survival and growth of neurons. Inhibiting this protein’s receptors caused the cells to produce less of the circular RNA.
The researchers noted that certain medical conditions could interfere with the accuracy of this blood test. For instance, the test performed poorly in depressed patients who had a family history of mania, which is often a sign of undiagnosed bipolar disorder. When the researchers excluded these patients from their analysis, the test’s predictive accuracy improved.
Medical events that disrupt the blood-brain barrier might also artificially alter the amount of circular RNA in the bloodstream. Severe head trauma or strokes could potentially cause these brain molecules to leak into the blood at abnormal rates. Future research will need to verify how such physical injuries influence the test results.
The study authors noted that high baseline levels of the molecule correlated with specific depression symptoms like anhedonia and social withdrawal. These symptoms are often associated with a subtype of depression that is historically harder to treat with SSRIs. Further studies will need to explore exactly how this biological marker overlaps with different clinical subtypes of the disorder.
The study, “A brain-enriched circRNA blood biomarker can predict response to SSRI antidepressants,” was authored by Grigorios Papageorgiou, El Chérif Ibrahim, Victor Gorgievski, Gabriella Maxson, Evelyn Lozano, Eric Gordon, Antoine Lefrere, Marie-Julie Toupet, Philippe Courtet, Raoul Belzeaux, Jane Foster, Thomas Carmody, Roy H. Perlis, Madhukar H. Trivedi, Eleni T. Tzavara, and Nikolaos Mellios.

Boxer built with room to upgrade its weapon station
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:19 BST
23:00:19 KST

The British Mechanised Infantry Vehicle was designed with capacity for future upgrades including to its remote weapon station, though no decision has been taken to replace the current system, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what assessment he had made of the potential merits of upgrading from the Kongsberg RS4 to the Kongsberg RS6 remote weapon station on Boxer.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The United Kingdom Mechanised Infantry Vehicle was designed with capacity for future upgrades, including to its Remote Weapon Station. The Army continues to assess capability, priority and affordability options across the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Programme and wider Armoured Fighting Vehicle fleet. No decision has currently been taken to upgrade the current Remote Weapon System.”
Boxer entered British service with the Kongsberg Protector RS4, a stabilised mount carrying a 7.62mm or 12.7mm machine gun with a day and thermal sight, operated from inside the vehicle. The RS6 is a heavier station in the same family, rated to carry a 30mm cannon or a 40mm grenade launcher along with anti-tank missiles, and Kongsberg has marketed it to armies wanting a protected weapon fit without the cost and weight of a full turret.
Australia selected the RS6 for its own Boxer order under Land 400 Phase 2, mounting a 30mm turret on its reconnaissance variants, and Germany has fitted heavier stations and turrets to Boxers for several customers.

The Cornell 7 and the Problem with Writing as Punishment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:04 UTC
23:00:04 KST

Justice is elusive, and there are few clearer examples of this than when people who commit acts of sexual violence are given rote tasks as a means of atonement.
Recently, the “Cornell 7” case has inspired new conversations about what accountability and atonement involve. When college administrators investigated a report of sexual violence, some of the alleged perpetrators were reportedly assigned to write “reflection papers,” along with other punishments. The writing assignments drew such ire that Cornell issued a statement stating that "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."
I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, which started when I was 11 years old. Abuse from my step-father went hand-in-hand with punishment. He knew how much I loved words, reading, and writing, and began to use them to discipline me.
Our household was governed by an elaborate set of rules. We were not allowed to speak during dinner without permission. We were required to stand while playing board games. Our bedrooms were inspected every evening, and our beds had to be made with hospital corners.
Any infraction could result in punishment. One of the preferred methods was to require me to write an essay outlining what I had done wrong and how to correct my misdeeds. If I didn't wash the dishes carefully enough, I would have to write an essay about why I needed to take better care when cleaning up after dinner.
Other times, I was ordered to write the same sentence hundreds of times.
If I complained about dinner, I had to write 100 times, “I will appreciate my mother’s cooking.”
If I made fun of one of my siblings, I had to write 250 times, “I will not make fun of my brother.”
And if I resisted attempts to assault me, the punishment could be a thousand repetitions of “I will listen.”
I was being punished for trying to protect myself from the person who was abusing me. In doing so, I learned that writing the correct words was not the same as believing them. I could produce an essay explaining what I might have done wrong and promise to be better, but it didn’t mean that I believed that I misbehaved. It meant that I understood what was required of me. The punishment was complete when the writing was complete, but whether I had learned anything was beside the point.
More than 50 years later, I find myself wondering what we believe an essay can accomplish when it is assigned in response to allegations of sexual violence. Cornell’s disciplinary proceedings have resulted in different sanctions for different students, including expulsions and suspensions. “Reflection papers” were among the educational requirements imposed on some students.
But what, exactly, can an assigned essay demonstrate?
An essay can be thoughtful and persuasive; it can express regret, recognize harm, and promise change. But how do we know whether the person who wrote it believes any of what is written? What happens when completing an assignment becomes a substitute for demonstrating genuine understanding or changed behavior?
I have spent my adult life writing, teaching, and interviewing people about their lives. I believe in the ability of language to help us understand ourselves and one another, and I know how easily language can be used to conceal the truth.
My abuser understood the power of words, and used them to dictate the terms of my obedience. He controlled what I was allowed to say. He warned me that no one would believe me and threatened violence against those I love if I spoke out. I believed him, and I remained silent and ashamed.
I was required to write about my smallest infractions while being forbidden, through fear, to speak about the most terrible thing happening in my life. And the person who demanded that I explain my wrongdoing was the person committing the most serious wrongdoing of all.
This is why the relationship between language and power matters so much to me. The person with authority often gets to decide what constitutes an acceptable explanation, a credible account, or a sufficient expression of remorse.
Jane Doe, the young woman at the center of the Cornell case, reported the incident to university police in 2024. Since then, the timing and content of her disclosures have become subjects of intense public scrutiny. Public debate has focused in part on differences between her initial statements and her subsequent allegations.
I cannot speak for her, and our experiences are different. But I understand how fear can determine what someone is willing to reveal, even when she desperately needs help.
There is something troubling about how much we expect words to prove in cases of sexual violence. We scrutinize the accounts of those who report abuse, searching for inconsistencies. Now we are asking those found responsible for misconduct to demonstrate understanding through written reflection.
I believe writing can lead to meaningful change. But an essay is evidence that someone has completed an assignment. It cannot establish whether that person understands the harm they have caused or whether their behavior will change.
Why are we putting so much faith in the words people are required to write, while questioning the words that others struggle to say?

The Defence Secretary spoke on British industry and sovereign production capacity at the official opening of Telford Gun Hall.

Today is a vote of confidence in our country, a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country, and proof that we are rebuilding the capabilities of our armed forces.

All of this adds up to a new era of hope and opportunity for this town, this region, and our country as we face up to a new era of threat and jeopardy.

Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.
But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.
To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.
Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.
And that’s what Rheinmetall here in Telford will help us to achieve. Here is also where our ambition to turn defence investment into jobs, skills and growth in every postcode becomes reality. The threat environment requires us to deliver the biggest sustained increase in defence investment since the end of the Cold War.
And I’m acutely aware that investment in defence comes with trade-offs and choices in other areas of government spending, and at a cost to the taxpayer. So investment in defence will only command lasting public support if people can see not only how that investment strengthens our national defence, but also if they can see how it improves their lives, how it makes sure that we have a Britain that is worth fighting for.
That means bringing opportunity to every corner of the country. Almost seventy percent of defence investment is already spent outside London and the South East, and we’re setting out shortly how people and communities in every nation and region of the UK will feel benefits and do feel benefits from the defence dividend.
Here in the West Midlands, the defence economy is worth £1.8 billion and directly support around 8,000 jobs, with Rheinmetall at the forefront. Defence can also help us to tackle the moral emergency of more than a million young people out of work or education or training.
So it’s not just about spending more, although spending more is necessary. Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. Does it strengthen our industrial base? Does it push the frontier of innovation? Does it create skilled work, especially for young people? Over the next decade, this facility will emphatically answer yes to all those questions.
And as it does, it will inject more than £400 million into the UK economy. That’s precisely what I mean when I say that the Ministry of Defence can also be a ministry for growth and a ministry for opportunity, not simply spending more, but investing more wisely, backing the people, places and businesses that strengthen our national security and drive our national renewal.
Every country across the NATO alliance faces similar challenges in the headwinds of rising threats and tighter finances. As we confront that reality, we need to avoid healthy competition becoming self-defeating rivalry and protectionism.
And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.
On so many fronts. UK and German interests align – nowhere more so than when it comes to our defence and security. We are the two biggest economies in Europe, the two biggest investors in defence, so it makes sense that we should come together in common purpose. Our partnership matters not as an end in itself, but because of what it allows our countries to deliver together.
The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.
This has Armin alluded to, is what lies behind the Trinity House agreement that deepens defence cooperation between our two countries. By working as one, we can build manufacturing capability home so that we can deliver faster and ultimately strengthen NATO, which is in all our interests.
In this new age of insecurity, we need to spend more and better, and we are. We need to prepare more, and we are, with better training and more kit and equipment in the hands of our armed forces. And we need to produce more, and we are. We are right here in a region rich in industrial heritage, honouring its past by investing in its future. The threats we face are real, and they are closer to home. We need to step up and together we are.
So thank you very much for being here and for the amazing work that’s gone into this incredible facility. Thank you.

Major rail works to disrupt traffic on Israel's busiest highways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:54:37 UTC
22:54:37 KST

Major infrastructure work by Israel Railways is expected to disrupt traffic on two key highways in central Israel this weekend, with lane reductions and traffic diversions planned along the Ayalon Highway and Route 531, ynet has learned.
The work, scheduled from Friday evening through Saturday, will affect motorists traveling through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and the Sharon region to its north. Although neither highway will be completely closed, the temporary traffic arrangements could cause significant congestion.
Israel Railways has not issued a special public announcement about the disruptions as the work does not involve full highway closures. However, authorities responsible for the affected roads have been formally notified, and the changes have been incorporated into the Waze navigation app.
The construction is part of a nationwide project to extend railway station platforms, allowing them to accommodate newer, longer trains and increase passenger capacity as demand for rail travel grows.
Under the approved traffic arrangements, crews will carry out the work by reducing the number of available lanes and diverting vehicles around construction zones rather than shutting down entire highways.
Where and when traffic will be affected
On the Ayalon Highway, also known as Highway 20, work will begin Friday at 8 p.m. and continue until Saturday at 8 a.m.
The highway is one of Israel's busiest transportation arteries, running through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and connecting major cities and employment centers along the country's central coastal plain.
Northbound traffic will be affected along two stretches: between the Shiv'at HaKochavim interchange and the HaMa'apilim area, and between the HaHalakha and KKL interchanges.
Southbound motorists will face changes along three stretches: between Shiv'at HaKochavim and HaMa'apilim, between HaHalakha and KKL, and between the Mevo Ayalon and Komemiyut interchanges.
Work on Route 531, a major east-west highway serving communities in the Sharon region north of Tel Aviv, will last longer. It is scheduled to begin Friday at 8 p.m. and continue until Saturday at 4 p.m.
Traffic arrangements will affect both eastbound and westbound lanes along the section between the Kfar Saba and Hod Hasharon railway stations.
Drivers traveling through either area are advised to allow additional time and consult navigation apps for updated routes.
Years of construction strain central Israel's roads
The latest disruptions come amid persistent traffic congestion across central Israel, where motorists have faced frequent delays over the past year as several of the country's largest transportation infrastructure projects advance simultaneously.
Among them is the construction of a fourth railway track along the Ayalon corridor, a major project intended to increase rail capacity through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area, where the existing tracks form a critical bottleneck in the national railway network.
Israel Railways is also carrying out an extensive electrification program to replace diesel-powered rail services with electric trains, while separate projects are expanding the Tel Aviv light rail network and preparing infrastructure for the planned metropolitan subway system.
Together, the projects have brought construction crews to major transportation arteries on an almost nightly basis, requiring recurring lane restrictions and temporary changes to traffic patterns.
Although much of the work is scheduled overnight to minimize disruption, construction frequently extends into periods of lighter daytime traffic and the early morning hours, creating bottlenecks and heavy congestion even when roads would ordinarily be relatively clear.
The overlapping projects have compounded the challenges facing drivers in the densely populated Tel Aviv metropolitan area, where major highways already carry substantial commuter traffic.
With another round of construction scheduled this weekend, motorists are being urged to prepare for possible delays, exercise patience and use navigation apps to check traffic conditions before setting out.

Trump’s tariffs loom over Maine Senate race between Collins and Jackson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:53:23 UTC
22:53:23 KST

PORTLAND, Maine — The same week President Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on imported steel, the domestic supplier of the wire mesh Mark Brooks uses to make lobster traps in Maine hiked prices by 20%.
When diesel prices began rising as the U.S. war with Iran escalated, Brooks started paying freight surcharges on his materials and saw sales slow as lobstermen tightened their belts. And when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney slapped 50% tariffs on U.S. lobster traps in September as retaliation for Trump's own duties on Canadian goods, the roughly $2 million in annual shipments Brooks typically sends over the northern border dried up virtually overnight.
"It's basically the worst business climate for us that I've ever seen in 40 years," said Brooks, a third-generation lobster-trap manufacturer and supplier, who along with his siblings runs Brooks Trap Mill and its seven locations across Maine. "We've eaten as much cost as we can to try to keep our prices down, but we just can't eat any more than we have already."
Few states have been as vulnerable in the U.S.-Canada trade war as Maine, which sends more than 40% of its exports to the U.S.'s northern neighbor. Those challenges are also piling on top of cost-of-living issues that were already spiraling, especially relating to things like home heating oil, on which Maine depends more than any other state. As a result, tariffs specifically — and affordability concerns more broadly — are center stage in this year's "toss up" Senate race between GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former president of the Maine Senate.
Polls show the economy is at the top of the list of voters' concerns this election, in Maine and nationwide. More than 90% of respondents in a Suffolk University poll this month of likely Maine voters rated the state's economy as "fair" or "poor," while a majority said the state is on the wrong track and 57% gave Trump an unfavorable rating.
The key question here is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Collins, or whether she will be able to separate herself from an unpopular piece of Trump's and the Republican Party's agenda. 
"That's one of the big issues in this campaign: How independent is Susan Collins from Donald Trump?" said Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington.
Across the country, Republican candidates in competitive seats have been working to find ways to distance themselves from the White House.
In Michigan, GOP candidate Mike Rogers has criticized the Canada tariffs and called for a quick end to the Iran war. In Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate, came out against Trump's decision to temporarily lower tariffs on imported ground beef, which she said would hurt U.S. cattle ranchers. And GOP Senate hopefuls in New Hampshire, Alaska, Ohio and Nebraska have all expressed concerns over Trump's decision to allow imports of Russian diesel, reversing course weeks after signing legislation to expand sanctions on Russia.
But Maine presents the ultimate test of whether voters this year will distinguish between the president and the rest of his party. Collins, long known and praised for her independent streak, is the lone GOP incumbent running for reelection in a state that voted against Trump in 2024. And polls show the race is tight, with Jackson leading by an average of 2 percentage points in polls compiled by FiftyPlusOne.
'We shouldn't be in a trade war with Canada'
Both Collins and Jackson have sharply criticized the tariffs, which are deeply unpopular here: Seven in 10 likely Maine voters say duties on Canadian goods are bad for the state, while only 12% called them "a good thing," according to a CNN poll last month.
But the candidates disagree over who bears responsibility for the economic damage, and who could better do something about it.
Collins has repeatedly pushed back against the Trump administration on duties and was able to secure exemptions from the Canada tariffs for some key items, including concrete, wood pulp and road salt. Jackson argues that Congress should have been able to prevent the tariffs altogether, and that Collins, for all her seniority in Washington, should have been able to do more to help her state.
"The bottom line is Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs," Collins said in an Oct. 13 debate, the third of four held between the two candidates. "But I have been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list — Troy would have gotten nothing."
"I'm not going to give Sen. Collins credit for taking things off the list, when we should have never had a list," Jackson replied. "We shouldn't be in a trade war with Canada."
"Troy spent most of his life working along the Canadian border, so he knows how important this relationship is to Maine's economy, and he sees Trump's tariffs for what they are: a tax on Maine families and small businesses," Maggie Amjad, Jackson's campaign spokesperson, said in response to CNBC's request for comment about the effects of tariffs and the Iran war.
"There's a fundamental difference between Senator Collins and Troy Jackson: she delivers results; he would get nothing," Blake Kernen, Collins' campaign spokesperson, told CNBC. "They both would have voted against the tariffs, but Senator Collins secured exemptions and delivered for Maine."
The lobster industry escaped the worst of the Canada tariffs, after Ottawa made a last-minute decision to leave lobster off its retaliation list. Collins' team says that move, too, was partly due to her influence: She met with Canada's ambassador in Washington to discuss lobster and seafood exclusions, and released a statement afterward warning that tariffs "would have caused tremendous harm to Maine's lobstermen."
But lobster fishermen say nearly everything else they use on the boat every day is still getting more expensive. The traps that Brooks makes are selling for $180 now, versus $130 two years ago. The diesel fuel that runs the boats is up 67% statewide over the past year, according to AAA. The rope, much of which is imported from India, and the bait, which largely comes from Europe, is also more expensive due to the combination of tariffs and higher fuel costs.
"Everything we do in this business costs more money right now," said Steve Train, a lobsterman who hauls 400 lobster traps a day out of Casco Bay. "These tariff wars are not helping us."
Train faults Trump for the tariffs and criticizes him for "bypassing Congress" to "issue executive orders to do things that cause us a problem." But he credits Collins for the work she has done to help the lobster industry. A registered independent, he says he will split his vote between the parties this election, but one vote will be for Collins.
"She has been like a guardian angel for the lobster industry for many years," he said. "I can't oppose her because she's in the same party as somebody I don't like."

Gambling regulator hits illegal casino with record €37m fine
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch gambling regulator KSA has issued a record fine of €37 million on a company for running a dozen unlicensed online casinos.
EOD Code SRL, which says it is registered in Costa Rica, offered games to players in the Netherlands through sites including Instantcasino and Skyhills without a Dutch licence, KSA said on Thursday.
KSA inspectors were able to register and gamble on the sites with no measures in place to stop people in the Netherlands using them. Several of the sites had no visible age checks and accepted cryptocurrency and other anonymous payment methods.
The investigation began with Instantcasino and later uncovered 11 more sites run by the same company. The KSA based the fine on an estimate of the company’s Dutch revenue.
Online gambling was legalised in October 2021, with the government arguing a regulated market would draw players away from illegal sites. But the KSA estimated last year that more money goes to unlicensed sites than to legal ones.
In August, radio station BNR found that illegal operators were targeting Facebook and Instagram ads at people on Cruks, the national register that bars them from gambling. The cabinet set out plans in June to ban online gambling advertising and bonuses.
If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s use of alcohol, drugs, or gambling, the Jellinek addiction helpline can be reached on 088 505 1220 or at jellinek.nl. The line is staffed in Dutch and English on weekdays, 1pm to 5pm.

Gaza’s Health Ministry warned Thursday that hospital electricity generators could stop working after stocks of operating oil were completely exhausted amid Israel’s continued blockade of the enclave, Anadolu reports.
The ministry said in a statement that engineering teams are working under difficult conditions to monitor the generators and keep electricity supply to critical hospital departments.
“Generators have been running for thousands of continuous hours without sufficient oil or maintenance, bringing them to the final point of mechanical danger,” the ministry said.
“If generator engines burn out because of the lack of oil, they could become permanently unusable even if supplies become available later,” it warned.
The ministry renewed its call for urgent intervention, saying the issue was no longer limited to securing operating oil but also involved protecting the remaining generators from complete failure.
On Wednesday, the ministry said stocks of oil needed to operate hospital generators had run out, adding that more than 2,500 liters (660 gallons) are urgently needed each month to prevent the remaining generators from breaking down amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of operating and maintenance supplies.
The ministry warned that the continuing shortage threatens the shutdown of life-saving medical departments.
In September, it said 70% of hospital generators had already gone out of service because of shortages of fuel, oil and spare parts caused by the Israeli blockade.
READ: Gaza hospitals face risk of power outages as generator oil runs out
Separately, Gaza’s Social Development Ministry warned Thursday of “catastrophic humanitarian consequences” threatening displaced Palestinians after most bakeries stopped operating amid Israeli restrictions on flour and essential food supplies entering the enclave.
“Continued restrictions on flour and supplies needed to operate bakeries amounted to an extension of the systematic starvation policy and the use of food as a weapon against civilians,” the ministry said.
“The restrictions are causing the collapse of the last line of food defense for vulnerable families, children and women who depend heavily on humanitarian aid and international relief organizations,” it added.
The ministry attributed the bakery shutdowns to Israel holding up flour shipments and preventing the entry of supplies needed to keep them operating, describing the restrictions as a violation of international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Hospitals in Gaza have relied heavily on generators to power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators, and dialysis machines since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023.
Gaza’s sole power plant stopped operating on Oct. 11, 2023, after running out of fuel, causing a complete electricity blackout, while power lines, cables, and distribution networks suffered widespread destruction during the war.
Damage to the electricity network has prevented hospitals from reconnecting to the grid, forcing them to depend on generators for prolonged periods.
The electricity crisis has continued despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, amid continued Israeli restrictions on supplies needed to rehabilitate Gaza’s health system.

"International reserves changed only slightly over the week, standing at $723.2 bln as of the end of October 16, 2026," the regulator said.

International reserves are highly liquid foreign assets held by the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They consist of foreign currency assets, special drawing rights, the reserve position in the International Monetary Fund, and monetary gold.
Western countries imposed sanctions on the Bank of Russia after Russia launched its special military operation in Ukraine. In addition to freezing Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, they banned all transactions related to the management of the Central Bank’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization, or body acting on behalf of or at the direction of the Central Bank.

Putin appoints 5 new government members in Russian Cabinet reshuffle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:49:52 UTC
22:49:52 KST

Elena Teslova
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday signed decrees appointing five new members of the government's Cabinet following their approval a day earlier by the lower chamber of parliament, the State Duma, the Kremlin said.
Under the decrees, Anton Siluanov was appointed deputy prime minister and finance minister, while Andrey Nikitin became deputy prime minister.
Irina Okladnikova was appointed deputy prime minister and chief of the government staff, Oleg Kozhemyako became deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District, and Dmitry Yadrov was appointed transport minister.
The reshuffle also introduced a new position of deputy prime minister and finance minister, increasing the number of deputy prime ministers from 10 to 11.
Siluanov, who has headed the Finance Ministry since December 2011, was relieved of his previous position as finance minister following his appointment to the new post.
Putin also dismissed Dmitry Grigorenko as deputy prime minister and chief of the government staff. Sberbank said its supervisory board would consider his appointment as the bank’s deputy chair on Nov. 10.
According to Sber, Grigorenko is expected to oversee strategic projects, including cooperation with the government and regional authorities on digitalization and the use of artificial intelligence in the public sector.
Yury Trutnev was also dismissed as deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District. Putin appointed him as a presidential aide.
Nikitin previously served as transport minister, a position he had held since July 2025. Yadrov headed the Federal Air Transport Agency, known as Rosaviatsiya, since September 2023.
Okladnikova previously served as first deputy finance minister, while Kozhemyako was governor of Primorsky Krai. During his career, he has also headed three other of Russia’s Far Eastern regions.
The newly restructured Cabinet is scheduled to hold its first meeting on Thursday, according to the government press service.
According to expert assessments, the reshuffle is aimed at strengthening the Cabinet’s economic bloc amid rising Western sanctions on Russia.

Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

22:48:46 KST

Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC)
The Defence Serious Crime Command investigates serious crime committed by people subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas. Investigations are carried out independently of the single Service chains of command.
Introduction
The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) investigates serious, complex and major crime where the person alleged to have committed the offence is subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas.
Anyone can report a crime to the Service Police. You do not need to be a member of the Armed Forces. If you are unsure whether an offence comes under Service Police jurisdiction, you can still contact the Service Police for advice.
The DSCC operates independently of the Royal Navy, Army and Royal Air Force chains of command. This means investigations and policing decisions are made independently of an individual’s Service chain of command.
Serious and complex crime
We investigate serious and complex crime where the Service Police has jurisdiction.
Investigations are conducted impartially and based on the evidence available. Victims and witnesses are kept informed about the progress of an investigation and the support available to them.
Major crime
We investigate major crime and other cases which require specialist investigative skills and resources.
Global policing
Our role extends beyond the UK. We investigate crime reported to have been committed by people subject to Service law overseas.
Investigations remain independent of the single Services’ chains of command regardless of where they take place.
Public protection and safeguarding
We work to protect vulnerable people and prevent harm.
Public protection and intelligence support the identification and management of risk and inform investigative activity.
Support for victims and witnesses
If you are a victim or witness of serious crime, committed by a person subject to service law, information and support is available to you throughout the Service Justice process.
The Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provides specialist support and information to victims and witnesses.
Location
The DSCC Headquarters is based at Southwick Park, Fareham. The DSCC also operates from locations across the UK and overseas.
Reporting a crime
If you or someone else are in immediate danger in the UK, or you need support right away, call 999.
Contact the Service Police
To report a crime, whether in the UK or overseas, or to speak to the Service Police in a non-emergency:
- call the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630
- attend or call a local Service Police station - the Service Police Crime Bureau will be able to provide location and contact details
Crimestoppers
If you are in the UK, you can contact Crimestoppers by:
- calling 0800 555 111 at any time of day or night
- completing the online information form on the Crimestoppers website – the form is completely secure and designed to protect your anonymity
If you are serving abroad, you must use the online information form to contact Crimestoppers. This will ensure your anonymity.
Fraud defence confidential hotline
Call the Fraud defence confidential hotline on 0800 161 3665 (UK) or +44 1480 44 638 (overseas).
Contact the DSCC

Southwick Park
1st Floor
Overlord Building
PO17 6EJ
Make a complaint
To make a complaint about the DSCC or VWCU, contact the Professional Standards Department at People-DSCC-PSDMailbox@mod.gov.uk

Please visit the Ministry of Defence homepage, where guidance can be found under ‘make an FOI request’.
