Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:18:36 UTC
22:18:36 KST

With less than two weeks to go before the congressional elections, Americans are nearly as gloomy about the economy as they were when the nation was emerging from the pandemic, and President Donald Trump's economic approval rating is hitting an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey.
Eight out of 10 Americans rate the economy as fair or poor, the highest number since December 2023 and one of several ominous signs for Republicans in the new polling data released Thursday that show why their candidates are facing an uphill battle in the midterm.
Downbeat views on the economy are most intense among Democrats and independents, but there's been a strong move toward economic pessimism even among Republicans in recent months. Overall, 63% of the public is pessimistic about the current state of the economy and the outlook, up 1 percentage point from the July survey. But that percentage now includes 35% of Republicans, up 6 points from July and the highest level of Republican pessimism of either of Trump's two terms.
"We got there not because of independents or Democrats getting more sour — it's because Republicans have," said Micah Roberts, partner at Public Opinion Strategies, the Republican pollster for the survey. "Since Trump has been president, [Republicans] have held on to a small margin saying that the current economy is either excellent or good. And now that has kind of broken and changed."
The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1%, found Americans preferring Democratic control of Congress by a 52% to 45% margin. The 7 percentage point Democratic edge represents a 3 percentage point gain for Democrats from the July survey.
The poll contained other foreboding signs for Republicans as well. It showed 72% of Democrats highly interested in the midterm election on Nov. 3, compared with just 62% of Republicans. Women are 10 percentage points more interested in the election than men, and they prefer Democratic control of Congress by 22 points. Independents prefer Democratic control by a wide 49% to 33% margin. And the majority of survey respondents said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans on many of the issues they singled out as their top concerns, including corruption and the cost of food and gas.
Read the full survey results here.
In the eight states with competitive Senate races, respondents prefer Democratic congressional control by 4 percentage points. Trump carried those eight states by a combined 10 points in the 2024 presidential election.
The survey shows "things moving either away from Republicans or toward Democrats, depending how you want to look at it, in a way that would make me very nervous if I was leading Republican campaigns leading into these last two weeks," said Jay Campbell, partner at Hart Associates, the Democratic pollster for the poll.
Despite the economic gloom, Trump's overall approval rating has remained stable, though at just 40% approving and 59% disapproving. His current net approval of -19 percentage points compares with -8 a year ago.
More striking is the sharp 9-point drop in the president's net economic approval rating from just the last survey in July. The president's economic approval fell to 34% from 38% in three months and disapproval rose to 65% from 60%. The net -31 economic approval is the lowest of either of Trump's two terms. The 65% disapproval rating is 1 percentage point higher than former President Joe Biden's worst showing and the highest for any president surveyed by CNBC going back to President Barack Obama.
Government corruption was identified as the top concern by 36% of respondents, and Democrats hold a 4-point lead on addressing the issue. On the cost of food and groceries, the second-most important issue, the Democratic lead widened to +16 from +7 in the July survey. Democrats also topped Republicans on protecting democracy as well as dealing with the high price of gas.
Among those most interested in the election are respondents who identify corruption and protecting democracy as top issues, and they prefer Democratic congressional control by wide margins.
Republicans continued to hold a strong advantage on border security and immigration, but the lead on immigration fell to +9 from +15. Democrats, meanwhile, are seen as better at handling the issues of jobs and unemployment and Iran, which flipped from +2 for Republicans to +5 for Democrats.
The public continued to be skeptical of the value of the Iran war. The survey found just 46% of the public believe the military action was worth it to disrupt development of Iran's nuclear capabilities, down from a 53% majority in April. And just 35% say the military action was worth it given the rise in the price of gasoline.
While the survey showed continued deep divisions by party, there was near unity on the corruption issue. Ninety-three percent said elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should not be allowed to personally own or trade stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. And 89% said companies owned by or invested in by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government.
While corruption was a top issue, prices are clearly top of mind for registered voters. Taken together, concern about the cost of food, gas and housing is the top concern for 57% of respondents. Eighty percent say prices are rising, up 5 percentage points from a year ago, with 55% saying they are rising faster than usual, also up 5 points. The cost of food actually eclipses gas as a greater concern in the survey 34% to 23%. It's a top worry among most major demographic groups but is most elevated among those making $30,000 or less and supporters of the agenda of Democratic Socialists of America. Yet it's also the top issue for those Republicans who don't count themselves as MAGA supporters.
Both pollsters were cautious about how extensive Democratic gains could be. Roberts from POS said it's a battle between "the map and momentum."
"There are several indications nationally that the electorate is tilting more toward Democrats … but the movement is also fairly concentrated, each party's base is consolidating, and a 'big change' is dependent on Democrats flipping a lot of districts and states that Trump won handily just two years ago," he said.
Campbell doesn't see a "realignment" election like in 1994 and 2008, saying, "This looks like a return to the mean—young voters and voters of color returning to the Democratic fold, bolstered by independents being fed up with Trumpenomics." He adds, "At no point did anyone expect that Democratic candidates would suddenly pull 15% of the Republican vote."

Interpol arrests over 1,400 suspects across Africa in $105M cybercrime crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:17:59 UTC
22:17:59 KST

Andrew Wasike 
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Interpol arrested at least 1,462 people across Africa in an operation which led to the recovery of $105 million in illicit funds, it said Thursday.
"Cybercrime networks operate without regard for borders, exploiting technology to target victims on an unprecedented scale," Interpol's Director of Cybercrime Neal Jetton said in a statement.
The criminal activities linked to these individual led to more than $385 million in losses, it said.
The operation, conducted between June 29 and Aug. 31 under the name Serengeti III, involved law enforcement agencies from 21 countries and resulted in the disruption of 10,909 malicious networks.
Nearly 66,000 victims identified
Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims of cybercriminal activities involving online investment scams, ransomware, digital extortion and fraudulent business communications.
In Uganda, police dismantled two international fraud operations and arrested 365 foreign nationals accused of targeting victims in Asia through elaborate investment and pension scams.
The suspects operated call centers where workers used prepared scripts, counterfeit investment websites and fraudulent trading platforms to convince victims, including pensioners, to invest in nonexistent financial opportunities.
In Angola, authorities shut down two illegal cryptocurrency mining facilities, arrested nine suspects and confiscated more than 2,000 mining devices.
Police also seized six unauthorized electrical installations, with the confiscated power infrastructure alone valued at more than $1 million.
In Nigeria, investigators arrested a suspect accused of operating a large-scale phishing scheme that collected software login credentials and approximately 2.1 million email addresses.
A separate Nigerian investigation uncovered an international investment fraud operation promoted through messaging applications, with investigators tracing more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of it moved through cryptocurrency transactions.
Authorities also disrupted fraudulent mobile lending operations in Tanzania, an online vehicle import scam in Gabon and a cybercrime network in the Republic of Congo, where 30 suspects were arrested.
 
AI being exploited by cybercriminals
Kenya was among the participating countries, alongside Ghana, South Africa, Rwanda, Cameroon, Zimbabwe and the United States.
Interpol said intelligence sharing and cooperation with technology companies helped investigators identify suspicious online infrastructure and trace criminal activity across borders.
The agency warned that artificial intelligence is increasingly being exploited by cybercriminals, allowing fraudsters to develop more sophisticated schemes and reach larger numbers of victims.
"Operation Serengeti III reinforces a clear message: while cybercrime is increasingly borderless, international cooperation remains one of the most effective tools for disrupting criminal networks, recovering criminal assets and protecting communities from digital harm," Jetton said.
Interpol said several investigations remain underway as authorities pursue additional suspects and examine digital evidence recovered during the operation.

Istanbul’s vanished historic mosque to rise again after 70 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:16:19 UTC
22:16:19 KST

Aise Humeyra Akgun
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Bostancilar Tabhanesi Mosque, also known as the Yedekciler Mosque, which disappeared from Istanbul’s historic skyline around 70 years ago, is being restored in the city’s Sarayburnu district.
Built during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent to serve sick palace gardeners, the mosque was located outside the sea walls of Topkapi Palace, between Sarayburnu and Ahirkapi. It was demolished during coastal road development works in the 1950s.
Restoration efforts led by Fatih Municipality aim to return the structure to Istanbul as part of the city’s historical and cultural heritage.
For centuries, the mosque served as a place of worship and formed part of daily life around the Ottoman palace. Its story also sheds light on the fate of historical buildings lost during Istanbul’s modernization.
Urban development projects carried out between 1956 and 1960, which altered Sarayburnu’s coastline and urban fabric, permanently transformed not only the area’s transport network but also its historic skyline.
Academic studies have also identified the mosque among the structures that disappeared from the coastline during this period and whose former locations have been traced through historical photographs.
 
‘Mosque had completely disappeared by 1950s, 1960s’
Bostancilar Tabhanesi Mosque was the only mosque located immediately outside Istanbul’s sea walls, Fatih Mayor Mehmet Ergun Turan told Anadolu.
“When crossing over to this side from Uskudar or by sea, this was the first mosque whose minaret came into view. However, the structure began falling into disrepair in the 1930s. Its minaret was demolished in the 1940s. By the 1950s and 1960s, when the coastal road was built, the mosque had completely disappeared,” he said.
“Today, we are delighted to restore this mosque to Istanbul’s skyline, perhaps nearly 100 years later. We have photographs of it in numerous documents, its location is marked on maps, and it appears in engravings.”
Underlining that they aimed to restore all lost works of ancestral heritage, he said: “We do not use public funds to build any of the mosques we restore. They are funded by donors. So far, we have completed the reconstruction of eight mosques. We are currently working on the restoration of 10 similar mosques.”

How TIME and Statista Determined America's Growth Leaders of 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:15:59 UTC
22:15:59 KST

The ranking "America’s Growth Leaders 2027" is the result of a comprehensive analysis conducted to identify the top performing publicly listed companies in the US. The analysis is based on three primary dimensions: Growth Performance, Financial Stability and Stock Performance.
Methodology
The first dimension, Growth Performance, was assessed using data from Statista’s revenue database, which contains company growth data for the last five years. To be considered for the evaluation the companies had to be headquartered in the USA, publicly traded and demonstrate strong revenue growth in the last five years. Relative growth and the number of years in which growth was achieved were considered in the evaluation.
The second dimension, Financial Stability, was investigated by analyzing the companies’ profitability as well as using classic metrics such as the Piotroski F-Score and Altman Z-Score, which refer to a company’s overall financial health and the probability to file for bankruptcy. Industry specific KPIs were utilized to portray financial stability of companies within the banking, insurance and REIT sector.
The third dimension, Stock Performance, was evaluated based on multiple KPIs, that underline the companies’ strengths as a stock investment. The analysis process focused on the average annual growth rate, recent returns, a comparison to the overall market and the stocks’ volatility for the past 5 years.
Once the data was collected and evaluated, it was consolidated and weighted within a scoring model. The scores of all three dimensions were added on an equal percentage basis to form the final ranking score of a maximum of 100 points. The 500 companies with the highest score were awarded as “America’s Growth Leaders 2027” by TIME and Statista.

Why is Libya-Turkey maritime deal causing a regional dispute?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:07:51 UTC
22:07:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Why is the Libya-Turkey maritime deal causing a regional dispute?
Libya's parliament has unanimously approved a controversial maritime agreement with Turkey, reversing years of opposition and reigniting a regional dispute over territorial waters, energy resources and political influence in the eastern Mediterranean.
The vote on Tuesday by Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives marked a significant shift in the country's divided political landscape, bringing rival authorities in Tripoli and Benghazi into agreement on a deal first signed in 2019.
But the decision has drawn strong objections from Egypt, Greece, Cyprus, the European Union and Israel, which have challenged the agreement's legitimacy and its implications for maritime sovereignty.
Turkey has rejected the criticism, insisting that the agreement is lawful and protects the rights of both countries.
The dispute goes beyond maritime boundaries, touching on competition for offshore gas, Turkey's growing influence in Libya and the shifting alliances of regional powers.
So what does the agreement involve, why has it caused such controversy, and what happens next?
What is the Libya-Turkey maritime agreement?
The agreement was signed on 27 November 2019 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Fayez al-Sarraj, then head of Libya's internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA).
It establishes maritime jurisdiction zones between Libya and Turkey across the eastern Mediterranean, giving both countries a basis to claim rights over areas believed to contain potentially valuable oil and gas resources.
The deal was signed during Libya's civil war, when Turkey was providing military support to the Tripoli-based government against an offensive by forces loyal to eastern commander Khalifa Haftar.
Turkey subsequently deployed drones and military advisers to help repel Haftar's assault on the capital.
At the time, Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives, which supported Haftar, rejected the agreement.
However, on Tuesday, the parliament unanimously voted to ratify the deal, reversing its previous position.
The decision was welcomed by Libya's Government of National Unity, Presidential Council and High Council of State, as well as Ankara.
Why are Egypt, Greece and the EU opposed?
The agreement has faced longstanding opposition from several eastern Mediterranean countries that argue it infringes on their maritime rights.
Greece maintains that Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coastlines that would justify the maritime boundary established under the deal.
Athens argues that the agreement disregards the maritime rights of Greek islands, including Crete, Rhodes and Karpathos.
The Greek foreign ministry has warned that it will take appropriate measures to defend the country's sovereign rights and has raised the issue with the UN Security Council.
Egypt has also rejected the ratification, arguing that the agreement encroaches on its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf.
Cairo's foreign ministry said the deal "constitutes a clear infringement upon Egypt's sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf", insisting that Libya's parliamentary approval has no legal consequences for Egypt.
The European Union has similarly reaffirmed its opposition.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa said in a joint statement that the agreement infringes on the sovereign rights of third countries and is incompatible with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
The bloc reiterated its support for Greece and Cyprus, both EU member states.
Turkey, which is not a party to UNCLOS, rejects these objections.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described the agreement as "entirely legitimate", while Omer Celik, spokesperson for the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), argued that it rested on strong legal foundations.
The dispute also has implications for the planned Great Sea Interconnector, a subsea electricity cable intended to connect Greece and Cyprus, and eventually Israel.
The project, estimated to cost approximately $2.1 billion, has already encountered delays linked to maritime disagreements between Greece and Turkey.
Why is the agreement important for oil and gas?
The eastern Mediterranean has become an increasingly important region for energy exploration, with competing maritime claims affecting access to potential offshore oil and gas reserves.
The Libya-Turkey agreement defines maritime economic zones and creates a framework for exploring natural resources, including hydrocarbons.
Neither country has announced proven reserves in the maritime areas covered by the deal.
However, a 2021 assessment by the US Geological Survey estimated that the wider eastern Mediterranean region contained an average of 286.2 trillion cubic feet of undiscovered, technically recoverable conventional natural gas resources.
Energy cooperation between Ankara and Tripoli has continued despite the political dispute.
In October 2022, Turkey and Libya's Government of National Unity signed a separate hydrocarbons cooperation agreement covering scientific, technical, legal and commercial collaboration.
In June 2025, Libya's National Oil Corporation and Turkish Petroleum signed a memorandum of understanding to conduct geological and geophysical studies in four offshore areas.
The arrangement included discussions over a two-dimensional seismic survey covering 10,000 kilometres.
For Libya, offshore exploration could attract investment and diversify energy revenues beyond its existing production of approximately 1.4 million barrels of oil per day and 72 million cubic metres of natural gas daily.
For Turkey, the deal could strengthen its position in the eastern Mediterranean energy sector and support efforts to reduce its dependence on imported energy.
However, the existence of a maritime agreement does not guarantee commercially viable discoveries or immediate production.
Why has eastern Libya changed its position?
The parliamentary reversal reflects significant changes in Libya's internal politics and Turkey's relations with the country's eastern leadership.
When the agreement was first signed, Ankara was supporting the Tripoli government against Haftar's forces.
Since then, Turkey has worked to improve relations with the eastern authorities, including Haftar and his son Saddam, the deputy commander of the Libyan National Army.
In July, Ankara and the eastern military leadership reportedly reached agreements involving military facilities, surveillance systems and training programmes.
The parliamentary vote also followed a change in leadership.
On 6 October, Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi replaced Aguila Saleh as speaker of the House of Representatives after more than 12 years.
Saleh, who was considered close to Cairo, had long resisted ratifying the agreement.
His successor, who previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee, oversaw its approval as one of his first major decisions.
Youssef Essaied, an academic and researcher specialising in oil and energy economics, told The New Arab that the timing of the vote was linked to broader political developments, including US-backed efforts to unify Libya's rival authorities.
He pointed to the role of Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump's adviser, in attempting to bring together the rival administrations in Tripoli and Benghazi.
The shift suggests that Ankara's influence now extends beyond its traditional allies in western Libya.
Does this mean Libya's rival authorities are uniting?
Not necessarily. The approval is significant because both Libya's rival centres of power now support the maritime agreement. However, the country's deeper political divisions remain unresolved.
Libya continues to have competing authorities, while disputes over control of the national budget, armed forces and electoral institutions remain central obstacles to political reunification.
The agreement therefore represents a notable area of cooperation between rival political camps rather than evidence of a comprehensive political settlement.
What happens next?
Despite parliamentary ratification, implementing the agreement could take years and face substantial legal, political and economic obstacles.
Essaied told The New Arab that the agreement was not an operational contract and that commercial energy production would require extensive geological surveys, exploration, financial assessments and negotiations.
He warned that Libya's political instability and unresolved maritime disputes could discourage international investment.
Companies may be reluctant to invest in offshore projects exposed to legal challenges from Greece or Egypt, particularly where competing sovereignty claims remain unresolved.
Essaied also highlighted concerns about corruption, weak oversight and the need for transparent management of Libya's energy resources.
Beyond the economic challenges, there is a risk that exploration activities in contested waters could provoke further tensions.
In August 2020, Turkey deployed the seismic survey vessel Oruç Reis to waters claimed by Greece, bringing the two NATO members close to military confrontation.
For now, the ratification represents a diplomatic gain for Ankara and a significant change in eastern Libya's position.

France reports first human detection of Shamonda virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:07:13 UTC
22:07:13 KST

France reports first human detection of Shamonda virus
French health authorities have reported the first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus in a severely immunocompromised patient who died in early October, according to a press release published by France’s Ministry of Agriculture, Agri-Food and Food Sovereignty, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The patient had been treated at the Hospices civils de Lyon for a serious illness. Clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations are in progress, the ministry said.
“Given the available knowledge about this virus, no health risk to the general population has been identified to date,” the ministry said.
The leading hypothesis is that the patient was infected through the bite of a Culicoïdes biting midge in eastern France, where the virus had circulated among animals during the spring and summer of 2026.
Clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are continuing in coordination with experts in human, animal and environmental health.
French health authorities have notified the World Health Organization (WHO) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), according to the press release.
What is the Shamonda virus?
The Shamonda virus is an Orthobunyavirus transmitted to animals by biting midges of the genus Culicoïdes, according to the France’s Ministry of Agriculture.
The virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and Southern Africa, as well as Japan.
In the summer of 2026, the virus was identified for the first time in Europe, including France, on cattle farms. Cattle are considered the main hosts among animal species that can be infected. Sporadic infections in small ruminants and equines were also identified in France during the summer, the ministry said.
The virus had previously been considered non-transmissible to humans. The infection reported in France is the first documented and reported detection of Shamonda virus in a human.
Despite decades of circulation in Africa and Asia, no human cases had been documented before this patient, according to the ministry.
The authorities described the case as exceptional because the patient was severely immunocompromised. Investigations are continuing, and the ministry reiterated that no health risk to the general population has been identified based on the knowledge currently available.
Earlier, Russian authorities reported on October 6 that no recent cases of plague had been recorded in the Irkutsk region and that around 200 people had been placed under quarantine. Qazinform News Agency has also explained the warning signs of plague, the dangers of its different forms, and when to seek medical attention.

Silence of Podgorica: how Montenegrins fight against Ukraine with impunity
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:06:00 EEST
22:06:00 KST

Silence of Podgorica: how Montenegrins fight against Ukraine with impunity
For some time now, videos and social media posts featuring men apparently from Montenegro serving in Russian military formations have been appearing in my feeds.
They wear Russian military uniforms, carry weapons, and display Serbian, Russian, and, somewhat surprisingly, Montenegrin flags on their uniforms.
In one photograph, a group of masked and armed men pose beside a sign reading "Donetsk".
Two of them have Montenegrin flags on their uniforms.
Their videos offer glimpses into everyday life. They talk about their military assignments, families, jobs, and connections to Montenegro.
Some discuss inquiries from people interested in joining the fighting. They seem remarkably open about their activities, showing their faces, weapons, and surroundings.
Their posts combined Serbian nationalist symbolism with support for Russia's war, presenting military service on Russia's side as part of a broader ideological commitment.
This was not unfamiliar rhetoric. Serbian ultranationalist movements have promoted precisely this understanding of the war for years.
Without government's response
On 23 September, I raised the issue in my regular column for the Montenegrin news portal Cafe del Montenegro (CdM). Rather than identifying individuals, I asked whether our security institutions knew who these people were, whether they were Montenegrin citizens, and whether anyone was investigating their activities.
One of the most relevant earlier reports appeared in the Montenegrin newspaper Vijesti in July 2025. According to Montenegro's National Security Agency (ANB), five Montenegrin citizens had fought alongside pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015.
One had been convicted, while the others reportedly had not returned to Montenegro. At the time of the newspaper's inquiry, ANB maintained that it had no confirmed information about Montenegrin citizens fighting in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Yet the material circulating on social media raised questions about whether that assessment still reflected the situation.
My column generated little public discussion, and I saw no significant institutional reaction. Last week, I therefore decided to formally notify Montenegro's judicial and security authorities.
I collected screenshots, video recordings, links to Instagram accounts, and specific posts showing armed men serving in Russian military formations. I submitted the information to the Supreme State Prosecutor's Office, the Special State Prosecutor's Office, the Police Directorate, and the National Security Agency.
I also approached Parliament's Committee on Security and Defense, requesting that it examine the broader institutional response.
My requests were to establish the identities and citizenship of the individuals concerned, investigate their possible participation in Russian military formations, examine indications of recruitment, and preserve relevant digital evidence.
Four days after my submissions, I had received no acknowledgment of receipt, no registration number, and no indication that the information had been formally recorded.
Threats on social media
Meanwhile, the accounts I had been monitoring began deleting their posts.
The photographs and videos that had prompted my investigation disappeared from public view. I cannot establish whether this was connected to my reports or resulted from unrelated decisions by the account holders.
Fortunately, I had preserved copies.
Then something considerably more disturbing occurred.
One of the accounts published images of pro-Ukrainian billboards I had personally designed following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Those billboards had been displayed at prominent locations across Montenegro for several months, including around Independence Day on 21 May.
The account also published what appeared to be threats against the author of the billboards, accompanied by the display of a machine gun at what appeared to be a military position.
I interpreted this as an indirect threat directed at me.
I cannot establish the author's intentions, but the timing and specific reference to my previous public activities were deeply unsettling.
The irony was difficult to miss. I had reported material suggesting possible participation in Russia's war against Ukraine.
That material subsequently disappeared, while I encountered content I perceived as intimidation. Meanwhile, the institutions I had contacted remained silent.
How mercenaries are being recruited
Montenegro has a complicated relationship with Russia. Historically close cultural and religious ties coexist with its strategic decision to join NATO in 2017, support Ukraine's territorial integrity, and align with European sanctions against Moscow.
The country's political environment nevertheless remains deeply divided over its relationship with Serbia, Russia, NATO and the European Union. Serbian nationalist political organisddations, pro-Russian media and religious and ideological networks sympathetic to Moscow continue to exercise considerable influence.
Within radical Serbian nationalist circles, Russia is portrayed not merely as a foreign ally but as the protector of Orthodox Christianity, Slavic civilisation and Serbian national interests.
Russia's war against Ukraine is frequently presented as a continuation of Serbia's historical confrontation with NATO and the West. In this narrative, fighting for Russia becomes an act of loyalty to a wider national and civilisational cause.
Serbian nationalist ideology has been used to mobilise volunteers for Russia's military campaigns since the beginning of the war in Donbas in 2014.
Appeals to Serbian-Russian brotherhood, the defense of Orthodoxy, resentment over NATO's 1999 intervention, and the unresolved Kosovo question have helped justify participation in a war taking place hundreds of kilometers from the Balkans.
The connection between Serbian nationalist ideology and recruitment is well documented. In October 2025, an investigation by the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) exposed recruitment networks operating through Telegram, where experienced Serbian fighters were attracting new volunteers from Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The investigation documented offers of military contracts, financial compensation, Russian citizenship and other benefits, alongside appeals to solidarity among Serbs fighting for Russia.
This combination of nationalist ideology, geopolitical resentment, religious identification, and financial incentives has created a recognizable framework for recruitment. It helps explain why people from the Western Balkans might view participation in Russia's war as something more than military employment.
Montenegro is especially exposed to this ideological influence
because Serbian nationalism operates across the border between Serbia and Montenegro through the Serbian Orthodox Church, a dominant religious organisation in the country, as well as through political movements, media and shared nationalist networks.
The accounts I documented displayed precisely this combination of Serbian nationalist identification, pro-Russian military symbolism and connections to Montenegro.
One Instagram biography contained the Russian-language descriptions "Russian Armed Forces" and "contract service," alongside the geographical reference "Budva–Donetsk". Another account published videos discussing inquiries from people interested in joining the fighting and criticising those motivated exclusively by financial compensation.
Montenegro has legislation addressing unlawful participation in foreign armed formations. Article 449b of its Criminal Code, introduced in 2015, also covers recruitment, organization, financing and related activities under the conditions established by law.
Its original adoption came during a period when public concern about foreign fighters was largely focused on Islamist radicalisation and departures to Syria and Iraq.
There is no reason why the authorities should be less attentive when the ideological motivation is Serbian ultranationalism and the destination is Russia's war in Ukraine. The law must be applied consistently, regardless of the political, ethnic or religious narratives invoked by those involved.
What makes the institutional silence particularly frustrating is
that Montenegro's security services have recently demonstrated their ability to act against Russian-linked activities.
On 9 October, Montenegrin authorities detained Mikhail Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defence Ministry press officer and founder of the influential pro-war information network Rybar, along with four other Russian nationals. The authorities subsequently ordered their expulsion on national security grounds.
I intend to continue documenting the available material and seeking answers.
I have preserved the relevant screenshots and recordings and remain prepared to provide them to competent authorities and investigative journalists.
Publications in the Expert Opinion section are not editorial articles and solely reflect the author's point of view

How to Fix South Korea-Ukraine Relations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

The transfer of two North Korean soldiers to South Korea was intended to be a quiet diplomatic success. Ukraine captured them in January 2025 while they were fighting for Russia in the Kursk region. After months of bilateral talks, they arrived in South Korea in mid-September. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer at the U.N. General Assembly on September 23. That started a spat that culminated in South Korea recalling its ambassador to Ukraine on October 8, its first protest recall since 2008.
Seoul is still demanding acknowledgment and an apology, while Kyiv considers the matter closed. On October 20, Seoul announced plans to withdraw roughly half its embassy personnel, citing what it described as Ukraine’s failure to take constructive steps to resolve the dispute.
Ukraine had a clear strategic interest in drawing the world’s attention to North Korea’s participation in Russia’s war. Instead, the episode exposed something else: a lack of sufficiently clear ground rules for managing the sensitive political consequences of South Korea-Ukraine cooperation.
Nearly a month after Zelenskyy’s revelation, the two governments still can’t agree on what they agreed on in terms of confidentiality. Seoul says confidentiality governed the talks from the start, even though no formal nondisclosure document was signed. It says internal records support that account and that it told Kyiv before Zelenskyy’s speech not to breach the understanding. Kyiv initially denied that a confidentiality agreement existed; Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later said the dispute stemmed from differing interpretations of the confidentiality requirements at various stages of the transfer.
Sybiha’s explanation points to the more useful lesson. An informal diplomatic understanding is not inherently defective, but whatever understandings and consultation process existed were not enough to prevent the disclosure dispute. Seoul had substantial reasons for discretion, including possible risks to the soldiers and their relatives who remain in North Korea. Ukraine had strong motives for publicity: North Korean troops are participating in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, and more are expected to arrive on the frontlines.
South Korea’s intelligence service has also told lawmakers that Ukraine originally requested secrecy, partly because the transfer of North Korean POWs could invite criticism that Ukraine had forgone a possible prisoner-exchange opportunity. If that account is correct, the incentives for secrecy and publicity shifted over time. Agreements that must survive shifting incentives need to be written down.
Of course, given the lack of clarity around confidentiality, Kyiv should have consulted with Seoul rather than proceeding with a public announcement. South Korea was justified in demanding an explanation and safeguards to prevent a recurrence. Ukraine later sent language that South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said contained an apology, but Seoul deemed it insufficient. Kyiv later declared the controversy closed.
For now, the two governments are stuck defending incompatible accounts of the past. What they should be doing is figuring out how to handle the next case.
The deeper problem is that the issues passing through their bilateral channels have evolved faster than the practices for handling them. To give an idea of the robustness – or lack thereof – of bilateral mechanisms before Russia’s invasion, the eighth round of foreign ministry political consultations in 2019 came after a seven-year gap and focused largely on conventional bilateral diplomacy.
As recently as September 16, a week before Zelenskyy’s speech, Ukrainian officials were discussing reviving those consultations. But the older platforms for discussion aren’t fit for purpose anymore. After North Korean troops entered Russia’s war, Zelenskyy and then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol agreed in October 2024 to intensify intelligence and expertise exchanges. Their foreign ministers have discussed battlefield conditions, North Korean prisoners, and Russia-North Korea military cooperation. In 2019, they were talking about “trade, investment, science, technology, and agriculture” – far less sensitive topics.
That means the same questions are likely to recur in South Korea-Ukraine relations. Ukrainian forces encounter North Korean troops and weapons in combat; South Korea wants to know what those encounters reveal about tactics, missile performance, battlefield adaptation, and Russian assistance. Future cases could involve another prisoner, captured equipment, debriefing materials, sanctions intelligence, or evidence of Russian technology transfers. Each could raise the same basic questions: what information is jointly sensitive, who may disclose it, and what happens if the other government objects?
Ukraine’s foreign minister has called the two countries “natural allies,” but Seoul has not adopted Kyiv’s strategic position toward Russia and continues to withhold direct lethal assistance. Seoul has its own reasons to preserve diplomatic space with Moscow and Pyongyang. The two governments do not need identical interests, but they do need ground rules for handling the information they are already sharing.
First, South Korea and Ukraine should define confidentiality in writing. For jointly handled information or information shared under agreed restrictions, the two governments should document what is protected, how long the restriction applies, and who may authorize disclosure. In the POW spat, Kyiv’s first response was to deny that any agreement existed; a written text would have clearly established the existence and scope of any commitment.
Second, an objection should trigger a defined escalation process. Advance notice was insufficient in the POW case. Kyiv warned that Zelenskyy would speak at the U.N. and might raise the case, and Seoul responded by objecting to public disclosure. But the speech went ahead, even though the disagreement remained unresolved. Future cases should require another round of consultation when either government objects to disclosure – first among the officials handling the issue and, if necessary, between senior political offices. That would not guarantee compromise, nor should it give either government an indefinite veto over the other’s public statements. It would move the disagreement to a point where compromise remains possible.
Third, South Korea and Ukraine need to give Russia-North Korea security cooperation a standing, quiet place within the bilateral relationship. If Seoul and Kyiv do revive their political consultations, those talks should include a regular security track to compare assessments of North Korean battlefield performance, weapons, Russian assistance, North Korean personnel returning from the war, and other lessons relevant to the Korean Peninsula. Their existing intelligence and expertise exchanges should feed into this track.
The point is continuity: officials should not have to rebuild priorities, contacts, and disclosure boundaries every time a new incident forces the issue. The same track should host the written terms and escalation contacts, so officials who know one another can try to resolve an objection before it reaches the leaders.
These principles could help resolve the current standoff. Seoul wants Ukraine to acknowledge that confidentiality was part of the talks; Kyiv maintains that there was never a firm agreement. A possible compromise would acknowledge that confidentiality was discussed, that the two sides understood its scope differently, and that future sensitive cases will use written terms and a defined consultation process before any disclosure. The first two elements broadly align with Sybiha’s own formula, so the statement would ask Kyiv to concede less than it may seem.
Ukraine could also express regret for any added risk to soldiers’ relatives. That would differ from the regret Kyiv’s Foreign Ministry has expressed so far, which focused on the dispute’s escalation into public criticism, and would give Seoul something closer to the acknowledgment it has sought. Such a statement would not require Seoul to abandon its account of the negotiations or Kyiv to admit a deliberate breach. Three European governments have reportedly offered to help ease tensions, suggesting that outside assistance may be available.
Even as Seoul reduces its diplomatic presence in Kyiv, it says humanitarian and reconstruction support for Ukraine will continue. Still, the expanding confrontation shows how difficult it can be to keep one grievance from overshadowing broader cooperation. Ground rules will not eliminate the larger differences between the two governments – Seoul’s interest in preserving room for dialogue with Pyongyang and Kyiv’s in exposing North Korea’s role in the war – and leaders can always ignore procedures. But a written agreement and clear procedures for handling disclosure will help head off similar cases before they erupt into public view.
Russia and North Korea have built a partnership suited to the war they are now fighting together. Seoul and Kyiv don’t need a formal alliance, but they do need better channels to handle the sensitive information that’s now a part of their partnership: the next prisoner, the next captured weapon, the next intelligence finding, and the next disagreement over who gets to tell the world.

Türkiye is seeking international partners for its planned second and third nuclear power plants. It has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRéalis, South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation and China’s State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building the facilities.

Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
Russia has handed over the remains of 252 Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict and received the bodies of 25 Russian troops in return, according to multiple reports.
The transfer reportedly took place on Thursday in Belarus near the Novaya Guta border crossing with Ukraine. Officials and media outlets in all three countries confirmed the details of the repatriations.
Footage from the scene shows monitors from the International Committee of the Red Cross overseeing the transfer.
The disparity in the number of bodies returned is typical, unlike prisoner-of-war swaps, which are generally conducted on an equal basis.
Pro-Kiev commentators have long argued that the imbalance does not reflect the actual ratio of battlefield casualties, as advancing Russian forces are better positioned to recover the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers. Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially publishes comprehensive figures for its military casualties. Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has cited death tolls that even pro-Kiev commentators consider implausibly low. In July, he claimed that “about 50,000” Ukrainian troops had been killed, down from the 55,000 deaths he reported in February.
Many Ukrainian battlefield casualties are classified as missing in action, which allows the cash-strapped government to defer compensation to the families of the fallen soldiers.
In summer 2025, Russian officials accused their Ukrainian counterparts of refusing to take hundreds of remains. The Ukrainians rejected the allegations, which the Russians said could be explained by a shortage of bodies in Kiev’s reserves and its concerns over the bad optics of a one-sided repatriation.
On three separate days in mid-June 2025, Russia unilaterally returned 1,200 bodies to Ukraine.

New nuclear sub design review finished ahead of schedule
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:48 BST
22:00:48 KST

The SSN-AUKUS Preliminary Design Review was conducted in June and concluded on 1 July, three months earlier than the September date it had been expected to meet, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for what reason the scheduled September 2026 Preliminary Design Review date for SSN-AUKUS was missed and what the new date was.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The SSN-AUKUS Preliminary Design Review was conducted in June 2026 and concluded on 1 July as part of the ongoing Detailed Design and Long Lead (D2L2) phase of the programme.”
A Preliminary Design Review on a submarine programme locks the overall configuration before detailed design work proceeds at scale, covering the hull form, the compartment arrangement, the propulsion and combat system integration and the weight and stability margins. Passing it allows long lead items to be ordered against a stable design, which matters on a programme where reactor components and large forgings have ordering lead times measured in years.
SSN-AUKUS is the replacement for the Astute class and the design Australia will also build, developed by BAE Systems at Barrow with Rolls-Royce providing the reactor plant and a trilateral arrangement governing the common elements. The boat is larger than Astute, carries vertical launch capacity and is intended to accommodate uncrewed systems alongside torpedoes and cruise missiles.
Detailed Design and Long Lead runs to 2028, and the programme is midway through it, with Pollard confirming in a separate answer the same day that the number of boats will be settled before the phase closes. Steel will be cut on the first British hull next year, a milestone this publication has covered as it approached.
Design reviews slipping to the right has been the pattern across large defence programmes for a generation, which is what prompted the question. Submarine design on this programme has run with a deliberately conservative schedule built around the Barrow drumbeat, and Dreadnought holds the priority on the same design and build resources.
Australia’s Osborne yard in South Australia will build to the same design, and the Australian Submarine Agency has its own review gates aligned to the British ones, so an early conclusion on the British side gives both partners margin before detailed design work peaks. Rolls-Royce in Derby is producing reactors for both classes from a doubled site.
Obese-Jecty’s question assumed a missed milestone and received a date that had already passed. The review closed on the first of July and the programme has been running on from it since.

How long does it take to feel forgiven by God? New study tracks Christians day by day after wrongdoing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:10 UTC
22:00:10 KST

After committing a moral wrongdoing, Christian adults who initially feel unforgiven by God tend to experience rapid increases in both repentance and feelings of divine forgiveness during the first few days, followed by a gradual leveling off over the next two weeks. New research published in Psychology of Religion and Spirituality suggests that actively turning back to God in repentance tends to precede the internal sense of being pardoned, which in turn was modestly linked to a renewed sense of spiritual closeness.
Reconciliation with God is the psychological and spiritual process of restoring relational harmony with the divine after a believer feels they have violated moral or religious standards. In Christian traditions, maintaining an ongoing, intimate bond with God (often referred to as communion) is a central life aim. Becoming aware of a personal sin or wrongdoing can disrupt that bond, creating inner unrest, guilt, and spiritual strain.
To repair that strain, believers often move through two connected processes: engaging in repentance and experiencing absolution. Repentance is an active, approach-oriented response where a person acknowledges their wrongdoing and turns back toward God rather than withdrawing in shame. Experiencing absolution is the receptive counterpart, characterized by an internal assurance that God is moving toward the believer with mercy and has wiped away their guilt.
While psychologists have extensively studied how people forgive one another or themselves, the psychological dynamics of divine forgiveness have received far less empirical attention. In the interpersonal realm, a 2010 longitudinal study demonstrated that forgiving another person after an offense tends to follow a curve of diminishing returns, rising rapidly in the immediate aftermath before gradually leveling off. More recently, scholars began looking at how spiritual repair unfolds over time; for instance, a 2024 two-study investigation indicated that actively seeking God’s pardon is an initial step that predicts whether a person actually feels forgiven six to twelve weeks later.
Other recent work has highlighted how everyday shifts in feeling pardoned by God can ripple outward into daily life. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in July 2026 found that on days when individuals felt more forgiven by God than usual, they were more forgiving and willing to make amends with their romantic partners.
The new study was conducted by Richard G. Cowden, a research scientist with the Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University (which coordinates the Global Forgiveness Movement) and the Department of Epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and Kaye V. Cook, dean of the School of Psychology and Human Services at Gordon College. Building on a theoretical framework that positions repentance and absolution within a broader system of spiritual closeness and struggle, the authors designed their study to track the exact day-by-day timeline of divine reconciliation immediately after a moral misstep.
“Most studies have taken a relatively faith-neutral approach to divine forgiveness,” Cowden and Cook told PsyPost. “That can be useful for identifying processes that may be shared across religious traditions, but it may overlook beliefs, practices, and relational meanings that are especially important within a particular faith tradition. In the Christian faith, for example, personal wrongdoing may be understood not only as moral failure but also as personal sin that can disrupt one’s sense of communion with God.”
“Our earlier work showed that many Christians may affirm that God is forgiving while still struggling to personally experience God’s forgiveness following specific instances of wrongdoing,” the researchers explained. “To explore how this experience unfolds over time, we focused on two related experiences within a Christian-sensitive understanding of experiencing reconciliation with God.”
“We wanted to know how these two processes unfold in the days after Christians become aware of a particular instance of wrongdoing,” Cowden and Cook added. “Does engaging in repentance with God tend to precede experiencing absolution from God, or vice versa? Do they develop together? And how are they related to a renewed sense of communion with God?”
To capture this process as it unfolded in real time, the researchers used an online research platform to screen 2,481 practicing Christian adults across the United States. They looked for participants who had committed a specific personal sin within the past 24 hours, could describe the event in writing, and currently felt little to no assurance that God had forgiven them for it. From this screening, 175 eligible adults enrolled in the main study and completed surveys on Days 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 following their wrongdoing.
“One distinctive feature of the study is that participants answered questions about the same instance of personal wrongdoing on Days 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 of the study,” Cowden and Cook noted. “This allowed us to examine change within each person rather than simply comparing people at one point in time.”
The sample ranged in age from 19 to 78, with an average age of about 42, and was roughly 59 percent female and 74 percent White. Participants represented a variety of Christian traditions, primarily identifying as Catholic (38 percent), nondenominational (23 percent), or Baptist (16 percent). The recent wrongdoings they described were most often rated as moderate in severity (40 percent), with the most common offenses involving sexual sin (22 percent), anger or resentment (21 percent), and dishonesty or lying (15 percent).
At each of the five survey waves, participants were reminded of the specific wrongdoing they had written about and rated their current levels of repentance and absolution on a 4-point scale. They also answered questions measuring their current sense of communion with God on a 5-point scale. On the first day, the researchers additionally measured participants’ general perception of God as benevolent versus strict, their baseline tendency to feel forgiven by God across life in general, and their divine struggles, meaning feelings of conflict, anger, or fear of punishment in their relationship with God since the incident.
When testing which factors predicted faster or slower change, the authors controlled for a wide range of background factors. These included age, sex, race, education, marital status, geographic region, frequency of prayer, Bible reading, and church attendance, as well as adverse childhood experiences, Big Five personality traits, and baseline anxiety and depression.
By comparing several mathematical growth models, the researchers found that both repentance and absolution followed a logarithmic trajectory over the 16-day window. In plain terms, both processes showed rapid increases during the first few days after the wrongdoing, followed by progressively smaller gains that tapered off over the second week. Although the two processes tended to rise in tandem across participants, they started at different levels and moved at different speeds.
On Day 1, average repentance scores were already relatively high at 2.52 out of 4, whereas feelings of absolution started lower at 1.90 out of 4. Over the 16 days, however, absolution increased at a steeper rate than repentance (growth estimates of 0.28 versus 0.19). At the same time, individual patterns varied considerably from person to person, and where a participant started on Day 1 had almost no bearing on how quickly their scores changed over the two weeks.
“Among Christians, taking appropriate responsibility for personal sin before God and experiencing God’s forgiveness are connected, but they are not the same thing,” the researchers said. “A Christian may acknowledge wrongdoing and turn toward God in repentance while still struggling to experience absolution from God.”
“On average, both engaging in repentance with God and experiencing absolution from God increased most quickly early in the study and then leveled off, but people differed quite substantially in how these experiences unfolded,” Cowden and Cook added. “The findings therefore do not establish a universal timetable for when a Christian should feel forgiven or how the process of experiencing divine forgiveness ought to unfold.”
When looking at what predicted faster spiritual recovery, the researchers found that ongoing relational experiences with God mattered more than abstract beliefs about God’s character. General perceptions of God as benevolent and a person’s general trait tendency to feel forgiven did not meaningfully alter the speed of change for either process. By contrast, participants who reported fewer divine struggles on Day 1 experienced steeper increases in both repentance (a growth rate of 0.23 for those with low struggles versus 0.15 for those with high struggles) and absolution (0.34 versus 0.22).
In addition, a stronger baseline sense of communion with God on Day 1 predicted a steeper rise in feeling absolved over the 16 days (a growth rate of 0.33 for those with high initial communion compared to 0.23 for those with low communion). This suggests that feeling close to God and free of spiritual conflict may provide a supportive foundation for internalizing forgiveness after a misstep.
“One particularly interesting finding was that the quality of participants’ lived relationship with God was more consistently associated with rates of change than their more general beliefs about God,” Cowden and Cook said. “An important contribution is showing why it helps to ask about both engaging in repentance with God and experiencing absolution from God. Simply asking, ‘Do you feel forgiven by God?’ misses whether someone is also acknowledging the wrongdoing and turning toward God, as well as how those experiences relate over time.”
The researchers also examined how fluctuations within an individual from one survey to the next predicted their responses on the very next survey. When a participant reported a higher-than-usual spike in repentance at one time point, they tended to report higher levels of absolution at the following assessment. The reverse was not true: spikes in feeling absolved did not predict subsequent changes in repentance.
Looking at downstream spiritual outcomes, experiencing a higher-than-usual increase in absolution at one wave modestly predicted a stronger sense of communion with God at the next wave. Fluctuations in repentance alone did not directly predict subsequent shifts in communion, and the link between absolution and later communion fell just short of statistical significance when both processes were analyzed together, likely because they overlap so closely. Taken together, the findings are consistent with a sequence in which repentance tends to come before feeling pardoned, and feeling pardoned tends to come before a renewed sense of closeness with God, though the evidence for that second step was weaker.
“These findings offer tentative evidence that experiencing absolution from God may precede a deeper sense of relational harmony with God, but leave unclear whether it has an association independent of engaging in repentance with God given that the two processes tended to unfold together,” the researchers explained. “One possible practical implication is that supporting Christians after personal sin may involve attending to both sides of experiencing reconciliation with God: taking wrongdoing seriously through engaging in repentance with God while also helping individuals more fully receive and internalize God’s forgiveness.”
There are a few caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study was not preregistered. Because the researchers intentionally selected Christian adults who still felt unforgiven up to 24 hours after their transgression, the findings may not apply to believers who immediately feel at peace with God after making a mistake. This screening approach may have also favored individuals who view God’s forgiveness as conditional upon human repentance rather than automatic, which could help explain why repentance preceded absolution in the timeline.
“We studied the psychological experience of reconciliation with God,” Cowden and Cook emphasized. “We could not determine whether God had forgiven someone, when God forgave them, or what theologically constitutes divine forgiveness.”
“The finding that engaging in repentance with God tended to precede experiencing absolution from God does not mean that Christians must earn God’s forgiveness through engaging in repentance with God,” the authors continued. “Rather, it describes the temporal ordering of two experiences. In some Christian understandings, forgiveness may be freely available while repentance helps a person become more able to receive or internalize it. Because this was an observational study, the temporal patterns are suggestive and should not be interpreted as demonstrating causality.”
In addition, about half of the participants committed their wrongdoing between 12 and 24 hours before the screener survey, and Day 1 repentance scores were already relatively high. Because some initial spiritual repair had likely already begun before the first measurement, future studies could track individuals even closer to the moment of a transgression. Finally, the participants who completed all five surveys attended church more frequently and had higher general perceptions of divine forgiveness than those who missed at least one survey, which raises the possibility of some attrition bias. Testing these patterns across other Christian traditions and other religions will also be important.
Looking ahead, the researchers are exploring practical ways to help believers navigate spiritual distress after moral missteps. “We have developed a freely available self-directed intervention to support Christians who are struggling to experience reconciliation with God following specific instances of personal wrongdoing, which is called the RECEIVE Forgiveness workbook,” Cowden and Cook told PsyPost. “We have completed a randomized controlled trial showing initial efficacy in a sample of adult Indonesian Christians, and we are looking to conduct further trials in other cultures and contexts.”
“More broadly, we are interested in understanding how engaging in repentance with God, experiencing absolution from God, and experiencing reconciliation with God differ across cultures and Christian traditions, particularly traditions that differ in beliefs and practices related to addressing personal wrongdoing and receiving divine forgiveness,” the researchers concluded. “We also want to understand why some Christians are able to internalize God’s forgiveness relatively readily after personal sin, whereas others remain caught in guilt, shame, divine struggle, or perceived distance from God. We are also interested in whether changes in reconciliation with God contribute over time to renewed communion with God and flourishing more broadly across different aspects of life.”
The study, “Temporal Dynamics of Experiencing Reconciliation With God After Personal Wrongdoing: An Incident-Anchored Longitudinal Study of U.S. Christian Adults,” was authored by Richard G. Cowden and Kaye V. Cook.

US, Israel develop plans for renewed strikes on Iran: Report

An Iranian actor wearing a mask depicting US President Donald Trump is seen inside a mock prison cell installed onto a street billboard at Tajrish Square in Tehran on October 21, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, with preparations advancing for a potential short but intensive campaign, The New York Times reported on Oct. 21.
Citing U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations, the newspaper reported that the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including flights over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers.
Potential targets could include Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenal and energy infrastructure, according to the report.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss possible new strikes, the newspaper reported.
Plans to target Iran’s nuclear program could include a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site, according to the Times.
The report said it is far from certain that Trump will approve the strikes, noting that he has repeatedly vetoed plans to return to major combat this year.
Earlier this month, Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections because the two sides were engaged in “productive discussions.”
A White House official told the Times that the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist,” adding that Trump is keeping all options on the table to ensure Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons.
The U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks in the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
A memorandum of understanding signed in June by the U.S. and Iran following Pakistani and Qatari mediation has since stalled amid disagreements, including over navigation in the strait.
