This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
A new CAR T cell therapy may be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.
In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.
For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”
Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”
But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.
Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”
The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.
Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.
But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.
For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”
No approved therapies
There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.
Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”
Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.
Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they start fighting one another, Piquet says. That’s when people can end up in a stuck position, leading to stiffness. But because everyone’s immune system is different, patients’ experiences with the disease can vary greatly.
For Tara Zier, a former dentist based in Maryland, SPS started with extreme neck pain, blood pressure spikes, shortness of breath and feelings of impending doom. While some people struggle with mobility, Zier’s difficulties include standing and extreme fatigue. When she holds herself upright, her muscles clamp down on her spine like it’s in a vise. “Have you ever had a charley horse in your calf?” she asks. “Imagine one in your whole body that stops you in your tracks.”
Zier and Montgomery-Haga went years before learning what was behind their symptoms. Their cases mystified doctors — Zier saw 13 specialists and visited the emergency room nine times before getting a diagnosis. When she finally found out she had SPS three years after her first symptoms, Zier says she felt validated, like medicine was confirming what she already knew: “Something’s wrong with me.”
Montgomery-Haga’s 2018 diagnosis put her “over the moon,” she says. For nearly four years, she had gotten sicker and sicker — but doctors couldn’t tell her why. She felt as if they were giving up on her. With the diagnosis, Montgomery-Haga not only learned that SPS existed, she says, “I was told it’s treatable.”
Current treatments include muscle relaxers, anti-seizure medications and Botox injections in body parts that feel especially stiff. Although these off-label therapies can address people’s symptoms, they’re “doing nothing to treat the underlying autoimmune disease,” Piquet says. And some can come with potent side effects, like mental fog.
Zier, who has tried multiple combinations of different meds, remembers frequently losing her train of thought. She has since tapered off all but one drug, a low dose of Valium. “The trade-off,” she says, “is pain.”
People with SPS can also receive intravenous infusions of healthy antibodies, a treatment called IVIG, to decrease muscle spasms and stiffness. Montgomery-Haga found it helpful but time-consuming. She’d go to the clinic every three weeks for an infusion, which could take up to six hours.
“The bottom line is there are no FDA-approved therapies for this disease,” Piquet says. Now, the one most likely to cross the finish line first is something no one would have expected even a few years ago, CAR T pioneer June says. If you told doctors that CAR T cell therapy was going to be FDA approved for an autoimmune disease, he says, “people would have laughed.”
To catch a killer
June may be best known for his work in cancer, but he’s been keenly following the progress in auto-immune therapy. His daughter, now in her 30s, was diagnosed with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis when she was 9 years old. For her, that’s meant over 20 years of treatment with drugs that bring a bundle of side effects, such as fatigue and risk of infections. “It would be much better to be cured,” he says.
In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and SPS, a person’s own antibodies attack tissues throughout the body, from blood vessels to cartilage to neurons. Wiping out these rogue antibodies can stop the attacks. But CAR T cell therapy doesn’t act on the antibodies themselves. It goes straight to the source, snuffing out the cellular factories that manufacture them.
Those antibody factories are known as B cells. To eliminate them, doctors recruit T cells, which act as the body’s security system and work together to hunt down and destroy problematic cells. In the lab, scientists fine-tune these hunters, outfitting them with a molecular homing device called a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. When infused back into patients’ bodies, the newly-engineered T cells can target the antibody factories directly — like a saboteur told exactly what to destroy.
A new treatment
The CAR T cell therapy Lynn Montgomery-Haga received wipes out B cells, including the ones likely driving her disease. Doctors hope this therapy “resets” her immune system, getting rid of harmful B cells and letting healthy new ones take their place.
“The secret behind CAR T cell therapy is that you completely deplete B cells in the body,” says Georg Schett, a rheumatologist at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. Temporarily wiping out a person’s B cells lets the body replace them with fresh, unproblematic ones, Schett says. He calls it an “immune reset.”
CAR T cell therapy got its start in the 2010s, when researchers used engineered T cells to target cancer. In 2017, the FDA approved the first CAR T cell therapies for two blood cancers, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and large B cell lymphoma. Soon after, scientists saw the first tantalizing hints that it might work for autoimmune diseases, too. In some cases, cancer patients with autoimmune disorders reported improvements in both conditions after treatment.
But most researchers didn’t think it could be that easy, Schett says. After all, autoimmune diseases were driven by a complex network of cell types. How could targeting just one of them work?
That thinking underwent a paradigm shift in 2021 when Schett and his team published the first major paper reporting a successful treatment with the therapy. The patient was a 20-year-old woman with a severe case of lupus, a complex, sometimes-fatal illness that can damage the kidneys and other organs. Within five weeks of CAR T cell therapy treatment, signs of her disease began to vanish.
Results like these were “unheard of,” says rheumatologist Maximilian Konig of Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. Lupus is extremely difficult to treat, and for decades, most drugs tested against it failed. No one had ever seen the kind of improvements that Schett’s patient experienced.
After the paper came out, “everybody was talking about it,” Konig says. Today, more than five years later, the woman’s lupus hasn’t returned, Schett says. “We consider this patient cured,” he says.
The woman’s response was no fluke. The following year, Schett’s team reported similar results in five more lupus patients. All went into remission after CAR T cell therapy.
This was the true tipping point, June says. “It’s rare, very rare, that you get such striking results.”
What followed was an explosion of research around the world. Scientists are now testing CAR T cell therapy in nearly a dozen autoimmune diseases linked to harmful B cells, including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and a connective-tissue disease known as systemic sclerosis.
Kyverna, the California-based company behind the SPS trial, is also running trials for neurological autoimmune conditions including generalized myasthenia gravis and progressive multiple sclerosis, or MS.
One reason using CAR T cell therapy for neurological conditions excites researchers is because of the cells’ potential to slip past the blood-brain barrier. That means they might be able to access pockets of smoldering inflammation inaccessible to other drugs, says neurologist Rebecca Farber of Columbia University.
That could be a huge help in diseases like MS, in which a person’s antibodies attack the protective sheaths around nerve cells, causing numbness, brain fog and difficulty walking. Still, Farber doubts that CAR T cell therapy could fix existing damage. “We’re not expecting it to repair the nervous system,” she says. But it’s possible the treatment could freeze the disease’s progress. Patients are already asking her team about future treatments.
For Piquet, who cares for roughly 100 people with SPS, Kyverna’s trial offered a compelling opportunity to help her patients. Montgomery-Haga cried when Piquet told her about the trial at one of their regular Zoom appointments. She recalls wondering, is this the treatment that “might help me be normal again?”
The good, the bad and the potentially ugly
Though Montgomery-Haga leapt at the chance to try Kyverna’s treatment, called miv-cel, CAR T cell therapy is no walk in the park. Before starting, doctors sit patients down to “talk about the good, the bad and the potentially ugly,” Piquet says.
That includes the rigorous prep work needed before people receive their engineered T cells. Patients must first get low-dose chemotherapy, which flushes T cells from the body and makes space for the new ones. Chemo can ambush the body with symptoms including hair thinning, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Treatment itself also carries risks. It destroys most B cells in the body — not just the ones that cause disease. That can lead to fever, inflammation and potentially risky infections. In Kyverna’s trial, for example, 15 percent of participants had severely low white blood cell counts after treatment. Such symptoms were expected, Piquet says, and were easily treated.
Other CAR T treatments seem to have fared far worse. In August, the pharmaceutical company Novartis paused clinical trials of its therapy, rap-cel, across a spectrum of autoimmune diseases after three patients died. Bristol Myers Squibb has also paused similar studies after some patients experienced neurological complications, according to the Wall Street Journal. Details of the incidents were slow to emerge and have set the field on edge. “It’s a tragedy,” Konig says. He calls such outcomes an important wake-up call.
But red flags in one trial don’t mean all CAR T products are dangerous, Konig says. That’s because many different designs and manufacturing processes exist, and scientists can’t always predict what will make one product toxic and another safe. Kyverna’s miv-cel, for instance, has been consistently well-tolerated in the more than 100 patients treated, a spokesperson for the company says.
CAR T cell therapies are transformative, Konig says. “They’re going to change the field — but there are risks.”
Another risk is that the once-vanquished disease will return. Doctors don’t know all the genetic and environmental conditions that trigger autoimmune disease. Some researchers wonder whether vulnerable individuals remain vulnerable, even after treatment. But because it often takes multiple insults for someone to tip into a state of disease, Scherlinger says, CAR T cell therapy could buy patients lots of time.
“Now I can”
After 10 days in the hospital for her treatment, Montgomery-Haga returned to recover at home. In the following months, she started to notice some changes. It was easier getting around the house, for one. And she felt her balance and stability improving. She can now kneel down to garden and clean without the days of recovery it used to require. “I can vacuum my house,” she says. “It seems so little, but now I can vacuum!”
Montgomery-Haga can even sit down “crisscross applesauce,” she says. “I couldn’t do that for, like, 10 years.”
Four months after the treatment, Piquet’s team tested Montgomery-Haga’s walking ability. In a hallway at University of Colorado Anschutz’s research building, the team marked out 25 feet with little orange cones. At one end stood Montgomery-Haga. At the other, Piquet watched behind a video camera. This time, Montgomery-Haga’s gait was smooth and her arms were down, not hovering out into the air to catch herself if she fell. “You could see that she was walking with a lot more confidence,” Piquet says.
The team saw similar results in other SPS patients. Some who had difficulty walking before treatment now wanted to run, Piquet says. “It’s incredible to just see those patients speeding down the hallway.” She remembers smiles, high fives and a sense of celebration in the air. Eight of 12 people who had used a walking aid for the initial test didn’t need one for the follow-up, Piquet reported at the American Academy of Neurology meeting in April.
In September, Kyverna reported the trial’s one-year results: Patients maintained mobility improvements, with a third completing their 25-foot walk about as fast as a healthy adult. Additionally, nearly all patients no longer rely on immuno-suppressive drugs to tamp down harmful immune activity. That’s good news because such drugs can bring all sorts of nasty side effects, like vomiting, bleeding and infections.
The results with SPS are “really something to celebrate,” June says. But only time and many more treatments will reveal how safe CAR T really is, he says.
That’s a concern for Zier, who says she wouldn’t feel comfortable trying the therapy at this point. Zier doesn’t know how she’d respond. She’s a single mother with two kids; even a rare side effect could disrupt her life in a way she may not be able to manage. And these days, she’s managing as well as she can. Zier is the founder and CEO of The Stiff Person Syndrome Research Foundation, which supports research for SPS treatments.
Kyverna is in the process of submitting miv-cel for FDA approval. The company is seeking priority review and hopes the treatment might be available to patients in 2027. If SPS is the first autoimmune disease to have an FDA-approved CAR T cell therapy, myasthenia gravis could be the second, says Warner Biddle, Kyverna’s CEO. What’s more, miv-cel also appeared to improve symptoms in six patients with severe cases of rheumatoid arthritis, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.
As for what’s next, the door is wide open. Some scientists are working to make off-the-shelf forms of CAR T that wouldn’t require personalized engineering. Others are trying to reprogram T cells directly inside people’s bodies, rather than in the lab. Still others are trying to make T cells that target only the B cells responsible for disease. In the future, doctors might use such drugs to help patients avoid the cumbersome treatment process that Montgomery-Haga endured.
Montgomery-Haga’s own future looks far different than what she had imagined a few years ago. In 2026, she took a trip to Washington, D.C., to see the monuments. Now she’d like to visit Paris, Scotland and Ireland, too.
For so many years, Montgomery-Haga has looked at trips and activities — and even household chores — that most people take for granted, thinking, “Man, I wish I could do that,” she says. “Now I can.”

Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.
As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.
That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.
“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.
According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.
It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.
It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.
The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.
The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.
Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”
OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.
It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.
“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”
The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.
Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.
Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.
“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”
Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.
“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”
When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.
“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”
Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.

Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
Unknown

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.
Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.
During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.
📍 New Delhi | Premier @donaldtusk spotkał się z Premierem Indii @narendramodi. pic.twitter.com/Y9HPLQsvf4
— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026
Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.
Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.
“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.
Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”
Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.
Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.
“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”
However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals.
The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".
"Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw

According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility.
To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.
Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.
The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors.
Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations.
Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War.
“In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”.
The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.

Sanctions-hit ICC wins top EU rights prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

A general view of the exterior of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, March 12, 2025. (AP File Photo)
Facing U.S. sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Oct. 22 awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick,” furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as U.N. rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month, a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful,” arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the U.S. sanctions, which will come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.

Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:46:24 UTC
21:46:24 KST

Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Southern California - Health Sciences
- Summary:
- A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.
- Share:
Millions of Americans take fish oil supplements in hopes of protecting their memory and keeping their brains healthy as they age. These products have become a major business, with Americans spending more than $1 billion each year on supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids. These essential nutrients help build and maintain the connections between brain cells that support memory, learning, and other cognitive functions.
But a new study suggests that getting more omega-3s into the brain through supplements may not provide the protection many people expect.
Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC found that even when high doses of omega-3s successfully reached the brain, they did not produce measurable improvements in memory, thinking abilities, or protection against brain shrinkage.
The findings, published in eBioMedicine, come from a two-year clinical trial involving older adults considered to be at increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Despite taking omega-3 supplements daily, participants showed no significant cognitive advantage over those who received a placebo.
"We all wish there was a silver bullet for preventing Alzheimer's, but our findings showed that fish oil supplements do not appear to protect brain health," said Hussein Naji Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health and lead investigator of the study. "While omega-3s play an important role in forming brain cell connections needed for cognition, our results do not support fish oil supplements as a preventive measure against Alzheimer's."
A Two-Year Study Tests Fish Oil's Brain Benefits
To investigate whether omega-3 supplements could protect the aging brain, researchers enrolled 365 adults between the ages of 55 and 80. All participants rarely ate fish, a major dietary source of omega-3 fatty acids, and were considered at elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease.
Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4, a gene variant associated with a substantially higher risk of developing Alzheimer's later in life. Although having this variant does not mean someone will necessarily develop the disease, it is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's.
Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily fish oil supplement or a placebo, an inactive treatment used for comparison. The supplements provided 2,000 mg of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid that is especially important for the brain.
DHA is a major component of brain cell membranes, helping maintain the structure and function of neurons. It also supports communication between nerve cells, making it an important nutrient for normal brain activity.
The study was double-blind, meaning neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving the active supplement during the trial. This approach helps reduce bias and makes it easier to determine whether any observed benefits are actually caused by the treatment.
Omega-3 Levels Rose, but Memory Did Not Improve
Before evaluating whether the supplements improved brain health, researchers needed to answer a fundamental question: Were the omega-3 fatty acids actually reaching the brain?
To find out, they measured DHA concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord. Examining this fluid can provide information about substances entering and circulating within the central nervous system.
After six months, DHA levels in the cerebrospinal fluid had increased by an average of 17% among participants taking the supplements. This provided evidence that the omega-3 fatty acids were reaching their intended destination.
However, getting DHA into the central nervous system was only part of the goal. The more important question was whether those higher levels would translate into better brain health.
Researchers assessed participants' memory and other cognitive abilities at the beginning of the trial and again after two years. Despite the increase in DHA, those taking fish oil performed no better on the cognitive tests than participants receiving the placebo.
Brain imaging revealed similarly disappointing results.
The supplements did not prevent shrinkage of the hippocampus, a region deep within the brain that plays a central role in forming and organizing memories. The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable to changes associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease, making its size an important indicator researchers use when studying brain health.
Taken together, the results suggest that simply increasing DHA availability in the brain is not enough to produce measurable cognitive benefits in this group of older adults.
Why Fish Oil Supplements May Work Differently Than Food
The unexpected findings have raised a new question for researchers: If omega-3s can reach the brain, why don't higher levels necessarily improve its function?
Yassine and his colleagues are now investigating how the brain absorbs, processes, and uses these nutrients. Their earlier research suggests that omega-3s may be more beneficial when consumed as part of a broader dietary pattern rather than taken in isolation as a supplement.
One possibility involves the Mediterranean-style diet, which emphasizes foods such as fish, vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and olive oil. This eating pattern naturally supplies omega-3 fatty acids alongside other nutrients and has been associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
The researchers suspect that the combination of nutrients in a balanced diet, along with an individual's overall health, may influence how effectively omega-3s support the brain.
"We're focused on better understanding how the brain processes omega-3s and whether factors, such as poor health, dietary pattern, genetic risk and age, may change the brain's ability to effectively absorb and use omega-3s," said Yassine. "We are working to develop medications that may help the brain better utilize these nutrients to preserve cognitive function."
Understanding these differences could eventually help scientists identify why certain people might respond better to omega-3s than others and whether new treatments could improve the brain's ability to benefit from these essential fats.
Importantly, the findings do not mean omega-3 fatty acids are unnecessary or that eating fish offers no health benefits. Instead, they indicate that taking high-dose DHA supplements alone did not provide measurable protection against cognitive decline or hippocampal shrinkage in the population studied.
Healthy Habits Remain Key to Alzheimer's Prevention
Although the trial focused specifically on fish oil supplements, the researchers emphasize that protecting brain health requires a much broader approach.
Rather than relying on a single supplement, they recommend maintaining healthy habits throughout life, including regular physical activity, sufficient high-quality sleep, and a nutritious, balanced diet.
These behaviors support overall health and may help reduce factors associated with cognitive decline. Physical exercise, for example, promotes cardiovascular health and blood flow, while sleep plays an important role in memory formation and normal brain maintenance.
"Staying healthy throughout life remains the most powerful tool we have for reducing Alzheimer's risk, including regular exercise, quality sleep and a balanced diet," said Yassine. "Living a healthy lifestyle is the brain's equivalent of getting regular car maintenance and high-quality oil changes. The brain is more likely to lose greater function if health issues in other parts of the body go unaddressed, in the same way that car engines stop working if regular maintenance is skipped."
While these lifestyle factors were not directly tested in the trial, the researchers believe they offer a more promising foundation for long-term brain health than depending on fish oil supplements alone.
The results also highlight an important distinction: A nutrient can be essential for healthy brain function without providing additional protection when consumed in large doses as a supplement. Understanding why that happens may open new avenues for research into Alzheimer's prevention and the nutritional needs of the aging brain.
The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, grant numbers RF1AG076124, R01AG055770, R01AG067063, R01AG054434, R21AG056518, P30AG066530 and R01AG054434 and the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation, grant number GC-201711-2014197.

France confirms first Shamonda virus infection in a human death of 'severely immunocompromised' individual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

21:46:00 KST

France confirms first human infection of Shamonda livestock virus
October 22, 2026
French health officials on Thursday confirmed that they had detected the Shamonda virus in a human — who died early this month — in what they say was the first-ever case of a human contracting the livestock disease.
"Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," said France's Ministries of Health and of Agriculture in a joint statement.
"No health risk to the general public identified at this time," they said, adding that the human infection appeared to be, "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient."
The World Health Organization (WHO) said the virus was unlikely to spread.
"Based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this is an isolated human case and it is unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time," WHO told Reuters in a statement.
How is Shamonda virus transmitted?
First identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the insect-borne Shamonda virus is a variant of the Orthobunyavirus, a genus that contains 138 species, and primarily affects livestock, particularly cattle.
It is transmitted by culicoides, or biting midges.
The virus has been detected in animals in Africa and Japan for years and has been spreading across Europe this year.
Until now, it was not thought to be transmissible to humans.
According to a press statement on the Ministry of Agriculture's webpage, "At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the case resulted from vector-borne transmission via the bite of a culicoid midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was reported to be circulating among animals in the spring and summer of 2026."
The ministry said biological, clinical and epidemiological investigations are being carried out by experts in human, animal and environmental health, adding that authorities at the WHO and European Center for Disease Control had been notified of the incident.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Thursday that they had launched attacks against Saudi Arabia's Defense Ministry in Riyadh, Saudi Aramco oil facilities in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, where Saudi authorities confirmed two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack Wednesday evening.
The claims mark another escalation in the Houthis' campaign against Saudi military, aviation and energy infrastructure, as fighting intensifies between the group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.
Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed attacks on the Defense Ministry in Riyadh or Aramco facilities in Yanbu, and there was no independent verification that either site had been hit.
The kingdom has, however, confirmed the deadly attack on Dammam airport, although its civil aviation authority did not specify the weapon used or identify those responsible in its initial statements.
The Houthi announcement comes after a series of deadly strikes against Saudi airports and oil facilities in recent weeks, prompting Washington to withdraw some government personnel from the kingdom and Britain to announce additional military assistance.
Two killed at Dammam airport, two more at Saudi oil field
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said Thursday that the death toll from Wednesday evening's attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam had risen to two after an additional fatality was confirmed.
The victims were identified as a Saudi citizen and an Indian national living in the kingdom. Eight other people were injured, including a Saudi citizen and seven foreign nationals from India, Yemen, Bangladesh and Nepal.
The injuries ranged from minor to serious, with the wounded receiving treatment at several hospitals.
The authority said the airport had sustained material damage, but that operations had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal. Officials continued assessing the damage and coordinating security measures to protect passengers and airport employees.
The airport, located in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province near the Persian Gulf, had already been targeted during the recent escalation.
In a separate incident Wednesday, two foreign workers were killed and two others injured after Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone attempting to strike a processing facility at Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field.
According to the Saudi Energy Ministry, falling debris from the interception sparked a fire in a contractor's vehicle outside the facility's perimeter.
The two fatalities were a Filipino and a Nepali national, while the injured were Pakistani and Indian citizens.
The ministry said operations at the oil field were unaffected.

Every Moment Is a Life: Gaza in the Time of Genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:44:30 UTC
21:44:30 KST

“To write stories in the heart of an unfolding genocide is to draw ink from the depths of your own heart,” writes Huzama Habayeb, the Arabic editor of Every Moment Is a Life. “To read stories of genocide, while the slaughter rages relentlessly, unceasingly, means that—at the very least—your heart will be crushed.”
She is right. Reading this anthology is a crushing experience. More than once the book has to be put down, and each time the reader picks it up again, because the people who wrote it deserve to be heard to the end.
The collection was compiled by the Palestinian American novelist Susan Abulhawa. It brings together heart-rending true stories by eighteen young writers from Gaza. They wrote in Arabic while Israel’s bombs fell around them, and the book is published in a bilingual Arabic-English edition by Atria/One Signal Publishers, an imprint of Simon & Schuster. All proceeds go to the contributors in Gaza and to the Palestine Writes Literature Festival.
The origin of this compilation has its roots in two journeys made by Abulhawa to Gaza in 2024. On both visits, she crossed into the besieged enclave with as many bags of aid as she could carry. While there, she collected stories from women recovering in hospital. Many wept as they described what they had seen, heard and felt, often exploring those details aloud for the first time, and the sessions became what Abulhawa calls “a kind of Indigenous therapy”.
Two friends, Majeda Saqqa and Maha elRa’ee, asked Abulhawa to run a writing workshop for young people at the Culture and Free Thought Association (CFTA). Every writer included in the collection had been displaced and had lost people they loved. Struck by the writers’ talent for storytelling, Abulhawa decided that the most useful thing she could do was to help Palestinians in Gaza tell their story of living through genocide.
READ: What is life like for Palestinians with disabilities during Israel’s genocide?
The workshops were held on the beach and in the CFTA courtyard, under the constant buzz of Israeli drones. The stories that emerged draw the reader into the heart of their reality: ordinary human moments, buying bread, mending a shoe, sharing a meal, set against what Abulhawa describes as “the first live-streamed genocide”.
Habayeb spent more than three months editing the Arabic stories with the writers entirely over WhatsApp. She calls it an “emotional odyssey”. She would send her notes and then wait, sometimes for days, fearing the worst. One reply read: “I buried my wife yesterday; please bear with me until the mourning period ends.” Another writer apologised for the delay because the family had fled to the sea and still had nowhere to sleep. A third hoped to send the final version at the weekend, adding: “my brother was martyred.”
In Every Moment Is a Life, the story that gives the book its title, Rizq Ahmad describes four families sharing a makeshift nylon shack, which they carry from one so-called “safe zone” to another. They nickname it “The Four Coupons”, after their food-aid vouchers.
There is no mirror in the shack. Anyone wanting to check their appearance turns to Ahmad’s mother, Hanan, who finds them beautiful whatever they look like. Ahmad’s trousers barely stay up, even with a belt wrapped around his waist. As he leaves the shack, his brother calls after him: “Don’t stay out long! I need the pants later.”
Even in these impossible times, Ahmad finds warmth in the family’s life together. They still gather for meals around a rickety table or on a mat on the ground, and lunch turns into lively political debate. They laugh as they squeeze together to sleep, sharing whatever food they have.
“A new intimacy formed among us—no blame, no complaints, no regret,” he writes. “Maybe because every minute of life is a whole life, one that cannot be taken for granted.”
In Ma’rouf, Ghassan Salam tells the story of Sami, who spends a night hiding in a greenhouse after fleeing Khan Younis. Across an open field, a baby is crying in his dead mother’s arms. Sami fears that trying to reach the child will get them both killed. For hours he listens, blaming himself each time the crying fades. After daybreak, he reaches the boy and carries him to safety.
Sami cares for the child as his own and names him Ma’rouf, which means “known”. Later, he finds papers showing that the boy’s real name is Adam and returns him to his uncle. When the uncle’s house is bombed, killing the rest of the family, Sami rushes to the scene and recognises the boy, alive but injured, as medics rescue the casualties.
BOOK REVIEW: How to Sell a Genocide: The Media’s Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza
“I recognized him by his little toes. I had kissed them so many times.”
An aunt later takes the child north to Jabalia. Sitting in a café some time afterwards, Sami watches breaking news of an Israeli air strike there and sees the boy among the bodies in the street. “Ma’rouf was gone. And I was left behind.”
In Khadija Abu-Lebdeh’s The Decision, the narrator, Ghada, has lost both her parents in the genocide and watched her brother Qasim die of illness. She clings to his bed, the last trace of their life together, its headboard covered in his drawings. But the family has burned everything else they own for cooking, and her older brother asks her to give it up.
“Are memories of our departed loved ones more important than those still living?”
Ghada lets it go and watches the fire take Qasim’s drawings. One charred scrap of paper drifts into her lap with just two words left on it: “the living”.
In Coffee by Old Blue, Muhammad Mu’ammar’s narrator takes his morning coffee to the sea he calls Old Blue, his friend since childhood. He had always dreamed of living by the sea. Now he does, in a tent, after being driven from his home and helping gather the remains of thirty or more relatives.
“My dream came true at last, but not as I dreamed.”
The narrator and his wife used to sit there together. Now he sits alone, having buried her with his own hands. “I do not dare call her name now.” He has come back to the sea, he says, “to become like you. An old blue soul. An immensity of silence.”
Umbilical Cord by Maysa Salama is a love story told in sign language. At an Israeli checkpoint, soldiers order the men to fall back. The husband is deaf, and his wife translates the orders for him with her hands. Before they part, he writes their three-year-old daughter’s name on his wife’s hand and ties the girl’s wrist to her mother’s with rope, like a new umbilical cord that might deliver the child safely into the world a second time.
The mother walks on, still bleeding after giving birth only days earlier, the newborn crying at her chest, until she faints. When she comes round, her daughter tells her: “Mama, you were going to fly away if I hadn’t held on to you.”
Not every writer offers the steadfastness the world expects of Palestinians. In For Gaza to Leave Us Something, Nebal Al-Najjar describes being displaced four times and her wish to escape Gaza’s destruction. Abulhawa praises her for daring to write what a world that expects Palestinians to be superheroes may not want to hear.
No review can do justice to this book. It is not one to be read once and put away. In the hospital in Gaza, the women who first spoke of what they had seen, heard and felt found comfort in being listened to. Every Moment Is a Life asks the same of its readers: to sit with these writers, to take in every detail of their loss, and to grieve with them. It is painful, but it can also be healing, the kind of “Indigenous therapy” Abulhawa found among those women. It is a book to be read, and read again.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:44:23 BST
21:44:23 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.
Attending a misconduct hearing
Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).
Please note the following conditions of entry:
- any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)
- any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time
- priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)
- any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing
- members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session
- no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing
- any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing
- where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment
- no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time
- no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient
- we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible
- members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted
If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.
Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.
Private hearings
Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.
Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:
- all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private
- a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing
- specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness
- specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome
If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.

ISTANBUL, October 22. /TASS/. No overproduction of liquefied natural gas (LNG) is on the market, CEO of the Russian gas producer Novatek Leonid Mikhelson said at the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
"Sometimes there is even heard an opinion at present that LNG overproduction will be in coming years. As long as Novatek deals with LNG, we always hear this phrase. Nevertheless, the actual market practice shows that no overproduction takes place. If the price goes down, LNG simply starts substituting coal. On the other hand, LNG shortage may occur. It is because of that we see gas price spikes. This is what is taking place in the current year," Mikhelson said.

Bulgaria’s Growth to Reach 3.5% in 2027, EY Forecasts
Bulgaria’s economy is expected to grow by 2.9% in 2026 and accelerate to 3.5% in 2027 before slowing to 3% in 2028, according to an October economic outlook
Iliaana Yotova and Kiril Valchev lead Bulgaria’s presidential election race with 43.4% support, ahead of Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev at 28.9%, according to a nationally representative survey by polling agency Myara for the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR).
The poll, reflecting voter preferences in mid-October, puts Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin in third place with 10.2%. Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva receive 3.1%, followed by Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov with 2.9%, and Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova with 1.9%.
“These figures represent a snapshot of electoral sentiment as of mid-October. There are hundreds of thousands of eligible Bulgarian voters who have yet to make up their minds,” the sociologists said.
Other candidates, including Georgi Dimov, Ivaylo Simeonov, Rosen Milenov, Volen Siderov, Rumyana Chenalova and Ivanka Tsvetanova-Petkova, have declared support levels of around 1%. Myara said it was too early to determine how much support they would ultimately attract. A further 2.5% of respondents said they would select the option “I do not support anyone.”
Based on respondents’ stated intentions, projected voter turnout stands at 39.4%, apparently slightly above the level recorded in previous surveys.
Myara’s team also found that more than three-quarters of Bulgaria’s adult population consider the person holding the presidency important. The vice president’s role is also significant to respondents, although to a lesser degree, with 57.4% attaching importance to the office. Meanwhile, 67.8% support expanding the powers of Bulgaria’s presidential institution.
“It appears that the presidency, as an institution, is significant to Bulgarian citizens. For more than three-quarters of the country's adult population, the individual holding the office of president is of substantial importance. The same applies to the office of the vice president, though to a lesser extent - 57.4%. Furthermore, a majority of 67.8% agree that the powers of the presidential institution in Bulgaria should be expanded. Naturally, these figures may reflect a certain automatic response, yet this in itself is revealing of broader public instincts,” the Myara team commented.
The poll also examined BNR’s role in informing voters during the presidential campaign. More than one-third of adult Bulgarians rely on the public broadcaster to some extent for information about the candidates and their platforms.
For 8.2% of respondents, BNR is their main source of information about the presidential candidates, while 13% regard it as one of their primary sources. Nearly 15% use the broadcaster as an additional source. Another 9.5% rely on BNR for general news and current affairs, but not specifically for coverage of the presidential election.
More than one-third of respondents said they do not follow BNR during the campaign, while the remaining participants were unable to assess the broadcaster’s role or declined to answer.
The survey was conducted between October 8 and October 19, 2026, through face-to-face tablet-assisted interviews with 1,009 adult Bulgarian citizens. The maximum margin of error is ±3.1% at a 50% share. One percent of the total sample, rather than of the electorate, represents approximately 53,000 people.

WHO was not told that Nigeria's Ebola patient travelled to Congo, official says

Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says
DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday.
Nigeria reported the case, its first Ebola case in more than a decade, on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May and has since become the fastest-spreading on record.
Ugandan authorities have said the woman who fell ill in Nigeria had travelled to eastern Congo before transiting through Uganda. But the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman had travelled to Congo.
The woman "has been in a private clinic in Abuja for around a week with symptoms. She is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda around two weeks ago," said an emailed statement from the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
"Her husband is in isolation; he has not shown any symptoms. He was travelling with his wife when she is believed to have contracted Ebola."
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters late on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases.
"That's a fact. If we did, as has happened before, we'd be the first to say," he said.
Asked whether the Ugandan government had proof that the woman had travelled to Congo, Kasujja said, "Like what? A passport stamp? Without infringing on the patient’s rights?"
AFRICA CDC, WHO SAY NO INFORMATION THAT PATIENT WENT TO CONGO
Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention official Wessam Mankoula said on Thursday that Nigeria and Uganda were sharing information to establish the patient's movements and possible source of exposure.
"So far, there is no validated information (that) this case traveled to DRC (Democratic Republic of Congo)," Mankoula told an online press conference.
The WHO said information it had received about the case did not include travel outside Uganda.
"The facts which we have received is that the patient returned to Abuja on October 3, being away from September 16 in Uganda," WHO representative to Nigeria Pavel Ursu told the press conference.
Ursu said the focus in Nigeria was now on containing the viral infection and that the patient remained hospitalised, with her biochemical markers improving.
Jean Kaseya, Africa CDC director, told Reuters on Wednesday that the patient had been on a two-week holiday in Uganda.
Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.
One issue under investigation is which health facilities the woman visited in Abuja after the onset of her symptoms and before her hospitalisation 48 hours later, Otim said.
KENYA TRACES ALL CONTACTS OF FIRST CASE
Separately, a senior Kenyan health official said authorities there had now traced all 135 contacts of the country's first Ebola case, which was confirmed on October 6 and after which a further eight cases have been reported.
"We have been able to account for them 100%," health ministry director-general Patrick Amoth said. He said the last contact to be traced was a Ugandan citizen who had arrived in Kenya in early October on the same flight as the index patient but exited by road via the Namanga border post with Tanzania, which meant it took more time to find him.
Africa CDC is investigating whether the Kenyan case may have come into contact with the patient being treated in Nigeria, as both travelled from Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day, Mankoula said. Transmission between the two was one of the possible scenarios being examined, he said.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people across the four African countries that have reported cases, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS

US university professor warns China seeks to divide Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:40:15 UTC
21:40:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Texas’ University of St. Thomas Professor Yeh Yao-yuan (葉耀元) warned Thursday that China is interfering in elections to deepen political divisions and undermine public trust in democracy, CNA reported.
Speaking at a National Taiwan University Hospital forum on election interference and democratic defense, Yeh said Beijing's main goal was not necessarily to help particular candidates win or lose elections. Instead, he said, China seeks to turn voters against one another and undermine confidence in democracy.
Yeh said China uses disinformation and online influence campaigns to reinforce existing political divisions. He warned that growing distrust could deepen disagreements over national defense and relations with China, leaving Taiwan more vulnerable to outside pressure.
China's interference should not be judged solely by election results, the professor said. The greater concern, Yeh said, is whether people with different political views become increasingly unwilling to accept one another.
The National Security Bureau has also warned of growing Chinese information campaigns ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections. The bureau said that it identified about 2.5 million items of contentious online content from January to September, up from 1.69 million during the same period last year, per Liberty Times.
China uses fake accounts, AI-generated videos, and coordinated online campaigns to spread misleading information, the bureau said. Social media and online forums were among the main platforms used for such activity.
Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥), the bureau's director-general, said that Chinese election interference was becoming more targeted. He identified six methods, namely illegal campaign funding, subsidized trips to China, discounted flights, disinformation, illegal betting, and cyberattacks, per SETN.
Yeh called for a foreign agents law to address activities carried out on behalf of foreign governments. He said stronger legal measures were needed to protect Taiwan's democracy from outside interference.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), director of the University of Taipei's Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience, warned that China could step up election interference. He said Beijing would use the results to assess its efforts to influence Taiwan ahead of the Chinese Communist Party's 21st National Congress in 2027, per CTS News.
Hung said Greater Taipei could be major targets because of their political importance and competitive elections. The director warned that foreign funding and local networks could also be used to influence election campaigns.
He urged national security, law enforcement, and election agencies to share more intelligence and investigate suspicious foreign funding and coordinated online campaigns. Hung also called for tougher penalties to ensure elections are decided by voters.

Macron targets Trump over French riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:38:28 UTC
