Commission criticises University of Zurich senior leaders
The Zurich Cantonal Council’s Supervisory Commission for Education and Health (ABG) has criticised the university, or rather its management. It claims that there are people in management positions who are not suited to the role.
Normally, the approval of an annual report in the Cantonal Council is a mere formality. The relevant committee, which prepares the matter, recommends that Parliament approve the annual report. In the vast majority of cases, this is then carried out without a hitch.
Not so this year. In its statement on Thursday, the ABG criticised the University of Zurich quite sharply. The criticism goes so far that it intends to withhold its approval of the annual report.
The reason, according to the ABG, is the university’s “outdated approach to leadership”. Greater attention must be paid to leadership skills when selecting and training senior staff. The ABG, in particular, sees major shortcomings among the university’s senior management.
‘Concerned’ about ongoing problems
The Commission has also criticised the collaboration between the University and the University Hospital. The Commission is “concerned” about the ongoing problems. While the exchange of information between the two institutions has improved significantly, according to the ABG, when it comes to dual appointments – that is, people who work at both the university and the university hospital – it is difficult to find joint solutions when problems arise.
+ Tribunal rules Zurich university unfairly dismissed professor
The Commission is also dissatisfied with the exchange of information between itself and the university. The members of the Cantonal Council are calling for this to become more transparent. This is necessary for the ABG to effectively exercise its supervisory role and verify whether the university is actually implementing its recommendations.
The Cantonal Council will debate the University of Zurich’s annual report at one of its forthcoming meetings. These issues will also be raised during the debate.

Who are the Americans detained in Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

20:36:33 KST

Who are the Americans detained in Russia?
Oct 22 - Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a retired US schoolteacher, from prison on Wednesday, as Moscow and Washington held a new round of talks about settling the war in Ukraine.
At least nine publicly identified Americans are believed to remain imprisoned in Russia, although the full number may be higher.
While Hubbard was in prison, the US State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained, a status that placed his case under a dedicated US government process for securing his release. Other imprisoned Americans lack that designation, potentially reducing the scope for efforts to free them.
Here are details on some of the cases:
ALEKSANDR ANTONOV
A US-Russian-Ukrainian citizen, Antonov was detained at passport control in Russia in spring 2025 after travelling to attend to business in Russian-controlled Crimea and family in Ukraine.
He was later sentenced to six years in a prison colony on charges of inciting terrorism and extremism, based on pro-Ukrainian comments posted online. He pleaded guilty.
CHUCK ZIMMERMAN
Zimmerman, a US Navy veteran, was intercepted in June 2025 by the Russian Navy as he sailed on the Black Sea during a round-the-world sailing trip, according to his family. He was charged with arms smuggling after a rifle was found on board his boat.
He was sentenced in late 2025 to five years in prison, according to a verdict published in January.
GORDON BLACK
An active duty US Army staff sergeant formerly based in South Korea, Black was detained in May 2024 in Russia's Far East on suspicion of stealing money from his Russian girlfriend.
A court found Black guilty of stealing 10,000 roubles ($123) from the woman and threatening to kill her, sentencing him to three years and nine months in prison. The sentence was reduced by seven months in 2025, following an appeal.
US officials have said the Army has stopped paying Black's wages and may prosecute him for violating its rules if he returns to the US.
DANIEL JOSEPH SCHNEIDER
A court in Kaliningrad region sentenced Schneider to six years in prison in September 2024 for kidnapping his own son, after he tried to leave Russia with the 4-year-old without permission from the boy's mother.
Schneider was detained near Poland by Russia's border service while trying to cross the border in a forest swamp, the court said.
MICHAEL TRAVIS LEAKE
A musician and former US serviceman, Leake was sentenced to 13 years in prison in July 2024 on drug-related charges.
Leake pleaded not guilty following his arrest in June 2023.
ROBERT ROMANOV WOODLAND
A US citizen adopted from Russia as a child, Woodland had moved back to Russia and was working as an English teacher when he was arrested on charges of attempting to sell drugs.
He was sentenced in July 2024 to 12 years and six months in prison. His lawyer said Woodland had partially admitted guilt. In 2025, a court reduced his sentence to nine years and six months.
EUGENE SPECTOR
A Russian-born US citizen and former pharmaceutical executive, Spector was convicted of espionage in a closed trial and sentenced in late 2024 to 15 years in a penal colony. He was first arrested in 2020 on bribery charges.
Before his arrest, Spector served as chairman of the board of Medpolymerprom Group, a company specialising in cancer drugs, state media said. He had pleaded guilty to helping bribe an assistant to a former Russian deputy prime minister. It was not clear how he pleaded to the espionage charge.
DAVID BARNES
Barnes was sentenced by a Russian court in February 2024 to 21 years on charges of abusing his two sons in the United States. Barnes, who had been involved in a custody dispute with his Russian ex-wife, denied all the charges.
The allegations had previously been investigated in Texas, where authorities found no grounds to charge him. In 2025, a court increased his sentence by six months.
ANDRE KHACHATOORIAN
An Armenian-American from Los Angeles, Khachatoorian was sentenced to eight years in prison in 2023 for arms smuggling. He was arrested in 2021, while travelling from California to Armenia via Moscow, after a firearm was found in his luggage.
Khachatoorian said that his firearm was legally owned in the US, and that he was tricked into applying for a Russian visa at the airport, and removed from the transit zone, where he could be arrested under Russian law. REUTERS

Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

20:35:43 KST

Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Thirty websites were taken offline and three men arrested earlier this week in connection to sites that sold counterfeit pills that led to the deaths of three people.
The suspects – a 35-year-old man from Kwintsheul, a 39-year-old man from Rotterdam and a 66-year-old male from The Hague – are suspected of “offering, selling and supplying illegal drugs”, including sedatives, sleeping pills and painkillers like oxycodone, which contained extremely potent synthetic opioids known as nitazenes.
Nitazenes can be many times stronger than morphine and more lethal than fentanyl.
Police say the victims bought the prescription-only pills on websites Slaappillen.net or regionapp.net shortly before they died, and are holding the suspects responsible for running them.
Whack-a-mole
Even though Slaappillen.net was taken down last year, police say the men continued to sell the counterfeit drugs through other websites, which kept popping up as soon as others were taken down.
But according to police, this time they not only took the web shops offline, but confiscated the servers they ran on.
“We have taken down the entire technology behind the websites,” Ron van Brussel told NOS. He is responsible for tackling serious organized crime at the National Investigation and Interventions Unit. “This makes it more difficult to make a restart.”
Both the servers and data have been seized for investigation, and more arrests have not been ruled out.
The police searches were carried out in five locations, including homes and a storage box in The Hague. Crypto wallets, cash and valuables were seized.
With this week’s arrests, police say the main players from the group are now in custody. But, they add, the sale of illegal drugs is far from over.
“There are several criminal groups that keep these types of sites online,” said Van Brussel.

France’s Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest
PARIS, Oct 22 - French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that "illegitimate" protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed "seditious" ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend's riots and looting.
Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organised by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to go ahead but could be diverted along alternative routes to protect businesses.
"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said.
His comments came as authorities across France prepared for fresh protests following some of the country's worst urban unrest in years.
All protests planned for Saturday in Lyon, France's second-largest city, have been banned, local authorities said. Yet fresh demonstrations are already taking shape ahead of what officials fear could be another volatile weekend.
France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, the anti-establishment force that emerged in 2018, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.
Businesses in central Paris have begun boarding up their shop windows in case of violence. Luxury goods group Hermes said it had stepped up security measures at its French stores.
Elsewhere, authorities in the northern city of Orleans were bracing for potential unrest as the far-right National Rally was due to hold an annual meeting and unions and left-wing groups planned demonstrations.
A student protest called for Thursday in Paris was banned, though metro stations in central Paris were nonetheless shuttered by transit authorities in anticipation of unauthorised gatherings.
France was rocked on October 17 by some of its worst urban unrest in years, on the fringes of nationwide protests, exposing the depth of public anger and raising questions about the security services' ability to keep order.
Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on Limoges city hall, French officials and media said.
A third consecutive night of local curfews passed without major incidents in areas affected by the violence, offering the government some respite ahead of the weekend.
The unrest has laid bare a deeper malaise in France, where soaring energy costs, pressure on household budgets and concerns over deteriorating public services have fuelled growing frustration among workers and younger people.
The French political class has also descended into a bitter blame game, with the government accusing far-left political groups of stoking the unrest.
Highlighting investor unease, yields on France's 10-year government bonds rose above those on equivalent US Treasuries on Thursday for the first time since 2013. REUTERS

Late detection in Nigeria raises alarm as Ebola spreads across Africa
- Nigeria’s first Ebola case in over a decade was tested 13 days after falling ill, raising fears about delayed detection and harder contact tracing.
- The case is part of a wider outbreak across four African countries, with Africa CDC saying “no one is safe today” and warning the risk may spread further.
- Officials are still checking whether the patient was infected in Uganda or Congo, while experts say the outbreak is “far from over” and screening may be failing.
AI generated
ABUJA/DAKAR – Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in over a decade was not tested for the disease until 13 days after falling ill, officials said, a delay that raises questions about the authorities’ ability to contain an outbreak already spanning four African nations.
The epidemic, first detected 3,000km away in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May, is the second largest on record and had already hit Uganda and Kenya before the Nigerian case was confirmed on Oct 20 – the widest known spread on the continent.
The patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, arrived in Nigeria’s capital Abuja, a major travel hub, on Oct 3, after a two-week holiday in Uganda, Jean Kaseya, the head of Africa’s top public health body, told Reuters.
‘No one is safe today’
She fell ill three days later, Kaseya said, citing the account given by the Nigerian authorities. Initially suspecting malaria, she sought treatment at several facilities before being tested for Ebola on Oct 19.
“When we identified at-risk countries, Nigeria was not part of this list. It is now,” said Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
That list would have to be redrawn and North and Southern Africa could also be at risk, he added. “We need to consider that no one is safe today.”
The late detection would complicate efforts to trace people the woman may have infected, he said. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone showing symptoms.
“We need to identify all the contacts... this one is a little bit tough for someone who took almost two weeks without being tested, coming into contact with health workers, family members, friends,” Kaseya said.
Nigeria has identified 44 contacts so far, a number Kaseya and other Ebola experts said was bound to rise.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, for which there is no vaccine or treatment. It has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 in Congo alone.
‘This is far from over’
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the country Ebola-free in August.
The Ugandan authorities have said the woman who fell ill in Nigeria had travelled to eastern Congo before transiting through Uganda.
Nigerian officials said they have not confirmed that.
“Our case did not have confirmed travel to DRC. So we presume it was likely picked (up) in Uganda,” Nigeria’s Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told state TV on Oct 20.
Kaseya said the Africa CDC was seeking clarification from both countries and from the woman herself.
Whether she was in Congo is an important question, said Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist who sits on the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee.
If she was, it would reinforce worries about the efficacy of screening at borders and in airports, she said. If not, it would raise the possibility that she somehow got infected in Uganda.
“Either way, it confirms that this is far from over,” she said.
Nigerian officials have pointed to the country’s handling of a case during the West African outbreak in 2014-2016, saying the country is fully prepared to deal with the disease.
But Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician and co-chair of a Group of Seven committee for investment in global health, noted that the first case to reach Nigeria in that outbreak involved a patient who flew from Liberia and was immediately hospitalised.
“It’s a very different scenario,” she said. REUTERS

A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
A revolutionary laser-powered microscope could reveal a hidden world inside human cells, opening an entirely new window into life and disease.
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Researchers have developed a revolutionary microscope that uses an incredibly powerful laser to make previously invisible cellular structures easier to see. The technology dramatically improves image clarity, allowing scientists to examine small proteins that conventional electron microscopes struggle to capture. It could eventually reveal how tiny molecular machines interact inside cells, providing an unprecedented look at the hidden workings of life.
- Share:
Almost a century ago, a breakthrough in microscopy gave scientists an entirely new way to examine the inside of cells. Known as phase contrast, the technique made previously faint or nearly invisible cellular structures much easier to distinguish. Its importance was recognized with a Nobel Prize in 1953.
Now, physicists at the University of California, Berkeley, have brought that same principle to electron microscopy, a technology capable of magnifying objects roughly 10,000 times more than conventional light microscopes.
The researchers have developed a device called a laser phase plate that could significantly improve cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM). This powerful imaging method has transformed the study of protein structures and helped speed up drug discovery over the past decade. Even so, it has a major limitation: Most human proteins are so small that obtaining clear images of them remains extremely difficult.
The new laser technology could help overcome that obstacle, potentially allowing scientists to image proteins as small as one-third the size of those that challenge current microscopes.
An even greater impact could come from improvements to cryoelectron tomography (cryo-ET). This newer approach combines images captured from multiple angles to construct three-dimensional views of proteins and other molecules. Unlike techniques that study isolated molecules in a solution, cryo-ET can reveal how proteins are arranged and interact within their natural cellular surroundings.
“Cryo-EM has become the new, fastest-growing method for resolving the structure of biological macromolecules, and cryo-ET is expected to show how these molecules work together in their natural, cellular context,” said Holger Müller, a UC Berkeley professor of physics and faculty scientist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory who led the development effort. “But because of signal-to-noise limitations, the majority of human and animal proteins are too small to be analyzed by these methods. The increase in signal-to-noise ratio provided by this laser phase plate is expected to overcome these important limitations.”
An Extraordinary Laser Reveals Hidden Cellular Structures
The breakthrough relies on what the researchers describe as the world's most intense focused continuous-wave laser. Rather than simply illuminating a specimen, the laser interacts directly with the microscope's electron beam, altering its phase to increase image contrast.
This adjustment makes it easier to distinguish small molecules, including hemoglobin, from their surroundings. It could also improve the visibility of structures inside cells, such as the nucleus and mitochondria.
“With cryo-ET, we're looking at small, very complicated cellular material that’s incredibly crowded inside the cell,” said Bridget Carragher, founding technical director of imaging at Biohub in Redwood City, California. “It’s like a forest of trees, and you’re trying to find one leaf on one tree in there. Cryo-ET needs a dramatic step forward in contrast, so we can start to see what's going on inside the cell. That's what the laser phase plate promises to give us.”
With financial support from Biohub, Müller acquired an advanced cryo-EM instrument and equipped it with the new laser phase plate. He named the resulting microscope Theia, after the ancient Greek Titaness associated with light and radiance.
Meanwhile, Carragher is directing the construction of a related microscope at Biohub's imaging facility in Redwood City. Her team's instrument uses two lasers rather than one, building on theoretical research conducted by Müller and his collaborators.
The two laser beams are arranged at right angles to one another and each operates at approximately half the power. This configuration helps prevent components from burning out while also reducing optical distortions that could interfere with image quality.
Both research teams are working with Thermo Fisher Scientific, the leading manufacturer of cryo-EM instruments.
“Theia is the Formula 1 microscope,” Müller said. “It has extra electron optics that give it better resolution than the standard cryo-EM, even without the laser. With the addition of the laser phase plate, we hope that it really becomes the world's best instrument overall.”
The Berkeley team's latest images and technical findings are presented in the journal Science. Details of Biohub's two-laser design are available in a recently posted preprint.
How a Nobel Prize-Winning Discovery Changed Microscopy
To understand why the new technology matters, it helps to look at a longstanding challenge in biological imaging.
Because plant and animal cells consist largely of water, they are relatively transparent when viewed under an ordinary light microscope. Although this transparency might seem beneficial, it creates a problem. Small cellular structures, including mitochondria and nuclei, scatter very little light and therefore appear only slightly darker than the surrounding material.
Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem by adding stains to create greater contrast. However, staining also kills the cells.
In 1930, Dutch physicist Frits Zernike realized that light passing through biological material changes in more ways than simply becoming brighter or dimmer. When light scatters inside a cell, it also experiences a tiny delay that changes its phase, or the timing of its wave peaks.
Although the human eye cannot directly detect this phase shift, Zernike discovered that it could be converted into a visible difference in brightness. By shifting the phase of the unscattered light by 90 degrees, he made subtle cellular features stand out more clearly against their background when the light reached the viewer's eye.
This innovation became the foundation of phase-contrast microscopy, earning Zernike the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.
By the early 1940s, scientists had already recognized how useful phase contrast was for studying cells. They began exploring whether the same idea might improve electron microscopes, which use electrons instead of light to examine structures as small as individual proteins.
Unfortunately, early attempts encountered serious technical difficulties. Devices designed to alter the phase of electron beams often weakened the beam too much, introduced image instability, or reduced resolution.
A possible solution emerged in 2010, when Müller and Robert Glaeser, now a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of molecular and cell biology, proposed using an intense laser to produce the necessary phase shift. Their approach offered a way to improve contrast without sacrificing electron beam intensity.
Overcoming the Limits of Electron Microscopy
Glaeser has played an important role in developing cryo-EM, which offers a potentially simpler way to determine molecular structures than traditional X-ray crystallography.
X-ray crystallography requires researchers to grow crystals of the molecules they want to study and obtain access to an intense X-ray source. Cryo-EM avoids the need to crystallize molecules, but it presents difficulties of its own.
One of the biggest problems is that an electron beam can heat and eventually damage the specimen being examined. This limits how much information can be collected and how detailed the resulting images can become. Covering specimens with metal can reduce damage and improve contrast, but it also makes the images less sharp.
During the 1960s, researchers began investigating whether freezing biological samples could protect them from radiation damage.
Glaeser demonstrated that cooling specimens helped preserve them during imaging. He also proposed using a less intense electron beam to examine thousands of frozen molecules at once, further limiting the damage.
Because the molecules would be positioned at different angles, computers could analyze and combine their images to reconstruct a highly detailed molecular structure.
These advances helped establish the foundations of modern cryo-EM, whose developers received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. During their acceptance remarks, the Nobel laureates acknowledged Glaeser's contributions.
The Nobel Committee praised the technology, explaining that cryo-EM “both simplifies and improves the imaging of biomolecules. This method has moved biochemistry into a new era.”
A 15-Year Quest to Harness an Exceptionally Powerful Laser
Turning the laser phase plate concept into working technology required years of engineering.
Following their 2010 proposal, Müller spent 15 years pursuing the idea, with part of the research supported by the National Institutes of Health.
The first major challenge was generating an extraordinarily intense laser beam concentrated into a tiny area. The researchers needed enough light intensity to change the phase of an electron beam by 90 degrees.
It took a decade to develop the necessary system.
Their solution was to confine a continuous laser beam inside a spherical chamber lined with mirrors. As the light repeatedly reflected through the cavity more than 10,000 times, its intensity increased dramatically while the beam became focused into an extremely small spot.
“It’s 75 kilowatts focused to a few microns,” Müller said. “That’s more powerful than what you use for welding. It's more power than a military laser. It builds up the brightest continuous laser focus ever.”
The team first demonstrated that the concept worked by installing a laser phase plate in one of Glaeser's older electron microscopes.
Additional funding from Biohub then made it possible to acquire a customized, state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Krios cryo-EM microscope and modify it to accommodate the laser technology.
In their latest research, the scientists tested the upgraded microscope using six different samples that varied in size and preparation method. The laser consistently improved image resolution, with particularly important gains for specimens that are difficult to image using standard methods.
“For the most challenging cases — small particles, bad specimens — the laser produces a very considerable advantage,” Müller said.
Sharper Images of Proteins Once Too Small to Study
To demonstrate the new microscope's capabilities, the researchers reconstructed images of two different proteins.
The first was aldolase, a protein found in muscle that modern cryo-EM systems can already image relatively easily. The second was hemoglobin, the protein responsible for carrying oxygen through the bloodstream.
Hemoglobin is much smaller and lies near the lower size limit of proteins that conventional cryo-EM instruments can reliably analyze.
Using the laser phase plate, the researchers improved the resolution of both protein structures. The improvement was especially pronounced for hemoglobin, highlighting the technology's potential to overcome the difficulties associated with smaller molecules.
“The bottom line is, if you have a large protein and a really good sample — a fresh one or one frozen without bubbles, for example — you may not need the phase plate to get a single, high-quality image. But for a small protein and a bad sample, laser-on is best,” Müller said. “This could fill an enormous gap in our knowledge of protein structures that can’t be crystallized or are too small for today’s cryo-EM. And it will be revolutionary for cryo-ET.”
Protein mass is typically expressed in daltons, a unit named after English chemist John Dalton. One dalton is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Conventional cryo-EM struggles to image proteins smaller than approximately 70 kilodaltons. That limitation is particularly significant because proteins below this threshold account for about 90% of the human proteome, the complete collection of proteins produced by the human body.
With the laser phase plate, researchers can now image proteins as small as 50 kilodaltons, although doing so remains challenging. Such proteins are even smaller than hemoglobin.
The Next Goal Is to Reveal Even Smaller Proteins
Müller believes the technology could eventually allow scientists to study proteins as small as 17 kilodaltons (the size of the protein myoglobin).
Reaching that goal may require another improvement: using a tightly focused electron beam rather than the defocused beam currently needed to produce sufficient contrast without the laser phase plate.
According to Müller, the laser system should make it possible to obtain contrast directly from phase changes in a focused electron beam.
If successful, this adjustment could double the contrast and signal-to-noise ratio again, adding to the improvement already achieved with the laser phase plate.
Such progress could make it possible to study a far larger proportion of the body's proteins and provide unprecedented insight into how they interact within the complex environment of cells.
“This technology is a step function change for biology,” said Stephani Otte, Biohub’s Vice President of Imaging Science. “We are going to be able to see how molecular machines operate inside the living cell, in context, for the first time. What was once invisible will become visible — and that changes everything about how we understand disease.”
The Berkeley research team also includes Glaeser; postdoctoral fellows and co-first authors Petar Petrov and Jessie Zhang; staff scientist Jonathan Remis; postdoctoral fellow Hang Cheng; and current and former physics graduate students Jeremy Axelrod, Eric Cooper, Ian Hicklin, Shahar Sandhaus, and Cooper Schnurr.
At Biohub, Carragher and David Agard, the organization's founding scientific director of imaging, jointly lead the Dynamic Structural Cell Biology group. Both are co-corresponding authors of the Biohub preprint, alongside Biohub engineer Pavel Olshin.

Chalmers says investors feel good about Australia despite gloom at home

Jim Chalmers declares optimism about business investment despite domestic gloom
In short:
Jim Chalmers says business investment is on track to grow nearly twice as fast as was forecast in May.
On the other hand, Treasury is expecting to forecast higher unemployment and lower economic growth when the mid-year budget update is published in December.
What's next?
The economic conditions are adding to political pressure on the Albanese government.
Business investment is booming in Australia despite stubborn inflation and a stagnant economy, according to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, as global investors rush to park their money in what they see as "an island of opportunity and stability" in troubled times.
Speaking to a gathering of investors in Sydney on Friday, the treasurer will boast of the warm reception he received in a string of international visits last week and reveal that business investment is growing more than twice as fast as was previously expected.
The optimism comes in the midst of a difficult period for Mr Chalmers, who has been weighed down by gloomy domestic conditions and backlash to his tax hikes on wealth, which have angered business lobbies and unsettled some Labor MPs.
Though acknowledging what he calls Australia's "fair share of challenges" and revealing that Treasury will forecast higher unemployment and lower growth, Mr Chalmers will frame the investment boom as a bright spot.
"I [have] heard the same message over and over: in a world of ratcheting risk, Australia is more and more reliable," he will tell investors at the Citi A50 Economic Forum, according to an excerpt of his remarks seen by the ABC.
"You wouldn't be here with your $25 trillion of capital if you disagreed."
Investment $50 billion better than expected
Mr Chalmers will reveal Treasury now expects business investment to grow faster than 5 per cent this financial year, doubling the May forecast.
That forecast will be formally updated in December's mid-year budget update, and while acknowledging that "potential surprises" could change this early figure, Mr Chalmers will say it would amount to an extra $50 billion in extra investment.
Earlier this year, Australia's peak business lobby the BCA declared Australia was in the middle of the pack as a global investment destination, more favourable than China, South Korea and France, but less than the United States, the UK and New Zealand.
Among the BCA's recommendations was for Australia to streamline the application process for foreign investors, something the government was already progressing.
Mr Chalmers will argue it is working, with $278 billion approved so far this year and more than half of all applications now processed within a month by the Foreign Investment Review Board.
Investment in data centres for artificial intelligence has been a big factor. The ABC reported in September that Australian data centre investment had reached $35 billion for the calendar year, more than one-10th of the total $278 billion investment.
Reserve Bank burnishes inflation concern
While this investment will boost Australia's growth figures, it is also one of a handful of factors concerning the Reserve Bank as it grapples with inflation.
The bank raised the cash rate to 4.60 per cent last month, above the previous 2024 peak. Markets believe another rate hike in early November is possible.
RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser sounded pessimistic in public remarks on Wednesday, saying the inflation outlook was "materially worse" than forecast.
The unemployment rate hit a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September. Mr Hauser said it was "a little weaker" than had been expected but did not suggest that this would deter a rate hike, adding: "I stress the 'little' … we need to see some easing in the economy."
The economic conditions have added to political pressure on the Albanese government, with usually placid backbenchers increasingly willing to bemoan the government's handling of economic conditions in private commentary.
For some, the tax hikes on capital gains and discretionary trusts and the clumsy handling of the issue of credit card surcharges, described by one backbencher as "compounding attacks on small business", have fuelled a sense of mid-term malaise.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has seized on the prospect of a rate hike, which he attributes to the government's "spending addiction".
"I think a lot of households are looking at it right now and saying, 'We cannot bear any more'… It's quite worrying," he said in an interview on 2GB on Wednesday.
But those within government ranks who are defensive of the treasurer's performance believe that the domestic debate over economic conditions does not give enough recognition of the contribution of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
This was a regular feature in Mr Chalmers's international meetings, which included a G20 Finance Ministers' meeting in Bangkok, an APEC Finance Ministers' meeting in Hong Kong, and a bilateral meeting with China's Finance Minister.
The two wars [are] impacting almost every economy in one way or another, posing risks to global growth, pushing up global inflation, and pushing up borrowing costs," he will say on Friday.
"In this sea of uncertainty and risk … Australia's strengths and stability are clear and they are compelling."

Mao Ning: There is no gray zone on the Taiwan question. The Philippine side should abide by the one-China principle with concrete actions. External interactions of China’s Taiwan region should be handled in strict accordance with the one-China principle.

Governments, companies take websites offline over PHP flaws

Governments, companies take websites offline over PHP flaws
Oct 22 - Several government, school and hospital websites across Europe and beyond were taken offline on Wednesday as organizations rushed to protect themselves from two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers a large share of the internet.
Cybersecurity agencies across the world warned that organizations unable to apply fixes in time should consider taking affected sites offline. PHP's developers said a set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was available.
Here are some major websites and services taken offline or otherwise affected:
GERMANY
A spokesperson for the German digital ministry said on Wednesday the federal IT service provider ITZBund had taken several websites offline due to the discovery of PHP vulnerabilities. The temporary deactivation was purely preventive and no security incidents were known to have occurred, the spokesperson said.
FRANCE
The Interior Ministry said it had temporarily taken offline the websites of prefectures, which are local government administrative offices, while awaiting a security fix for the PHP framework they use. It said the move was a precaution pending a patch from the framework's publisher.
BELGIUM
Belgium's foreign ministry said it had temporarily taken its websites offline following reports of cyberattacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, although the country's cybersecurity centre said it had not recorded any attacks on Belgian websites.
NETHERLANDS
Many organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and preventively took their public-facing sites offline. They included the Port of Rotterdam, government site Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites of the five largest political parties and numerous hospital websites across the country.
FINLAND
State IT centre Valtori shut down the government's public web services on Wednesday as "a precautionary measure." Valtori said it had not identified any attempt to exploit the flaws and that the outage was not the result of a data breach.
CZECH REPUBLIC
The Czech government took its website offline on Wednesday at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) at the recommendation of the country's cyber watchdog to "allow for the implementation of necessary security patches."
"The measure aims to ensure the secure operation of the website. During the shutdown, the site and its content will not be accessible to the public. Services will be restored once the recommended security updates have been applied," the government office said.
WIKIMEDIA
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language. All foundation-supported systems and volunteer-run systems that use PHP are affected, the foundation said in a statement.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," the foundation added.
INTERNET ARCHIVE
The non-profit digital library took its portal offline on Wednesday due to emergency maintenance and security patches, it said in a X post. The website is back online.
ORANGE SA
The French telecoms group temporarily suspended access to a number of websites and applications using the PHP programming language as a precaution. The measure affects websites, services and applications across several subsidiaries and entities.
JAPAN
Japan's Ministry of Finance and Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan's National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service.
Several Japanese companies, including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway said on Thursday they were also temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures.
UNITED KINGDOM
The British public service broadcaster BBC said it had taken down some web portals on Wednesday. The broadcaster also reported several municipalities taking down their web services, including the city of Edinburgh. REUTERS

Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:11:10 UTC
20:11:10 KST

Partner content
Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?
New to the Netherlands or a longer-term resident looking to get your finances organised to make the most of your Dutch life? A little planning, a few local habits and some expert coaching will soon have you in the best financial shape.
The foundation of any fitness plan is the basics, so first of all you need to establish what your monthly costs are likely to be. Alongside your rent or mortgage repayments, you’ll have to pay for health insurance, council taxes, public transport, gas and electricity, and perhaps a gym membership.
“If you are financially fit, you are able to meet all your monthly and annual payments, save some money and live the life you would like to have at that moment,” says Ame Pots, a financial health coach with ABN Amro who helps expats make the most of their money.
What costs can you expect?
ABN Amro is hosting a free webinar on October 28 to explain how to get financially fit in the Netherlands.
You will have to pay for insurance. Health insurance, for example, will cost you upwards of €160 a month from next year, and you will have to pay the first €400 of insured treatment. You can cut the monthly premium by around €25 if you raise your voluntary deductible by €500, but that means you’ll need to increase your savings so you can pay if you do fall ill. If you want supplementary insurance, such as dental coverage or extra physiotherapy, you will pay more.
By the way, the six-week window for changing health insurer kicks off in mid-November, so now might be a good time to start shopping around for a better deal.
You’ll also have to pay your local authority for waste collection and the water board for water usage. How much you pay depends on the size of your home and how many people live there, but between €250 and €450 a year is the norm in most places. If you are a homeowner, you will pay slightly more. These bills often arrive at the same time of year, in the spring, so you’ll need to make sure you have enough savings to cover them as well.
“We rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people,” Ame says.
Some bills are monthly, others come once a year
If you live in rented accommodation, you may have to pay service costs, which can range from around €50 to over €250 a month if you live in a building with a lift and lots of amenities such as co-working spaces or a gym. The monthly service fee is an estimate, and you will get a final invoice once a year. Rents also go up once a year, usually in July, by a percentage set by the government. For 2027, the increase in the non-rent-controlled sector, where most expats live, will be 4.4%.
You can keep an eye on your gas and electricity bills if you have a smart meter. If you pay too little to cover your usage, you will be invoiced for the extra costs and your monthly payment is likely to increase. If you pay too much, you’ll get the difference back.
“All this means that you need to really plan out your spending over the year,” says ABN Amro expert Ame. “For example, if you have the 30% ruling, will you still be able to meet your payments when it ends in five years’ time?”
Once you understand the costs you face, create a budget that includes fixed spending, savings and fun stuff. Remember to adjust it if your financial situation changes.
Why is banking in the Netherlands different?
“It’s important to explain to new arrivals how the financial system works in the Netherlands, because it may be very different to back home,” says Ame. “For example, we rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people from countries where they use a credit card as part of their regular spending.”
You’ll need a Dutch bank account for your salary, your rent and pretty much everything else. The Netherlands runs on digital payments, with debit cards, internet payments and payment request apps dominating how the Dutch spend their money.
“If I ask people how much they spend on rent or groceries, they often give a round number – €100 or €200 – but in practice it is more than that,” says Ame. “Once you are aware of what is really happening in your finances, you will understand how much you can actually spend each month.”
How can you improve your financial fitness?

French health authorities on Thursday reported the first human case of Shamonda virus after a patient died in early October.
France’s Health Ministry said the authorities reported a Shamonda virus infection in a patient with "severe immunodeficiency" who was receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon in the country’s third-largest city.
They said the patient died in early October and that clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are ongoing.
"The Shamonda virus had previously been considered non-transmissible to humans. The infection in this patient therefore constitutes the first documented and reported detection of the virus in a human," the ministry said in a statement.
It said no human cases had been documented earlier despite several decades of circulation in Africa and Asia.
"This is therefore an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient," the statement added.
It reaffirmed that no health risk to the general population has so far been identified.
The ministry said the virus was first identified in Europe this summer, including France, on cattle farms. The cattle are considered the main hosts among animal species that can be infected.
"At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the patient was infected through vector transmission, via the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was circulating among animals in spring and summer 2026," it added.

Cuba’s public transport plunges to all-time low amid US fuel blockade, minister says
- Cuba’s transport system has hit a record low after the US fuel blockade, with bus routes cut from 419 to 11 and passenger trips expected to fall 75% in 2026.
- Minister Eduardo Rodriguez Davila said families are struggling to travel, visit sick relatives, or reach hospitals, while freight transport may drop to 20 million tonnes.
- Cuba is turning to electric vehicles and solar charging, but high costs and weak power supply still cause delays, including idle tricycles and limited charging stations.
AI generated
HAVANA – Cuba’s Transportation Minister Eduardo Rodriguez Davila faces daily what appears to be mission impossible: moving millions of people by plane, train and automobile across an island nation that spans 1,250km – with virtually no fuel.
Since the US imposed a de facto ban on fuel imports on Cuba’s communist-run government in late January, the Caribbean’s largest island has seen an unprecedented collapse in public transportation.
“Traditional public transportation is at one of its lowest points of all time,” Rodriguez Davila, a mechanical engineer turned minister, told Reuters in an exclusive interview in Havana this week.
The island’s top transportation official estimates passenger trips on public transportation would plunge 75% in 2026 versus the last. Public bus service to the provinces from the capital Havana dropped from 419 daily in 2025 to just 11 in 2026, he said. Bus routes island-wide have been slashed from more than 100 to just 21. Inter-urban transportation – a mainstay for Cuban workers – would fall 90%, he said.
“These are families that can’t move around, people who can’t visit their sick loved ones, others who can’t get to a hospital,” he said. “The drama behind these shortfalls is complex.”
Even domestic freight transport is expected to fall to around 20 million tonnes in 2026, Rodriguez Davila said, less than a third of the 70 million tonnes moved across the country in 2025.
The US says the now nine-month-long fuel blockade and recent beefed-up sanctions are necessary to upend Cuba’s government, which it calls inept and corrupt.
Cuba and the United Nations have called the blockade illegal and a violation of the human rights of all Cubans.
Electric revolution
While tension soars between governments, Cubans have turned to hitchhiking, impromptu carpooling and, increasingly, far pricier private transportation.
Electric options have also flourished, the minister said.
“It’s what we have to work with, but it comes with a high investment cost,” he said, noting that such vehicles are often twice the price of those that utilize gas or diesel.
Rodriguez Davila says Cuba now has 150,000 electric cars, bikes and tricycles, double the number in 2025 and around 15% of the total one million vehicles in Cuba.
The actual proportion of electric vehicles is likely far higher, he said, given the large numbers of unregistered plug-in cars and bikes, and the prohibitively high price of running a car on petrol or diesel.
By August, 40% of vehicle imports were electric, he said, up from just 3.5% in January 2025, thanks to import incentives that waive or reduce taxes for electric-powered cars and bikes.
“Electric vehicles have increased more quickly than the supply of renewable energy,” the minister said.
Cuba is scrambling to construct solar-charging stations for vehicles, to move soaring demand from the decrepit, mostly fuel-fired electrical grid to the sun. Rodriguez Davila said the Transportation Ministry had just purchased 60 solar charging stations to be distributed countrywide.
Examples abound across Cuba of experiments that have ended in success, and failure.
Transmed, a state enterprise, will soon inaugurate a fleet of cargo vans and charging stations that will move medicines to pharmacies throughout Havana without using hard-to-source fuel.
But even on a government-led press tour, not everything was running like clockwork.
At one stop, dozens of yellow electric tricycles owned by a state company sat idle in a parking garage because there was no electricity to charge them. Frustrated taxi drivers vented.
The minister grimaced.
“These are the problems we face,” he said. REUTERS

NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:03:49 UTC
20:03:49 KST

NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a spectacular new panorama of Mars, providing its clearest look yet at a series of mysterious cliffs shaped by wind. Scientists have been eager to examine these distant formations up close, and the latest images offer an exciting preview of what lies ahead. Taken at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the scene reveals striking blue tones across the foreground while morning sunlight illuminates rugged cliffs known as yardangs along the horizon.
Curiosity recorded the panorama using its Mastcam on August 11, during the mission's 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. Six separate photographs were transmitted to Earth and combined to create the sweeping view. Unlike most Mastcam photographs, the images were processed without white balancing, allowing the scene to retain the distinctive colors and lighting of the Martian morning.
Curiosity Approaches Mysterious Martian Cliffs
The yardangs stretch approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern portion of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014. The rover recently achieved a major milestone, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, a greater climb than any other rover has completed on Mars.
As Curiosity continues toward these unusual formations, researchers anticipate increasingly detailed views of the cliffs. More importantly, they hope that examining the rocks firsthand will help explain how the remarkable landscape developed.
What Mars' Ancient Rocks Reveal About Its Past
Mount Sharp contains numerous layers of sedimentary rock, each preserving evidence from a different chapter of Martian history. Investigating these layers has helped scientists reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams existed in this region of Mars.
As the planet's environment changed, those bodies of water eventually disappeared, leaving deposits of salty minerals behind. Once additional material stopped accumulating on the mountain, powerful winds may have gradually eroded portions of the existing rock, carving out the distinctive yardangs visible today.
Yet the unusual appearance of this particular layer has raised questions about its origins. Its color differs from the surrounding terrain, and its rock layers are tilted in an unexpected direction. Scientists suspect that processes beyond ordinary wind erosion may have contributed to its formation.
"The yardang layer looks out of place. It's the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "But that's what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions."
NASA Plans to Investigate the Cliffs in 2027
Curiosity is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an investigation of unusual spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. Over roughly the next year, the rover will continue traveling through rock layers containing abundant sulfates and carbonates, minerals that provide evidence of ancient drying conditions on Mars.
Mission scientists aim to reach the bottom of the yardang formations sometime in 2027. Once there, Curiosity should be able to examine the mysterious cliffs using its robotic arm, gathering unique measurements that could help determine how they formed and reveal more about the environmental changes that shaped Mars billions of years ago.

Beneath psilocybin’s apparent brain chaos, scientists find signs of a hidden order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

A new neuroimaging study suggests that the psychedelic compound psilocybin does not simply scramble brain communication into random disorder, but instead reorganizes neural activity to align with a person’s immediate environment. Using brain scans and advanced computational modeling, researchers found that under the drug, brain activity formed structured patterns that tracked what participants were doing and experiencing, especially in those who reported a dissolving sense of self. The findings were published in Nature.
Psilocybin is a psychoactive chemical compound found naturally in certain species of mushrooms. After ingestion, the body converts it into psilocin, which binds mainly to serotonin 2A receptors on brain cells, changing how distinct neural networks interact and altering perception, emotion, and self-awareness. Earlier neuroimaging work characterized psychedelic states as predominantly chaotic, marked by a breakdown of coordinated brain rhythms. An influential 2013 study recorded brain signals after psilocybin administration and found widespread drops in coordinated electrical oscillations, suggesting that the drug plunged neural circuits into an uncoordinated state.
Building on these observations, the authors of a 2018 review led by Robin Carhart-Harris, who is also a co-author of the new study, updated what is known as the entropic brain hypothesis, arguing that psychedelics make brain activity more varied and unpredictable, a property known as entropy, and that this makes the brain unusually sensitive to a person’s mindset and physical setting. Later work began to test this idea directly: a study first posted as a preprint in 2020 and later published in a peer-reviewed journal indicated that sensory inputs like music and video alter the diversity of brain signals under psychedelics, showing that external context helps determine neural activity.
Brain imaging has also shown that psychedelics modify how higher regions of the brain communicate with sensory systems. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, psilocybin was found to strengthen signals traveling from higher-order thinking regions down to visual areas, providing a biological basis for vivid closed-eye mental imagery. Despite these insights, scientists still lacked an understanding of whether the brain under psychedelics is truly disorganized or if it follows hidden patterns that track real-world experiences as they unfold over time.
The project was led by Devon Stoliker, a Turner Impact research fellow in the Computational Neuroscience Laboratory at Monash University‘s Turner Institute for Brain and Mental Health, and Adeel Razi, a professor of computational neuroscience and director of the laboratory. Stoliker told PsyPost that the project was motivated by a desire to understand how mindset and setting interact with brain function.
“Psychedelic experiences vary considerably with mindset and setting, but how these differences are reflected in brain activity remains unclear,” Stoliker explained. “Brain-imaging studies often describe disrupted networks or increased disorder, leaving a gap in explaining experiences that people find coherent and deeply meaningful. We wanted to understand how brain activity becomes reorganized during psychedelic experiences, how that reorganization is modulated by what a person is doing and experiencing, and how it relates to subsequent psychological change.”
To carry out the project, the research team recruited 65 healthy adults between the ages of 18 and 55 who had no meaningful prior experience with psychedelic substances. Three participants reported minor or remote exposure without noticeable effects, while the remaining participants had never taken a serotonergic psychedelic. Two individuals left the study before drug administration due to protocol exclusions, leaving 63 participants who received a standardized oral dose of 19 milligrams of psilocybin.
Each volunteer took part in two separate testing visits spaced roughly one week apart: a baseline visit with no drug and an active dosing visit. During each visit, participants completed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in blood oxygenation across the brain, followed by electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical brain waves through sensors on the scalp. The imaging sessions began about 80 minutes after taking the capsule, while electrical recordings started roughly 150 minutes post-dose, during the drug’s acute effects.
In both the brain scanner and the EEG session, participants moved through four distinct conditions designed to present varying levels of sensory engagement. These conditions included resting quietly with eyes closed, following a guided audio meditation, listening to an emotionally evocative music playlist with eyes closed, and watching a silent video of drifting clouds with eyes open.
The sequence progressed from low-stimulus to high-stimulus contexts in the scanner, while the movie was presented first in the EEG session. Half of the participants had also completed an eight-week mindfulness meditation course before their scans, but differences between meditators and non-meditators were not statistically significant, leading the authors to combine both groups for the primary analyses.
After applying quality checks to exclude scans affected by excessive head movement, the final analyzed functional imaging dataset included 60 participants during rest, 59 during meditation, 56 during music listening, and 57 during movie watching. A balanced group of 54 participants with complete data across all four conditions was used for machine learning models. The final electrical recording dataset included 58 participants per condition during the psilocybin session.
When the authors analyzed overall communication across the brain, they discovered that psilocybin redistributed functional connections depending on whether participants had their eyes open or closed. During eyes-closed conditions, overall connectivity decreased in sensory regions by up to 39 percent while increasing in associative thinking areas by up to 72 percent. During the eyes-open movie condition, by comparison, connectivity increased across both sensory and associative areas. Overall, the differences in brain connectivity between having eyes open and having eyes closed shrank by 85 percent in the visual system after psilocybin, indicating that eyes-closed states began to resemble eyes-open processing.
The traditional measure of brain modularity, which quantifies how cleanly the brain divides itself into separate functional communities, dropped under psilocybin across all four conditions. Modularity decreased during rest with an effect size of minus 0.63, during meditation at minus 0.60, during music at minus 0.70, and during video viewing at minus 0.91. However, these static, time-averaged modularity scores failed to predict how participants actually felt during the session, and correlations with subjective reports were not statistically significant.
“The striking finding was that reduced separation between the usual brain networks, a common finding known as reduced modularity, coexisted with the organization detectable using machine learning,” Stoliker observed. “Only the machine learning methods, which preserve each individual’s brain activity over time, identified an association with subjective effects.”
To look beyond static averages, the researchers used machine learning to map moment-by-moment brain activity into smooth, lower-dimensional geometric trajectories. An automated classifier could identify which condition a participant was engaged in based on their brain trajectories, and its accuracy rose with the intensity of the experience. In a closer analysis of six participants with strong subjective effects, accuracy climbed from roughly 62 percent at baseline to about 98 percent under psilocybin.
“Uniquely, this method measured each individual separately, rather than an average across the group of participants,” Stoliker remarked. “We think the development of similar measures that preserve each individual’s brain activity over time is an important next step, but whether the current methods can help predict or improve treatment outcomes remains to be tested.”
To capture different facets of this neural reorganization, the scientists used a second machine-learning tool, called TAVRNN, that tracks how connections between brain regions shift over time. “The main analysis captured context-aligned patterns in each person’s brain activity over time, while a complementary machine learning analysis, TAVRNN—developed in-house by co-author Moein Khajehnejad—showed greater cohesion in the connectivity within and across networks,” the researchers pointed out. “Both analyses showed that organization varied with the strength of subjective effects and both showed that the apparent disorder of the psychedelic state contained structure that became visible when we examined brain activity differently.”
This organizational structure tracked the emotional and psychological quality of each participant’s experience. Higher classification accuracy correlated strongly with overall scores on a questionnaire measuring mystical-type experiences (r = 0.64), while correlations with anxiety or impaired thinking were low and not statistically significant. Among specific kinds of experience, accuracy tracked most closely with positively felt ones, such as bliss, unity, and spiritual feelings. Participants who experienced strong feelings of unity showed tightly packed neural patterns aligned with each condition, a pattern the authors call context alignment; they reserve a separate term, embeddedness, for the felt experience that accompanied it.
“Psychedelics may provide a window into how the brain ordinarily maintains the experience of being a separate self within the world,” Stoliker elaborated. “We use the term embeddedness to describe the felt continuity with a broader physical and psychological context that some participants reported. Embeddedness is the phenomenological correlate of context alignment, thus our findings suggest that this change in experience has a measurable counterpart in how brain activity is organized.”
A perturbation analysis indicated that this context-aligned organization depended most heavily on two major brain networks: the default mode network, which typically supports internal self-reflection, and the visual network, which processes external visual inputs. In those six participants, when researchers mathematically replaced the psilocybin-altered signals in either network with that person’s drug-free data, classification accuracy dropped noticeably, with each network contributing roughly 23 percent to the total accuracy gain.
Subjective questionnaires confirmed the profound psychological impact of the session. More than half of the participants rated the experience among the most meaningful of their lives, with 24 placing it in their top five, and most rated the overall intensity at nine or ten out of ten. Participants also completed follow-up assessments one day later, showing positive mindset improvements related to inner peace, patience, and feelings of connection to nature and other people. Mindset change was most strongly associated with feelings of insightfulness during the session (r = 0.65), followed by mystical, blissful, and spiritual experiences.
“The authors acquired neuroimaging data from individuals at baseline and after a dose of psilocybin, the serotonergic psychedelic contained in ‘magic mushrooms’ of the Psilocybe genus,” said Enzo Tagliazucchi, a researcher at the University of Buenos Aires who was not involved in the study. “Instead of obtaining neuroimaging data just during rest, as is most frequent in this type of study, they acquired the data under different conditions, including music and movie viewing, and meditation. There are multiple results included in this paper, but in my opinion the most salient result is the psilocybin-induced enhancement of context sensitivity.”
“In other words, under psilocybin the neuroimaging data allowed for a much clearer distinction between the different experimental conditions, relative to the baseline,” Tagliazucchi told PsyPost. “Moreover, the authors linked this sensitivity to the occurrence of mystical-type experiences under the drug. This experience is interesting from the perspective of basic and clinical neuroscience, as it can predict symptom improvement after psychedelic therapy.”
The findings are in line with a 2024 study covered by PsyPost, which found that psilocybin causes brain networks to shift into temporary states of heightened communication that predict feelings of ego dissolution. The results also align with an international brain imaging analysis covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that psychedelics consistently bridge the gap between sensory and associative systems, though that study found weak evidence for within-network breakdown while the current work observed drops in within-network connectivity.
In addition, the findings offer a different emphasis from research covered by PsyPost in May 2026, which linked increased brain entropy under psilocybin to later insight and well-being. The new study also found signs of higher entropy, but argues that this apparent disorder contains structured organization aligned with context.
Tagliazucchi also highlighted how the results fit with longstanding concepts in psychedelic science. “The findings in this study align with the context-dependent effects of psychedelics,” he noted. “Today, we are familiar with terms such as ‘set’ and ‘setting,’ coined decades ago to represent the mental and environmental aspects that can influence a psychedelic trip, respectively. From this perspective, the authors found a neural signature of this sensitivity to context; that is, a much easier distinction between the ‘settings’ explored in the study during the psychedelic state compared to the baseline.”
The authors note that earlier psychedelic imaging studies often relied on small samples of experienced users. A second outside expert highlighted the size of the new dataset.
“Psilocybin can produce a rich range of subjective experiences, such as changes in perception to shifts in mood and sense of self,” said Alex Kwan, a professor in the Meinig School of Biomedical Engineering at Cornell University and head of the Kwan Lab, who was not involved in the study. “What makes this study exciting is that it begins to connect these different aspects of the psychedelic experience to distinct patterns of brain activity. One strength of this study is its relatively large sample size, drawing on brain imaging data from more than 60 people. That is a substantial dataset for this type of psychedelic research.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. All participants knew they were receiving psilocybin, as the study used an open-label design without an active placebo group. Although an active placebo that convincingly mimics a psychedelic trip is difficult to implement, expectations could have influenced participants’ subjective reports and emotional responses. The four conditions were also presented in a fixed order during imaging to prioritize safety and comfort for first-time participants.
“I think the authors did an excellent job in several aspects, including data collection, participant number, and computational analyses,” Tagliazucchi evaluated. “The latter, especially, are a ‘tour de force’ in neuroimaging data analysis.”
“My only concern relates to the experimental design,” he added. “This study did not include a placebo condition, and the order of the conditions was fixed across all participants. Therefore, the authors’ analysis might be capturing the differential temporal effects of psilocybin on factors such as vigilance, arousal, attention, or even the temporal evolution of the subjective intensity of the effects, which spans several hours.”
For their part, the authors note that context-aligned organization was already strong during rest, the very first condition scanned, before order effects or fatigue could accumulate. In addition, the types of stimuli presented during the scan sessions represent an important consideration for understanding what context meant in this experiment.
“It would be important to distinguish ‘context’ in a broad sense from a more fine grained definition of ‘context’ which implicates the specific contents of consciousness present at any given time,” Tagliazucchi explained. “The authors used visual stimuli composed by slowly drifting clouds, this stimulus is interesting for inducing a certain global ‘setting,’ but it lacks semantic content. The same applies to the auditory stimulation, which comprised slow, ambient music but lacked strong temporal dynamics. A new study would be required to test whether the context-sensitivity also extends to different forms of conscious content, such as faces, objects, or complex situations like those seen in movies.”
Kwan told PsyPost that the physical environment of brain imaging introduces its own unique influences. “Context is indeed important,” Kwan pointed out. “For this study, we should keep in mind that the participants are lying inside a large and loud brain scanner while they are under the influence of a psychedelic drug. That itself is an unusual context that can affect the results and the qualities of the subjective experience.”
In addition, the participants were healthy volunteers who were generally curious and willing to experience an altered state in an imaging scanner, meaning the findings might not generalize directly to clinical populations undergoing psychedelic-assisted therapy for specific psychiatric disorders. Future investigations will need to examine whether similar patterns of brain reorganization occur in individuals being treated for depression, anxiety, or addiction.
The authors also highlighted important caveats regarding how brain scans are interpreted. “‘Organization’ here is inferred from the structure of patterns observed in the machine learning results derived from the fMRI signal. fMRI measures changes in blood oxygenation associated with neural activity, rather than recording neuronal activity directly,” Stoliker cautioned. “Under psilocybin, this context-aligned structure became more detectable, particularly in participants reporting stronger positive subjective effects, but not in those reporting negative subjective effects or just visual effects—the profound changes to self and boundary, a reduced sense of separation, or continuity with the internal and externally oriented environment, seemed to occur with the emergence of the organization we observed.”
“We want to identify the conditions that make this organization more likely, and whether changing those conditions improves outcomes,” Stoliker said. “This means studying individual characteristics, expectations and preparation before dosing, psychological state around administration, and context and support during the session. Behavioral and brain measurements prior to dosing could help establish which factors are modifiable and whether preparation should differ between people. The clinical goal is to determine whether tailoring these conditions can support more reliable and sustained benefit.”
The study, “Psychedelics align brain activity with context,” was authored by Devon Stoliker, Leonardo Novelli, Moein Khajehnejad, Mana Biabani, Matthew D. Greaves, Tamrin Barta, Martin Williams, Sidhant Chopra, Olivier Bazin, Otto Simonsson, Richard Chambers, Frederick S. Barrett, Gustavo Deco, Katrin H. Preller, Robin L. Carhart-Harris, Anil K. Seth, Suresh Sundram, Gary F. Egan, and Adeel Razi.

Britain still plans new nuclear sub every eighteen months
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:24 BST
20:00:24 KST

Ministers have confirmed that the intention remains to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, and that the investments needed to establish industrial capacity for a submarine every eighteen months from the mid-2030s have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase total hull numbers in the submarine service.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), the Ministry of Defence intends to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.
“The programme is currently midway through the Detailed Design and Long Lead (D2L2) phase and we anticipate that the number of submarines will be confirmed before the end of this phase in 2028.
“Through the DIP, the Government has made the investments necessary to establish the industrial capacity required to ultimately deliver a submarine every 18 months from the mid-2030s to ensure we can deliver an expanded SSN force.”
Britain currently operates seven Astute class attack submarines, and this publication reported the government’s commitment to build twelve new nuclear attack submarines when the plan appeared. A drumbeat of one boat every eighteen months would be the fastest sustained British submarine production rate since the Cold War, and the figure follows from the capacity being built at Barrow.
Barrow has been expanding through the Barrow Infrastructure Programme, with new build halls, a reconfigured yard and a recruitment effort that has taken the BAE Systems workforce there past twelve thousand. Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby has doubled its site to produce reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and the Sheffield Forgemasters work on large forgings feeds the same chain.
Confirmation of the final number before the end of the detailed design phase in 2028 ties the fleet size to what the yard can actually sustain. Senior officials told the Commons Defence Committee earlier this year that submarine fleet size was conditional on Barrow output, and a decision due in 2028 falls inside this Parliament.
Australia will build its own SSN-AUKUS boats at Osborne in South Australia to a common design, and the two production lines are intended to share a supply chain, which is part of the case for the industrial investment on the British side. Dreadnought holds priority at Barrow through the late 2020s, so attack submarine production builds up behind the ballistic missile boats.
Pollard confirmed in a separate answer the same day that steel will be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS next year, and that the Preliminary Design Review for the class concluded on the first of July. Twelve boats remains an upper bound until the design phase closes.
