Snowy 2.0 to cost 12 times more than initial budget with further delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:08 UTC
20:00:08 KST

Review finds delayed Snowy 2.0 hydropower project could cost up to $25b
In short:
A major review of Australia's biggest renewable energy project has found it could cost up to $25 billion, which is about 12 times the original price.
Snowy 2.0 was initially set to cost $2b and come online in 2021.
What's next?
The project is now expected to be delivered in 2029.
The cost of delivering Australia's biggest renewable energy project has doubled since the last estimate and is now set to become fully operational a year later than expected, according to a major review.
Snowy Hydro has released its much-anticipated cost reassessment for the Snowy 2.0 hydropower project, revealing it could cost up to $25 billion, with first power expected in early 2029 and the project to be fully operational later that year.
While the Commonwealth-owned company has set a target cost of $22 billion, it is allowing for an additional $3 billion to be spent on the project if required.
Snowy 2.0, which started being built seven years ago, had an initial budget of $2 billion and was originally expected to start operating in 2021.
Those figures were revised as part of a project reset three years ago, which projected first power would be delivered in late 2027.
It was expected Snowy 2.0 would be fully operational a year later, at a cost of $12 billion.
Late last year it was announced the project's contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) would conduct a "line-by-line reassessment", which has now been released three months later than initially expected.
Snowy Hydro chief executive Dennis Barnes said he was "incredibly disappointed" with the update.
"We had a project that was stalled and had billions of dollars of claims on the table in 2023," he said.
"I'm pleased we've got progress. Progress doubled in the first year after the reset.
"What I'm disappointed about is obviously the resultant costs of the progress we're making."
Mr Barnes said the "design immaturity" that was faced before the 2023 reset had contributed to the latest cost blowouts.
"We've understood that we're going to need a lot more people for a lot longer to deliver this job," he said.
"This job is 80 per cent people costs. We've got 5,000 people on the job now working across multiple work fronts and that's obviously a lot more than we thought in 2023."
The review found 65 per cent of machine tunnelling and 90 per cent of cavern excavation had now been completed and work to build the underground power station was underway.
While Mr Barnes said the project was in its "strongest position yet", he could not rule out further cost blowouts beyond the most recent targets.
"There's never any guarantees with mega projects. We're doing a world-first thing in many respects in really complex conditions," he said.
"But the project is hitting its milestones of late. We have a lot of the risks behind us."
How did Snowy 2.0 get here?
Snowy 2.0 is designed to underpin Australia's electricity security and affordability over coming decades, as the country transitions away from fossil fuels.
Based in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, the project will link two dams through about 27 kilometres of tunnels and include an underground pumped hydro station the size of the Sydney Opera House.
The project will act like a giant battery, pumping water upstream when electricity is cheap and releasing it back downstream to generate power when demand is high.
It has a total capacity of 2,200MW and is expected to power three million homes for a week, the equivalent of about 26 million household batteries.
Unlike batteries, pumped hydro offers long-duration storage, meaning it is designed to be a renewable energy insurance policy during days when there is limited sun or wind.
But Snowy 2.0 has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes.
A major setback came after one of the initial three tunnel boring machines, Florence, got stuck in early 2023 for 11 months after hitting soft ground and creating a sinkhole.
The National Audit Office gave Snowy 2.0 a glowing review in 2022 but the most recent audit, released earlier this year, found "significant deficiencies" in the management of the project.
In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry examining the project's delivery, Snowy Hydro said initial "design immaturity" and the project's "inherent complexity" had been the primary drivers of additional costs.
"Productivity underperformance and cost escalation have also been significant factors," the submission read.
"Others have related to project-specific complexities that have developed during delivery.
"Snowy Hydro has learned and taken action in response to these challenges."
A submission from FGJV said "unprecedented geotechnical uncertainty" and "significant geopolitical upheaval" had contributed to cost escalations.
"Unlike metropolitan tunnelling projects, where initial ground investigations are typically well-developed, ground investigations within a national park are necessarily limited," the submission said.
"As a result, conditions only become fully apparent as excavation progresses."
Project benefits report released
Along with the cost reassessment, Snowy Hydro has also released an economic study conducted by engineering consultant GHD.
It found the project would contribute $18 billion to Australia's economy during the delivery phase and reduce wholesale electricity costs by more than $7 billion by 2075.
It comes as batteries start to reshape the market, with the Australian Energy Market Operator confirming within its latest snapshot of the national electricity system that they were starting to drive down wholesale energy costs.
Mr Barnes said all technologies were needed for the energy transition, including batteries, pumped hydro and gas for firming.
"We issued a report earlier in the year to show what the grid looked like with and without Snowy 2.0 and on those periods, which are pretty common, where we get no wind and we get no sun for days on end, batteries run out of juice, they don't get recharged," he said.
"We actually saw that in January in South Australia. There was a period where the batteries ran out of juice and prices went very high.
"So with Snowy 2.0 in the grid, we see that the prices in those periods were $7,000 a megawatt hour lower."
A joint statement from Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said abandoning the hydropower project would undermine grid reliability, scrap 5,000 jobs and lead to higher electricity bills.
"Once completed, Snowy 2.0 will be an incredible national asset, supporting Australia's energy security, price stability and the transition to renewable energy," the statement read.
"The pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices.
"The former Coalition government left behind a project facing major delays, rising costs and serious delivery risks."
Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan called for Mr Bowen to resign over the cost blowouts but sidestepped questions about whether the Coalition supported the project.
"Chris Bowen should apologise to the Australian taxpayer and resign. His incompetence means the PM has no choice. He should seek his resignation or he should sack him," he said.
"We have to look at this very closely, look at the model on which it's been funded, and also we will have to consider the poles and wires, the connecting of this project into the grid."

Exclusive: Ben-Gvir’s Plan to Push Netanyahu Right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

In a small office in the industrial district of Lod, a city outside Tel Aviv where Israeli forces expelled thousands of Palestinians during the 1948 war, sits the campaign headquarters of Otzma Yehudit, or “Jewish Power.” The ultra-nationalist party is led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right firebrand once deemed too extreme to serve in Israel’s military. He now sits in Benjamin Netanyahu’s cabinet as national security minister, overseeing the country’s police and prison services.
If Ben-Gvir has his way, the Oct. 27 election will give his party more seats in parliament and himself greater leverage over another right-wing government led by Netanyahu. His ambition is not to replace the prime minister but to make him even more dependent on the hardline parties pushing for Palestinians to leave Gaza and the West Bank—and for Israel to extend sovereignty over the territories.
“I want Netanyahu to be prime minister. He’s a leader. I prefer him a million times over Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir tells me in a rare interview on Oct. 19, referring to Netanyahu’s chief rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Pounding his chest, he adds: “What will really help Netanyahu be right wing is if I, Ben-Gvir, will be a senior minister and it’s a full right-wing government.”
The post he covets is defense minister, which would give him command over Israel’s armed forces and greater authority to pursue his vision for Gaza and the West Bank: fewer constraints on military operations, the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from both territories, and the expansion of Israeli control over lands he believes belong to the Jewish people. Netanyahu has resisted giving Ben-Gvir the portfolio. But Ben-Gvir and his allies hope to win enough seats to force Netanyahu to accommodate their demands or risk losing power. He may benefit from the rightward shift of Israeli politics, particularly among younger voters drawn to his confrontational style and uncompromising vision of Jewish sovereignty. In a Channel 12 survey of first-time Jewish voters, nearly three-quarters identified as right-wing or center-right.
Polls suggest a tight contest, with Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party edging ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud in several recent surveys, but neither the prime minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition appears close to the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. An average of four recent polls puts the two camps at roughly 50 and 53 seats, respectively, leaving Arab parties and smaller factions potentially pivotal. The result could be another fragile coalition; an unlikely unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot; or a prolonged deadlock that sends Israelis back to the polls.
Ben-Gvir, dressed in a white shirt and white kippah, speaks halting English. Under his leadership, Israel’s prison service has drawn allegations of abuse for its treatment of Palestinian detainees. But he wants a more direct role in determining Israel’s future in Gaza and the West Bank.
“If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza,” he says. “We have to promote voluntary emigration. Gaza could be a Riviera. It’s a beautiful place. But we can’t have one Hamas member there.” His proposal would have Palestinians leave Gaza for countries willing to receive them, and then allow Israelis to establish settlements in the coastal enclave. It would reverse a defining decision of an earlier right-wing prime minister, Ariel Sharon, who in 2005 withdrew Israeli forces and evacuated more than 8,000 Jewish settlers from Gaza.
Ben-Gvir offers no clear explanation of which countries would accept large numbers of Palestinians, or how their departure could be considered voluntary under the conditions he proposes. “Gaza was always ours,” he says. “Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader. Hamas are terrorists who don’t just want to destroy Israel. They want to destroy the whole world.”
When I suggest that removing Palestinians from Gaza and resettling it would deepen Israel’s international isolation, he dismisses the concern. “I think that the stronger we are, we won’t be isolated,” he says. “Israel is isolated when it’s weak. If we help the population leave Gaza, we can be very strong.”
Ben-Gvir’s rhetoric and policy designs have drawn widespread condemnation at home and abroad, with critics across the political spectrum accusing him of inciting war crimes and eroding the foundations of Israeli democracy. “He’s a source of immense trouble,” Efraim Halevy, a former head of the Mossad, tells me.
His ambitions in the West Bank are no less sweeping. Ben-Gvir wants Israel to annex the territory, which he, like most Israelis, calls by its biblical names, Judea and Samaria. It is home to 3.3 million Palestinians and partially governed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), created by the 1993 Oslo Accords that envisioned a Palestinian state. Controlled by the Fatah party, the PA has a lightly armed security force that is trained by the U.S. military and historically works with Israel to suppress terror attacks. But Ben-Gvir wants Israeli security control over the area Palestinians envisage as the heartland of a future state. “We need to take away the weapons for the Palestinian Authority,” he says. “As of now, they are training in Jericho. They’re not training to direct traffic, are they? They want to do another Oct. 7.” A spokesperson for the PA did not respond to a request for comment.
The vision goes beyond annexation. Ben-Gvir says he would encourage millions of Palestinians who have lived in the West Bank for generations to pack up and go. “We want sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, where we also want voluntary emigration,” he says. “Just so we understand, we want voluntary emigration—not kicking anyone out. People will choose the option to leave.”
Whether Ben-Gvir can translate those ambitions into official Israeli policy will depend in part on the leverage his party wins on Oct. 27. He is counting on voters to strengthen his hand. “I hope the nation sends its message,” he says.
Ben-Gvir, 50, was born into a relatively secular Jewish family of Iraqi and Kurdish descent in Mevaseret Zion, a suburb of Jerusalem. His mother had belonged to the Irgun, the Jewish underground that fought British rule before Israel’s founding, but his parents were, by all accounts, not ideological zealots. Ben-Gvir took a different path. He became religious at 12 and, amid the violence of the first Palestinian intifada, gravitated toward the teachings of Meir Kahane, the American-born rabbi who advocated expelling Arabs from Israel and the occupied territories. By his teens, he was an activist in Kahane’s movement, which Israel eventually outlawed as a terrorist organization. Ben-Gvir was considered so extreme that the Israeli military barred him from compulsory service.
Today, Ben-Gvir continues to revere Kahane, even as he disavows some of his mentor’s most fanatical positions. “I went to his yeshiva. He did a lot of good things. He protected Jews. He was murdered sanctifying God’s name,” he tells me. “Not everything that he did do I fully agree with. In the past, I thought we should kick out all the Arabs from the land of Israel. Now I think there can be some. I accept that there are some Arabs who live here. And I have no problem with part of them. Those who recognize the State of Israel as the Jewish state. Those who are loyal to the Jewish State.”
As a young adult, Ben-Gvir moved to Kiryat Arba, a Jewish settlement overlooking the Palestinian city of Hebron, where Kahane’s legacy runs particularly deep. According to published accounts, he and his future wife, Ayala, visited the grave of Baruch Goldstein on their first date. Goldstein, an American-born physician and Kahane admirer, had massacred 29 Palestinian Muslims at prayer in Hebron in 1994 before being beaten to death by survivors. For years, Ben-Gvir displayed Goldstein’s portrait in his living room. He became an attorney for Jewish settlers and activists accused of extremist violence. He also acquired a criminal record, including convictions for incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization.
For years, Ben-Gvir remained on the fringes of Israeli politics, a familiar presence at settler demonstrations but an unlikely candidate for national office. Over time, he softened some of his rhetoric, publicly distanced himself from Kahane’s demand to remove all Arabs, and cultivated a more approachable persona without abandoning his annexationist aspirations.
His political breakthrough came under Netanyahu. Ahead of the 2022 election, the prime minister helped broker an alliance between Ben-Gvir’s party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, giving Netanyahu enough seats to assemble a government. Netanyahu’s decision to bring two Jewish supremacists into government became emblematic of Israel’s rightward turn—and one of the factors in its growing international isolation.
As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has pursued a hardline agenda: expanding civilian gun ownership, imposing an increasingly draconian regime on Palestinian prisoners, and pressing for tougher policing of anti-government protests. He wore a noose-shaped pin as he championed legislation imposing the death penalty on Palestinians convicted of deadly terrorist attacks, and released an AI-generated video depicting Palestinian prisoners emerging from Israeli jails emaciated and weeping, a grotesque statement about the conditions of their confinement.
Ben-Gvir also encouraged Jewish prayer at the Jerusalem holy site known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as Haram al-Sharif, challenging a decades-old arrangement governing the disputed religious site, which has traditionally permitted non-Muslims to visit but reserved the right to worship there for Muslims. Under Ben-Gvir, Israeli police have increasingly allowed Jews to pray at the site, a deliberate provocation to the Arab world, drawing condemnation from Palestinian and Jordanian authorities. “It used to be an apartheid up there and Jews could not pray,” he tells me. “That could not happen in any normal country. I returned justice to the Temple Mount.”
Ben-Gvir has also become one of the leading voices on the Israeli right seeking to shift responsibility for Oct. 7 away from Netanyahu and onto Israel’s military and intelligence establishment. Among the claims he repeats is that security officials failed to wake the prime minister as the attack unfolded—which is disputed by former security officials.
“Even if he’s not perfect, and even if he made mistakes, and he indeed made mistakes, what screwed him up on Oct. 7 was our intelligence,” Ben-Gvir says of Netanyahu. “The army, the intelligence, the Shin Bet. They are all to blame,” he adds. “Netanyahu is not clear of blame, but there are many people who are more at fault than him.”
Ben-Gvir’s relationship with the prime minister is not exactly warm. “I’m not backing him; I’m not his crony on everything. I think he’s much better than Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir says. “I want to be next to him. I want him to be very strong. I want to pull him to the right.”
He tells me he would not join a unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a possibility if neither can assemble a governing coalition. “Governments like that are never good,” he says. “It's dancing in two weddings.” Besides, he adds, “It won’t fulfill my dreams.”
What Ben-Gvir wants from another Netanyahu government would place him at odds with the diplomatic framework advanced by the Trump Administration and its partners in Europe and the Arab world. The American-led Board of Peace envisions Gaza’s reconstruction under Palestinian leadership, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, and a possible path toward Palestinian statehood.
Ben-Gvir, on the other hand, wants Israeli sovereignty and the departure of much of Gaza’s Palestinian population. He cites polling that he says shows 52% of Gazans want to leave the territory, devastated by years of war and Hamas rule. If Israel helps that majority leave, he reasons, those who remain will eventually want to follow. “They will see it is successful for them, they’ll see there’s a future, there’s a life,” he says. “There’s good places in the world. Pretty places.” He offers no evidence that the remaining population would choose to relocate, or how such a migration could be arranged without coercion.
For Ben-Gvir and his allies, the coming election offers a chance to advance a far-reaching transformation of Israeli politics and society—to move the country toward a maximalist vision of a Jewish state, one with expanded territorial ambitions, fewer judicial constraints, and a government less inclined to heed international objections. Ben-Gvir dismisses concerns that such policies would cement Israel’s status as a pariah state. In his telling, the military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran demonstrate the value of uncompromising power. “We made Israel stronger,” he says. “When Israel is stronger, the world respects that.”
– With reporting by Liam Forberg

- A soccer program iACT founded by late Redondo Beach activists Katie-Jay Scott and Gabriel Stauring helped refugees in Chad find hope.
- The program helped former refugees Mohammed Annour and Moubarak Abdallah thrive in Sweden, where they raise families and coach.
- Trump administration cuts to foreign aid and tighter refugee policies threaten the program as humanitarian needs grow.
Mohammed Annour spent much of his youth living in a flimsy shelter in a dusty, overcrowded refugee camp in east Africa, where the days were long, the food was poor and the future nonexistent.
“Go to the army and fight. That’s one option,” said Annour, who fled war in Sudan for the refugee camp in Chad when he was 9. “The other one is you stay there. But you don’t have a future.”
If he had stayed, Annour, now 33, has little doubt how his story would have ended.
“Probably,” he said, “I’m dead.”
Instead, he’s in Sweden, raising two boys, working as a quality control inspector for a textile company and playing amateur soccer for a team in the country’s fifth division. And the only thing that separates his experience from the tens of thousands of desperate people he left behind in the camp is the fact someone believed in him enough to give him a chance.
“Everybody needs a chance,” Annour said. “Don’t throw people out. People just need a chance in life.”
“And we got that chance,” he continued, “because of Katie-Jay and Gabriel.”
That would be Katie-Jay Scott and Gabriel Stauring, a pair of South Bay activists who showed up at Annour’s camp on a blazing hot day in 2011, rolled a battered soccer ball across a barren field and transformed an untold number of lives.
Scott and Stauring founded the humanitarian group iACT largely to respond to the crisis in Darfur, a semi-desert plateau in western Sudan that has known nothing but war this century. But unlike many of the dozens of other similarly minded people and groups working in Africa, Scott and Stauring came not to preach, but to listen. They came with questions, not answers.
And what they were told was that the children in the camps needed more than food and shelter. They needed a routine, they needed recreation, they needed joy and they needed hope.
In other words, they needed soccer.
“Many organizations came into the camps. They just came around and took some pictures and then they leave,” said Annour, a slight man with a serious countenance. “I think [Scott and Stauring] understood us as humans, not just these kids or these people who need food or shelter.
“They saw another side. They saw these people that can make something in life.”
Stauring and Scott were killed in a car accident in Manhattan Beach five years ago, but their legacy lives on in the unique advocacy and aid program they created, one that uses soccer to teach skills and provide structure to refugees stranded in camps, shelters and intolerable poverty in four countries on two continents.
“They were so kind, careful,” Annour said. “Listening to everyone. It didn’t matter where you came from, which color you are. They were open and gave time to everyone they met.”
“Honestly, I didn’t know they were going to change my life or anything,” added Moubarak Abdallah, another refugee introduced to soccer by Scott and Stauring. “I saw them as other people who just come and go. But they were quite special people.
“They wanted to help our ideas shine, to [give] other people hope. They were listening to what I needed.”
Today, there are more than 5,000 children participating in iACT soccer academies in Chad, the Central African Republic, Cameroon and Mexico. Another 1,800 children are enrolled in the group’s Little Ripples preschool program, which also served 475,000 meals to students and staff last year.
But the organization, like many similarly focused humanitarian groups, is fighting for its survival amid a global backlash against refugees and migrants.
The hostility has been especially strong in the U.S., where the second Trump administration has sharply restricted immigration and asylum access and drastically cut congressionally approved spending for life-sustaining programs previously funded through USAID. Many European countries have followed that lead, adopting a stauncher approach to border enforcement and deportations and slashing support for development assistance by 13.8% in 2025, the largest cut in a decade.
This summer, violent anti-immigrant protests in South Africa forced more than 178,000 people to flee to Zimbabwe, Malawi, Nigeria and other countries, reversing a trend that has seen the region’s richest country welcome migrants to work on farms, in construction and other low-paid jobs. Public sentiment toward refugees and migrants has also hardened elsewhere, creating a crisis for nonprofit aid groups.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, or UNHCR, this month warned the gap between humanitarian needs and donor contributions is widening, leading to deep cuts and forcing aid groups to fight one another for the shrinking dollars that remain — all at a time when conflicts in Syria, Gaza and Ukraine have swelled the number of refugees worldwide to nearly 42 million; another 69 million people are displaced.
A couple killed nearly a year ago in a Manhattan Beach car crash ran soccer clinics at refugee camps around the world. This is how work has continued after their death.
That’s more than 1 out of every 70 people on Earth, according to the UNHCR.
Annour and his family were once part of that wave, fleeing their home in Sudan in 2003, stepping around dead bodies and witnessing unimaginable horror, to escape one in a series of continuing civil wars that have given way to genocide. More than 15 million people have been displaced in the 23 years of fighting, with more than 1.3 million still stranded in teeming refugee camps in eastern Chad.
Annour said he would have perished there if not for Stauring and Scott, who introduced soccer to their camp. Three years after the pair arrived, an international tournament for stateless players, the CONIFA World Football Cup, was held and iACT entered a 20-man team comprised of players from 12 camps. Annour, a left back, made the cut as did Abdallah, a physical midfielder with a perpetual smile who would become the team captain.
“No one is thinking this [is] going to be life-changing,” Abdallah remembers thinking. “You know, there was like a small chance but it became big dreams for us.”
The team, Darfur United, was outscored 39-0 in its two games in Ostersund, Sweden, but most of the players chose to stay in Ostersund rather than return to their camps and were welcomed by the Swedish government. They received asylum and eventually formed an integration team, the Mighty Cosmos, that advanced as high as the fifth division of Swedish soccer.
Abdallah is a natural leader, said Alan Barker, chairman of the Mighty Cosmos, and the kind of person who receives total respect from the other players.
“He is a sort of guy you can rely on 100%,” Barker said. “Personally, I would trust him with my life. He is a doer, not a talker. A problem solver not a problem creator. And he always wants the best for everybody.”
Annour, he added, has been troubled by knee injuries on the field but remains “a strong and quiet yet forceful personality of the group.”
“He is a passionate believer in fair play and honesty and has no room for dishonesty or deception in any aspect of life,” Barker continued. “Maybe that’s a reflection of his childhood in the refugee camps and Chad, where there was no time for such things. He’s a sort of guy whose name would be first on the team sheet. The team sheet of football and life.”
More important is the fact that the players, teenagers or young adults when they arrived in Sweden, have married, had children of their own, become citizens and integrated into the local community, where their civic work was this year recognized with one of Sweden’s most prestigious awards.
“I never dreamed to be in this position when I was a kid. I was trying to survive, to live day by day,” said Annour, who is working three jobs to support his sons, aged 1 ½ and 4.
“I’m here. I can provide for my family. Moubarak provides for his family. It’s like saving a generation, not just me and Moubarak.”
A Redondo Beach couple who offered Darfur refugees hope and a way out via soccer are killed in a four-car traffic accident in Manhattan Beach.
“It’s about the chances,” agreed Abdallah, 35, who also lives in Sweden where he coaches the Mighty Cosmos while raising a 5-year-old son.
“The door has to open. That’s all.”
iACT offered a way to open those doors when it first rolled that battered soccer ball onto a dirt lot. Without that, “these guys wouldn’t be here, wouldn‘t have the lives they have,” said Darren Hamlin, a British filmmaker who has started a Kickstarter campaign to fund a documentary on the refugee players.
By focusing on single players and their game and not the vastness of the sprawling global refugee crisis, Hamlin says the film has the power to redefine these former refugees not as obscure numbers but as flesh-and-blood people with dreams and talents and aspirations. That was what inspired Scott and Stauring when they founded iACT.
“Football has this power to transcend sports. It becomes an emotional thing,” said Hamlin, who is behind on his goal of raising $66,000 by the end of the month to expand work on the documentary. “It doesn’t matter how many stats or things we put in front of people; they don’t really pay attention.
“But football kind of goes deeper sometimes. Football is kind of the vehicle that delivers the message.”
Redondo Beach’s Gabriel Stauring and Katie-Jay Scott are determined to grow the Refugees United Soccer Academy, which teaches soccer and life skills to displaced Darfuri people and other refugees.
Getting that message out, however, is becoming increasingly difficult. As government funding for refugee programs around the world has dried up, groups like iACT have found themselves fighting for the same slice of a much smaller funding pie.
“Fundraising at all levels has become more difficult with the gutting of USAID, especially with the increase in larger NGOs [non-government organizations] applying for foundation grants,” said Merri Weir, a retired teacher and iACT board member since 2016. “It is becoming harder and harder because we’re competing with larger NGOs. The funding stream has become tighter.”
At the same time, the need has swelled.
“The refugee camps in Chad are still very unstable,” said Weir, who has visited the camps multiple times. “The current war has not ended and shows no sign of ending. Refugees are still coming across the border, which has more than doubled the number of Sudanese refugees.
“It is critical that we are able to sustain our current refugee-led programs.”
In response, Weir’s group, which will hold its annual fundraising event in Manhattan Beach next month, has considered everything short of a corner lemonade stand and selling chocolate door to door to make up for the lost financial backing it needs to continue what Scott and Stauring started.
“In the past, it is our uniqueness and our innovation and our refugee-led action [that] set us apart,” said Weir. “It was very appealing.”
The Trump administration complicated things even further in June 2025 when it instituted a travel ban and entry restriction list on Chad, leading the Chadian government to retaliate by revoking visas for American citizens, including aid workers. That means fewer children playing soccer and attending preschool, fewer meals being served — and fewer success stories like the ones told by Abdallah and Annour.
Players representing 29 countries took part in the Homeless World Cup, a tournament that aims to raise awareness about people who are homeless or refugees.
“I spent 12 years in a refugee camp,” Abdallah said. “People just hope to get a meal for the day. [iACT] brought the footballs and then just brought the idea. A chance to change our lives. Opportunity.
“There’s a lot of people in the refugee camps [that] could be pilots, doctors, better football players. Maybe there is the next Lionel Messi, Cristiano [Ronaldo], Lamine Yamal in the camp. But they don’t have any opportunity to get out.”
“The world is crazy. It’s just war everywhere,” added Annour, who is about to begin a college course on sports science. “Those people who don’t like refugees, who don’t want the United Nations to bring more refugees, they need to put themselves in our shoes.
“People are so naive to think they can just ignore what’s going on. It’s getting bigger every day.“
Abdallah and Annour may have left the camps, but the camps have not left them. The work they have done in Sweden includes the construction of a community sports and culture center, addressing crime prevention and mental health, refugee resettlement, and fundraising efforts that support the work of iACT and other groups working with the people they left behind.
“My mom is still in the same camp, so I’ve been back three times now with a lot of footballs, football boots and football equipment,” Abdallah said.
Scott and Stauring, who lived in Redondo Beach before the fatal car crash, thought they were bringing soccer to the camps in Africa, but what they really brought was hope and proof that if someone just opens the door, you might be surprised what you find on the other side.

Taipei rejects Lee Chen-hsiu's bid to run for Zhubei mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:52:37 UTC
19:52:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei High Administrative Court on Thursday rejected former TPP Legislator Lee Chen-hsiu's (李貞秀) bid to run for Zhubei mayor after she challenged her disqualification.
CNA reported that the court said the Hsinchu County Election Commission had legal grounds to reject Lee's candidacy. It also warned that letting her run could spark election disputes and harm the public interest.
Lee registered to run for Zhubei mayor on Aug. 31. Still, the commission rejected her application on Oct. 8. Officials said she had not met the 10-year residency requirement because she submitted proof of canceling her Chinese household registration in March 2025.
Lee was born in China and moved to Taiwan after marrying a Taiwanese citizen. She established her household registration in the country in December 1999 but did not submit proof of canceling her Chinese registration until more than 25 years later, per CTS News.
Under an April 16 interpretation by the Mainland Affairs Council, the 10-year residency requirement begins when a person submits proof of canceling their Chinese household registration. The commission therefore ruled Lee was ineligible under cross-strait relations law, per UDN.
Lee challenged the decision and sought temporary permission to run while her case proceeded. However, the court found no clear evidence that the commission's decision was unlawful.
The court said further investigation would be needed to determine whether the government's interpretation imposed restrictions beyond those set by law. It added that Lee had not shown she was likely to win her legal challenge.
Judges warned that allowing Lee to run could create legal problems if she won the election but later lost her case. Such an outcome could lead to a challenge to her election victory or a new election.
The court ruled that the potential harm to the public interest outweighed the harm Lee would face from being barred from the election. It therefore rejected her request for temporary permission to run, although she can appeal the ruling.

India and Poland on Thursday agreed to boost defence, space, and nuclear energy ties as their prime ministers held talks in New Delhi.

Modi during his press remarks said the partnership between the two nations “has gained new momentum over the past two years.”
He said during Thursday's meeting they agreed to deepen ties in defence, space and nuclear energy sectors.
“We believe that reform is essential to make global governance institutions more empowered and effective,” he said.
Tusk during his remarks said: "We are building our friendship on the basis of trust, shared values, and ideas such as non-violence."
Tusk is currently on an official visit to India. He will conclude his visit on Friday, after holding meetings in southern India's Bengaluru city.
India and Poland, which established diplomatic relations in 1954, elevated their relationship to “Strategic Partnership" during Modi's visit to Poland in 2024.
Bilateral trade between the two countries witnessed an increase of 107.9 percent from $1.32 billion in 2010 to $2.73 billion in 2020.

South African police investigate killing of foreign national by crowd
JOHANNESBURG – South African police said on Oct 22 they were investigating the killing of a foreign national by a crowd of about 50 people in the city of Durban.
The South African Police Service said in a post on X that the victim, thought to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was beaten by the crowd and declared dead at the scene.
A group of people had been marching in central Durban when two men appeared to break away and approach the victim, after which he was assaulted by about 50 people, police said.
Police did not give the victim’s nationality and said the motive for the killing was unknown.
The incident follows months of anti-migrant protests in South Africa, some of which have turned violent and drawn international criticism, prompting thousands of migrants from elsewhere in Africa to flee affected communities.
Earlier in October, anti-migrant protests in Durban and Johannesburg's Soweto township turned violent, with foreign-owned businesses looted and vehicles set alight after demonstrations against the processing of asylum applications at a refugee reception centre. REUTERS

U.S. Congress Urges Trump to Allow Ukraine to Use Starlink for Strikes on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:45:45 UTC
19:45:45 KST

Twenty-three members of the U.S. House of Representatives have urged President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite network for military operations inside Russia.
According to The Hill, the lawmakers believe that such authorization would help Ukraine detect Russian missile launchers in a timely manner and strike them on Russian territory.
The initiative was led by Republican Joe Wilson. The letter was signed by 16 Democrats and seven Republicans, who urged Trump to personally contact SpaceX founder Elon Musk to secure the lifting of the relevant restrictions.
“We urge you to ask Elon Musk to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite internet system to locate missile launchers on Russian territory. One phone call could save lives and increase Vladimir Putin’s incentives to negotiate,” the lawmakers wrote.
According to lawmakers, if Ukrainian forces cannot reliably intercept Russian missiles, they should be able to strike the launchers from which those missiles are fired.
The letter also noted that Ukraine had already approached Elon Musk with a request for an exemption from the restrictions preventing the use of Starlink for such operations inside Russia.
The lawmakers believe that Donald Trump could help secure the decision.
In July 2026, during closed-door talks at the White House, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly asked the U.S. President Donald Trump to authorize the use of Starlink to guide long-range drones toward ballistic missile launchers on Russian territory.
In August 2026, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk held talks with former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
According to reports, the talks proved ‘extremely unsuccessful,’ after which Musk reportedly became firmly inclined to deny Ukraine permission to use Starlink for such operations.
Following his departure from office on August 7, Fedorov said he was continuing negotiations with Musk but did not specify their subject or outcome.

Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:43:13 UTC
19:43:13 KST

Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.
Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.
Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent.
“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.
Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.
LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed.
Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals.
Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product.

‘Inconsistent with policy’: Bikaner House on removal of photos from Raihan Vadra’s exhibition

2026-10-22
10:41:27 UTC
19:41:27 KST

Vadra had alleged that he had shared the exhibition layout a week earlier
NEW DELHI: Bikaner House Management Society on Thursday said it had requested the removal of certain photographs from Raihan Vadra’s exhibition, ‘No Idea Is Final’, after finding them inconsistent with its policy.The statement came after Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra, alleged that the venue’s management had asked him to remove photographs depicting youth movements in Delhi just hours before the exhibition’s scheduled opening at 7 pm.In a statement, the society said Bikaner House was a public cultural institution dedicated to promoting art and culture, and that exhibitions held at the venue must comply with its management policy."Certain photographs displayed as part of Mr Raihan Vadra’s exhibition, No Idea Is Final', at Bikaner House were found to be inconsistent with the policy of the Bikaner House Management Society. Accordingly, their removal was requested," it said, as quoted by news agency PTI."The photographs that are consistent with the Society's policy have continued to be displayed," the statement added.Speaking to ANI, Vadra said the management had first raised concerns about some images 24 hours before the opening.
He said he had asked officials to identify the photographs so that the matter could be discussed, but was approached again on Thursday afternoon, leaving him with only a few hours to address the issue.Vadra alleged that he had shared the exhibition layout a week earlier and questioned why the concerns had not been raised sooner. He also said he had requested written explanations for the proposed removals but had not received specific reasons.
According to Vadra, the management ultimately insisted that none of 70 photographs in question be displayed. He said his team initially turned the framed photographs around before they were subsequently removed and placed in storage. He also alleged that two photographs featuring the Indian national flag had been objected to."I don't know if there was any pressure or anything from anywhere else. I know that it was the management here that decided to, take that decision," he told ANI.

ICC wins EU's top human rights honor while in Trump's crosshair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

The EU awarded its top human rights prize to the International Criminal Court Thursday, defying U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently hit the war crimes tribunal with sweeping sanctions.
"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said Roberta Metsola, chief of the European Parliament, announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize "at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges."
"Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law," said Tomoko Akane, president of the ICC.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick by brick," furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, for war crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after former ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as U.N. human rights chief, received the Nobel Peace Prize this month. U.S. President Donald Trump slammed the choice as "disgraceful," arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of U.S. sanctions, which will come into force in six months and has said it is "ready to take any necessary measures" to make sure the court can continue working.
"The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission independently and without pressure or intimidation," said Ursula von der Leyen, chief of the EU, after the prize was announced.
Brussels hopes to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to persuade the U.S. to reconsider, but it is also considering implementing a "blocking statute" to shield the ICC from Washington.
Established in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organizations to recognize their fight for human rights and democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tundu Lissu, a Tanzanian opposition leader, and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, who represent those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are nominated by the political groups in the EU, and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania's opposition Chadema party, was detained on April 9, 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have been sentenced, respectively, to death and 36 years in prison for taking part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov Prize have been Maria Corina Machado, a Venezuelan opposition chief; the late Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

Missing lift fire door frames confined to Taizoom, Hong Kong authorities say

Inspections into lift safety across Hong Kong have found no missing fire-resistant door frames among contractors other than Taizoom Elevator, authorities have said, after 338 buildings served by the firm were confirmed to lack the crucial components.
The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department provided an update on the checks on Thursday after the government pledged to expand the inspection scope to cover lifts handled by other contractors as well to check whether the problem existed across Hong Kong.
Citywide inspections of lifts serviced by Taizoom were launched on October 16 after fire-resistant door frames were found missing from 48 newly installed lifts at two public housing estates.
The department eventually found that 338 buildings under Taizoom’s service lacked crucial components designed to prevent flames and smoke from entering the shaft in the event of a fire.

Evergrande liquidators recover US$435m in asset sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:35:10 UTC
19:35:10 KST

China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered US$435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about US$46 billion against the developer.
In their second progress report since a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande's liquidation in January 2024, the liquidators, Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong of Alvarez & Marsal, said on Thursday they aimed to make a first interim dividend payment to creditors in the first half of 2027, although the amount has yet to be determined.
Evergrande, once China's top property developer, defaulted on most of its roughly US$300 billion in liabilities.
The liquidators said they had raised the US$435.9 million through the sale of assets including aircraft, artwork and club memberships, as well as the settlement of loan receivables.
They said 96 of the 107 artworks found at Evergrande's Hong Kong headquarters had been sold for US$28.8 million at a loss. The collection included works by Picasso, Monet and Warhol, as well as sculptures by Moore and Hepworth.
Other assets being sold include a private jet expected to fetch about US$12 million in the fourth quarter. The liquidators are also seeking a US$2 million refund from a US university for part of a donation made in 2020. (Reuters)

Peter Thiel Says US Should Not Have Gone to War with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel has voiced opposition to the U.S. war with Iran, saying Washington should not have launched the conflict and putting him at odds with President Donald Trump over a major foreign policy decision of his administration, according to audio obtained by POLITICO’s Decoded.
Thiel made the remarks during a private event on October 12, in his most explicit publicly disclosed comments on the war to date. They came less than two weeks before midterm elections, as Trump’s Republican Party seeks to retain control of Congress.
“I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it,” Thiel said. “There were a lot of mistakes that were made.”
He also questioned whether the United States had sufficient influence to prevail, saying, “Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.”
During the full lecture, Thiel expressed strong opposition to neoconservatives and wars in the Middle East. Despite criticizing the Iran conflict, he reiterated his support for Trump and indicated that he wanted to protect the president.
His comments nevertheless mark one of the clearest instances so far of a prominent Trump ally expressing serious reservations about the war.
The remarks were made during Thiel’s lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has been documenting since it began this fall. In his latest lecture, Thiel also warned extensively about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, referring to comments by Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney, figures from the George W. Bush administration.
“I read the Cheney family’s Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” Thiel said. “And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran.”
Thiel also recounted a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, following the October 7 attack, during which he asked Netanyahu about his plans for Gaza. According to Thiel, the Israeli leader replied, “I can’t just Dresdenize it,” referring to the Allied bombing of Dresden in World War II, which killed approximately 25,000 people.
Thiel was the first major technology investor to support Trump in 2016 and delivered a high-profile speech at the Republican National Convention that year. He was also the largest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance’s Senate campaign in 2022.
POLITICO reported in March that Vance had been “skeptical” of U.S. strikes against Iran in the period leading up to the start of the war.
Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:30:38 BST
19:30:38 KST

Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence.
That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

Meta Sued in Australia Over Alleged Harm to Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:30:04 UTC
19:30:04 KST

Social media giant Meta was hit with a class action lawsuit in Australia on behalf of children and teenagers who allegedly suffered harm over the addictive design features and exposure to harmful content on its platforms Facebook and Instagram.
Australian law firm MinterEllison filed the class action in the country’s Federal Court on Oct. 9. The firm announced the suit on Wednesday, saying it seeks to “recover compensation for both current and former users” of the two Meta social media platforms.
The class action, funded by Sydney-headquartered Litigation Lending Services, was brought in the names of eight unnamed lead applicants. Australia’s Federal Court on Monday ordered a gag on reporting any information that could reveal the applicants’ identities and their statements of claim.
“This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia,” MinterEllison Partner William Nolan said in its press release. “Those questions will now be considered through the Federal Court process.”
TIME reached out to Meta for comment. A spokesperson told Reuters: “We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously.”
The Australian government, which enforced the world’s first social media ban for children under 16, is also set to take action against Meta and other social media companies. In a Bloomberg interview published Tuesday, Communications Minister Anika Wells, a 2026 TIME100 Next honoree, said that the government expects to bring Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, ByteDance’s TikTok, Snapchat, and Google’s YouTube to court for allegedly failing to comply with the country’s laws.
U.S. parallels
The Australian class action follows several civil victories against Meta in the U.S. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $6 million in damages to a 20-year-old plaintiff in a bellwether social media addiction trial. In August, a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay more than $900 million and introduce a slew of reforms to its platforms, including rigorous age verification, time limits for users under 18 years old, and enhanced protection against sextortion and child sexual exploitation. The same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a nationwide lawsuit that alleged its platforms were “addictive” by design and harmed children.
Rob Nicholls, a senior researcher at the University of Sydney with expertise on digital regulations, tells TIME in an email that he was “not surprised” with the class action, given the cases in the U.S.
“The U.S. lawsuits were primarily concerned with negligence,” Nicholls tells TIME. “It’s likely that in Australia the suit will be both negligence and the consequences of the supply of an unsafe product.”
Regulatory enforcement
Australia has led the way in trying to rein in social media platforms in the name of child safety. Last year, it enforced a blanket ban on children under 16 from having social media accounts, a move that other countries have followed.
The effort, however, has been criticized by some, including politicians and digital rights advocates, for not being aggressively enough enforced since the ban took effect in December 2025. The latest data from the country’s online regulator, eSafety, shows that 42% of children aged 10 to 15 still own a social media account.
In a podcast published Thursday, Wells, the Communications Minister, said there was a “great initial response” with 5 million accounts deactivated, but that has since “tapered off.” She added that the eSafety Commissioner believes the five platforms in particular could be doing more to comply with the law and the Commission is investigating potential violations.
Asked why there haven’t been any fines yet, Wells said: “Unfortunately, this isn't a police officer on duty pointing a speeding radar at a car and issuing an on-the-spot fine. This is asking the eSafety Commissioner, our independent regulator, to take on some of the biggest, richest, most resourced companies in the world.”
In September, the Australian government increased the fines for noncompliant social media firms. Failing to take “reasonable steps” to prevent underage Australians from creating or keeping accounts could incur a maximum penalty of 109.2 million Australian dollars (around $76 million).
But speaking to Bloomberg, Wells pointed to the multi-billion-dollar settlement Meta agreed to in the U.S. and said, “I’m not convinced that any particular dollar value is going to change it.” For her, the policy should be measured on how it creates cultural change. “And cultural change,” she said, “takes time.”

I Worked for a Whole Day Using Only the iPhone Duo. Here’s How It Went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

An iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199. An iPad is $449. If you want both—the iPhone as your primary device and the iPad to handle some work when you’re away from your desk—you'll be spending a total dollar amount that’s pretty close to the $1,999 price of Apple’s first folding smartphone, the iPhone Duo.
So can the Duo’s 7.6-inch screen pull double duty as a phone and a workstation? Does it make sense to shell out a few hundred more dollars for a single gadget that can theoretically handle the workload of two devices?
I wrote my entire iPhone Duo review on Apple’s new handset. I used a note-taking app called Bear, which was mercifully optimized for the Duo’s larger screen. (Read my review and you’ll hear about how most apps aren’t optimized; it could take weeks or months for everything to look right.) But surprisingly, I didn’t hate the experience.
I have run this experiment before on Android foldables and even smart glasses with virtual workspaces, but iOS has its own unique hurdles. Notably, iOS doesn’t recognize a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad by default. Instead, you have to go to the phone’s accessibility settings and enable AssistiveTouch—then you’ll get an iPad-like cursor that lets you navigate the Duo’s interface and select text without constantly reaching for the touchscreen.
Even with the cursor, small tasks like pasting hyperlinks into a written piece or quickly Googling topics for additional research are slower and more cumbersome, so I left those for the end when I moved everything into WIRED’s content management system. Even then, I had to switch over to my desktop for the final touches.
Apple also imposes arbitrary multitasking restrictions in iOS because, well, Apple likes to control how people use its devices. For example, if you open two apps in split screen mode, you can only view them in an equal 50-50 split. Unlike most operating systems that let you adjust how much of each app you can see by dragging the border in between the windows, iOS leaves you stuck with a view that gives both apps equal screen space. If you want to use the iPhone in portrait orientation and stack two apps vertically, one on the top part of the screen and the other on the bottom, you’re out of luck. In portrait mode, you can only pin video apps to the top with another app below.
One thing Apple did get right is app pairs. You can “pin” two apps together, and they will live in your Recents, ready when you need them. Say you always want to look at your email and calendar together; you can pair them and find them in Recents whenever you need them. (Tap the bar in the middle to lock and save the pair.)
My keyboard of choice is an old Seenda folding Bluetooth keyboard that is admittedly not very good. I imagine we'll see an array of compact keyboards hitting the market soon—like Nillkin or ProtoArc keyboards already available now—to cater to workaholics who need to work everywhere. I also used one of Apple's cases, the iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand, to keep the phone propped up. You can use various MagSafe kickstands, tripods, or cases with the Duo.
I typed most of the day, but I also had to juggle between apps to respond to coworkers or hop on a Zoom call. Thankfully, the Slack iOS app updated the day before my testing to fully support the iPhone Duo's larger screen and vertical navigation, making it very easy to bounce between multiple conversations in the two-pane view. I still think Apple should add a feature like the iPad's Slide Over, where you can “hide” a floating app off to the side and bring it back in when you need it. It’d be the perfect spot for messaging apps like Slack, WhatsApp, or Messages, and it wouldn’t interrupt your split screen experience.
Zoom wasn’t optimized for the Duo, though my editor said the video quality from the inner and outer selfie cameras was “really good.” I used the folio kickstand to Zoom on the big 7.6-inch screen until we realized my video was stuck in an awkward portrait orientation, so I laid the phone down on the table and pointed the 5.4-inch outer screen toward my face, which made it feel like a traditional laptop experience.
The app that annoyed me the most was Gmail. Even though Google updated the Google Search app to be compatible with the iPhone Duo early this week, the rest of Google's workspace apps currently look awful on the Duo. I imagine full support will come very soon, if not on Friday, when the Duo officially launches. The two-pane view in Gmail (or any email app) is a game changer for clearing a bunch of emails when you’re on the go.
By 6 pm, battery life was sitting around 45 percent, which is very impressive. That's with around six hours of screen-on time.
You probably won’t want to replace your laptop with the iPhone Duo. And anyone accustomed to the iPad’s larger screen may feel cramped on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas. But with a kickstand and the right portable keyboard? Knocking out focused, light work on the Duo is entirely doable. Things will get even more interesting once Apple Pencil support arrives later this year.
But as I packed up my keyboard, I couldn’t shake a familiar feeling. Maybe we’ll realize a single do-it-all device isn’t as great as it’s chalked up to be. Maybe it is better to kick back with a dedicated MP3 player. Or snap photos with a camera. Or write in a notebook. Or work off a laptop.
Speaking of which, did you hear Apple’s making a touchscreen MacBook?

Kazakhstan eyes localizing satellite manufacturing
Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov held a series of bilateral meetings with international companies on the sidelines of the ninth Kazakhstan Global Investment Roundtable (KGIR-2026) in Shymkent, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the government’s press service.
The meetings brought together representatives of Aksa Energy, Carlsberg Kazakhstan, Solico Group and CONTEC. Discussions covered ongoing and prospective investment projects in energy, agribusiness, food production and the space sector.
The parties examined prospects for expanding cooperation, developing processing industries and introducing new technologies in line with the priorities set by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Increasing the share of local content was also a key focus.
During a meeting with Aksa Energy CEO and Executive Committee Chairman Naci Ağbal, Bektenov discussed the results of the company’s cooperation with Kazakhstan and prospects for new energy projects.
The sides highlighted the launch of a combined-cycle power plant in Kyzylorda, valued at 215 billion tenge. The facility, with an electrical capacity of 240 MW and a thermal capacity of 277 Gcal per hour, entered commercial operation in June 2026. It is designed to meet the region’s growing demand for electricity and heat.
Further investment plans by Aksa Energy in Kazakhstan were also discussed.
At a meeting with Carlsberg Kazakhstan CEO Vyacheslav Maltsev, the discussions focused on food industry development, production localization and export expansion.
Carlsberg Kazakhstan has become the official distributor of PepsiCo products in Kazakhstan. As part of the cooperation between the two companies, a $344 million soft drinks plant was launched in Almaty region on October 1, 2026.
The facility supplies the domestic market and is also intended to serve export markets. It has created 230 permanent jobs.
Local content currently accounts for 71.5% of Carlsberg Kazakhstan’s operations. The meeting also addressed opportunities to expand cooperation with domestic suppliers of raw materials and packaging materials.
Bektenov also met with Alireza Mohammad Rahimi, CEO and Board Member of Solico Group in the CIS countries, to discuss construction of a cheese manufacturing plant in Almaty region.
The project represents an investment of nearly 45 billion tenge and is expected to have an annual production capacity of 41,000 tons. It is projected to create around 450 permanent jobs.
Construction and installation work is ongoing, with the facility scheduled to begin operations in 2029.
The sides also considered prospects for establishing additional processing facilities in Kazakhstan’s agricultural regions. Such projects are expected to support the expansion of exports of domestically produced goods.
During talks with CONTEC founder and CEO Lee Sung-hee, the sides discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in the space industry.
The proposals include joint production of satellites and satellite components in Kazakhstan, development of ground infrastructure and localization of selected manufacturing processes.
The discussions also covered the use of artificial intelligence to process satellite data, cooperation in training Kazakhstani specialists and opportunities to export jointly manufactured products to international markets.
Kazakhstan is seeking to attract new investment and implement projects focused on producing high-value-added goods. Prime Minister Bektenov instructed the relevant ministries and responsible organizations to provide the necessary support for investment projects.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan and Chinese company advance a $1 billion Kuryk port project.

In Iowa stronghold, Trump urges Republicans to turn out and vote
SIOUX CITY, Iowa, Oct 22 - President Donald Trump on Thursday tried to galvanize Republican voters in Iowa, a state he won by double digits two years ago but now faces a tougher battle in the November midterm elections due to dissatisfaction with rising prices and the Iran war.
The Midwestern stop is part of Trump's push through states Republicans usually expect to win, but where polling points to some tight races.
Trump held a rally in Sioux City as Republicans defend a Senate seat, three House districts and the governor's office, giving Democrats an opening after years of Republican gains.
"Pretend I'm on the ballot, because if you get out, we're going to win big," Trump told the crowd gathered in an airport hangar.
He has spoken repeatedly with confidence about his connection with voters, though his approval rating has fallen and some Republicans Trump is trying to help have broken with him over the Iran war, as higher fuel and grocery prices deepen voters' economic worries.
Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, who also addressed the Sioux City rally, has called for an "immediate end" to the war, saying Iowans should not bear higher fuel or grocery prices because of it. She is in a close Senate race against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek.
"If we lose this seat here in Iowa, the Democrats will control the US Senate. Mark my words," she said on Thursday.
Republican Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, facing difficult reelection races, joined Democrats last month in voting to limit Trump's war powers in Iran.
"The only thing is the fuel prices that are hurting him more than anything," said rally attendee Ron Sitzmann, 73, a semi-retired parts and service director for an automotive company in Iowa, adding that he thought prices would drop once the conflict ended.
"I just wish it would happen sooner than later because it’s kind of dragging on," said Sitzmann, who remains a strong Trump supporter.
'PREACHING TO THE CHOIR'
Trump was in Iowa to back his party's candidates but used the platform to attack Democrats from other states, including Somali American Minnesota lawmaker Ilhan Omar, suggesting that she should quit Congress in the wake of a raid by federal agents on her home.
Omar says the government is being weaponized to target her as a political enemy of Trump's, who has been ramping up anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric in recent weeks.
In the Iowa races, Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in recent polling for governor, while Democrats are targeting an open House seat in the state's second congressional district.
Republican losses would be a setback for Trump in a state where his popularity helped the party build a commanding advantage.
The Senate and House races could help decide control of Congress, shaping his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years.
Republicans also worry about rural voters who powered Trump's Iowa victories, with farmers facing higher costs and trade uncertainty.
A Marist poll this month found 42% of likely voters said their finances had worsened over the past year, including more than half of independents. Thirty-five percent viewed their vote as a vote against Trump, versus 21% who saw it as a vote for him.
Trump's Iowa stop follows rallies earlier this week in Kansas for Senator Roger Marshall and South Carolina for Senator Darline Graham, where the Republicans are defending seats.
"We know he’s preaching to the choir," said Harlan Grau, 70, a staunch Trump supporter and pig farmer from Iowa. The rallies encourage supporters to "go out and get them 10 people to go to the polls with us," he added.
Trump's campaign swing comes as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either presidential term, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday. The survey found 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
At recent rallies, his economic message has largely avoided the financial pressures facing many Americans. The Iran war has driven up gas prices, compounding broader cost-of-living concerns, while Trump has repeatedly promised prices will fall when the conflict ends.
Behind the scenes, Trump has questioned campaign spending, criticized redistricting efforts and second-guessed candidate choices, according to people familiar with the matter.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the people's characterizations, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Publicly, Trump has noted the tendency of a president's party to lose seats in midterm elections. REUTERS

How would a Netanyahu election loss change Israel’s policies towards the Palestinians?
