How would a Netanyahu election loss change Israel’s policies towards the Palestinians?
- Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot both reject an independent Palestinian state and would keep Israeli security control. This means no major shift away from the two-state solution's collapse.
- They differ on West Bank settlements. Netanyahu backs rapid expansion, while Eisenkot wants only legal settlements, removal of illegal outposts, and less settler violence.
- In Gaza, both say troops stay until Hamas disarms and fighting may resume. Eisenkot says Hamas rule is a failure and wants it replaced within 18 months.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot both oppose an independent Palestinian state, meaning next week’s election is unlikely to produce a sweeping shift in policies that have hampered a decades-old peace process.
Three years since the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023, attacks, they also share hawkish positions towards Gaza, saying they would resume the war there if the militant group, whose founding charter calls for Israel’s destruction, does not disarm.
But they differ on their positions on settlements in the occupied West Bank, and are likely to rely on different coalition partners to form governments, which could broadly set the country on diverging paths.
Here is a look at the candidates’ views on the conflict with the Palestinians:
West Bank settlements
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis live in the West Bank, settling in territory Israel captured in a 1967 war, a practice nearly all countries consider illegal under international law, although Israel disputes this.
Netanyahu has presided over a rapid expansion of settlements, including small outposts in parts of the West Bank reserved for civil administration by the Palestinian Authority, where settlements are illegal under Israel’s own laws. Settlers have increasingly attacked Palestinians, and critics say the government has turned a blind eye to such violence.
Eisenkot favours settlement in principle, but says that it should comply with Israeli law. He opposes settlements built without authorisation, would dismantle outposts in areas where they are forbidden, and has pledged to prevent violence by settlers against Palestinians.
He also opposes a decision by the Netanyahu government to build in territory known as E1, which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, which settlers say is intended to “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state.
Palestinian self-rule
In a sign of how far Israeli politics has shifted to the right, Netanyahu and Eisenkot, along with the leaders of nearly all other Jewish-led parties, oppose the establishment of a future independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.
This effectively repudiates the two-state solution that underpinned international peace negotiations for generations.
Netanyahu and Eisenkot both say Israel must retain ultimate security control over all territory between the Jordan River and Mediterranean Sea.
There are, however, differences in their emphasis. Eisenkot’s position on limiting settlements in the West Bank would reserve territory where Palestinians now exercise civil self rule. Netanyahu’s coalition includes parties that openly call for Israel to fully annex occupied Palestinian land.
Gaza
Three years since Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, prompting an Israeli invasion of the Gaza Strip, and a year since a US-brokered ceasefire ended major combat there, Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of the enclave.
Nearly the entire population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives in the remaining third, mainly in tents or damaged buildings, still under the full political control of Hamas. US-brokered talks have so far failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm, Israel to withdraw and reconstruction to begin under international auspices.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu say Israeli troops will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is disarmed, and that Israel is prepared to restart fighting to achieve this.
Eisenkot says the continued rule of Hamas in Gaza is a profound failure, and that within 18 months of taking office he would ensure that the Hamas administration had been replaced, either through a US-brokered plan or through military force.
Coalition partners
Netanyahu’s governing coalition now includes far-right Jewish nationalist groups led by settler activists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who support full annexation of Palestinian land and are under sanctions in several Western countries for promoting settler violence.
Netanyahu also relies on ultra-Orthodox parties that seek exemptions from military service for Jewish religious students.
Opposition parties likely to be courted by Eisenkot for a future coalition to unseat Netanyahu include several right-wing groups, but none with leaders as extreme as Smotrich or Ben-Gvir. His supporters are mainly opposed to the military exemption for religious students, which probably rules out an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox.
To unseat Netanyahu, Eisenkot is likely to require the support of the Democrats, which include the rump of the centre-left Labour Party that dominated Israeli politics for generations but has dwindled as the country has shifted to the right. The Democrats are now the only prominent Jewish-led party that supports a two-state solution.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have both said they would not form a government with parties primarily representing Israeli citizens of Palestinian descent, who comprise around a fifth of the population. REUTERS

Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:10:23 UTC
19:10:23 KST

Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.
- Share:
Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.
Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.
Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded
Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.
Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.
Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.
"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."
Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth
To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.
These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.
The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.
"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."
The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.
Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.
Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues
Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.
"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."
One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.
Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.
What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution
The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.
They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.
Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lidiia Tynianskaia, Cesar Mateo Bastidas-Betancourt, Esther Marie Grewe, Julia Marie Kniep, Neringa Liutikaite, Nesil Esiyok, İrfan Burak Göloğlu, Sabrina Heide, Nancy Rüger, Dimitri Lindenwald, Charis Drummer, Stoyan Petkov, Nataliya Di Donato, Michael Heide. Coordinated neural progenitor adaptations contribute to primate neocortical downscaling. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (39) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5563

Trump's tax-exempt diesel draws skepticism from farmers, eludes others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:06:52 UTC
19:06:52 KST

Trump's tax-exempt diesel draws skepticism from farmers, eludes others
CHICAGO, Oct 22 - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel as soaring prices frustrate voters ahead of midterm elections. But farmers say it is too risky to use the fuel on public roads, while some other drivers do not have access to it.
Trump has sought to lower prices and boost his sagging approval ratings through a series of actions focused on fuel, including an $8 billion financial support program he announced on Monday to offset diesel costs for farmers during the autumn harvest.
His administration also relaxed sanctions on Russian fuel shipments, pushed allies to release emergency oil stocks and temporarily lifted restrictions on foreign-flagged vessels moving between US ports. Still, prices remain elevated because of the US-led war with Iran.
Trump said his executive order would temporarily waive an off-road requirement for red-dyed diesel, which is generally sold for use in farm equipment. Red diesel is essentially the same as regular or clear diesel but exempt from highway fuel taxes. It is dyed red to indicate highway taxes have not been paid.
Farmers said potential savings from using dyed diesel in semi-trucks on highways were too small to justify the risk of red residue staying in fuel tanks after the order expires. States have their own taxes and rules for red diesel use, and can fine drivers thousands of dollars if authorities inspect fuel tanks and find signs red diesel was used improperly on public roads.
The Internal Revenue Service said it would not impose a penalty when dyed diesel is used on highways from October 1 to December 31 but that Trump's order had no effect on state taxes and penalties.
"In my mind, it's not anywhere near worth the risk," said Glenn Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, who raises crops and cattle near Wamego, Kansas. "That residue might be in there for years."
FINES UP TO $10,000 IN KANSAS
Farmers use the most diesel during the autumn harvest season, burning dyed fuel in tractors, combines and other machinery. Under Trump's order, they could also use red diesel to haul crops to market in semi-trucks normally fueled by clear diesel, if allowed by states.
Kansas, a major grain producer, prohibits using dyed diesel on public roadways unless it is purchased lawfully outside the state. Violators can be charged with a felony, have their driver's license suspended, and face penalties of $1,000 to $10,000, according to the Kansas Department of Revenue.
Governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat, said the state could not legally implement Trump's order as drafted. The Kansas Highway Patrol was concerned it "would result in law enforcement difficulties once red dye diesel returns to its normal usage restrictions," she said in a statement.
Democrats hope surging farm costs can help revive their support in the Republican heartland in November's midterm elections.
Trump wants lower fuel prices, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said.
"President Trump remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance, cutting costs, and putting more money back in the pockets of hardworking American families," Rogers said.
For Jay Sorg, a fifth-generation farmer in New Richland, Minnesota, the order could save $1,500 to $2,000, but that is not enough to offset higher costs for fuel and other inputs. Like many farmers, he buys diesel in advance to store in tanks.
"In the grand scheme of our business, it's kind of inconsequential, especially when we already have fuel bought and in the tank for highway use," Sorg said. "It's a move to try to win votes."
Ryan Wagner, a farmer in Roslyn, South Dakota, worried that increasing usage of tax-exempt red diesel could drain government funds used to maintain roads.
"It's a very short-sighted plan that could come back and haunt us in the future," he said.
LIMITED ACCESS
For other motorists, it can be hard to get their hands on red diesel.
Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican, issued a proclamation that allows vehicles to use dyed diesel on highways until February, but only if they are hauling specific agricultural products.
In Texas, drivers must register with the state to take advantage of a temporary suspension of restrictions on the use of red diesel on highways.
A Reuters reporter visited four sites around Houston that were listed online as selling red diesel by companies that offer fuel cards to commercial operators. Three of the sites sold only commercial diesel, and red diesel pumps at the fourth site were not working. A notice at the fourth site said red diesel was purely for agricultural use and should not be used on roads.
Vincenzo Lasalosi, a firefighter in Houston, said he considered using red diesel in his Ram 2500 truck due to high diesel prices but did not know where to find it.
"Even if I do find it, it's probably too far and not worth the drive to fill it up," he said. REUTERS

As Trump's support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:06:33 UTC
19:06:33 KST

As Trump’s support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
BLYTHEWOOD, South Carolina – US President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
With Republicans on the defensive amid record-low approval ratings for Trump, strong evangelical turnout could help the party limit losses driven by voter frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran.
That loyalty was on display last week at Village Church, an evangelical congregation in Blythewood, South Carolina, where hundreds of worshippers gathered for a weekly “Bible and Politics” sermon by pastor Erik Estep. The backdrop: an unexpectedly competitive race for a Republican-held US Senate seat.
Speaking in the main worship hall, framed by a giant video screen and concert-style lighting, Estep did not endorse a candidate or party. But as he spoke against gambling, following sermons on abortion and socialism, he urged his predominantly white parishioners to view politics through a biblical lens.
“I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation,” Estep said from the stage. “And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally.”
The message resonated with Karen Whiting, a 72-year-old retired pharmaceutical executive who plans to vote for Republican Darline Graham over Annie Andrews, the Democrat. Graham was appointed by the governor to fill the seat of her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.
Whiting cited concerns that Democrats would allow transgender girls and women to compete in female sports, echoing other white evangelicals Reuters interviewed in South Carolina last week who prioritised social and religious issues over economic concerns.
“I’m voting for biblical principles, and I do not believe the Democratic Party stands for biblical principles,” Whiting said. “Without God, this country’s going to fail.”
If visitors to Village Church needed more explicit guidance on how to vote, a candidate guide available in the church lobby left little doubt. Produced by the conservative Christian advocacy group Palmetto Family Council and distributed to churches across South Carolina, it awarded Graham green check marks on all seven issues it rated, including restrictions on abortion medication and gender-affirming care, while Andrews received mostly red X’s.
Andrews offered a different reading of evangelical voters’ priorities. In a statement to Reuters, she said she had visited evangelical churches and met voters of various faiths, political persuasions and backgrounds, finding that they were chiefly concerned about the economy. “They’re struggling with the cost of everything. That’s why I’m running,” she said.
Strong bonds
Reuters/Ipsos polling shows Trump’s support among white evangelicals fell to 63% in October from 77% in January 2025. The decline is slightly smaller than his drop among the electorate as a whole, from 47% to 31%, and white evangelicals remain the only major demographic group tracked by Reuters/Ipsos where his support tops 60%.
The thrice-married Trump’s bond with white evangelicals has survived a decade of scandals and investigations, including dozens of allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies, and a hush-money case involving a porn star. The question for Republicans is whether economic pressures and unhappiness over the Iran war, now in its eighth month, are weakening that bond.
Reuters interviews with 15 people at two South Carolina churches suggested that his hold on white evangelical voters remained strong. At Village Church and Carolina Baptist Church in the city of Spartanburg, about a 90-minute drive from Blythewood, only two of the 15 said they were considering Andrews, and none indicated they were abandoning Trump.
While several voiced frustration with the Iran conflict and rising gas prices, most said they trusted Trump to keep Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon or, like Trump, blamed inflation on policies enacted under Democratic president Joe Biden.
Chad Connelly, an evangelical activist who heads the Christian voter-engagement group Faith Wins, said that while evangelicals “don’t like paying higher prices”, they are equally animated by social issues. Concerns about transgender athletes are “really playing everywhere” across the nearly two dozen states he has visited this election cycle, he said.
White evangelicals’ loyalty to Trump reflects what Robert P. Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, a non-profit organisation that studies religion and politics, calls a “grand bargain” forged during the 2016 election.
Many evangelicals have overlooked his personal conduct in exchange for his commitment to curtail abortion and LGBTQ rights, advance a conservative Christian vision of American life and pursue strict immigration policies that some supporters see as preserving the country’s white Christian identity, Jones said.
“That has proven to be more powerful for this group than what they’re having to pay at the gas pump,” Jones, who has written extensively about the rise of Christian nationalism in American politics, told Reuters.
Why evangelicals matter
White evangelicals make up about 13% of US adults but nearly a third of Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, according to a PRRI survey and a validated-voter analysis by the non-partisan Pew Research Center. More than 80% voted for Trump in each of his three presidential campaigns, according to Pew. They differ sharply from black Protestant evangelicals, who overwhelmingly support Democrats.
Evangelicals’ loyalty could also prove pivotal in Senate races beyond South Carolina that may help determine control of Congress, including in Iowa and Kansas, where white evangelicals make up a significant share of the electorate.
Opinion polls suggest the race in South Carolina is close. This week Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning pollster, released a survey showing Andrews trailing Graham by 3 percentage points.
Part of Graham’s challenge stems from lingering unease among some conservatives over her appointment to the Senate seat. Even after a boost from Trump, the political newcomer only narrowly defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in the party’s August run-off, underscoring questions among some Republicans about her experience and conservative credentials.
A spokesperson for the Graham campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Yet even evangelicals lukewarm on Graham, like 53-year-old Kevin Thomas, said they felt they had no choice. Thomas, who attended the Village Church sermon, said he did not trust Andrews on transgender issues, despite a recent campaign ad in which she said she opposed both transgender women competing in women’s sports and gender-affirming surgical operations for minors.
“I’m leaning towards holding my nose and voting for Graham,” said Thomas, who had backed Norman. “I’m not willing to sacrifice six years of having a Democrat representing us in South Carolina.” REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hsinchu-based Elan Microelectronics Co. presented integrated drone technologies at the 2026 Taitronics trade show on Thursday, including a ground control station for defense and commercial use, the Commercial Times reported.
The three-day event runs from Tuesday to Thursday, during which Elan highlighted its drone station. Its touchscreen uses LED lighting for all-weather visibility, is waterproof, and supports fingerprint recognition for added security.
Elan Microelectronics Chair Yeh I-hau (葉儀晧) said the station processes video feeds from drones to identify and track targets. He noted that the station offers different interfaces for combat, rescue, and patrol missions.
Yeh said the station is expected to enter production in the second quarter of 2027. He said each unit could cost more than NT$100,000 (US$3,072), or up to NT$300,000 including communication modules.
Elan has also partnered with Ubec to combine AI vision with controller technology. Yeh said video compression causes latency, while communication quality affects drone performance.
Yeh said the technology is still being developed and improved. He added that communication and high-performance computing chips will be manufactured using a 28-nanometer process.
Elan's AI vision system uses four camera lenses for forward and downward vision up to 30 meters away and will be integrated with flight controls. Elan is also training drone swarms through simulations.
For drone landings, Elan said it is working to increase its detection range from 6 meters to 10 meters. It has sent samples for evaluation and expects mass production later this year.

Taiwan’s Arctic Ocean data made available to researchers worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:04:55 UTC
19:04:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Seawater temperature and salinity data collected by the National Academy of Marine Research (NAMR) during a 2024 Arctic scientific expedition have been archived on PANGAEA, an international platform for Earth and environmental sciences.
Fang Ying-chih (方盈智), an associate professor in National Sun Yat-sen University’s oceanography department, and NAMR associate research fellow Fu Ke-hsien (傅科憲) traveled aboard the German research vessel Polarstern from August to October 2024, per Liberty Times. The ship crossed the Arctic Ocean and passed through the North Pole.
Fu recorded oceanographic data along the route using expendable conductivity-temperature-depth probes to measure seawater temperature and salinity, according to Liberty Times. The measurements were taken between approximately 80 degrees north latitude and the North Pole.
The academy made two datasets publicly available on PANGAEA, covering raw and processed data, Liberty Times reported. It also released a comprehensive report, enabling international researchers to trace the data’s origins, processing procedures, and quality-control methods.
The academy said the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany and the University of Bremen’s Center for Marine Environmental Sciences jointly operate PANGAEA.

Greenlight Family Hub (2026): Finally, a Digital Wall Calendar With a Voice Assistant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

I set up a digital wall calendar at a friend’s house a couple of months ago. Her first question was one I’ve constantly asked myself as I test these devices in my own home: “Does it have a voice assistant?”
It feels like the one thing missing from these devices. Digital wall calendars have been on the rise in popularity this year, driven by the popularity of the Skylight Calendar. After testing multiple models in my own home, I can see why. These devices take any and all of the digital calendars you already have (Google Calendar, iCalendar, Outlook Calendar—you name it) and put them onto a single device in your home.
It’s great if you’re like my husband and me, who live by our Google Calendars but don’t want to be tied to our phones when discussing plans. These devices can also double as household management tools with meal planning, chore trackers, to-do lists, photo screen savers that double as a digital photo frame, and even financial management for your kids if you go with the Greenlight Family Hub.
The Greenlight Family Hub has been an interesting device in the world of digital calendars because of how many features it offers. It not only adds financial management, as the company was originally a banking tool for parents and their teens, but family location tracking, which uses the Greenlight app on a family member’s phone to show their location, or a GPS tracker that you can separately purchase for younger children.
But there’s one feature behind the paywall (a $10-a-month membership) that finally satisfies the thing I’ve always wanted: a voice assistant.
Greenlight’s proprietary voice assistant has been both easy to use and has given smart, thoughtful answers. So why isn’t there a voice assistant in every digital wall calendar? And conversely, why haven’t smart displays that do have smart voice assistants gained features like full-page calendars and chore charts?
Not Just a Calendar
Part of what makes Greenlight’s hub different from other digital calendars is that the company is using the calendar as a starting point for the offerings it already has. That’s also why it’s called the Family Hub instead of just a calendar like most other devices I’ve tested. Greenlight grew from a banking tool to a way to manage chores and money for kids and teens, and has now become a full family management platform where you can track your family’s calendars, chores, kids’ spending, and even family locations.
Greenlight says it noticed the lack of voice support among competitors’ offerings and baked that into its hub intentionally. “Voice assistants have been around for over a decade, yet when building the specs for Family Hub, we noticed that voice support was absent in the digital calendar market," says Sushil Sharma, chief product officer at Greenlight. "Our goal with Hub was to create an all-in-one command center for busy families to engage with technology in a way that feels natural and seamless. By combining a voice assistant feature with a centralized home display, we are able to limit the number of devices families need in their home.”
It’s also smart for families with younger children—Sharma pointed out that not all kids can read and type fluently, and voice support makes it more accessible for them and the rest of the family. But it’s also a way people are expecting to interact with their home devices after years of smart speakers and smartphones offering voice support.
Voice Report
Greenlight’s assistant reminds me of the modern, AI-powered iterations of Alexa and Google because it’s also powered by AI. Greenlight says its family AI assistant uses frontier large language models with Greenlight’s own proprietary safety tools that it designed with family safety in mind. That means the assistant shouldn’t get into sensitive or inappropriate topics (or accidentally tell your child Santa isn’t real) but will both schedule a timer and answer day-to-day questions. You’ll also see a conversation appear on the right-hand side, reminding me a lot of the Alexa+ experience on an Echo Show device.
Greenlight’s Hub is supposed to only wake at its wake phrase, “Hey Greenlight,” but in the days I’ve been testing it, I’ve found it to be a little sensitive and likely to wake at random. It also tends to keep listening, waiting to see if you’ll continue the conversation or give a new command, so if my family is having a general conversation after asking a question, Greenlight will try to pick up a question from that and answer it. I find myself often ordering Greenlight to stop.
That isn’t an issue just for Greenlight. My Google Gemini-powered smart speaker does the same thing, and both my son and I are quick to yell, “Google, stop!” to get it to stop trying to answer a question we didn’t ask. It’s a problem with these AI-powered voice assistants overall, but I’m finding I’d rather say the wake word multiple times than get interrupted.
Big Brother Energy
When I described to my editor the laundry list of features that the Greenlight Family Hub has, she said it sounded like a “Big Brother machine.” I see why, of course—tracking your location and financial information in a device that sounds like a simple calendar might come as a surprise to most people. It was certainly a surprise to me when I went to set up the hub through the app and ended up stuck on the financial pathway (Greenlight says it’s fixing this issue in the app but I had to have support clear my information so I could set up the hub without setting up a bank card for my child).
Still, I like how much it has to offer, even if it might feel a tad Big Brother-y for some. And while it does have a microphone, it doesn’t have a camera like most smart displays have, so in that sense it feels less creepy to me than other devices I’ve had in my home.
I also really like that most of the features are accessible without needing a premium subscription—notably the photo screen saver feature, which Skylight will charge you for. (Skylight’s business model in general has become charging for storage, for both its calendars and digital photo frames.) Greenlight charges instead for its AI assistant and voice interaction, along with family location sharing. If you’re less voice-inclined than I am, you’d be plenty happy with this hub without the premium subscription.
I am hoping we see more digital wall calendars add at least some kind of voice assistance, as well as offering some control of your smart home devices. Maybe I’m biased coming from a background in smart home technology, but it feels like a huge missed opportunity. Smart displays have existed for years (and Apple just announced its first one) but have lacked the key feature that digital wall calendars have to really make them a touch point in the home beyond your voice. I reached out to both Amazon and Skylight to ask why neither has introduced any such model yet, but both companies declined to comment.
Maybe, for a company like Skylight, it’s the cost of creating an assistant that would work with its platform and needing to change its hardware to include a microphone, but Amazon is well positioned to bring something like this to the market (especially since the newest version of Alexa, Alexa+, is already paywalled). I’m hopeful we’ll see the next generation of smart displays at least make some kind of calendar mode an option; I’d certainly rather see my calendar than another ad or piece of screen clutter on my Echo Show.
Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. Get best-in-class reporting and exclusive subscriber content that’s too important to ignore. Subscribe Today.

Ministers restate plan for combined force of 13 Type 26 frigates
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:57 BST
19:00:57 KST

Ministers have restated that a combined force of thirteen Type 26 frigates with Norway is expected to enter service from the late 2020s, with five Type 31 frigates in service by the early 2030s, and that the Type 23 fleet will go through phased retirement, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase the lifespan of the Type 23 frigate fleet.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, the Ministry of Defence will be implementing a phased retirement Type 23 Frigates after decades of proud and faithful service.
“The Government is investing in: new autonomous surface vessels; autonomous sub-surface; an amphibious fleet with the Netherlands; future Common Combat Vessels; and delivering a combined force of 13 Type 26 frigates with Norway expected to enter service from the late 2020s; five Type 31 frigates expected to be in service by the early 2030s; and new Fleet Solid Support ships.
“To avoid compromising operational security, the Ministry of Defence does not routinely disclose individual out of service dates or specific in-service dates for warships to avoid revealing elements of the Fleet’s long-term schedule. However, the Royal Navy continues to ensure that it has sufficient assets available to deliver operational outputs.”
Norway selected the Type 26 this year, ordering at least five ships to replace its Fridtjof Nansen class and signing a strategic partnership with Britain that runs beyond the hulls to joint operations, shared support and common training. Britain is building eight at Govan and Scotstoun, and the thirteen figure counts both navies as one force, which is how the partnership has been presented since the Norwegian decision.
The Type 23s are the ships carrying the burden in the meantime. Designed for a sixteen year life in the Cold War, several have served more than thirty years, and the general purpose ships have been leaving as their refits became uneconomic. Westminster and Argyll both went early after surveys found work that could not be justified, and the remaining hulls are the towed array ships that hunt submarines.

Indonesia haze: why Jakarta won’t declare wildfires a national disaster
Indonesia resists declaring the wildfires a national disaster despite health crises, facing criticism over political and budget priorities
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Resty Woro Yuniarin Jakarta
Indonesia’s government has resisted mounting calls to declare widespread forest and land fires a national disaster, insisting it can handle the crisis alone as residents report worsening health impacts and disaster experts warn that a broader, coordinated response is needed.
Critics suggest the reluctance may stem from concerns that a national declaration could force Jakarta to redirect funds from other political priorities, while exposing the administration to greater scrutiny over its disaster response.
The dispute intensified on Tuesday – the second anniversary of President Prabowo Subianto’s administration – when student protesters across the country demanded a national disaster declaration, the restoration of damaged ecosystems and action against both the rising cost of living and the perceived erosion of democracy.
A similar demand was included in a class-action lawsuit filed by civil society and indigenous groups in West Kalimantan last month, though the government maintains the fires do not warrant such a designation.
“If a national disaster is declared, there will inevitably be those who exploit the situation. Disaster management is now nationally mandated, no longer the responsibility of regional governments,” Dudung Abdurachman, Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, told reporters on Wednesday.

Press review: Russia-US-Ukraine peace hopes rise as Moscow offers Iran-US mediation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The prospects for peace and trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine following the October 21 St. Petersburg meeting; Moscow’s willingness to mediate between Tehran and Washington; and Russia’s potential agreement with the US to start shipping fertilizers alongside diesel. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Chances of peace and Russia-US-Ukraine talks following St. Petersburg meeting
US efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have resumed, perhaps the main visible and indisputable outcome of the October 21 talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The envoy left Russia with news of the release of an American citizen from a Russian prison and Moscow’s assurances that the proposals he brought would be reviewed. In addition, Putin expressed readiness to launch trilateral talks in the Russia-US-Ukraine format. The talks are scheduled for mid-November, after the US congressional elections, which are likely to bring significant changes.
Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg wrapped up a busy diplomatic round, international affairs expert Nikolay Novik told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The St. Petersburg talks were preceded by consultations in Oslo. Witkoff and Kushner, who participated remotely, met with Zelensky, European leaders, and EU and NATO representatives there, the expert recalled. "It is likely that Witkoff presented an updated plan to end the conflict and a proposal for direct talks involving Trump and Zelensky. There may also have been discussions about a meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping in China during the APEC summit on November 18-19: Washington doesn’t need a technical pause, but rather an outcome from the summit that can be presented as a tangible result," Novik said.
At the same time, the package of conditions that the US envoy might have brought - if these were the ones recently mentioned in the Western media - does not suit Russia, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin told Vedomosti. According to the expert, Moscow agreed to discuss not so much the settlement itself as possible ways to establish a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends. "By 2027, we will most likely still be in the midst of ongoing hostilities, though the US administration had certainly hoped to achieve tangible results by the end of this year," Trenin noted. The expert stressed that the future prospects of the negotiation process, including the development of specific terms, will be determined by the actual situation on the battlefield.
The current round of talks differs from previous ones because the agenda will include the issue of security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, an issue that was not included in negotiations with Kiev following the Istanbul consultations, Nikolay Silayev, a leading researcher at the MGIMO Institute of International Relations, said. However, the expert does not expect the upcoming negotiations with Ukraine to conclude any differently from the previous ones. "The main reason for the lack of confidence in a breakthrough is the public statements made by Ukrainian and European officials. Their position remains the same: an unconditional ceasefire," he stressed.
Izvestia: Russia ready to mediate between Tehran and Washington
Moscow is prepared to act as a mediator in settling the conflict between the US and Iran, provided both parties are interested. Talks between Washington and Tehran have reached an impasse, partly due to the unresolved question of Iran’s nuclear program. Russia previously proposed transporting Iran’s enriched uranium to its territory, but this initiative has yet to receive support.
The eight-month conflict between the US and Iran has stalled. Washington’s initial plan to quickly topple the country’s government has failed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains difficult, and diplomats have yet to make progress toward resolving the conflict. Under these circumstances, Russia could assume the role of mediator. Moscow is ready to take such a step, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "If all parties express interest, then we are ready [to act as mediators]," he noted. "We previously offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program could be resolved, but our proposals have not yet been supported," the senior diplomat said.
Thanks to its good relations with both Iran and Israel, Russia occupies a unique position as a universal intermediary in the Middle East, political analyst Alexander Kargin said. Moreover, Moscow is currently pursuing a negotiating track with the US as well. The expert noted that Pakistan, another potential mediator, has no diplomatic relations with Israel at all, whereas Russia does not face this problem.
Russian mediation would at least help establish a ceasefire, paving the way for a comprehensive resolution of the crisis, Kargin said. The analyst expects that, ultimately, the practical necessity of Moscow’s involvement will prevail, and the parties will bring Russia into the negotiations. At the same time, according to him, the parties to the conflict have diametrically opposed views on the nuclear program. While Russia’s proposal to remove the uranium would be ideal, heightened tensions in the Middle East are preventing the parties from making even the smallest compromises, Kargin stressed.
Izvestia: Russia may begin exporting fertilizers to US alongside diesel
Russia is ready to supply mineral fertilizers and fuel to the US, but expanding fertilizer exports would require a reallocation of shipments: currently, about 69% of fertilizer production is exported, experts said. Russian President Vladimir Putin has discussed the prospect of supplying fertilizers to the US market on a significant scale. In addition, the first shipment of 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel is scheduled to leave for the US on October 22, with other countries set to receive shipments by the end of the year.
During a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on October 21, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow could supply fertilizers to the American market in large quantities. However, it is difficult to gauge potential export volumes, since a significant portion of Russian production is already under contract with foreign buyers, Denis Prikhodko, an equity market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, told Izvestia. According to him, shipments will increase gradually, primarily through the redistribution of export flows among foreign markets rather than through higher production.
Increasing fertilizer and diesel fuel shipments to the US market could help bring down prices for these products both in the US and globally, which is especially important for agricultural producers. Such agreements with Russia would benefit both the Donald Trump administration and the Russian authorities, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed.
The European factor is also relevant. According to political scientist and German studies expert Yegor Belyachkov, the current leadership of most European countries will likely react negatively to an agreement between Russia and the US on fertilizer supplies, just as they did with the diesel deal. This approach directly reflects European countries' policy in recent years, under which the slightest compromise between Moscow and Washington prompts EU nations to attempt to block such agreements. Brussels could do so by tightening sanctions against Russia and coordinating with American Democrats, the expert said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Possibility of routing Persian Gulf oil around Strait of Hormuz
New pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and lead to seaports outside the Persian Gulf will address the problem of supplying Middle Eastern oil to the global market. In five years, the strait may become obsolete for oil trade as shipments are redirected along new routes. This is not the first attempt to find alternative ways to deliver oil from Persian Gulf countries. Previously, this idea was also proposed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to him, the construction of oil pipelines will render the Strait of Hormuz "a worthless piece of water" in as little as two to three years.
Bypass routes are currently more profitable, not because transporting oil via pipeline is inexpensive, but because of the increased costs linked to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Before the crisis, tanker transit cost the same as or less than pipeline transport, while now, that balance has reversed, the expert noted. However, maritime transport is cheaper in peacetime. The cost of pumping oil through a pipeline is up to five times higher than the cost of moving it by oil tanker per kilometer, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, pointed out.
Existing alternative routes do not resolve the problem because their combined capacity is less than half of the volumes that previously passed through the Strait of Hormuz, Malkov emphasized. Moreover, the Red Sea poses its own risks, such as Houthi attacks, and there are virtually no alternatives to tankers for transporting refined petroleum products, the expert noted. But even if the existing infrastructure that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz is expanded and new oil pipelines are built in parallel, the economic viability of these projects will be questionable, economist Boris Kopeikin stressed. If the situation in the region stabilizes in the long term, oil will once again follow the traditional route, through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
At the same time, the main advantage of alternative routes is the diversification of risks. They reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and allow exports to continue in the event of shipping restrictions, but they do not guarantee complete supply security, Ivan Timonin, a senior manager at the Implementa consulting firm, said. According to Abelev, pipelines are no safer than maritime transport. They are vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, and protecting them along their entire length is quite difficult. Unlike seagoing vessels, a pipeline is stationary and its location is precisely known. It cannot be replaced or rerouted. Maritime transport offers greater flexibility. Oil pipelines for the Persian Gulf states are an expensive insurance policy, not a cheap alternative, the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: French authorities trying to ease protests with talks and concessions
Ahead of another round of large-scale protests scheduled for the weekend, the authorities are trying to reach a deal with the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met with union representatives on October 21. The meeting produced no results; the government did not receive any promises to call off the protests. In fact, a general strike has been announced.
Nevertheless, Lecornu remains undeterred. The government has proposed an aid program for businesses affected by the unrest. Following his trip to the Persian Gulf states, President Emmanuel Macron issued a statement saying that he had secured additional fuel shipments to bring down prices in the country. The authorities are hoping these measures will have a rapid effect.
Rather than resorting to force, the French authorities have decided to address the wave of protests sweeping the country through persuasion. They have chosen to respond to the demonstrators’ main demands. Perhaps there is no other option: last weekend, more than half a million French citizens took to the streets across the country. The protests are no longer limited to schoolchildren and their parents who are dissatisfied with the education system. Labor unions are actively participating in the protests, which are directed against the rising cost of living and ultimately against the economic policies of the current president and government.
At the same time, the situation in the country is gradually returning to normal, although this will take some time, Tatyana Zvereva, a professor at the World Economy and World Politics Faculty of the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "The composition of the protesters is complex. It includes high school students, members of the ‘Yellow Vests’ movement, and others, including members of fringe political organizations," she noted. According to the expert, the French authorities are pursuing two main lines of action. On the one hand, they are restoring order, which society as a whole expects. The far-right National Rally party has been particularly vocal in demanding this. On the other hand, the authorities are negotiating with moderate protesters.
"The logic is this: the most aggressive protesters must be held accountable, and positive-minded citizens must be reached out to by addressing their socio-economic demands. However, the second point is much more difficult to achieve. Therefore, it seems unlikely that we can expect quick results from the negotiations. But dialogue can help defuse the situation and let off some steam," Zvereva emphasized.

South Korea's stranded celebrity shark swims back into canal after rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:59:38 UTC
18:59:38 KST

An endangered dusky shark that had been trapped in a canal in South Korea’s southeastern port city of Busan for more than a month returned hours after authorities guided it out to sea, local media reported on Thursday.
The female shark, nicknamed Bukang-i, was spotted on Thursday morning near the entrance to the canal at Busan’s North Port Waterfront Park after crossing a floating barrier late on Wednesday, according to The Korea Herald.
It was the second time the shark had slipped past barriers following rescue attempts.
Authorities had declared Wednesday’s operation successful at around 6.10 pm local time (0910GMT), but the shark was seen crossing the barrier again at around 11.05 pm (1405GMT).
Officials are considering reinforcing the barriers or capturing the shark and transporting it to open waters.
Lee Gwang-seok, an official with the oceans and fisheries ministry, said Bukang-i was unlikely to slip past more barriers and move farther up the canal, considering the density of the nets and the narrow waterway in that section that leaves little room for the shark to squeeze through.
The shark’s repeated returns have puzzled authorities, who remain concerned about its deteriorating health and falling water temperatures.
The National Institute of Fisheries Science has not observed Bukang-i feeding, while apparent injuries and footage showing it striking a canal wall have raised further concerns.
Sharing the Korean name of Busan’s North Port, where it was first spotted in mid-September, Bukang-i has become a major local tourist attraction as it slowly circled the canal, its fins slicing through the water’s surface. It has drawn more than 1.6 million visitors as of Sunday, according to Yonhap News Agency.
Previous rescue attempts on September 29 and October 2 failed. Authorities fear the shark could die if temperatures continue to fall.

Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:58:49 UTC
18:58:49 KST

Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.
The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.
Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.
Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.
Idriss Ghazi Kareem
Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.
The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.
Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.
“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”
The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.
Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.
“Floating coffins”
Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”
And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

Researchers warn of global decline in childhood measles vaccination
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:27 CST
18:56:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have warned of a global decline in childhood measles vaccination rates since the COVID-19 pandemic, contributing to a resurgence of the highly contagious disease.
Routine vaccine program disruptions and under-resourced health systems are driving the global decline, with estimated measles cases among children under five rising to 15.6 million worldwide in 2023, a 40 percent increase from 2019, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
The study, published in Nature Medicine, examined measles cases, deaths and vaccination gaps among children under five across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023.
Associate Professor Benn Sartorius from UQ's Frazer Institute said the resurgence coincided with pandemic-related disruptions to immunization programs, health systems and funding, reversing decades of progress, with measles cases falling nearly 80 percent worldwide between 1990 and 2019.
An estimated 23.7 million infants, or one in five worldwide, missed their first measles vaccine dose in 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa accounted for 50 percent of the missed doses, followed by South Asia at 20 percent, Sartorius said, adding the study's data could help authorities identify under-vaccinated populations to prevent future outbreaks. ■

Xinhua Headlines-Xi Focus: Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March
China
Unknown Publisher

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Yao Dawei)
BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
"Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary.
Under Xi's proposal, all participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China.
From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army marched through more than 10 provinces during the Long March, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said.
"This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," he noted.
Xi stressed that the Party's right leadership and the establishment of Mao Zedong's core position were decisive for the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
The Party and the Red Army relied on firm conviction, Xi said, adding that troops with noble ideals and firm beliefs are invincible.
Xi emphasized the importance of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities in addressing the country's issues and problems.
He further underscored that the people will always be the source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces.
Xi said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously."
He said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said.
To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements.
He underscored the need to unswervingly advance high-quality development and promote common prosperity for all.
Efforts must be made to better ensure both development and security and seize the historical initiative to overcome difficulties, combat risks and meet challenges, he stressed.
Xi also emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military.
It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added.
Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, as well as Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, attended the gathering.
Zhao, who presided over the event, said Xi's speech was of immense political, ideological and guiding significance, urging earnest efforts to study and grasp its essence and ensure its effective implementation.
He called on the whole Party, the entire military and the Chinese people of all ethnic groups to rally more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and strive to build a great country and advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.
Around 3,000 people participated in the gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. ■

Explainer: What's the cost of biodiversity loss?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:55:59 CST
18:55:59 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Your first glass of water today comes with an invisible bill.
Behind it is a vast network of life, from forests and wetlands to microscopic organisms, helping keep water supplies clean and reliable.
The United Nations calls this interconnected system the "web of life," on which we depend for food, water, medicine and a stable climate.
Biodiversity is the variety of life that makes up this web.
At the ongoing 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, countries are grappling with how to halt biodiversity loss and translate pledges into action.
VALUE OF BIODIVERSITY
From bacteria and fungi to forests and coral reefs, the biodiversity we see today is the product of 4.5 billion years of evolution, increasingly shaped by human activity.
Pollinating plants, dispersing seeds, sustaining food webs ... every species has a role to play in nature. Losing a single species can mean losing ecological relationships and genetic resources accumulated over millions of years of evolution.
The scale of the loss is alarming.
The 2026 Living Planet Report of the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) shows that the average size of monitored wildlife populations shrank by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022.
Conservation, meanwhile, is making progress.
In Colombia, conservationists are breeding, reintroducing and monitoring the critically endangered Orinoco crocodile, aiming to restore self-sustaining wild populations rather than simply releasing more animals.
Armenia has applied for funding from the Kunming Biodiversity Fund to cover projects bolstering the biodiversity of Lake Sevan, including the protection of the Sevan trout, an endemic species, said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
And the projects go beyond saving a particular fish species. They aim to preserve genetic diversity, which helps species adapt to changing conditions.
Such diversity is practically valuable for humans: crop varieties may carry genes for drought or disease resistance, while natural organisms provide compounds used in medicine. According to the WHO, more than half of modern medicines came from nature.
INVISIBLE SERVICES
Scientists call the benefits nature provides -- including water purification, pollination and carbon storage -- "ecosystem services."
They rarely appear on household bills or business balance sheets, but their loss can bring very real costs, from poorer water quality to damaged crops and increased exposure to environmental disasters.
According to the United Nations, more than half the world's gross domestic product is moderately or highly dependent on nature. More than 1 billion people rely on forests for their livelihoods. And land and the ocean absorb more than half of all carbon emissions.
As COP17 opened, forest fires in Indonesia's Kalimantan region had affected more than 57,000 hectares, with haze reaching communities in Malaysia and Singapore, said Theiva Lingam, co-chair of Friends of the Earth International.
She described the fires as "a stark reminder of the deeper biodiversity crisis which is unfolding across the Global South."
The vulnerability of peatlands helps explain why such environmental damage can have consequences far beyond the areas affected.
Peatlands cover only about 3 percent of the world's land but store roughly twice as much carbon as all the forests on Earth. When drained or burned, these ecosystems can release large amounts of stored carbon while losing their ability to regulate water and support wildlife.
FOOTING THE BILL
The economic gains from activities that harm biodiversity are often shared globally, while the environmental and social costs fall disproportionately on developing countries and local communities, Lingam said.
To help redress this imbalance, Article 20 of the Convention on Biological Diversity requires developed countries to provide "new and additional financial resources" to help developing ones cover the agreed costs of implementing the convention.
Likewise, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, calls for international biodiversity funding to developing countries to reach at least 20 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2025 and 30 billion dollars by 2030.
Preventing damage is particularly important as extinction is irreversible, while restoring degraded ecosystems can be costly and the outcome uncertain, experts said.
Celine Beaulieu, who works on biodiversity finance at the WWF, said funding must also translate into results, urging countries to "judge biodiversity finance not only by what is being pledged, but by what reaches implementation."
As Armenian Deputy Environment Minister Aram Meymaryan put it, conservation must be judged by results on the ground: Have threats been reduced? Have species' chances of survival improved? Are their populations recovering?
Nature may never send a bill, but the cost of losing the ecosystems behind it is real. Protecting biodiversity is not simply an act of generosity toward nature. It is an investment in the systems that sustain everyone's life. ■

Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up

Gerard Larcher, the president of the Senate, told Le Figaro this week it was worth considering whether LFI should be banned, a suggestion decried as "authoritarian" by LFI.
Laurent Jacobelli, a spokesperson for Marine Le Pen's National Rally (RN), blamed "the ultra-left, including France Unbowed", as well as what he called uncontrolled immigration, for creating a revolutionary climate.
Marc Fesneau, of centrist party MoDem, said Melenchon had long promoted the idea that "everything must be a battleground".
"When you turn everything into a confrontation, you run serious risks," Fesneau told Reuters.
The attacks underscore both Melenchon's central place in French politics and the unease he provokes as the country heads toward a presidential election expected to pit increasingly strong anti-establishment forces against a weakened political centre.
The unrest has reinforced that contrast, shifting scrutiny onto the hard left while allowing Le Pen to strike a more presidential tone on law and order, an issue that traditionally favours the far right.
Yet with France's political landscape fragmented into three rival blocs and traditional centre-left and centre-right parties struggling, analysts say Melenchon remains a formidable political force.
YOUTH APPEAL AND THE 'NEW FRANCE'
LFI has built its support by mobilising younger voters, many of whom have grown disillusioned with mainstream politics. An IFOP poll for LCI published this month put Melenchon on 16.5%, behind Le Pen's 36% but ahead of all other mainstream candidates.
A Cluster17 poll found nearly half of 18-to-24-year-olds and more than a third of 25-to-34-year-olds would back Melenchon.
That has made him a prominent voice for many students involved in the protest movement and wider unrest that has shaken France in recent weeks.
However, Frederic Dabi, head of pollster IFOP, said the unrest risked reinforcing one of Melenchon's biggest electoral weaknesses: his inability to win over older voters.
"The perception that Jean-Luc Melenchon has been too indulgent towards perpetrators of violence is an absolute red line for a large part of the electorate," Dabi said.
Nevertheless, the party has also built strong support in poorer urban areas and among many voters from immigrant backgrounds who see themselves reflected in Melenchon's vision of a "New France" — a multicultural republic that embraces ethnic and religious diversity and gives greater political representation to communities that often feel overlooked.
Supporters say that reflects social realities rather than identity politics.
"It's the unique synthesis between a programme of revolutionary rupture and the desire to govern the country," LFI lawmaker Hadrien Clouet told Reuters.
Clouet said that meant tackling inequality and reversing a decades-long transfer of wealth towards finance and a narrow oligarchic elite.
Yet critics say LFI often blurs the line between democratic protest and more radical political agitation.
UPRISING LANGUAGE DRAWS SCRUTINY
Melenchon has frequently invoked the language of popular uprising. During the pensions crisis of 2023, he urged supporters to "tear down the citadel" of President Emmanuel Macron's government and has at times spoken favourably of "citizen insurrection" as a democratic force.
Supporters say such language refers to mass political mobilisation, not violence. The party officially advocates non-violent action.
LFI and its allies argue some of the accusations are politically motivated. This week, investigative news outlet Mediapart reported, citing an anonymous intelligence officer, that officials had been instructed to portray LFI as being behind the protest movement despite what the source described as a lack of evidence. The government denied the allegation.
Still, opponents say Melenchon's messaging is often deliberately ambiguous.
"They say they are against vandals, but at the same time they justify masks at demonstrations," said Sylvain Maillard of Macron's Renaissance party. "They never calm things down. They always say it's the police's fault. They want chaos."
Former Socialist President Francois Hollande, however, warned against making Melenchon the sole focus of the debate.
"It is not one political party or one individual that poured fuel on the fire," Hollande told France Inter. While criticising LFI for sometimes drawing an equivalence between rioter violence and police violence, he said: "To fixate on LFI is to fail to see what is happening in the country." REUTERS

This Preamp Costs More Than a Fancy Sports Car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.
I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.
In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.
Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.
The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.
Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.
It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.
In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.
Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.
What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.
But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.
And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

Stubb and Costa Emerge as Possible EU Negotiators with Putin
