Washington’s ICC sanctions expose limits of international justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:49:25 UTC
17:49:25 KST

On the morning of October 9, 2026, the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo awarded its Peace Prize to the South African jurist who had led the UN commission that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza.
By the afternoon, the United States Secretary of State announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court as an institution. Not against individual officials, as Washington had done in 2020 and again in February 2025, but against the court itself, which the administration had declared rogue.
Three years of South African legal filings, Palestinian evidentiary submissions, UN commission hearings, and General Assembly resolutions produced the genocide finding Pillay announced, and the Pre-Trial Chamber warrants Rubio moved to punish.
Between the law’s formal reach and the impunity its founders assumed it would preserve, the sanctions were the closing instrument.
What October 9 made visible is not a crisis of international law but its constitutive condition: that the universality claimed by the institutions built to deliver accountability was always contingent on those institutions never seriously threatening the states that built them.
The distance between those two acts measures how far the Global South’s legal mobilisation pushed. The institutions the West built to represent universal justice after colonialism were never designed to deliver it against themselves.
What pushed the court past its limit
South Africa’s December 2023 genocide filing at the ICJ was the deployment of the system’s own instruments against a situation those instruments had never been activated on simultaneously.
The Genocide Convention’s Article IX compromissory clause went before the ICJ, the Rome Statute’s complementarity framework before the ICC, and the General Assembly’s Uniting for Peace mechanism across both.
Palestinian legal documentation had built the evidentiary record for decades. Invoking Article IX of the Genocide Convention before the ICJ required a state party with full standing to file, and Palestine did not hold that standing.
What South Africa provided was the jurisdictional key the evidence had been waiting for.
Four separate mandates, each operating under its own evidentiary standard and jurisdictional basis, reached the same conclusion.
The ICJ’s January 2024 provisional measures found a plausible right to protection from genocidal acts. Francesca Albanese’s March 2024 Special Rapporteur report found reasonable grounds that the genocide threshold had been met.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry chaired by Pillay attributed responsibility for specific genocidal acts to Israel’s senior leadership and found that its senior leadership had incited genocide within the meaning of Article III(c) of the Genocide Convention.
The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber issued warrants for war crimes and crimes against humanity against Netanyahu and Gallant in November 2024.
Its founding states had not designed the institution to produce that convergence for a Western-allied government. Once it emerged, they had no way to contain it without acting against the institution itself.
Pillay had sat on Trial Chamber I of the ICTR that delivered the Akayesu judgment in 1998, the first international conviction to establish rape as a constituent act of genocide.
The judge who helped build that jurisprudence from the bench was now the author of the most precise genocide determination the Gaza proceedings had produced.
Oslo honoured that tradition. Washington sanctioned the institution that applied it on the same day.
The threshold that was never named.
When the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber issued arrest warrants for the political and military leadership of an occupying power, nothing in the Rome Statute prohibited it from doing so.
What the warrants exposed was the distance between the law’s formal reach and the prosecutorial limit its founding states had assumed the court would never approach, a limit held in place by the interlocking operation of Article 98 bilateral non-surrender agreements, Security Council deferral rights under Article 16, and the financial leverage of states whose contributions fund over forty per cent of the court’s budget.
For two decades, that structure held without requiring activation, and no confirmed prosecution had reached the political or military leadership of a Western-allied government.
The African Union formally threatened mass withdrawal in 2017, accusing the court of concentrating its coercive reach on African leaders while investigations elsewhere stopped well short of confirmed charges against officials whose states Washington considered partners.
The founding states declined to engage with that challenge, because the Pre-Trial Chamber’s warrants had not yet required them to.
South Africa’s filing activated proceedings the existing architecture had no mechanism to stop. Article 98 bilateral agreements bound third states not to surrender US nationals to the ICC.
They had no reach over a Genocide Convention filing before the ICJ, which operates on an entirely separate jurisdictional basis.
Bilateral non-surrender agreements did not apply to a Genocide Convention filing before the ICJ.
The Article 16 deferral mechanism required a Security Council resolution that Russia and China would veto, and the kind of financial leverage Washington could deploy operates over years, not the months the proceedings took.
Prosecutorial reach had run in one direction for two decades not because the founding instruments required it to, but because the states that built those instruments had no reason to enforce the limit before anyone crossed it.
Built to protect its own
At Rome in 1998, the US voted against the Statute it had spent years shaping, demanding Security Council control over referrals and prosecutions, an end to automatic jurisdiction, and protection for nationals of non-party states.
The Like-Minded group, led by Canada and Australia, defeated all three demands. Washington left with a text it could not control and set about building a parallel architecture to constrain it from outside.
Marco Rubio’s declaration that the US neither needs nor wants the International Criminal Court is that legal framework, operating as its drafters intended.
Washington withdrew its signature in May 2002 after failing at Rome to secure the jurisdictional carve-outs it required, and spent the next two decades resisting: contesting the Afghanistan investigation, sanctioning the prosecutor and other officials in 2020, and imposing further measures against court personnel in February 2025.
All of Washington’s prior interventions had targeted individuals. Sanctioning the court itself was something it had never done.
Through negotiation, the United States shaped the Rome Statute into three layers.
By coercing over 100 states into bilateral non-surrender agreements under Article 98, Washington constrained cooperation obligations for its nationals. The Security Council deferral mechanism under Article 16, a multilaterally negotiated provision Washington pressed for, reserved the power to seek a twelve-month suspension of any specific investigation.
The American Service-Members Protection Act of 2002 authorised the President to use military force to recover any American held by the court.
The October 9 executive order prohibited American technology providers from servicing the institution, making the ICC’s dependence on United States commercial infrastructure an instrument of the sanctions themselves.
Washington tested that deferral mechanism early. Security Council Resolution 1422 (2002), extracted under threat of vetoing UN peacekeeping mandates, sought a blanket exemption for all non-party nationals involved in UN operations, not a deferral of any existing case, but a generic preventive suspension the article’s text does not authorise.
States and scholars condemned it as exceeding Article 16’s case-specific scope, and the resolution was not renewed after 2003.
The instrument Washington had pressed for proved legally indefensible when it was activated.
In 2011, Washington voted in the Security Council to refer Muammar Gaddafi to the ICC under Article 13(b), placing the leadership of a non-party state within the court’s jurisdiction while remaining outside it.
The same Security Council instrument it had pressed for as a defensive deferral mechanism it deployed offensively against a government it wished to remove.
The same text included both offensive referral and defensive deferral, and Washington used whichever served its interests at the time.
That duality held for two decades because the Pre-Trial Chamber’s warrants had never reached a government Washington was committed to protecting.
Faced with findings it could not contain through any of the instruments it had built for that purpose, the United States sanctioned the court itself.
The test the mobilisation now faces is whether the 124 states whose filings, mandates, and evidentiary work drove those findings will bear the cost of defending the institution under that pressure.
When Robert Jackson drafted the Nuremberg Charter in 1945, he wrote that no official position shields an individual from criminal responsibility for crimes against humanity, then confined the Charter’s jurisdiction to the defeated, leaving the victors' conduct outside the tribunal he was constructing as the foundation of a universal legal order.
That selective foundation has now been pushed, through the sustained legal mobilisation of non-Western sovereign states using the system’s own instruments, past the prosecutorial limit its founders assumed would never be crossed.
Sanctioning the institution that crossed it was the system working exactly as designed.

Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.
The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.
Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.
The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.
When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.
The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.
Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”
Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

U.S. Navy tests camera system that spots sailors overboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:39:04 UTC
17:39:04 KST

- U.S. Navy engineers tested a thermal camera system on Aug. 14 that automatically detects sailors falling overboard, using a rescue dummy at Port Hueneme, California.
- The prototype uses commercial cruise ship software, and the team is now seeking new funding to test it aboard an active destroyer.
U.S. Navy engineers in California have tested a prototype camera system designed to spot a sailor falling overboard and alert the ship’s bridge automatically, throwing a 35-pound rescue dummy off the side of a decommissioned destroyer to see whether the cameras would catch it.
The test took place on Aug. 14 aboard the Self Defense Test Ship, which was docked at Port Hueneme, California, where a team from Naval Surface Warfare Center, Port Hueneme Division temporarily mounted the Man Overboard Detection System on the starboard side of the bow. Branch manager Eric King said the system worked flawlessly, although the bridge alarm it is meant to trigger was not part of the test.
King said he believes the system “bridges a gap by providing immediate, automated man-overboard alerts, enabling rapid-response search and rescue operations when seconds count.”
The prototype uses thermal cameras, which detect body heat and can work in darkness, mounted on metal pedestals that extend horizontally from the deck out over the water. For the test, the team installed two cameras in each of two pedestals placed about 61 meters (200 feet) apart and held them to the deck with powerful magnets and counterweights, while permanent versions would be welded in place.
“We needed two thermal cameras per pedestal because one of them captures the short-range blind spot view of the ship and the other camera captures the medium- to long-range view of the ship,” said systems engineer David Dozal, who leads the project.
Dozal said the software compares the overlapping views from opposing cameras to confirm that someone has gone over the side, which allows it to sound the bridge alarm in real time and give responders the exact location where the person entered the water. In a full installation, the cameras would ideally cover the entire perimeter of a U.S. Navy destroyer.
To simulate a fall, the team bought a 1.8-meter (6-foot) vinyl water rescue training dummy named OSCAR, after the international signal flag for “man overboard.” Dozal and mechatronics engineer Daniel Lopez dropped the dummy over the side several times on a rope, hauling it back aboard between throws, while computer engineers Jessica Diaz and Nayeli Mateo checked on a laptop inside the ship that the system had recorded each event correctly.
Much of the hardware and software came from the commercial market. The video analytics software was developed by a private company for the cruise ship industry, and the Navy team used part of its research funding to license it, while the same company built the pedestals to a design drawn up in-house at Port Hueneme. The four thermal cameras were bought off the shelf. The Navy did not name the company.
The cruise industry has a regulatory reason to build such tools: the Cruise Vessel Safety and Security Act, passed by Congress in 2010, requires passenger cruise ships to integrate technology that can capture images of passengers or detect those who have fallen overboard, to the extent such technology is available.
The Self Defense Test Ship itself is the former USS Paul F. Foster (DD 964), a Spruance-class destroyer decommissioned in 2003 and now used by the Port Hueneme division as a floating test platform, often operated by remote control, for ship self-defense weapons and sensors.
The project was funded through the Naval Innovative Science and Engineering program, which supports early-stage research at Navy warfare centers, but that money has now run out. King said the team needed the test results to prove the concept and has started talks with potential sponsors, including the possibility of folding the system into a larger program.
Dozal said the next step would ideally be a temporary installation aboard an active destroyer in San Diego, tested both in port and at sea, which would require a longer window, such as a maintenance period, to fit cameras around the whole ship and route cables safely.
“We also need to calculate the complete MOB installation cost to put it entirely around one Navy ship; we need those numbers to show to a funding source,” Dozal said.

New rules coming into force in Switzerland on November 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:38:32 UTC
17:38:32 KST

New rules coming into force in Switzerland on November 1
New rules are coming into force in Switzerland on November 1 that concern the transmission of air passenger data and Schengen personal data, as well as the modernisation of identity documents.
AVIATION SECURITY: Airlines will be required to submit detailed passenger data to a national authority, the Passenger Information Unit (PIU). The new regulation sets out the formats and timelines for this submission, with a view to combating terrorism and serious crime more effectively.
In future, passengers will be informed about the collection of their data before making a booking. This measure implements the Air Passenger Data Act passed by Parliament and aims to enhance security in the sector, while ensuring compliance with data protection regulations.
SCHENGEN: A new ordinance sets out in detail the national component of the Schengen Information System (SIS) and the tasks of the SIRENE Bureau in Switzerland, which is the national reference and coordination centre for the SIS at the Federal Office of Police (Fedpol). The text sets out the procedures by which the Swiss authorities manage and exchange personal data within the framework of international police cooperation.
+ Switzerland to collect data from non-Schengen visitors
The aim is to strengthen internal security and make border controls more effective by standardising data processing. This amendment serves to implement Switzerland’s international Schengen obligations and aims to ensure smooth cooperation with other Member States in the fight against crime.
IDENTITY DOCUMENTS: Switzerland is modernising its identity documents and amending the relevant ordinance. From November 1, the current “provisional passport” will be referred to as an “emergency passport”, which should provide greater clarity. Furthermore, in future, identity cards will be explicitly offered in two versions: with and without a chip.
The collection of biometric data – such as fingerprints – for passports and identity cards with chips is clarified, in line with international standards. The fees for the various types of documents have also been revised to take account of the administrative burden and technical innovations. The changes affect all Swiss citizens applying for a new passport or identity card.
AGRICULTURE: A new regime for the management of bovine viral diarrhoea (BVD) will come into force on Swiss livestock farms. The previous classification of holdings as “not subject to restrictions”, “subject to restrictions” and “subject to restrictions for individual animals” is being abolished. From now on, there will be only two categories: “BVD-free” or “not BVD-free”, the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (FSVO) has announced.
From November, BVD-free farms will be able to move animals without restrictions. For non-exempt holdings, however, restrictions will apply. The new regime marks the end of a two-year transitional phase towards the elimination of BVD in Switzerland. The FSVO is, in fact, pursuing the objective of eradicating the disease. To date, over 99% of cattle holdings are free from the virus.

Nordic force should turn north, committee suggests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:30:20 BST
17:30:20 KST

The government should consider whether the Joint Expeditionary Force concentrates its finite resources on the High North instead of operating as often in the Baltic, and may need to build the British Army force in Estonia up to brigade strength to offset the change, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets out that Britain permanently leads the ten-nation force, which brings together the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and the three Baltic and five Nordic countries, and that Britain has taken over command of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk.
Dhesi said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
The report recommends: “The government should consider whether the JEF focuses on the High North, concentrating finite resources on maximising its ability to operate more frequently in the harsh climate there while undertaking the demanding anti-submarine mission, rather than operating as often in the Baltic as previously.”
On Estonia it states: “To offset this greater focus on the High North the UK may need to reassure Baltic members of the JEF by reinforcing its commitment there in other ways; for example, by building up the current British Army force in Estonia to brigade-size, to match what Germany is already doing in Lithuania.”
A separate recommendation asks the government, within a year of assuming leadership of Joint Force Command Norfolk, to reassess the added value the force brings to European security, stating that either it provides distinct value alongside NATO and should be strengthened and aligned more closely with it, or it does not and Britain should focus its finite resources on NATO.
The committee sets out that the force was established in 2014 for rapid, scalable operations with northern European allies, and that its principal value lies below the Article 5 threshold where it can respond to hybrid threats, protect undersea infrastructure and act more quickly than NATO’s full consensus-based machinery. During an overseas committee visit, one commentator referred to the force as “a jack of all trades and therefore master of no military tasks.”
The report records that the force overlaps with NATO tasks and has not always proved faster than NATO in practice, that it lacks some major NATO powers including Canada, and that it neither specialises in the shallow waters of the Baltic nor in anti-submarine operations in the harshness of the High North.
Canada applied to join the force in September 2026, and the committee notes that it could add valuable experience and capabilities given its long experience of operating in harsh regional conditions and its membership of the Five Eyes intelligence group, but that adding the North American Arctic to the European High North would significantly increase the force’s area of responsibility.
With Sweden and Finland having joined NATO, the committee observes that eight of the nine countries around the Baltic Sea are now members of the alliance and offer significant capabilities of their own in that region.
The Ministry of Defence told the committee that “[o]nce we transition into crisis, the chances are that the JEF will, in some way, fold into the regional plan north-west anyway. There is not a competition between the two; they are entirely complementary and one supports the other.”

Ukraine faces a new Russian cruise missile called Filin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:29:56 UTC
17:29:56 KST

- Ukrainian military intelligence published a 3D model and component breakdown of Russia’s Filin cruise missile, first used against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
- The ground-launched missile has a claimed range of up to 1,200 km and contains 35 American and 22 Chinese components.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has published a detailed breakdown of Filin, a new Russian ground-launched cruise missile that Moscow began firing at Ukraine in late summer 2026. According to the agency, the missile combines a composite airframe and a Russian jet engine with onboard electronics built largely from American and Chinese parts.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, known as HUR, released an interactive 3D model of the missile, its main assemblies and a catalog of its electronic components on the agency’s War & Sanctions portal. The agency did not say how many Filin missiles Russia has launched, which targets they hit or how investigators obtained the parts they examined.
Filin, Russian for “eagle owl,” is made by AO NPO Molniya, a company within Russia’s state-owned Tactical Missiles Corporation. HUR described the missile as the latest product of a Russian effort to build relatively cheap jet-powered strike weapons that launch from the ground instead of from aircraft or warships.
The missile is 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) long and has a wingspan of 3 meters (9.8 feet), with a maximum launch weight of 210 kg (463 pounds). Its fuselage is made of carbon fiber and fiberglass composites, and some of its parts are produced by 3D printing, an approach that can cut manufacturing time and cost compared with traditional machined components.
Russia claims Filin can reach a top speed of 800 km/h (497 mph) and fly up to 1,200 km (746 miles), although HUR’s specification sheet gives the range as 600 to 1,200 km (373 to 746 miles), which suggests the figure depends on the configuration. The missile can fly at very low altitude, where ground-based radar has a harder time detecting incoming threats, or climb as high as 6 km (19,700 feet).
Filin comes in versions with either a 50 kg (110-pound) or a 100 kg (220-pound) warhead, and HUR lists three warhead types: high-explosive fragmentation, penetrating and thermobaric. A thermobaric warhead first disperses an explosive cloud and then ignites it, producing a longer and more powerful blast wave than a conventional charge of similar weight.
The missile is fired from a ground launcher with the help of a solid-fuel booster, which pushes it up to flying speed before its small jet engine takes over for the cruise to the target.
HUR’s investigation also links Filin closely to Russia’s long-range attack drone program. The missile’s onboard equipment is produced by OOO PLAZ, which also makes equipment for the Garpiya, or “Harpy,” drone, a modification of the Geran-2 built in several series by the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol. The Geran-2 itself is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, and HUR said electronic units from Filin and Garpiya share a similar layout and similar markings.
For guidance, Filin relies on a Chinese-made inertial navigation system, which tracks the missile’s position using onboard motion sensors without any outside signal. It works alongside a 16-channel Kometa satellite navigation module, a jam-resistant receiver made by Russia’s VNIIR-Progress that has repeatedly turned up in Russian drones and guided bombs recovered in Ukraine.
HUR said Filin’s electronics resemble those found in other Russian missiles and drones, but with a larger share of Chinese parts and with the same design solutions reused across different units and circuit boards. Investigators counted 35 American components and 22 Chinese ones in the missile’s onboard equipment.
The identified suppliers include Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, NXP Semiconductors and STMicroelectronics, along with Chinese firms such as WinChipHead and Mornsun. Production markings on some parts date from 2021 and 2022, including an Ethernet switch chip made in May 2022, three months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Filin’s engine, by contrast, is Russian: an R500 turbojet built by OOO Reynolds. HUR had previously identified the same engine in Russia’s S-71K Kover air-launched cruise missile and in the S-71M Monokhrom.

Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The iconic Apekop train, officially known as Mat ’64 (Materieel ’64), made its last journey on Wednesday before heading back into retirement.
Originally retired from service in 2016, the passenger train was brought back by operator Keolis last year, to the delight of train enthusiasts, to run between Amersfoort and Barneveld Zuid after refurbishment work on newer trains led to a rolling stock shortage.
But its 12.25pm departure from Barneveld Zuid on Wednesday is said to be its final trip. The train will now return to Stichting 2454CRW, a volunteer organisation that maintains old trains.
First appearing on Dutch tracks in 1961, the Mat ’64, the last NS train built largely in the Netherlands, came to symbolise Dutch commuter travel. The trains served passengers for more than five decades, with hundreds in service at their peak.
The nickname Apekop, which translates as “monkey head”, comes from the train’s distinctive rounded nose.

Taiwan conducts observation flight to improve Typhoon Champi forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:12:38 UTC
17:12:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Weather Administration said Thursday that it had completed an observation flight to gather data on Typhoon Champi earlier that morning, according to a press release.
The CWA partnered with National Taiwan University and the Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation for the mission. An Astra jet departed Taichung’s Ching Chuan Kang Airport at 5 a.m. for a flight lasting about five hours.
The aircraft flew at an altitude of about 13,000 meters and deployed weather instruments called dropsondes around the typhoon and along its potential path. The instruments collected atmospheric temperature, pressure, humidity, wind direction, and wind speed data as they descended toward the sea.
The data were transmitted by satellite to the CWA to help forecasters analyze Champi’s structure and development. They were also fed into numerical forecasting models to improve predictions.
The CWA said observations over the ocean were relatively sparse, while forecasting models differed in their projections of Champi’s path and circulation. The flight gathered data from key areas to help address those gaps.
Taiwan has completed 92 observation flights under the program since 2003, improving typhoon monitoring and forecast accuracy, the CWA said. It also shared the Champi observations with weather agencies worldwide.

17:12:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Administration for Cyber Security (ACS) on Thursday urged government agencies, schools, and businesses to update PHP promptly after two critical vulnerabilities were found that could allow attackers to remotely execute malicious code.
PHP (Personal Home Page) is a programming language widely used to build websites, content management systems, and administrative interfaces. ACS urged organizations to check their PHP versions and install updates as soon as possible.
The two flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each received a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 under version 4.0 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, per CNA. Patches were released at 10 p.m. Taiwan time Wednesday, ACS said.
ACS Director-General Tsai Fu-lung (蔡福隆) said an inventory found approximately 28,000 publicly accessible websites use PHP, including about 200 government websites, per CNA. However, he said not all versions of PHP are affected, so the number of affected websites is expected to be lower.
PHP underpins platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, and may also be used in software that does not explicitly identify itself as PHP-based, the agency said. Organizations should inventory PHP-based systems and related packages, verify their versions, and apply patches according to instructions.
After updating, organizations should review system logs for unusual access and check the security of accounts and credentials if suspicious activity is found. The agency said it would continue monitoring vulnerabilities to help public and private organizations reduce risks.

“President Trump was forced into a memorandum of understanding which actually looked very much to be in Iran’s favour. Since then, he has been trying to claw back what the US lost in those first 40 days,” says Nasr, referring to the failed June agreement for a 60-day ceasefire.
“This can be resolved by them going into another bout of war. Or they can do what they have been doing, grinding this (out) going forward. The Iranians are now asking for more than they asked for in June.”
The 14-point agreement, reached in Islamabad, undertook to release substantial frozen funds of Iran, allowed Iran to resume oil exports, and envisaged a massive reconstruction fund for Iran. Tehran reaffirmed its commitment to never acquire or develop nuclear weapons and to allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to supervise the blending down of its uranium stockpile.

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and adviser, was given access to bank accounts containing billions of dollars by the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, including one account in the Israeli Central Bank, the new book Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East claims.
In an excerpt from the book published by Vanity Fair magazine, the author, Matthew Cole, described how the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) hacked Kushner's phone. The MIVD discovered that he had used it to log into a UAE bank account that had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan beginning in 2017.
The Azerbaijani national bank, the book explained, is often used for money laundering purposes for large transfers of foreign currencies into US dollars.
According to one source familiar with the deal between Kushner and the UAE, “Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” and had promised UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) he would push their agenda with Trump if they contributed money to a slush fund for diplomatic objectives, including Kushner's aim of eventual normalization with Israel.
“The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year," the source explained. "A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”
Kushner did not own this bank account. It was managed by the Emirati charity Watani Al Emarat Foundation as a cover, but he was a signatory to it. As such, he had access to the funds and could, in theory, conduct transactions.
"One way to view what Kushner did with the Alpha account is to imagine him as the director of the CIA," Cole wrote in the book.
"Had he been running the government entity that managed and ran secret foreign programs, maintaining the account, again, with presidential approval and congressional disclosure, Kushner’s conduct would have been within his job’s responsibilities.
"But he was not the director of the CIA, whose position is approved by the Senate and whose operations are overseen and accountable to Congress. Instead, Kushner was overseen only by his father-in-law."
Four sources cited by Cole, including two national security advisors, a White House chief of staff, and a former CIA director, said they were unaware of any presidential approval or authorization for Kushner's access to a foreign bank account.
Kushner's counsel, however, stated that the president's advisor had not made any agreements or arrangements with foreign leaders or officials without the full agreement of Trump and "in the best interests of the United States." His lawyer also denied any illegal activity Kushner had conducted while dealing with foreign leaders or officials, as well as any knowledge of and connection to the Emirati charity, its manager Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, or the UAE bank account.
MBZ funded account in Israel for Kushner, with Netanyahu's awareness
Another account reportedly funded by MBZ was located in Israel, and had at least one billion dollars transferred to it by spring of 2018, according to the book.
One person cited by Cole who worked with Kushner said that much of the money was transferred to Cyprus before being funneled elsewhere in order to grant him untraceable access.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was allegedly aware of the account and had encouraged Kushner to have the funds deposited into what appears to be a government account at the Bank of Israel.
KAN News noted that the Bank of Israel does not manage private accounts. Additionally, the bank requires the approval of two authorized persons in order to make transfers.
Netanyahu also reportedly required that Kushner inform him before making any transactions with the account, which Kushner did by passing messages through former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman.
Friedman, however, denied being involved in the reported affair.
“I know absolutely nothing about any of these allegations,” he said. “The specific allegations about me or my alleged involvement in this alleged scheme are 100% false.”
Kushner's counsel also denied all knowledge of the affair, claiming "there are no accounts and never were."
A third account, detailed by the book, was negotiated by Kushner to serve as a "rainy-day defense fund" for the UAE to pay Israel to support its defense from any major Iranian attacks, during the warming of Israel-UAE relations.
Kushner denies all allegations of misconduct, points to lack of evidence
In a response to the excerpt published by Vanity Fair, Kushner called the allegations "outrageous and categorically false."
In a post on X/Twitter on Thursday, Kushner said that, during the period covered by the book, he had been "one of the most scrutinized people in the world," and had cooperated fully with investigations that did not turn up any evidence of the book's claims.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said. "This is not journalism. It is a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent."
Kushner's attorney, Chad Mizelle, stated that they intended to pursue legal action against those responsible for publishing the "categorically false and defamatory allegations."

Two Finnish firms progress satellite plans for Ukraine

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:03:19 EEST
17:03:19 KST

Finnish space tech firm Iceye and networking giant Nokia are partnering with Ukraine's defence ministry to develop satellite communications in the war-torn country.
Ukraine is looking to reduce its dependence on the United States-based satellite internet service provider Starlink, owned by multi-billionaire Elon Musk's firm SpaceX.
A letter of intent about the firms' cooperation with Ukraine was signed on Thursday in Kyiv, during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's (NCP) visit to the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement is important for the country's defence and resilience, the Kyiv Independent reported.
Musk has recently capped the speed of Starlink services in Ukraine. The embattled country has used Starlink for military communications and operating drones — but hampered network speeds reduce Ukraine's capabilities on the battlefield.
However on Thursday, US President Donald Trump said that Musk had restored Starlink service in Ukraine — while at the same time declining to comment on reports that he had discussed the matter with the billionaire.
According to US and Ukrainian officials interviewed by the Wall Street Journal, the Starlink system began to function better after the reported discussion.
However, according to the Kyiv Independent, speed restrictions on Starlink's military version, Starshield, still haven't been lifted, despite reports that either Musk or Trump had ordered the restrictions — introduced just over a week ago — to be removed.
Ukraine needs secure, independent and powerful satellite communication systems that the country controls itself, Iceye chief executive Rafal Modrzewski said in a press release.
"We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. Iceye has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today," the CEO and co-founder said.
Iceye's and Nokia's cooperation was announced earlier this month.
At the time, Professor Jaan Praks from Aalto University told Yle that Iceye has a firm grasp on today's geopolitical realities.
According to Praks, Europe urgently needs its own, sovereign satellite system.
"Iceye knows what European states need, perhaps better than anyone else—perhaps even better than the really big satellite manufacturers like Airbus and others," Praks said earlier this month.
Praks is a space technology researcher, and Iceye's roots trace back to his research group at Aalto University.
Finding a European solution
Iceye was founded in Otaniemi, Espoo, in 2014 and now has more than 1,500 employees with operations in around ten countries. The firm operates around 80 satellites that transmit Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images of the Earth.
In its early days, Iceye's focus was on mapping storm and flood damage in real time as well as monitoring effects of climate change, but today its operations are increasingly security-focused.
The militaries of Finland, Poland and the Netherlands, among others, have made deals with Iceye, which had a turnover of over 250 million euros in 2025.
SpaceX has a network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites — far more than any European entity.
According to Marko Höyhtyä, research professor at the VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and satellite comms expert, it's unlikely anyone could access that kind of performance at the same price from any other operator — but other factors weigh in favour of a European solution.
"Price is hardly the decisive argument, especially not at this early stage. Other factors weigh more heavily, such as independence from the US and similar considerations," Höyhtyä told Yle earlier this month.

Taiwan manufacturing sentiment rebounds in September

08:09:52 UTC
17:09:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taiwan Institute of Economic Research said Friday that manufacturing and construction sentiment improved in September, while services sector sentiment declined for a third consecutive month.
TIER’s manufacturing business climate index rose 0.5 points from August to 101.39, while the construction index gained 2.81 points to 110.42, per UDN. The services index fell 3.15 points to 92.65. Among manufacturers, 26.8% rated business conditions as good, while 20.3% rated them as bad.
Manufacturing sentiment benefited from expanding global AI infrastructure and demand for smartphones, which boosted inventory-building, per CNA. These trends supported advanced semiconductor production, memory chips, and semiconductor packaging and testing. Higher oil prices also drove up plastic and rubber material costs.
However, manufacturers are more cautious about the next six months. The share expecting conditions to improve fell from 27.1% in August to 24% in September, while the share expecting them to worsen rose from 18% to 19.8%. The institute cited the Middle East conflict, high oil and raw material costs, and oversupply in traditional industries as key concerns.
Rising memory chip costs driven by AI demand could raise consumer electronics prices, weaken demand and reduce future orders, TIER explained. Meanwhile, new petrochemical capacity in China is adding pressure on traditional manufacturers already facing weak demand.
Services sentiment weakened despite stronger business for hotels and restaurants during major exhibitions, Mid-Autumn Festival celebrations, and travel. Restaurants reported lower revenue than in August, while banks faced lower investment returns amid rising US Treasury yields and reduced dividend income.
Construction sentiment improved on high-tech factory expansions, public infrastructure projects, and urban renewal. Property transactions across the six special municipalities rose 14.1% month over month in September, partly as delayed ownership transfers and new-home handovers were completed.
Looking ahead, TIER said department store anniversary sales, online shopping and the government’s universal cash payment could boost retail spending over the next six months. However, it said financial market volatility and uncertainty in overseas markets are expected to keep the services outlook cautious.

Taiwan's Nan Ya sees structural shift in PCB materials market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:09:48 UTC
17:09:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's Nan Ya Plastics Corp. has observed a shift in the printed circuit board materials market, with supply shortages reshaping product demand and supplier selection, CTEE reported Thursday.
PCBs are boards that hold and connect electronic components in devices. Copper-clad laminates (CCLs) form the base of circuit boards, helping determine their signal transmission and heat resistance. Fiberglass cloth, made by weaving fine glass fibers, is a key material in CCLs that provides heat resistance and electrical insulation, according to Pocket Securities and Business Next.
The supply chain expects prices for both fiberglass cloth and CCL to rise 10-15% starting in November, although increases will vary by product specifications and suppliers. This reflects a broader market shift, Nan Ya said, as manufacturers focus on higher-end products while demand for standard-grade materials remains strong.
Nan Ya noted that the tight supply has also changed how customers choose suppliers. In the early stages of price increases, customers tended to favor suppliers offering a wide range of products and specifications. As shortages have worsened, however, access to materials and reliable delivery schedules have become more important than product variety.
On the pricing front, China-based CCL leader Kingboard Laminates Holdings Ltd. has raised prices 12 times this year. Meanwhile, prices for thinner 1080-grade E-glass fiberglass cloth have climbed about 300% from their lows to their peaks.
Thin fiberglass cloth is in particularly short supply, as limited capacity to install additional weaving machines makes it difficult to ramp up production in the short term.
However, new production capacity may not ease shortages of thin fiberglass cloth. China Jushi Co., a leading manufacturer, is expected to begin mass production at its new facilities next year, but the added capacity will mainly produce thicker grades rather than the thinner varieties facing the most severe shortages.
Supply chain estimates suggest the shortage may gradually ease from the second half of 2027 through 2028. The timing will depend on equipment deliveries, the commissioning of new capacity, and how quickly manufacturers can shift production between product grades.
However, rising demand for higher-end applications could keep supplies tight even as capacity expands. Higher material costs are also expected to be passed on to manufacturers downstream.

Taipei's Royal Joying Soiree unveils seasonal crab feast

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Stepping into Taipei’s modern Chinese restaurant Royal Joying Soiree, diners are greeted by the rich, savory aromas of autumn.
Executive chef Li Kuan-yi (李冠儀) and dim sum chef Li Kuo-sheng (李國聖) have teamed up to debut an 11-dish seasonal crab menu blending Cantonese foundations with global and regional inspirations.
Among the standout dishes is the stir-fried mud crab with aged black vinegar. Inspired by Li Kuan-yi’s time working in Shanghai, where vinegar-simmered seafood is a staple, the dish features a measured touch of sugar and aged vinegar to create a caramelized glaze over the crab and vegetables.
Paired with crisp Japanese yam and purple sweet potato, it balances the rich crustacean meat.
Attention to detail drives the menu's soup selection. The lotus seed and intestine mud crab soup originally stemmed from a concept inspired by Shanghai’s traditional pork and bamboo shoot soup.
Due to seasonal availability constraints of authentic Jinhua ham and fresh bamboo shoots, the team instead adapted Taiwanese sishen soup. After simmering pork bone and lean meat for six hours to build a gelatinous base, they added daikon radish to draw out the crab's sweetness, incorporating handmade lotus seed intestines and Job's tears for a nourishing broth.
Another creation, the braised mud crab and ginger duck in clay pot, marries Taiwanese winter ginger duck tonic with traditional Fujianese dry-braising.
To keep the duck tender, the kitchen pressure-cooks ingredients on demand. Diners can enjoy the dry-braised dish before pouring in Wenchang chicken broth for a comforting second course.
Subtle touches elevate even the vegetable courses. To eliminate the raw, grassy taste of carrots in the golden pumpkin puree for the braised baby bok choy and sea cucumber, the kitchen slices and deep-fries the carrots first, locking in natural sweetness for a velvety finish.
On the dim sum front, chef Li Kuo-sheng navigates the technical hurdles of handling perishable, fresh crab meat without freezing.
The menu features steamed prawn dumplings with crab roe and mentaiko — combining tiger prawns, rich crab roe, and vegetarian shark’s fin — alongside crispy kataif-wrapped snow crab legs coated in a crab roe white sauce.
The autumn crab feast runs through Oct. 31. During the promotional period, orders of any mud crab dish include a complimentary nourishing soup, while red swimmer crab selections come with a complimentary serving of signature lava mushroom buns.

Shen calls for separating Taiwan stock trading from typhoon closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:09:22 UTC
17:09:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) on Thursday called for discussions on separating stock market closures from local government decisions to suspend work and classes during typhoons.
CNA reported that Shen said the city's role as the main financial center makes typhoon closure decisions more complicated. He suggested reviewing whether financial institutions and stock trading should follow separate closure rules.
Local governments should explain the weather conditions and other factors behind their decisions to suspend work and classes, Shen said. He added that changing stock market closure rules would require cooperation between central and local authorities.
Currently, the stock market closes for the day if Taipei announces a full-day or morning work suspension before trading begins at 9 a.m. If the city announces an afternoon suspension after trading has begun, regular trading continues until 1:30 p.m., but trading scheduled after that time is canceled.
This means Taipei's decision to suspend work can halt stock trading nationwide, even if other cities remain open. However, closures in other cities do not automatically stop trading, although affected securities firms may need special arrangements to complete transactions.
KMT Spokesperson Liu Tsai-wei (柳采葳) questioned how financial workers would be protected if trading continued during severe weather. She said Shen had not explained how securities transactions and bank settlements would be handled, while financial market rules fall under the central authorities, per UDN.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said the issue had been discussed before and could be reviewed with the central government. His campaign questioned why Shen, who is also a legislator, had not used his position to seek changes from financial regulators, per Nownews.
Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) said central authorities should assess whether online trading is widespread enough to support the change. New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) said public safety must remain the government's top priority during typhoons, per Taisounds.
The Financial Supervisory Commission said it was reviewing how other countries handle stock trading during severe weather. Securities and Futures Bureau Deputy Director-General Huang Chung-hao (黃仲豪) said the review included Japan and South Korea, but no decision had been made, per SETN.
Japan does not automatically suspend stock trading when a typhoon warning is issued. The Tokyo Stock Exchange considers the extent of damage, whether brokers can trade, and public safety before deciding whether to suspend trading.
Reuters reported that the Tokyo Stock Exchange suspended all stock trading on Oct. 1, 2020, after a hardware failure disrupted its trading system. The shutdown lasted the entire day, with trading resuming the following morning.
South Korea's stock market can remain open during typhoons, rather than automatically closing when severe weather strikes. Yonhap reported that the benchmark KOSPI index continued trading on Sept. 6, 2022, when Typhoon Hinnamnor struck the country.
However, trading can still be suspended when technical problems disrupt market operations. Yonhap reported that a system error halted all KOSPI stock trading for seven minutes, from 11:37 a.m. to 11:44 a.m., on March 18, 2025, marking the first such market-wide technical suspension since 2005.

"This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally... (puts) Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril," Blumenthal wrote in a letter addressed to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The move also "raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," the senator continued.
Neither Musk nor the Trump administration publicly claimed responsibility for the slowdown, but the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Oct. 21 that the order came from the SpaceX founder.
The outlet separately wrote a day later that Trump called Musk to lift the restrictions. However, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the 161 kph limit is still in place.
Blumenthal, who sits on the Senate's Subcommittee on Investigations, asked the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.
The pro-Ukraine lawmaker also stressed that the reports "raise further questions about the respective roles of (the Pentagon), the White House, and SpaceX in controlling and modifying the service."
"If the Pentagon cannot say plainly who has the authority to degrade a military communications network, our partners cannot rely on it, and our adversaries will look for ways to exploit that uncertainty."
Blumenthal asked Hegseth to provide information by Nov. 5. As the Democrats lack a majority in the Senate, they do not hold the subpoena power.
The Democratic Party aims to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from the Republicans during the upcoming midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Saab Q3 results 2026: Positioned to capture growing demand
Saab presents the results for January-September 2026.
“We delivered a quarter marked by high organic sales growth, significantly increased cash flow and strong order bookings. The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany’s new frigates. We continue to invest in future capabilities and expand capacity, while our strong order backlog and programme progress position us well for continued growth,” says Micael Johansson, President and CEO, Saab.
Key highlights Q3 2026
- Order bookings amounted to SEK 65,825 million (20,861). This included a SEK 24.6 billion order for Gripen E to Ukraine, a SEK 10.1 billion order for GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer and a SEK 8.7 billion order for systems for German frigates.
- Sales amounted to SEK 20,553 million (15,871), corresponding to an organic sales growth of 30.6 per cent (18.3).
- EBITDA amounted to SEK 2,833 million (2,173), corresponding to an EBITDA margin of 13.8 per cent (13.7).
- EBIT increased 42 per cent and amounted to SEK 1,945 million (1,374), corresponding to an EBIT margin of 9.5 per cent (8.7).
- Net income increased to SEK 1,432 million (975) and earnings per share amounted to SEK 2.57 (1.77).
- Operational cash flow increased to SEK 6,785 million (142).
- Net liquidity amounted to SEK 8,679 million compared to SEK 3,989 million at year-end 2025.
- Changes to Group Management were announced, see page 14 for more information.

ROK Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy Kim Hong-Cheol delivers a statement to Pyongyang; North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong and Marshal Pak Jong Chon inspect fencing at the inter-Korean border. | Images: KTV via YouTube (Oct. 23, 2026), KCNA (Oct. 21, 2026), edited by NK News
South Korea’s Defense Ministry renewed its proposal for military talks with North Korea to verify the exact location of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) on Friday, amid heightened tensions after land mine explosions injured three ROK soldiers last month.
Kim Hong-Cheol, Seoul’s Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy, said in a statement addressed to Pyongyang that the two sides should hold military talks “to mutually confirm the clear location of the MDL between the South and the North.”
He also proposed discussing the restoration of military communication lines and “ways to prevent accidental clashes in border areas.”

Military horses could carry loads in the field again
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:00:53 BST
17:00:53 KST

Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions, with further development needed on equipment, load carriage and operating endurance, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what findings were made on the feasibility of the operational use of horses during Exercise Copper Horse.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions. It also identified areas requiring further development, including equipment, load carriage and operating endurance before any judgement can be made on potential operational use.”
Britain’s forces keep around five hundred horses, almost all of them in ceremonial roles with the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment in London, the King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery at Woolwich, and the Defence Animal Training Regiment at Melton Mowbray, which trains horses and military working dogs.
A horse can carry around a fifth of its body weight, and United States special forces operated on horseback in northern Afghanistan in 2001, and the French, Italian, Austrian and Swiss armies retain mules or horses for mountain logistics.
We reported recently that the British Army has been experimenting with the use of horses for reconnaissance, patrol and security tasks in terrain where military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the Ministry of Defence.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment on the Barossa training area at Sandhurst, exploring how mounted troops could support battlefield activity beyond the Regiment’s familiar ceremonial duties.
The training was conducted across difficult terrain and focused on environments where conventional vehicles could face restrictions, giving soldiers an opportunity to examine how horses might provide an alternative means of moving personnel during reconnaissance and security operations.
